> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc04
URL JDBC de la base : [jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles]
Il y a eu 6 ligne(s) supprimée(s)
article [article1] inséré avec l'id 7
article [article2] inséré avec l'id 8
article [article3] inséré avec l'id 9
article [article4] inséré avec l'id 10
article [article5] inséré avec l'id 11
Article[id=7, nom=article1, prix=100.00, stockActuel=10, stockMinimum=1]
Article[id=8, nom=article2, prix=200.00, stockActuel=20, stockMinimum=2]
Article[id=9, nom=article3, prix=300.00, stockActuel=30, stockMinimum=3]
Article[id=10, nom=article4, prix=400.00, stockActuel=40, stockMinimum=4]
Article[id=11, nom=article5, prix=500.00, stockActuel=50, stockMinimum=5]
Articles dont le nom se termine par 3 :
Article[id=9, nom=article3, prix=300.00, stockActuel=30, stockMinimum=3]
  • Lines 24–27: a list of five items. The value 0 in [id] is irrelevant: it will not be inserted into the database;
  • Line 31: All items are deleted from the table. The [executeUpdate] method (line 87) returns the number of rows deleted this time;
  • line 35: [forEach(IO::println)] displays each item in the list using a method reference (Chapter 7). The results show the [toString] method generated for the record;
  • line 45: the method for inserting a list of items:
    • line 47: the query to insert an item. It has four parameters, denoted as [?]: the name (parameter #1), the price (#2), the current stock (#3), and the minimum stock (#4);
    • line 49: [prepareStatement] creates the configured order. The second argument, [Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS], instructs the driver to retrieve the primary keys generated by SGBD during the insertions;
    • Lines 51–56: The items are inserted one by one. Each of the four parameters is assigned a value by the [setXxx] method corresponding to its type, and then the query—now complete—is executed by [executeUpdate], this time without any arguments: the query text was specified when the command was created. The parameter values are retained from one execution to the next until they are changed (or until [clearParameters] is called);
    • lines 58–61: [getGeneratedKeys] returns, in the form of a [ResultSet], the primary key generated by SGBD for the inserted row. The results show [id] 7 through 11: MySQL does not reuse values 1 through 6 from the deleted rows. This is how to determine the identifier of a row that has just been inserted;
  • line 67: the method that returns items whose names match a pattern [like] from SQL (the character [%] represents any sequence of characters: [%3] refers to names ending in 3):
    • lines 68–69: the query has one parameter, the model;
    • line 72: the parameter is assigned a value;
    • lines 73–81: each row of the result becomes a [Article] object. The column type is known: the [getXxx] methods are used. They accept either the column number (lines 77–78) or its name (lines 78–79). Accessing by name is more readable and better handles changes to the query; accessing by number is slightly faster.

The name [PreparedStatement] (“prepared” statement) comes from the fact that a SGBD can “prepare” a parameterized query—that is, compile it once and for all. When a SGBD executes a SQL command, it performs analysis and optimization before executing it (it establishes an “execution plan”). A parameterized query is intended to be executed multiple times with different parameters, but its text does not change: this work need only be done once. With MySQL Connector/J, preparation is simulated by the driver by default: it inserts the parameter values—properly escaped—into the query text itself before sending it. The [useServerPrepStmts=true] parameter of URL causes it to use the preparation provided by the MySQL server. In both cases, the Java code is the same.

The main correspondences between the SQL types of MySQL, the methods of JDBC, and the Java types are as follows:

MySQL column typeJDBC methodsJava Type[INT][setInt], [getInt][int] ([Integer] for [getObject])[BIGINT][setLong], [getLong][long] ([Long])[DECIMAL(p,d)][setBigDecimal], [getBigDecimal][BigDecimal][DOUBLE][setDouble], [getDouble][double] ([Double])[VARCHAR(n)], variable-length string[setString], [getString][String][DATETIME][setObject(i, valeur)], [getObject(i, LocalDateTime.class)][LocalDateTime][DATE][setObject(i, valeur)], [getObject(i, LocalDate.class)][LocalDate][BOOL] (synonym for [TINYINT(1)])[setBoolean], [getBoolean][boolean] ([Boolean])

Dates are represented by the classes of [java.time] (Chapter 5), which JDBC has supported since version 4.2 (Java 8) via [setObject] and [getObject]. The older classes [java.sql.Date], [java.sql.Time], and [java.sql.Timestamp], derived from [java.util.Date], and the methods [getDate], [getTimestamp] that implement them, should no longer be used in new code. To assign the value SQL or [NULL] to a parameter, write [setNull(i, Types.INTEGER)], where the class [java.sql.Types] (or the enum [JDBCType], Java 8) specifies the parameter’s type, SQL.

docs.title: 10.5.2. The SQL injection
docs.text:
Preparation is not the only advantage of parameterized queries, nor is it the most important one. Consider searching for an article by its name. You might want to construct the query text programmatically, inserting the search term into it:

        String requete = "select id, nom, prix from articles where nom = '" + nom + "'";

(this is line 30 of the program [Jdbc05] below). If the name is “bike,” the query becomes:

select id, nom, prix from articles where nom = 'vélo'

But if the name is “oxygen tanks,” it becomes:

select id, nom, prix from articles where nom = 'bouteilles d'oxygène'

and it is syntactically incorrect because of the apostrophe in the name. Worse still: if the name comes from user input, the user could enter text that changes the meaning of the query. This is the SQL injection, one of the most widespread and serious security vulnerabilities in applications that use a database. The program [Jdbc05.java] demonstrates this with a search for an article by its name:

package jdbc;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.List;

// Injection SQL: Why You Should Use Parameterized Queries
public class Jdbc05 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String UTILISATEUR = "root";
    private static final String MOT_DE_PASSE = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // Article names, as a user might type them
        List<String> noms = List.of("vélo", "bouteilles d'oxygène", "x' or '1'='1");

        IO.println("1 - requête construite par concaténation");
        noms.forEach(Jdbc05::rechercherParConcatenation);
        IO.println("\n2 - requête paramétrée");
        noms.forEach(Jdbc05::rechercherAvecParametre);
    }

     // Searching for an article by name: the name is inserted into the query text
    private static void rechercherParConcatenation(String nom) {
        String requete = "select id, nom, prix from articles where nom = '" + nom + "'";
        IO.println("[" + nom + "] -> " + requete);
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
             ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery(requete)) {
            afficher(resultat);
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("   erreur : " + ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

     // Searching for an item by name: the name is the value of a parameter
    private static void rechercherAvecParametre(String nom) {
        IO.println("[" + nom + "]");
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             PreparedStatement ordre = connexion.prepareStatement(
                     "select id, nom, prix from articles where nom = ?")) {
            ordre.setString(1, nom);
            try (ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery()) {
                afficher(resultat);
            }
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("   erreur : " + ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

     // displaying the result of a SELECT query
    private static void afficher(ResultSet resultat) throws SQLException {
        int nbLignes = 0;
        while (resultat.next()) {
            IO.println("   " + resultat.getInt(1) + " " + resultat.getString(2) + " "
                    + resultat.getBigDecimal(3));
            nbLignes++;
        }
        IO.println("   " + nbLignes + " ligne(s)");
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc05

   1 vélo 500.00
   1 ligne(s)
[bouteilles d'oxygène] -> select id, nom, prix from articles where nom = 'bouteilles d'oxygène'
   erreur : You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual that corresponds to your MySQL server version for the right syntax to use near 'oxygène'' at line 1
[x' or '1'='1] -> select id, nom, prix from articles where nom = 'x' or '1'='1'
   1 vélo 500.00
   2 pompe 10.00
   3 arc 600.00
   4 flèches - lot de 6 100.00
   5 combinaison de plongée 300.00
   6 bouteilles d'oxygène 120.00
   6 ligne(s)

2 - requête paramétrée
[vélo]
   1 vélo 500.00
   1 ligne(s)
[bouteilles d'oxygène]
   6 bouteilles d'oxygène 120.00
   1 ligne(s)
[x' or '1'='1]
   0 ligne(s)
  • line 20: three names that a user might type: a regular name, a name containing an apostrophe, and malicious text;
  • line 29: the first search method inserts the name into the query text (line 30), executed by a standard [Statement]:
    • row 3 of the results: with a regular name, everything works fine;
    • line 6: the apostrophe in the name prematurely terminates the SQL string; the query is invalid (line 7). An article whose name contains an apostrophe cannot be found;
    • line 8: the user entered text containing apostrophes placed in such a way as to produce a valid query, but for which the condition [nom = 'x' or '1'='1'] is true for all rows: the query returns the entire table (line 15). If the query were verifying a username and password, the same process would allow the user to log in without knowing the password. With a driver that accepts multiple SQL commands in a single query, the user could even add a command of their choice after a semicolon, such as a [delete]. Connector/J rejects this by default (setting [allowMultiQueries=false]), which limits the scope of the injection without eliminating it;
  • Line 42: The second method uses a parameterized query (lines 45–47). The parameter’s value is never interpreted as SQL: it is treated as data, regardless of its content. The name with an apostrophe is found (line 22 of the results), and the malicious text is simply the name of an article that does not exist (line 25).

One could “neutralize” the apostrophes by doubling them, but the rules depend on SGBD, and it’s easy to overlook a case. The rule is simple: values provided by the user (or any external source) must never be concatenated with the text of a SQL request; we always use a PreparedStatement and parameters. The interactive program [Jdbc01.java] does not follow this rule by its very nature: it executes the SQL commands typed by the user. It is an administrator tool, not an example to follow.

docs.title: 10.6.1. General Information
docs.text:
A transaction is a sequence of SQL commands executed “atomically”:

  • either all operations succeed;
  • or one of them fails, in which case all preceding operations are rolled back.

Ultimately, either all the operations in a transaction were successfully applied, or none of them were. The classic example is a bank transfer: the debit from one account and the credit to another must both be completed or neither at all. When the application itself controls the transaction, it validates it with a [COMMIT] command or cancels it with a [ROLLBACK] command.

In our previous examples, we did not use a transaction. And yet there were transactions, because in a SGBD, a SQL command is always executed within a transaction. If the application does not start an explicit transaction itself, the SGBD uses an implicit transaction. There are then two cases:

  • each SQL command is part of a transaction, opened by the SGBD command before the command and committed afterward. This is referred to as autocommit mode. It behaves as if the application were creating a transaction for each SQL command;
  • SGBD is not in autocommit mode: it begins an implicit transaction with the first SQL command issued outside a transaction and allows the application to complete it. All subsequent SQL commands are part of this implicit transaction, which can end due to various events (connection closure, start of a new transaction, etc.), according to the rules specific to SGBD. This mode should be avoided.

JDBC enforces the first case: a JDBC connection is in autocommit mode when it is opened, regardless of the setting for SGBD (MySQL, with the InnoDB storage engine used by default, is also in autocommit mode).

The SQL commands from different users execute simultaneously, within transactions that run in parallel. Operations performed by one transaction may affect those performed by another. There are four levels of isolation between transactions from different users:

  • Read Uncommitted;
  • Read Committed;
  • Repeatable Read;
  • Serializable.

Read Uncommitted

This isolation level is also known as “Dirty Read.” Here is an example of what can happen in this mode:

  • A user named U1 starts a transaction on table T;
  • a user named U2 starts a transaction on the same table T;
  • user U1 modifies rows in table T but has not yet committed the changes;
  • user U2 “sees” these changes and makes decisions based on what they see;
  • User U1 rolls back their transaction using [ROLLBACK].

In step 4, user U2 made a decision based on data that later turned out to be incorrect.

Read Committed

This isolation level avoids the previous pitfall: in step 4, user U2 does not “see” the changes made by user U1 to table T. They will only see them after U1 has committed their transaction with a [COMMIT]. In this mode, however, the following situation may occur:

  • a user U1 starts a transaction on table T;
  • a user U2 starts a transaction on the same table T;
  • user U2 executes a [select] to calculate the average of column C for rows in T that meet a certain condition;
  • user U1 modifies ([update]) certain values in column C of T and commits the changes ([commit]);
  • User U2 repeats the same [select] as in step 3. They discover that the average of column C has changed due to the modifications made by U1.

User U2 now sees only the changes committed by U1, but while still within the same transaction, two identical operations yield different results. This situation is called a “non-repeatable read.” It is problematic for anyone who wants a consistent view of table T.

Repeatable Read

In this isolation level, a user is guaranteed to obtain the same results from database reads as long as they remain within the same transaction. They work on a “snapshot” of the data that does not reflect changes made by other transactions, even if those changes have been committed. They will only see those changes once they have completed their own transaction.

This isolation level is not yet perfect in theory: another transaction ([insert]) could add rows that satisfy the condition in step 3, which would change the result of a subsequent read. These rows are called “phantom reads.” This is the default isolation level for MySQL (InnoDB), which also prevents phantom reads for simple reads.

Serializable

In this isolation mode, transactions are completely isolated from one another: the result of two transactions executed simultaneously is the same as if they had been executed one after the other. To achieve this, the SGBD locks the data being read and causes transactions that attempt to modify it to wait (or fail). This level reduces parallelism and, consequently, performance.

The four isolation levels are not available in all SGBD instances. The default isolation level is generally Read Committed (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle) or Repeatable Read (MySQL). The desired isolation level can be explicitly specified by the application.

docs.title: 10.6.2. Transaction Management (API)
docs.text:
With JDBC, transactions are managed by the connection. There is no “transaction” object: a connection has at most one active transaction, and all SQL commands executed on that connection are part of it. The relevant methods of the [Connection] interface are as follows:

MethodRole[setAutoCommit][setAutoCommit(false)] exits autocommit mode: the subsequent SQL commands are part of a transaction, which begins with the first of them and ends with [commit] or [rollback]. A new transaction then begins with the next command. [setAutoCommit(true)] returns to autocommit mode, committing the current transaction.[commit]Confirms the transaction: The results of the SQL orders issued in the transaction become final and visible to other transactions.[rollback]Cancel the transaction: The results of the SQL commands issued in the transaction are rolled back.[setSavepoint]Sets a savepoint (a [Savepoint] object) in the current transaction.[rollback(Savepoint)]rolls back the SQL commands executed since the savepoint, without rolling back those that preceded it: the transaction continues.[setTransactionIsolation]sets the transaction isolation level for the connection. It must be called before the start of a transaction.

The isolation level is one of the constants of the [Connection] interface:

ValueMeaning[TRANSACTION_READ_UNCOMMITTED]The transaction can read data written by another transaction that it has not yet committed. Should be avoided.[TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED]The transaction cannot read data written by another transaction that it has not yet committed. However, data read twice in a row within the transaction may change, because another transaction may have modified it in the meantime; another transaction may also have added rows (ghost rows).[TRANSACTION_REPEATABLE_READ]The data read by the transaction does not change until the transaction is complete. In theory, this does not prevent another transaction from adding rows.[TRANSACTION_SERIALIZABLE]Everything behaves as if the transaction were running alone. This reduces performance because transactions no longer run in parallel.

A connection that has exited autocommit mode must be closed after the transaction has been committed or rolled back. If it is closed while a transaction is in progress, the result depends on the driver (MySQL Connector/J rolls it back): you must always explicitly commit a transaction.

docs.title: 10.6.3. The sample program
docs.text:
The program [Jdbc06.java] demonstrates the effect of a transaction:

package jdbc;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Savepoint;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.List;

// Transactions
public class Jdbc06 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String UTILISATEUR = "root";
    private static final String MOT_DE_PASSE = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        IO.println("URL JDBC de la base : [" + URL + "]");

         // Two items with the same name: the uniqueness constraint UNQ_NOM will reject the second one
        List<Article> articles = List.of(new Article(0, "article", new BigDecimal("100"), 10, 1),
                new Article(0, "article", new BigDecimal("200"), 20, 2));

        try {
             // 1 - Insertion without an explicit transaction
            IO.println("\nInsertion sans transaction...");
            executeUpdate("delete from articles");
            try {
                insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articles);
            } catch (SQLException ex) {
                IO.println("Erreur d'accès à la base de données (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
            }
            afficherArticles();

             // 2 - the same thing within a transaction
            IO.println("\nInsertion dans une transaction...");
            executeUpdate("delete from articles");
            insertArticlesInTransaction(articles);
            afficherArticles();

             // 3 - a transaction with a savepoint
            IO.println("\nInsertion dans une transaction avec un point de sauvegarde...");
            executeUpdate("delete from articles");
            insertArticlesWithSavepoint(articles);
            afficherArticles();
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("Erreur d'accès à la base de données (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

     // inserting a list of items without an explicit transaction (autocommit mode)
    private static void insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(List<Article> articles) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             PreparedStatement ordre = creerOrdreInsert(connexion)) {
            for (Article article : articles) {
                insererArticle(ordre, article);
            }
        }
    }

     // Inserting a list of items within a transaction
    private static void insertArticlesInTransaction(List<Article> articles) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE)) {
             // Start of the transaction: exiting autocommit mode
            connexion.setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED);
            connexion.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (PreparedStatement ordre = creerOrdreInsert(connexion)) {
                for (Article article : articles) {
                    insererArticle(ordre, article);
                }
                 // Everything went well: commit the transaction
                connexion.commit();
                IO.println("transaction validée...");
            } catch (SQLException ex) {
                 // An insertion failed: roll back the transaction
                connexion.rollback();
                IO.println("transaction invalidée (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
            }
        }
    }

     // Insertion within a transaction: a failed insertion only rolls back what follows
     // the last save point
    private static void insertArticlesWithSavepoint(List<Article> articles) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE)) {
            connexion.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (PreparedStatement ordre = creerOrdreInsert(connexion)) {
                for (Article article : articles) {
                     // A savepoint before each insertion
                    Savepoint avantInsertion = connexion.setSavepoint();
                    try {
                        insererArticle(ordre, article);
                    } catch (SQLException ex) {
                         // Only the failed insertion is rolled back
                        connexion.rollback(avantInsertion);
                        IO.println("insertion de [" + article.nom() + ", " + article.prix() + "] annulée ("
                                + ex.getMessage() + ")");
                    }
                }
                connexion.commit();
                IO.println("transaction validée...");
            } catch (SQLException ex) {
                connexion.rollback();
                IO.println("transaction invalidée (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
            }
        }
    }

     // the configured order for inserting an item
    private static PreparedStatement creerOrdreInsert(Connection connexion) throws SQLException {
        return connexion.prepareStatement(
                "insert into articles(nom, prix, stockactuel, stockminimum) values(?, ?, ?, ?)");
    }

     // insertion of an item using the configured order
    private static void insererArticle(PreparedStatement ordre, Article article) throws SQLException {
        ordre.setString(1, article.nom());
        ordre.setBigDecimal(2, article.prix());
        ordre.setInt(3, article.stockActuel());
        ordre.setInt(4, article.stockMinimum());
        ordre.executeUpdate();
        IO.println("article [" + article.nom() + ", " + article.prix() + "] inséré");
    }

     // Execution of an update command
    private static void executeUpdate(String requete) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement()) {
            IO.println("Il y a eu " + ordre.executeUpdate(requete) + " ligne(s) modifiée(s)");
        }
    }

     // displaying the table contents
    private static void afficherArticles() throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
             ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery(
                     "select id, nom, prix, stockactuel, stockminimum from articles")) {
            IO.println("Contenu de la table [articles] :");
            while (resultat.next()) {
                IO.println("  " + resultat.getInt(1) + " " + resultat.getString(2) + " "
                        + resultat.getBigDecimal(3) + " " + resultat.getInt(4) + " " + resultat.getInt(5));
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc06
URL JDBC de la base : [jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles]

Insertion sans transaction...
Il y a eu 6 ligne(s) modifiée(s)
article [article, 100] inséré
Erreur d'accès à la base de données (Duplicate entry 'article' for key 'articles.UNQ_NOM')
Contenu de la table [articles] :
  7 article 100.00 10 1

Insertion dans une transaction...
Il y a eu 1 ligne(s) modifiée(s)
article [article, 100] inséré
transaction invalidée (Duplicate entry 'article' for key 'articles.UNQ_NOM')
Contenu de la table [articles] :

Insertion dans une transaction avec un point de sauvegarde...
Il y a eu 0 ligne(s) modifiée(s)
article [article, 100] inséré
insertion de [article, 200] annulée (Duplicate entry 'article' for key 'articles.UNQ_NOM')
transaction validée...
Contenu de la table [articles] :
  11 article 100.00 10 1
  • Lines 24–25: a list of two items with the same name, [article]. The uniqueness constraint [UNQ_NOM] on table [articles] prevents both from existing in the database at the same time: inserting the second one will trigger a [SQLException]. To demonstrate the effect of a transaction, the two items will be inserted in three ways:
    • first, outside of any explicit transaction. Since the connection is in autocommit mode, each insertion is performed in its own transaction. The first record will be inserted, but the second will not;
    • next, within a transaction encompassing both inserts. Because the second insert will fail, the first will be rolled back: ultimately, neither insert will be performed;
    • finally, within a transaction with a savepoint before each insertion: the failure of the second insertion will roll back only itself, and the transaction will be committed with the first;
  • lines 28–36: the table is cleared, then both items are inserted without an explicit transaction. Since we know the second insertion will throw an exception, it is caught by a [try] / [catch]; finally, the table is displayed;
  • lines 38–42: We repeat the same sequence, but with a transaction. This time, the exception is handled in the [insertArticlesInTransaction] method;
  • lines 44–48: the same applies to savepoints;
  • line 55: the insertion method without a transaction. It uses two methods: [creerOrdreInsert] (line 113), which creates the parameterized insertion command, and [insererArticle] (line 119), which assigns values to the parameters and executes the command;
  • line 65: the method for inserting within a transaction:
    • line 68: the isolation level [TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED], set before the transaction begins;
    • line 69: the connection exits autocommit mode; the transaction will begin with the first insert;
    • lines 71–73: the inserts;
    • line 75: everything went well: the transaction is committed, and the inserts are permanently added to the database;
    • lines 77–80: an insert failed: the transaction is rolled back;
  • line 87: the insertion method using savepoints:
    • line 93: a savepoint is set before each insertion;
    • line 98: if the insertion fails, we roll back to the savepoint: only the failed insertion is rolled back, and the loop continues;
    • line 103: the transaction is committed, with the successful inserts.

In the results:

  • line 5: displayed by command [delete]: there were six rows in the table;
  • line 7: the exception caused by the second insertion. The message indicates that the constraint [UNQ_NOM] on table [articles] was not satisfied;
  • row 9: the table is not empty: the first record was inserted;
  • row 12: displayed by command [delete]: there was one row in the table;
  • line 13: the first insertion was successful… within the transaction;
  • Line 14: The message displayed when the transaction fails;
  • line 15: the table is empty: the transaction's [rollback] rolled back the first insert;
  • Lines 19–21: With the savepoints, the second insert was rolled back and the transaction committed;
  • line 23: the table contains the first item. Its [id] value is 11, not 8: each insertion attempt—even if rolled back or rejected—consumed a value from the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column, and MySQL does not reuse these values.

With MySQL, the failure of a SQL command cancels only that command, and the transaction can continue: the savepoint is therefore not essential here. This is not the case for all SGBD commands: with PostgreSQL, even the slightest error renders the transaction unusable until it is rolled back or until a rollback point is reached. The code with rollback points works with both.

docs.title: 10.7. Queries that return a single value
docs.text:
Some queries return only one value, such as [select count(*) from articles]: a row from a single column. JDBC does not have a specific method for these: you execute the query using [executeQuery] and read the first column of the first row of the result. The program [Jdbc07.java] implements a method for this and demonstrates a few ways to use it:

package jdbc;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;

// queries that return a unique value
public class Jdbc07 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String UTILISATEUR = "root";
    private static final String MOT_DE_PASSE = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
             // unique values returned by SELECT statements, in the type chosen by the driver
            Object prixMoyen = valeurUnique("select avg(prix) from articles");
            IO.println("Prix moyen des articles = " + prixMoyen + " (type " + type(prixMoyen) + ")");
            Object nbArticles = valeurUnique("select count(id) from articles");
            IO.println("Nombre d'articles = " + nbArticles + " (type " + type(nbArticles) + ")");
            Object nom = valeurUnique(
                    "select nom from articles where prix = (select max(prix) from articles)");
            IO.println("Article le plus cher = " + nom + " (type " + type(nom) + ")");
            Object absent = valeurUnique("select nom from articles where prix > 10000");
            IO.println("Article de plus de 10000 euros : " + absent);
            Object vide = valeurUnique("select max(prix) from articles where prix > 10000");
            IO.println("Prix maximal au-delà de 10000 euros : " + vide);

             // the same values in the requested data type: the driver performs the conversion
            BigDecimal moyenne = valeurUnique("select avg(prix) from articles", BigDecimal.class);
            Integer nombre = valeurUnique("select count(id) from articles", Integer.class);
            IO.println("Moyenne arrondie = " + moyenne.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)
                    + ", nombre = " + nombre);
             // A direct type cast fails: `count` returns a `Long`, not an `Integer`
            int n = (int) nbArticles;
            IO.println("n = " + n);
        } catch (SQLException | ClassCastException ex) {
            IO.println(ex.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

     // Execution of a SELECT statement that returns a single value: the first column of the first row
     // The result is null if the SELECT statement returns no rows or if the value is SQL NULL
    private static Object valeurUnique(String requete) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
             ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery(requete)) {
            return resultat.next() ? resultat.getObject(1) : null;
        }
    }

     // The same thing, with the value converted by the driver to the requested type
    private static <T> T valeurUnique(String requete, Class<T> type) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
             ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery(requete)) {
            return resultat.next() ? resultat.getObject(1, type) : null;
        }
    }

     // the simple class name of an object
    private static String type(Object objet) {
        return objet == null ? "null" : objet.getClass().getSimpleName();
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc07
Prix moyen des articles = 271.666667 (type BigDecimal)
Nombre d'articles = 6 (type Long)
Article le plus cher = arc (type String)
Article de plus de 10000 euros : null
Prix maximal au-delà de 10000 euros : null
Moyenne arrondie = 271.67, nombre = 6
ClassCastException : class java.lang.Long cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer (java.lang.Long and java.lang.Integer are in module java.base of loader 'bootstrap')
  • Line 48: The method [valeurUnique] executes the query and returns the first column of the first row via [getObject(1)], or [null] if the query returns no rows (line 52);
  • line 21: the average price of the items. The Java type of the result depends on the SQL type of the value: the average of a [DECIMAL] column is a [BigDecimal], in this case with six decimal places (line 2 of the results);
  • line 23: the number of items. MySQL returns an integer of type [BIGINT], which becomes a [Long] in Java (line 3);
  • lines 25–26: the name of the most expensive item, a string. The query contains a subquery, enclosed in parentheses;
  • line 28: if the query returns no rows, the method returns [null] (line 5);
  • line 30: if the query returns a row whose value is SQL [NULL] (the maximum of an empty set), [getObject] also returns [null] (line 6). Our method therefore does not distinguish between the two cases—no row or a value of [NULL]; if the distinction matters, one must test the result of [next] oneself;
  • line 57: a second, generic version of the method (Chapter 4) receives the desired type in the form of a [Class<T>] object and returns a value of that type. [getObject(1, type)] (line 61) instructs the driver to convert the value to that type;
  • lines 34–35: the driver converts the value to the requested type: the average to [BigDecimal], and the number of items ([BIGINT]) to [Integer]. [setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)] rounds the average to two decimal places (line 7);
  • line 39: a direct type conversion fails because the object is a [Long]: the [(int)] conversion of a [Object] requires a [Integer], which is then unboxed, and a [Long] is not a [Integer]. A [ClassCastException] is initiated (line 8). This code would work with a SGBD whose [count] returns an integer of type [INT] and would fail with MySQL: This is an example of the peculiarities of SGBD that JDBC does not hide. Reading using [getInt], [getLong], or [getObject(i, type)], which leaves the conversion to the driver, is safer;
  • line 41: a multiple [catch] clause (Java 7) catches both types of exceptions.

docs.title: 10.8. JDBC is blocking: the virtual threads
docs.text:
Chapter 9 showed that I/O operations should not block an application thread in applications that serve many users (servers, web services): while a SQL command is executing on the server, the thread that issued it waits. However, JDBC is a blocking API: [getConnection], [executeQuery], [next], [commit]… only yield control once SGBD has responded. There is no asynchronous version of JDBC: a project for an asynchronous API (ADBA) was abandoned in 2019, and the reactive API (R2DBC), which exists outside of JDK, did not replace JDBC.

Since Java 21, the Java platform’s solution has been the virtual thread (Chapter 8): a lightweight thread managed by JVM, of which thousands can be created. When a virtual thread is waiting for a response from the network, the JVM sets it aside and frees up the system thread that was executing it, allowing that thread to execute another virtual thread. The code remains sequential and blocking—simple to write and read—but the wait no longer incurs any overhead. Recent JDBC drivers, including Connector/J 9, are written to work with virtual threads, and since Java 24 (JEP 491), a virtual thread waiting in a [synchronized] block no longer monopolizes the system thread.

One limitation remains: the number of connections. A thousand virtual threads querying the database do not have a thousand connections; they share the connections in the pool and wait for a connection to become available. The program [Jdbc08.java] demonstrates this, using a pool HikariCP of four connections:

package jdbc;

import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariConfig;
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.SQLTimeoutException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import javax.sql.DataSource;

// JDBC is blocking: concurrent requests executed by virtual threads
public class Jdbc08 {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
         // the data source: a pool of up to 4 connections to the database [dbarticles]
        HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles");
        config.setUsername("root");
        config.setPassword("");
        config.setMaximumPoolSize(4);

        try (HikariDataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config)) {
             // 1 - an update statement, within a transaction
            try (Connection connexion = dataSource.getConnection()) {
                connexion.setAutoCommit(false);
                try (PreparedStatement ordre = connexion.prepareStatement(
                        "update articles set prix = prix * 1.1 where prix < ?")) {
                    ordre.setInt(1, 200);
                    int nbLignes = ordre.executeUpdate();
                    connexion.commit();
                    IO.println(nbLignes + " prix augmenté(s) de 10 %");
                }
            }

             // 2 - six concurrent queries, each in its own virtual thread
            long debut = System.nanoTime();
            List<Future<Article>> taches = new ArrayList<>();
            try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
                for (int id = 1; id <= 6; id++) {
                    int idArticle = id;
                    taches.add(executor.submit(() -> getArticleLentement(dataSource, idArticle)));
                }
            } // The executor waits for all six tasks to complete before closing
            for (Future<Article> tache : taches) {
                IO.println(tache.get());
            }
            IO.println("6 requêtes d'une seconde exécutées en %.1f s avec %d connexions"
                    .formatted((System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1e9, config.getMaximumPoolSize()));

             // 3 - a single value
            try (Connection connexion = dataSource.getConnection();
                 Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
                 ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery("select sum(prix * stockactuel) from articles")) {
                resultat.next();
                IO.println("Valeur du stock : " + resultat.getBigDecimal(1) + " euros");
            }

             // 4 - a request blocked by another transaction, abandoned after one second
             // The transaction [bloquante] modifies item #1 and does not complete:
             // the row remains locked
            try (Connection bloquante = dataSource.getConnection()) {
                bloquante.setAutoCommit(false);
                try (Statement ordre = bloquante.createStatement()) {
                    ordre.executeUpdate("update articles set stockactuel = stockactuel - 1 where id = 1");
                }
                 // Another connection attempts to modify the same row: it must wait for [bloquante] to complete
                long chrono = System.nanoTime();
                try (Connection connexion = dataSource.getConnection();
                     Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement()) {
                    ordre.setQueryTimeout(1);
                    ordre.executeUpdate("update articles set prix = prix * 2 where id = 1");
                } catch (SQLTimeoutException ex) {
                    IO.println(ex.getClass().getSimpleName() + " au bout de "
                            + Math.round((System.nanoTime() - chrono) / 1e9) + " s : " + ex.getMessage());
                }
                 // The transaction [bloquante] was not committed: it is rolled back
                bloquante.rollback();
            }
        } catch (SQLException | ExecutionException ex) {
            IO.println("Erreur d'accès à la base de données (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

     // A record read by a query that takes one second (the MySQL sleep function simulates a slow query)
    private static Article getArticleLentement(DataSource dataSource, int id) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = dataSource.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ordre = connexion.prepareStatement("select id, nom, prix, stockactuel, "
                     + "stockminimum, sleep(1) from articles where id = ?")) {
            ordre.setInt(1, id);
            try (ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery()) {
                resultat.next();
                return new Article(resultat.getInt(1), resultat.getString(2), resultat.getBigDecimal(3),
                        resultat.getInt(4), resultat.getInt(5));
            }
        }
    }
}

Article[id=4, nom=flèches - lot de 6, prix=110.00, stockActuel=12, stockMinimum=20]
Article[id=5, nom=combinaison de plongée, prix=300.00, stockActuel=8, stockMinimum=2]
Article[id=6, nom=bouteilles d'oxygène, prix=132.00, stockActuel=10, stockMinimum=5]
6 requêtes d'une seconde exécutées en 2,4 s avec 4 connexions
Valeur du stock : 12550.00 euros
MySQLTimeoutException au bout de 1 s : Statement cancelled due to timeout or client request
  • lines 24–28: configuration of a pool with a maximum of four connections;
  • line 30: the data source [HikariDataSource], closed at the end of the program by the try-with-resources statement;
  • lines 32–41: an update statement within a transaction, using a connection obtained from the pool. The implicit [close] on line 41 returns the connection to the pool. The results show that the three prices below 200 euros were increased by 10% (line 2 of the results);
  • line 93: the [getArticleLentement] method reads an article in a query that takes one second: the MySQL and [sleep(1)] functions (lines 95–96) wait one second before returning 0. This simulates a slow query;
  • lines 44–56: six article reads, executed simultaneously:
    • line 46: [Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor] (Java 21, Chapter 8) creates an executor that launches each task in a new virtual thread. The executor is closed at the end of the try-with-resources block (line 51), and its method [close] (Java 19) waits for all tasks to complete;
    • line 49: Each task is a lambda that returns a [Article]: a *[Callable<Article>]*, whose *[call]* method can throw controlled exceptions, in this case the *[SQLException] from *[getArticleLentement]*. [submit] returns a [Future<Article>]. The lambda uses the copy [idArticle]* of the loop variable (line 48), because a lambda can only use local variables that are not modified;
    • lines 52–54: the items are displayed in the order of the tasks. [Future.get] returns the result of the task; if the task threw an exception, [get] throws a [ExecutionException] that encapsulates it (intercepted on line 87). [get] can also throw a [InterruptedException], which [main] declares (line 22);
    • lines 55–56: the total duration. Six one-second requests executed one after the other would take six seconds; executed simultaneously with six connections, one second. With four connections, it takes about two seconds (line 9 of the results): four virtual threads obtain a connection and execute their requests simultaneously, while the other two wait in [getConnection] for a connection to be returned to the pool, then execute theirs. The remaining time is spent opening connections from the pool. A thread that waits too long for a connection (30 seconds by default, setting [connectionTimeout] in HikariCP) receives a [SQLTransientConnectionException];
  • lines 59–64: a single value, the stock value;
  • lines 69–86: Aborting a query that is taking too long:
    • lines 69–73: a first connection exits autocommit mode and modifies item No. 1 without completing its transaction. The SGBD has locked the modified row until the end of the transaction;
    • lines 76–79: a second connection attempts to modify the same row. It must wait for the first transaction to complete… which it will not do. [setQueryTimeout(1)] (line 78) limits the command’s execution time to one second: after one second, Connector/J instructs the server to abort the request (command MySQL [KILL QUERY]), and [executeUpdate] initiates a [SQLTimeoutException], in this case from the driver’s [MySQLTimeoutException] class (line 11 of the results). Without this timeout, the request would have waited for the lock timeout of MySQL—50 seconds by default—and then failed;
    • Line 85: The transaction [bloquante] is never committed; it is rolled back. The connection is then returned to the pool.

Virtual threads offer no benefit to a small console program that performs one task at a time: they do not make a request any faster. But they allow a server application—such as the Spring Boot web services in Chapter 13 (where the [spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true] property is sufficient)—to serve many users at once using ordinary JDBC code. The size of the connection pool then becomes the true control for parallelism with respect to the database.

docs.title: 10.9. Batch Execution
docs.text:
Each execution of a SQL command involves a round trip between the application and the server. When multiple SQL commands need to be executed, they can be sent to SGBD in a single exchange, in the form of a batch. JDBC has supported this since version 2.0:

  • for a [Statement], [addBatch(sql)] adds a SQL command to the batch;
  • for a [PreparedStatement], [addBatch()] adds the current parameter values to the batch: the batch contains the same SQL command executed with different values;
  • [executeBatch] executes the batch and returns an array of integers: the number of rows modified by each command in the batch. If a command fails, it launches a [BatchUpdateException], whose method [getUpdateCounts] returns the results of the executed commands.

The program [Jdbc09.java] uses the following batches:

package jdbc;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.Arrays;

// Batch processing: multiple SQL commands sent to SGBD in a single exchange
public class Jdbc09 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String UTILISATEUR = "root";
    private static final String MOT_DE_PASSE = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE)) {
            IO.println("Le pilote sait exécuter des lots : "
                    + connexion.getMetaData().supportsBatchUpdates());

             // 1 - a batch of three different update commands
            try (Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement()) {
                ordre.addBatch("insert into articles(nom, prix, stockactuel, stockminimum) "
                        + "values('canoë', 800, 5, 1)");
                ordre.addBatch("update articles set stockactuel = stockactuel + 10 "
                        + "where stockactuel < stockminimum");
                ordre.addBatch("delete from articles where nom = 'pompe'");
                int[] nbLignes = ordre.executeBatch();
                IO.println("Lignes modifiées par chaque ordre : " + Arrays.toString(nbLignes)
                        + ", total : " + Arrays.stream(nbLignes).sum());
            }

             // 2 - 1,000 inserts via a batch of the same configured command, first without and then with batch rewriting
            insererLot(URL, 1000);
            insererLot(URL + "?rewriteBatchedStatements=true", 1000);
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("Erreur d'accès à la base de données (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }

         // 3 - two SELECT statements sent in a single exchange: one query, two successive results
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL + "?allowMultiQueries=true",
                UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement()) {
            ordre.execute("select nom, stockactuel from articles where stockactuel < stockminimum + 5;"
                    + "select count(*), sum(prix * stockactuel) from articles");
            IO.println("Articles à surveiller :");
            try (ResultSet resultat = ordre.getResultSet()) {
                while (resultat.next()) {
                    IO.println("  " + resultat.getString(1) + " : " + resultat.getInt(2));
                }
            }
             // moving to the next result
            ordre.getMoreResults();
            try (ResultSet resultat = ordre.getResultSet()) {
                resultat.next();
                IO.println(resultat.getLong(1) + " articles, valeur du stock : " + resultat.getBigDecimal(2)
                        + " euros");
            }
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("Erreur d'accès à la base de données (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

     // Insertion of n items via a batch in a single transaction, followed by deletion of those items
    private static void insererLot(String url, int n) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(url, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE)) {
            connexion.setAutoCommit(false);
            long debut = System.nanoTime();
            try (PreparedStatement ordre = connexion.prepareStatement(
                    "insert into articles(nom, prix, stockactuel, stockminimum) values(?, ?, ?, ?)")) {
                for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
                    ordre.setString(1, "lot-" + i);
                    ordre.setBigDecimal(2, BigDecimal.TEN);
                    ordre.setInt(3, i);
                    ordre.setInt(4, 0);
                     // Parameter values are added to the batch
                    ordre.addBatch();
                }
                int[] nbLignes = ordre.executeBatch();
                connexion.commit();
                long duree = (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000;
                IO.println("%d insertions (%s) en %d ms : %s...".formatted(nbLignes.length,
                        url.replaceFirst(".*/", ""), duree, Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOf(nbLignes, 3))));
            }
             // the table is restored to its previous state
            try (Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement()) {
                ordre.executeUpdate("delete from articles where nom like 'lot-%'");
                connexion.commit();
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc09
Le pilote sait exécuter des lots : true
Lignes modifiées par chaque ordre : [1, 1, 1], total : 3
1000 insertions (dbarticles) en 2341 ms : [1, 1, 1]...
1000 insertions (dbarticles?rewriteBatchedStatements=true) en 207 ms : [-2, -2, -2]...
Articles à surveiller :
  arc : 4
  flèches - lot de 6 : 22
  canoë : 5
6 articles, valeur du stock : 17200.00 euros
  • Lines 21–22: The [supportsBatchUpdates] method in the connection metadata indicates whether the driver can execute batches;
  • Lines 25–34: A batch of three different update commands, added to the batch of a [Statement] by [addBatch]:
    • line 31: the three commands are executed. [executeBatch] returns the number of rows modified by each: one insertion ([canoë]), one update (the stock of arrows, which is below the minimum stock), and one deletion ([pompe]);
    • Lines 32–33: [Arrays.toString] displays the array, [Arrays.stream] converts it into a stream of integers ([IntStream]), and [sum] calculates the sum (line 3 of the results);
  • lines 37–38: the method [insererLot] is called twice, with two different URL instances;
  • line 68: the [insererLot] method inserts [n] items with a batch:
    • line 70: the insertions are performed in a single transaction, which is also much faster than committing each one individually;
    • Lines 74–81: For each item, the parameters are assigned their values, then [addBatch()] adds these values to the batch;
    • lines 82–83: the batch is executed, then the transaction is committed;
    • lines 84–86: the number of inserts, the duration, and the first three elements of the array returned by [executeBatch] are displayed;
    • lines 89–92: The inserted items are deleted to restore the table to its previous state;
  • row 4 of the results: with the simple URL, the MySQL driver sends the 1,000 inserts one after another: the batch adds almost nothing. Each element of the array is 1;
  • Line 5 of the results: With the [rewriteBatchedStatements=true] parameter of URL, Connector/J rewrites the batch as a few [insert into articles(…) values (…), (…), (…)…] commands, each of which inserts numerous rows. Execution is ten times faster. The array elements are then set to -2, the value of the constant [Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO]: the command succeeded, but the driver does not know how many rows each batch element modified. This is an important setting to be aware of: without it, batches are of little use with MySQL;
  • lines 43–64: two [select] commands sent in a single exchange:
    • lines 44–45: the connection is opened with the parameter [allowMultiQueries=true], which allows multiple SQL commands separated by semicolons in a single request. As we have seen, this is disabled by default to limit the scope of SQL injections;
    • lines 47–48: both commands are executed by [execute], which accepts any command;
    • line 50: [getResultSet] returns the result of the first command;
    • Line 56: [getMoreResults] moves to the next result (it closes the current result and returns [true] if the next result is [ResultSet]);
    • Line 57: The result of the second query: a row with two columns.

Batches are useful for large-scale inserts and updates (such as data imports). Hibernate (Chapter 11) also supports them.

docs.title: 10.10. Offline mode: CachedRowSet
docs.text:
The offline mode of JDBC is based on the [javax.sql.rowset.CachedRowSet] interface, derived from [ResultSet]: A [CachedRowSet] is a query result copied into memory, which can be browsed in both directions and modified offline, after which the changes are sent back to the database. The program [Jdbc10.java] demonstrates this:

package jdbc;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import javax.sql.rowset.CachedRowSet;
import javax.sql.rowset.RowSetFactory;
import javax.sql.rowset.RowSetProvider;

// Offline mode: a memory copy of the rows, modified offline, then sent back to the database
public class Jdbc10 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String UTILISATEUR = "root";
    private static final String MOT_DE_PASSE = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
             // the RowSet factory on the Java platform
            RowSetFactory fabrique = RowSetProvider.newFactory();
            try (CachedRowSet articles = fabrique.createCachedRowSet()) {
                 // connection parameters and the query
                articles.setUrl(URL);
                articles.setUsername(UTILISATEUR);
                articles.setPassword(MOT_DE_PASSE);
                articles.setCommand("select id, nom, prix, stockactuel, stockminimum from articles");
                 // the table to be updated and its primary key (column #1)
                articles.setTableName("articles");
                articles.setKeyColumns(new int[]{1});
                 // Connection, copying rows to memory, disconnection
                articles.execute();
                IO.println(articles.size() + " lignes copiées en mémoire");

                 // offline processing: restocking out-of-stock items
                while (articles.next()) {
                    int stockActuel = articles.getInt("stockactuel");
                    int stockMinimum = articles.getInt("stockminimum");
                    if (stockActuel < stockMinimum) {
                        articles.updateInt("stockactuel", stockMinimum + 10);
                        articles.updateRow();
                        IO.println("[" + articles.getString("nom") + "] : stock " + stockActuel + " -> "
                                + articles.getInt("stockactuel"));
                    }
                }
                 // Add a row: ID 0 requests that MySQL generate one
                articles.moveToInsertRow();
                articles.updateInt("id", 0);
                articles.updateString("nom", "canoë");
                articles.updateBigDecimal("prix", new BigDecimal("800"));
                articles.updateInt("stockactuel", 5);
                articles.updateInt("stockminimum", 1);
                articles.insertRow();
                articles.moveToCurrentRow();
                 // Delete the second line
                articles.absolute(2);
                IO.println("suppression de [" + articles.getString("nom") + "]");
                articles.deleteRow();

                 // The database has not yet been updated
                afficherArticles("Base avant acceptChanges :");
                 // Log in, submit changes in a transaction, log out
                try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE)) {
                    connexion.setAutoCommit(false);
                    articles.acceptChanges(connexion);
                }
            }
            afficherArticles("Base après acceptChanges :");
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("Erreur d'accès à la base de données (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

     // displaying the table contents, read in connected mode
    private static void afficherArticles(String titre) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
             ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery(
                     "select id, nom, prix, stockactuel, stockminimum from articles")) {
            IO.println(titre);
            while (resultat.next()) {
                IO.println("  " + resultat.getInt(1) + " " + resultat.getString(2) + " "
                        + resultat.getBigDecimal(3) + " " + resultat.getInt(4) + " " + resultat.getInt(5));
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc10
6 lignes copiées en mémoire
[flèches - lot de 6] : stock 12 -> 30
suppression de [pompe]
Base avant acceptChanges :
  1 vélo 500.00 10 5
  2 pompe 10.00 10 2
  3 arc 600.00 4 1
  4 flèches - lot de 6 100.00 12 20
  5 combinaison de plongée 300.00 8 2
  6 bouteilles d'oxygène 120.00 10 5
Base après acceptChanges :
  1 vélo 500.00 10 5
  3 arc 600.00 4 1
  4 flèches - lot de 6 100.00 30 20
  5 combinaison de plongée 300.00 8 2
  6 bouteilles d'oxygène 120.00 10 5
  7 canoë 800.00 5 1
  • Lines 23–24: [RowSetProvider.newFactory] (Java 7) returns a factory ([RowSetFactory]) from various types of RowSet derived from JDK, from which [createCachedRowSet] creates a [CachedRowSet]. A [CachedRowSet] is a resource closed by the try-with-resources statement;
  • lines 26–29: the [CachedRowSet] receives the connection parameters and the query that will populate it;
  • lines 31–32: to be able to commit the changes to the database, it must know the modified table and its primary key—in this case, column #1—[id];
  • line 34: [execute] opens a connection, executes the query, copies all rows of the result into memory, and closes the connection. The rest of the work is done offline;
  • Lines 38–47: A [CachedRowSet] is a [ResultSet]: it is iterated through using [next], and the columns are read using [getXxx]. The [updateXxx] methods modify a column in the current row, and [updateRow] saves the change… to the in-memory copy. The arrow count, which was below the minimum, is increased to 30 (row 3 of the results);
  • lines 49–56: adding a row. [moveToInsertRow] places the cursor on a special row, the “insertion row,” whose columns are specified by [updateXxx]; [insertRow] adds it to [CachedRowSet], and [moveToCurrentRow] returns the cursor to its previous position. [CachedRowSet] requires a value for all [NOT NULL] columns, including [id]: the value 0, inserted into a [AUTO_INCREMENT] column, instructs MySQL to generate one;
  • lines 58–60: [absolute(2)] places the cursor on the second line, which is enabled by [CachedRowSet]—allowing the cursor to move in any direction—and [deleteRow] removes it;
  • line 63: the database has not yet been modified (lines 5–11 of the results);
  • lines 65–68: [acceptChanges] commits the changes to the database: a [update], a [insert], and a [delete], executed in a transaction that is committed at the end. For each modified row, the implementation of JDK verifies that the database row has not been modified by someone else since it was read (an “optimistic” check); otherwise, it launches a [SyncProviderException]. The parameter-less version of [acceptChanges] opens the connection itself, but leaves it in autocommit mode and then calls [commit], which Connector/J refuses; therefore, it is passed a connection that has exited autocommit mode;
  • line 70: the database has been modified (lines 12–18 of the results).

[CachedRowSet] has the advantage of being a standard API version of JDK, but its limitations are evident: it manipulates rows and column numbers, not business objects; the modifications are made by an implementation whose SQL we do not fully understand. This is why it is rarely used today: working with in-memory objects and subsequently saving the changes is the domain of ORM frameworks such as Hibernate (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 10.11. Sample Application—Version 6
docs.text:
Let's revisit the sample application [Impots]. The latest version, version 5, was discussed in Chapter 6. It was a three-tier application whose [dao] tier retrieved its data from a text file, a JSON file, or its own code, and whose tiers were integrated by Spring’s dependency injection container. We’re writing a new layer, [dao], that retrieves its data from a database, MySQL:

We reuse the Version 5 modules as-is, via Maven dependencies, and write only what is new: the [dao] layer and the program that integrates the layers.

docs.title: 10.11.1. The database
docs.text:
Tax brackets are stored in the [tranches] table within the MySQL database, created by the [sql/dbimpots.sql] script:

-- Created the database [dbimpots] for the application [Impots] (version 6)
-- Execution: mysql -uroot < dbimpots.sql

-- the script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;

-- The database is recreated each time the script is run
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbimpots;
CREATE DATABASE dbimpots CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
USE dbimpots;

-- the tax bracket table (2004 tax schedule for 2003 income)
CREATE TABLE tranches (
    id      INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    limite  DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    coeffr  DECIMAL(6,3) NOT NULL,
    coeffn  DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO tranches (limite, coeffr, coeffn) VALUES
    (4962, 0, 0),
    (8382, 0.068, 291.09),
    (14753, 0.191, 1322.92),
    (23888, 0.283, 2668.39),
    (38868, 0.374, 4846.98),
    (47932, 0.426, 6883.66),
    (0, 0.481, 9505.54);

-- an application-specific user who has access rights only to the database [dbimpots]
CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'admimpots'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'mdpimpots';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON dbimpots.* TO 'admimpots'@'localhost';
  • Lines 13–18: The table [tranches] has four columns: the primary key [id], generated by SGBD, followed by the three columns [limite], [coeffr], and [coeffn], which represent a tax bracket of type [DECIMAL]: these are amounts and coefficients that must be exact. They will be read in Java as [BigDecimal], the field type of the [TrancheImpot] record;
  • lines 19–26: the seven brackets of the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, used since the beginning of the course (this is an exercise: the schedule is not up to date). The brackets are listed in ascending order of their thresholds, and the [id] column reflects this order;
  • lines 29–30: creation of a user MySQL [admimpots], with password [mdpimpots], who is granted full permissions ([GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES]) on all objects in the database [dbimpots] ([dbimpots.*]), and only on those objects. The application will run as this user rather than as the administrator [root]: if the administrator’s password were to be compromised, only the database [dbimpots] would be at risk. [IF NOT EXISTS] allows the script to be run multiple times.

The script is executed by the administrator:

> mysql -uroot < dbimpots.sql

then we verify that the user [admimpots] has access to the segments (the [-p] option alone prompts for the password, which is not displayed as it is typed):

> mysql -uadmimpots -p -t dbimpots -e "select * from tranches"
Enter password: 
+----+----------+--------+---------+
| id | limite   | coeffr | coeffn  |
+----+----------+--------+---------+
|  1 |  4962.00 |  0.000 |    0.00 |
|  2 |  8382.00 |  0.068 |  291.09 |
|  3 | 14753.00 |  0.191 | 1322.92 |
|  4 | 23888.00 |  0.283 | 2668.39 |
|  5 | 38868.00 |  0.374 | 4846.98 |
|  6 | 47932.00 |  0.426 | 6883.66 |
|  7 |     0.00 |  0.481 | 9505.54 |
+----+----------+--------+---------+

docs.title: 10.11.2. The ImpotsV6 project
docs.text:
Version 6 is a Maven project consisting of two modules, located in the [10-jdbc/ImpotsV6] folder, which uses three modules from version 5:

java-oct-2026/
  06-architectures/ImpotsV5/            la version 5, réutilisée
    pom.xml                               projet parent impots-v5
    impots-dao/                           entités, interface IImpotDao, implémentations de la version 5
    impots-metier/                        couche [metier]
    impots-ui/                            couche [ui] (classe Dialogue) et programme de la version 5
  10-jdbc/
    sql/
      dbimpots.sql                        script de création de la base
    ImpotsV6/
      pom.xml                             projet parent impots-v6
      impots-dao-mysql/                   la nouvelle couche [dao]
        pom.xml
        src/main/java/impots/dao/
          MySqlImpot.java
        src/test/java/impots/dao/
          MySqlImpotTests.java            tests JUnit de la nouvelle couche [dao]
      impots-ui-mysql/                    intégration des couches
        pom.xml
        impots.properties
        impots-base.properties
        impots-motdepasse.properties
        impots-serveur.properties
        impots-requete.properties
        impots-postgresql.properties
        src/main/java/impots/ui/mysql/
          Main.java

The Version 5 modules are not part of the [ImpotsV6] project: they are dependencies, such as the JDBC driver or Spring. For Maven to find them, you must first install them in the local Maven repository (the [.m2/repository] folder in the user’s home directory), where Maven stores all the libraries it downloads. This is what the [mvn install] command does, which is entered once and for all in the version 5 folder:

> cd 06-architectures/ImpotsV5
> mvn install

It compiles the three modules, runs their tests, creates their archives [impots-dao-5.0.jar], [impots-metier-5.0.jar], and [impots-ui-5.0.jar], and copies them, along with the [pom.xml] from the parent project, to the local repository under the identifiers [exemples.impots:impots-dao:5.0], [exemples.impots:impots-metier:5.0], and [exemples.impots:impots-ui:5.0]. Any Maven project on the machine can then use them just like any library from Maven Central.

This illustrates the value of a layered architecture. The layers [metier] and [ui] only recognize the [IImpotDao] interface, defined in the [impots-dao] module of version 5; the new layer [dao] implements this interface in a new module. No lines of code in version 5 are modified, and its source files are not even recompiled.

The [pom.xml] from the parent project is as follows:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- parent project of the application [Impots], version 6: the layer [dao] reads a database -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
    <artifactId>impots-v6</artifactId>
    <version>6.0</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>

     <!-- the two new modules; those from version 5 are dependencies -->
    <modules>
        <module>impots-dao-mysql</module>
        <module>impots-ui-mysql</module>
    </modules>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

     <!-- library versions, common to all modules -->
    <dependencyManagement>
        <dependencies>
             <!-- the modules from version 5, installed in the local Maven repository by [mvn install] -->
            <dependency>
