docs.title: 10.11.3. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [pom.xml] file in the [impots-dao-mysql] module is as follows:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

     <!-- the parent project provides the shared versions and configuration -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
        <artifactId>impots-v6</artifactId>
        <version>6.0</version>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>impots-dao-mysql</artifactId>

    <dependencies>
         <!-- the entities and the IImpotDao interface from version 5 -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-dao</artifactId>
        </dependency>
         <!-- the JDBC driver for MySQL: the code only uses it at runtime -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
            <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>
         <!-- for testing: the [metier] layer in version 5 and JUnit -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-metier</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

</project>
  • lines 8–12: the parent project;
  • lines 18–21: the [impots-dao] module from version 5, which contains the entities ([TrancheImpot], [ImpotException]) and the [IImpotDao] interface;
  • lines 23–27: the JDBC driver for MySQL, with the scope ([scope]) [runtime]: it is not used at compile time, but it is present at runtime and during testing. This provides a guarantee: if the code mistakenly used a class from the driver, it would not compile. The layer [dao] depends only on JDBC;
  • lines 29–38: for testing only (scope [test]), the [metier] layer from version 5 and JUnit.

The class [MySqlImpot] implements the interface [IImpotDao]:

package impots.dao;

import impots.entites.ImpotException;
import impots.entites.TrancheImpot;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

// a [dao] layer that reads the tax brackets from a MySQL database
public class MySqlImpot implements IImpotDao {

     // error codes specific to this implementation
    public static final int ACCES = 101, DONNEES = 102;

     // the default query: tax brackets must be returned in ascending order of thresholds
    public static final String REQUETE_PAR_DEFAUT = "select limite, coeffr, coeffn from tranches order by id";

     // tax brackets
    private final List<TrancheImpot> tranchesImpot;

     // constructor with the default query
    public MySqlImpot(String url, String utilisateur, String motDePasse) {
        this(url, utilisateur, motDePasse, REQUETE_PAR_DEFAUT);
    }

     // constructor: tax brackets are read once and for all
    public MySqlImpot(String url, String utilisateur, String motDePasse, String requete) {
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = new ArrayList<>();
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(url, utilisateur, motDePasse);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
             ResultSet resultat = ordre.executeQuery(requete)) {
             // one tax bracket per result line: threshold, coeffR, coeffN
            while (resultat.next()) {
                tranches.add(lireTranche(resultat));
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
             // Database access error: encapsulated in a ImpotException
            throw new ImpotException("Erreur d'accès à la base des tranches d'impôt", e, ACCES);
        }
         // An empty table is also an error
        if (tranches.isEmpty()) {
            throw new ImpotException("La base ne contient aucune tranche d'impôt", DONNEES);
        }
         // returns a read-only copy of the list
        tranchesImpot = List.copyOf(tranches);
    }

    @Override
    public List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }

     // the section of the current row: three numeric columns, with no values NULL
    private static TrancheImpot lireTranche(ResultSet resultat) {
        try {
            BigDecimal limite = resultat.getBigDecimal(1);
            BigDecimal coeffR = resultat.getBigDecimal(2);
            BigDecimal coeffN = resultat.getBigDecimal(3);
            if (limite == null || coeffR == null || coeffN == null) {
                throw new ImpotException("Une tranche d'impôt de la base a une valeur NULL", DONNEES);
            }
            return new TrancheImpot(limite, coeffR, coeffN);
        } catch (SQLException e) {
             // a missing or non-numeric column
            throw new ImpotException("Les tranches d'impôt de la base sont incorrectes", e, DONNEES);
        }
    }
}
  • line 1: the class is in the package [impots.dao], like the other implementations of [IImpotDao], although it is in a different archive;
  • line 15: the class [MySqlImpot] implements the [IImpotDao] interface from version 5: a method [getTranchesImpot] that returns the list of slices (line 54);
  • line 18: the error codes specific to this implementation, modeled after those of [FileImpot] and [JsonImpot]: 101 for a database access error, 102 for incorrect data;
  • line 21: the query that returns the slices. The [order by id] clause is important: the [metier] layer expects the slices in ascending order of bounds, and a [select] without [order by] returns the rows in an order that SQL does not guarantee;
  • lines 27–29: a constructor that uses the default query, calling the other constructor via [this(…)];
  • line 32: the constructor receives the connection parameters and the query. The slices are read once and for all within the constructor: the [dao] layer is a singleton in the application, and the database is not queried again afterward. A connection opened by [DriverManager] is therefore sufficient; a connection pool would serve no purpose;
  • Lines 34–36: the connection, the query SQL, and the result, as in the previous examples;
  • lines 38–40: Each line of the result becomes a [TrancheImpot] object, created by the [lireTranche] method;
  • lines 41–44: A database access error is encapsulated in a [ImpotException] with code [ACCES], just as [FileImpot] and [JsonImpot] did with input/output errors. [ImpotException] is an unhandled exception: the [ui] layer does not need to be aware of [SQLException], which are handled exceptions of JDBC;
  • Lines 46–48: An empty table is a data error;
  • line 50: the list is made read-only by [List.copyOf] (Java 10);
  • lines 59–72: reading a slice:
    • lines 61–63: [getBigDecimal(i)] reads column #i as a [BigDecimal];
    • lines 64–66: a column with the value [NULL] yields a [BigDecimal] [null]: this is a data error;
    • lines 68–71: A query that returns fewer than three columns, or a non-numeric column, results in a [SQLException] in [getBigDecimal]: this is also a data error. The [ImpotException] raised on line 65 is not a [SQLException]: it passes through the [catch] clause on line 68 without being intercepted, and then the one on line 41; the constructor’s try-with-resources block nevertheless closes the connection.

Note that the class name is the only place where MySQL appears: the code uses only the interfaces of [java.sql]. We’ll come back to this.

docs.title: 10.11.4. Tests for the [dao] layer
docs.text:
The tests for the [dao] layer are in the [src/test/java] folder of the module:

package impots.dao;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertInstanceOf;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertNotEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrowsExactly;

import impots.entites.ImpotException;
import impots.entites.TrancheImpot;
import impots.metier.IImpotMetier;
import impots.metier.ImpotMetier;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.List;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;

// tests of the layer [dao] MySqlImpot (the database [dbimpots] must exist)
class MySqlImpotTests {

     // the test database
    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbimpots";
    private static final String UTILISATEUR = "admimpots";
    private static final String MOT_DE_PASSE = "mdpimpots";

     // The slices read from the database are those from the “hard-coded” version
    @Test
    void memesTranches() {
        List<TrancheImpot> reference = new HardwiredImpot().getTranchesImpot();
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = new MySqlImpot(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE).getTranchesImpot();
         // "equals" also compares the scale of BigDecimal: 4962.00 (database) is not equal to 4962 (hard-coded)
        assertNotEquals(reference, tranches);
         // compareTo compares only the values
        assertEquals(reference.size(), tranches.size());
        for (int i = 0; i < reference.size(); i++) {
            assertEquals(0, reference.get(i).limite().compareTo(tranches.get(i).limite()));
            assertEquals(0, reference.get(i).coeffR().compareTo(tranches.get(i).coeffR()));
            assertEquals(0, reference.get(i).coeffN().compareTo(tranches.get(i).coeffN()));
        }
    }

     // the [metier] layer from version 5 with the new [dao] layer
    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource({
        "true, 2, 60000, 4282",
        "true, 3, 60000, 2959",
        "false, 0, 60000, 11519"
    })
    void calculerImpot(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire, int impot) {
        IImpotMetier metier = new ImpotMetier(new MySqlImpot(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE));
        assertEquals(impot, metier.calculerImpot(marie, nbEnfants, salaire));
    }

     // database does not exist (or is restricted to the user)
    @Test
    void baseInexistante() {
        ImpotException e = assertThrowsExactly(ImpotException.class,
                () -> new MySqlImpot(URL.replace("dbimpots", "dbimpotsinconnue"), UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE));
        assertEquals(MySqlImpot.ACCES, e.getCode());
        assertInstanceOf(SQLException.class, e.getCause());
    }

     // incorrect password
    @Test
    void motDePasseIncorrect() {
        ImpotException e = assertThrowsExactly(ImpotException.class,
                () -> new MySqlImpot(URL, UTILISATEUR, "x"));
        assertEquals(MySqlImpot.ACCES, e.getCode());
    }

     // server unreachable
    @Test
    void serveurInjoignable() {
        ImpotException e = assertThrowsExactly(ImpotException.class,
                () -> new MySqlImpot(URL.replace("3306", "3399"), UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE));
        assertEquals(MySqlImpot.ACCES, e.getCode());
    }

     // query returns only two columns
    @Test
    void requeteIncorrecte() {
        ImpotException e = assertThrowsExactly(ImpotException.class,
                () -> new MySqlImpot(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE, "select limite, coeffr from tranches"));
        assertEquals(MySqlImpot.DONNEES, e.getCode());
    }

     // query that returns no rows
    @Test
    void aucuneTranche() {
        ImpotException e = assertThrowsExactly(ImpotException.class,
                () -> new MySqlImpot(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE,
                        "select limite, coeffr, coeffn from tranches where id < 0"));
        assertEquals(MySqlImpot.DONNEES, e.getCode());
    }

     // query in which one column is NULL
    @Test
    void valeurNull() {
        ImpotException e = assertThrowsExactly(ImpotException.class,
                () -> new MySqlImpot(URL, UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE,
                        "select limite, coeffr, null from tranches"));
        assertEquals(MySqlImpot.DONNEES, e.getCode());
    }
}
  • Lines 22–24: The tests use the database [dbimpots], which must have been created by the script [dbimpots.sql]. These are therefore no longer unit tests in the strict sense—which would test a class in isolation—but rather integration tests: they verify that the [dao] layer works with SGBD. For these tests, we often use an in-memory H2 database, created at the start of the tests, or a SGBD instance launched in a Docker container by the Testcontainers library; here, we’ll simply use the machine’s MySQL database;
  • Lines 28–40: The slices read from the database are those of the “hard-coded” version [HardwiredImpot]… but not in the sense of [equals] (line 32)! The [equals] method for a record compares its fields with their [equals] method, and the [BigDecimal] method compares the value and the scale (the number of decimal places): the [BigDecimal] values read from the database have two decimal places ([4962.00]), as does the [DECIMAL(10,2)] column, whereas those of [HardwiredImpot] have none ([4962]). [compareTo], on the other hand, compares only the values (lines 35–39). This is a classic pitfall of [BigDecimal] (Chapter 3);
  • lines 43–52: the [metier] layer in version 5 calculates the expected taxes using the new [dao] layer. [@CsvSource] provides the parameters for the three test runs;
  • lines 55–61: a nonexistent database triggers a [ImpotException] with code [ACCES], which encapsulates the original [SQLException] ([assertInstanceOf] accepts a derived class);
  • lines 64–69: the same applies to an incorrect password;
  • lines 72–77: an unreachable server (no server is listening on port 3399) also causes an access error;
  • methods [requeteIncorrecte] (line 81), [aucuneTranche] (line 89), and [valeurNull] (line 98): A query that returns only two columns, returns no rows, or has a column with the value [NULL] triggers a [ImpotException] error with code [DONNEES].

The tests are run using [mvn test] in the module folder (or [mvn install] in the [ImpotsV6] folder, which also runs the tests). Maven displays only the summary; IDE and the JUnit launcher in console mode display the following tree (the summary following the tree is abbreviated):

╷
└─ JUnit Jupiter ✔
   └─ MySqlImpotTests ✔
      ├─ motDePasseIncorrect() ✔
      ├─ calculerImpot(boolean, int, int, int) ✔
      │  ├─ [1] marie=true, nbEnfants=2, salaire=60000, impot=4282 ✔
      │  ├─ [2] marie=true, nbEnfants=3, salaire=60000, impot=2959 ✔
      │  └─ [3] marie=false, nbEnfants=0, salaire=60000, impot=11519 ✔
      ├─ serveurInjoignable() ✔
      ├─ aucuneTranche() ✔
      ├─ baseInexistante() ✔
      ├─ valeurNull() ✔
      ├─ memesTranches() ✔
      └─ requeteIncorrecte() ✔
...
[        10 tests successful      ]
[         0 tests failed          ]

docs.title: 10.11.5. Layer Integration
docs.text:
The [impots-ui-mysql] module contains the program that integrates the layers. Its [pom.xml] file is as follows:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

     <!-- the parent project provides the shared versions and configuration -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
        <artifactId>impots-v6</artifactId>
        <version>6.0</version>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>impots-ui-mysql</artifactId>

    <dependencies>
         <!-- the new layer [dao] (and, by transitivity, the driver JDBC for MySQL) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-dao-mysql</artifactId>
        </dependency>
         <!-- the [metier] and [ui] layers from version 5, unchanged -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-metier</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-ui</artifactId>
        </dependency>
         <!-- the Spring dependency injection container -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
             <!-- `mvn exec:java` executes the main class -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>impots.ui.mysql.Main</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
  • Lines 18–21: the new layer [dao]. By transitivity, the JDBC driver for MySQL—a scope dependency of [runtime] in this module—is part of the application’s libraries;
  • Lines 23–30: the [metier] and [ui] layers from version 5. The [impots-ui] module contains the main program for version 5, but we only use its public class [Dialogue];
  • lines 32–35: Spring’s dependency injection container, as in version 5;
  • lines 41–47: the class executed by [mvn exec:java].

The configuration file [impots.properties] is as follows:

# application configuration [Impots], version 6: the [dao] layer reads a database
dao.implementation=MySqlImpot
dao.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbimpots
dao.utilisateur=admimpots
dao.motdepasse=mdpimpots
dao.requete=select limite, coeffr, coeffn from tranches order by id
  • line 2: the implementation of the [dao] layer;
  • Lines 3–5: the URL and JDBC from the [dbimpots] database and the user identifiers [admimpots];
  • line 6: the query that returns the slices. Including it in the configuration allows you to use a different database—even one with tables or columns that have different names—without modifying the code.

The class [Main] is the one for version 5, with the exception of the record in layer [dao]:

package impots.ui.mysql;

import impots.dao.HardwiredImpot;
import impots.dao.IImpotDao;
import impots.dao.MySqlImpot;
import impots.entites.ImpotException;
import impots.metier.IImpotMetier;
import impots.metier.ImpotMetier;
import impots.ui.Dialogue;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.Reader;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Properties;
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext;

// the [Impots] application, version 6: the [dao] layer reads tax brackets from a database
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // the configuration file: impots.properties by default, or the one passed as an argument
        String fichierConfig = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "impots.properties";

         // integration of layers
        IImpotMetier metier;
        try {
             // reads the configuration from the current directory
            Properties config = new Properties();
            try (Reader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of(fichierConfig))) {
                config.load(reader);
            }
            String implementation = config.getProperty("dao.implementation", "MySqlImpot");
            String url = config.getProperty("dao.url");
            if (url == null) {
                throw new ImpotException("Le paramètre [dao.url] est absent de la configuration");
            }
            String utilisateur = config.getProperty("dao.utilisateur", "");
            String motDePasse = config.getProperty("dao.motdepasse", "");
            String requete = config.getProperty("dao.requete", MySqlImpot.REQUETE_PAR_DEFAUT);

             // the Spring container: layers are registered here
            GenericApplicationContext contexte = new GenericApplicationContext();
             // the layer [dao]: the implementation is selected by the configuration
            contexte.registerBean(IImpotDao.class, () -> switch (implementation) {
                case "MySqlImpot" -> new MySqlImpot(url, utilisateur, motDePasse, requete);
                case "HardwiredImpot" -> new HardwiredImpot();
                default -> throw new ImpotException(
                        "Implémentation [" + implementation + "] de la couche [dao] inconnue");
            });
             // the [metier] layer from version 5: the container will pass the [dao] layer to its constructor
            contexte.registerBean(ImpotMetier.class);

             // Container startup: it creates the [dao] layer, then the [metier] layer
            contexte.refresh();
            metier = contexte.getBean(IImpotMetier.class);
        } catch (IOException | RuntimeException e) {
             // Displays the error and terminates the program
            Dialogue.afficherErreur(e);
            System.exit(1);
            return;
        }

         // User interaction: the [ui] layer from version 5
        Dialogue.run(metier);
    }
}
  • line 1: the class is in a package specific to version 6, [impots.ui.mysql], to avoid confusion with the version 5 class [impots.ui.Main], which is also present in the classpath;
  • line 22: the configuration file, [impots.properties] by default, or the one passed as an argument;
  • lines 28–31: reading the properties file from the current directory;
  • lines 32–39: the parameters for the [dao] layer. The absence of URL is an error; the request has a default value;
  • lines 44–49: the [dao] layer is registered in the Spring container under the [IImpotDao] interface, with a [Supplier] that creates it according to the configuration: a [MySqlImpot] (line 45) or, for comparison, the “hard-coded” version from version 5 (line 46). The [FileImpot] and [JsonImpot] implementations from version 5 could be added in the same way: they are in the classpath;
  • line 51: the [metier] layer of version 5;
  • line 54: when the container starts, it creates the [dao] layer, and thus reads the database, followed by the [metier] layer;
  • lines 56–61: a configuration or database access error is displayed by the [afficherErreur] method from version 5, and the program terminates;
  • line 64: the Version 5 dialog box, unchanged.

To run the application, first install the Version 6 modules in the local repository (the [dao] layer must be available for the [impots-ui-mysql] module), then run the program from the [impots-ui-mysql] folder, which contains the configuration files:

> cd 10-jdbc/ImpotsV6
> mvn install
> cd impots-ui-mysql
> mvn -q exec:java

Running with the [impots.properties] file:

> mvn -q exec:java
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : o 2 60000
Impôt=4282 euros
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : o 3 60000
Impôt=2959 euros
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : n 0 60000
Impôt=11519 euros
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter :

The course reference values are as follows: 4,282 euros for a couple with two children, 2,959 euros for a couple with three children, and 11,519 euros for a single person without children, with an annual salary of 60,000 euros.

With the file [impots-base.properties], where URL refers to a base file [dbimpotsinconnue]:

docs.title: 10.11.6. Change the database
docs.text:
The [dao] layer ([MySqlImpot]) uses only the interfaces of JDBC: despite its name, it is not specific to MySQL (a name like [JdbcImpot] would be more appropriate). To use a PostgreSQL database (or SQL Server, or Oracle), simply:

  • create the slice table in a PostgreSQL database—for example, a table named [data] with columns [data1], [data2], [data3], to highlight the benefit of placing the query in the configuration;
  • to add to [pom.xml] of the [impots-ui-mysql] module the dependency of the JDBC driver on PostgreSQL, [org.postgresql:postgresql] (or [com.microsoft.sqlserver:mssql-jdbc], [com.oracle.database.jdbc:ojdbc11]), with scope [runtime];
  • to write a configuration file similar to [impots.properties], such as the [impots-postgresql.properties] file from the module:
# the same application with a database PostgreSQL (org.postgresql driver: PostgreSQL to be added to pom.xml)
dao.implementation=MySqlImpot
dao.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/dbimpots
dao.utilisateur=admimpots
dao.motdepasse=mdpimpots
dao.requete=select data1, data2, data3 from data order by id

Only MySQL is installed on the machine used to write this course: we did not run this configuration. The layers [metier] and [ui], the class [MySqlImpot], and the program [Main] do not need to be modified: only the configuration and the driver in the classpath have changed. Note that the request from [MySqlImpot] has no parameters and uses only standard SQL functionality: this is what allows it to be executed by any SGBD. A more feature-rich [dao] layer (searches, updates) would quickly encounter the specific characteristics of each SQL as seen above: that’s where a ORM like Hibernate takes over.

docs.title: 10.12. Conclusion
docs.text:
This chapter has covered database access using JDBC:

  • JDBC is a set of interfaces ([Connection], [Statement], [PreparedStatement], [ResultSet], [DataSource]…), from the [java.sql] and [javax.sql] packages, implemented by a driver specific to each SGBD (MySQL Connector/J for MySQL), which [DriverManager] selects based on the URL and JDBC in the database;
  • a connection is opened as late as possible and closed as early as possible, using a **try-with-resources statement; a connection pool such as HikariCP, via the [DataSource] interface, makes this practice inexpensive;
  • [executeQuery] executes a [select] and returns a [ResultSet], which is traversed line by line using [next], reading the columns, numbered starting from 1, using the [getXxx] methods; [executeUpdate] executes a [insert], [update], or [delete] and returns the number of modified lines;
  • Errors are [SQLException], controlled exceptions, which return an error code specific to the SGBD and a standardized SQLSTATE code;
  • external values are always passed via the parameters of a [PreparedStatement] and are never concatenated with the query text, which protects against SQL injection;
  • transactions ([setAutoCommit(false)], [commit], [rollback], savepoints) ensure that a sequence of SQL commands is atomic;
  • JDBC is blocking: Java 21 virtual threads allow serving many users with standard JDBC code, within the limits of the pool size; batches ([addBatch], [executeBatch]) reduce the number of exchanges with the server;
  • offline mode ([CachedRowSet]) exists, but working with in-memory objects is now the domain of ORM.

Version 6 of the [Impots] application demonstrated that, thanks to the layered architecture, switching from a file to a database requires only writing a new [dao] layer and modifying the configuration. The next chapter will create a seventh version of this layer using Hibernate, which generates the SQL commands itself.

To learn more:

  • Oracle’s JDBC tutorial: JDBC Database Access (written for Java 8, but API has hardly changed since then);
  • the MySQL Connector/J documentation: MySQL Connector/J Developer Guide;
  • the documentation for HikariCP: HikariCP;
  • The SQL injection, explained by the OWASP: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: 15.1. SGBD and MySQL with Laragon
docs.text: Chapters 10 and 11 of this document use SGBD and MySQL 8. The easiest way to install it on Windows is to install Laragon, a portable development environment that includes MySQL, the graphical client HeidiSQL, a configured terminal, Apache, and PHP. The author also uses it for his courses PHP.

docs.title: 15.1.1. Installation
docs.text:
Laragon can be downloaded from https://laragon.org. The installation is standard; you can use the suggested installation folder ([C:\laragon]). Laragon provides MySQL 8 (the exact version depends on the Laragon version), with a [root] administrator account that has no password and a server listening on port 3306 on the local machine. This is the configuration assumed by the examples in the document, where the URL and JDBC are in the form:

jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles

with the username [root] and an empty password. If MySQL was installed differently, with a password for [root], you must update the examples accordingly ([.properties] files or constants at the top of the programs).

For a system without Laragon, you can also install MySQL Community Server from https://dev.mysql.com/downloads/mysql/, or its open-source derivative, MariaDB. However, the examples have only been tested with MySQL 8: the scripts in Chapter 10 use a collation specific to MySQL 8 ([utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci]), and with MariaDB, it would need to be adapted, as would the driver JDBC (MariaDB provides its own).

docs.title: 15.1.2. Starting and Stopping MySQL
docs.text:
The Laragon main window includes a “Start All” button that starts the servers (Apache and MySQL) and a “Stop” button that stops them. MySQL is not a Windows service that runs at system startup: it only runs when started from Laragon, which prevents it from consuming resources when not in use. The Laragon menu (right-click in the window) also allows you to start only MySQL and to choose its version.

When MySQL is not running, the programs in Chapters 10 and 11 fail with an exception from the JDBC driver indicating that no connection could be established ([CommunicationsException]: “Communications link failure”): this is the first thing to check in case of an error.

docs.title: 15.1.3. The command-line client
docs.text:
The Terminal button in Laragon opens a terminal where Laragon commands are available, including the command-line client MySQL ([mysql]). To connect to the server, use:

> mysql -u root

then enter commands ending with a semicolon ([show databases;], [use dbarticles;], [select * from articles;]) and [exit] to exit. The client can also run a script SQL, which is what Chapter 10 does to create its databases:

> cd java-oct-2026\10-jdbc\sql
> mysql -u root < dbarticles.sql
> mysql -u root < dbimpots.sql

The scripts completely recreate their database each time they are run: you can rerun them to restore the data to its initial state after testing.

docs.title: 15.1.4. The HeidiSQL graphical client
docs.text:
The Laragon Database button launches the graphical client HeidiSQL. Upon first launch, HeidiSQL offers a connection session that is already configured for the Laragon server MySQL (host [127.0.0.1], user [root], blank password, port 3306); simply open it. You will see:

  • on the left, the tree view of the server’s databases and their tables;
  • on the right, tabs showing a table’s structure, its data (which can be edited directly), and a field for entering SQL queries (the “Query” tab), which are executed by [F9].

To create a database using a script from Chapter 10, open the script (via the “File” menu, using the command to load a file: SQL) in a query tab, then execute it ([F9]). You can also create a database, a user, and user permissions using the menus in HeidiSQL (right-click on the connection / “Create New” / "Database"; "Tools" menu / "User Manager"), but the SQL scripts have the advantage of being reproducible and able to be rerun.

The IDE scripts can also connect to a database: IntelliJ and IDEA via their “Database” window, VS Code via an extension such as “SQLTools” or “MySQL.”

docs.title: 15.1.5. Databases Used in This Document
docs.text:
Chapters 10 and 11 use the following databases, all located on the local MySQL server:

DatabaseChapterCreation[dbarticles]10Script [10-jdbc/sql/dbarticles.sql]: Table [articles] from the examples JDBC[dbimpots]10Script [10-jdbc/sql/dbimpots.sql]: Table [tranches] from version 6 of the application [Impots] and user [admimpots][hbpremier], [hbarticles], [hbboutique], [hbclients], [hbconcurrence]11created by the programs themselves (option [createDatabaseIfNotExist=true] of URL and JDBC; tables created by Hibernate or by versioned scripts)[hbimpots]11Created and populated by the [CreationBase] program in version 7 of the [Impots] application

docs.title: 9. Asynchronous Programming
docs.text:
The previous chapter introduced threads: we can execute multiple pieces of code “at the same time,” synchronize them, and assign tasks to a thread pool via an executor ([ExecutorService]). This chapter addresses a related but distinct issue: how to write a program that waits a lot (for the disk, the network, or a database) without tying up threads during these waits.

Java does not have language keywords for this (other languages, such as C# or JavaScript, have the keywords [async] and [await]). It offers two solutions, which complement each other and are both presented in this chapter:

  • the [CompletableFuture<T>] class (Java 8, since enhanced) represents an ongoing operation whose subsequent steps are composed using callback methods: “when the result is ready, do this, then that” ([thenApply], [thenCompose], [thenCombine], [allOf]…). No thread waits: it is the completion of the operation that triggers the next step;
  • virtual threads ( Java 21) allow you to write blocking, sequential code that reads from top to bottom: when a virtual thread waits for input/output, the JVM detaches it from the system thread that was executing it (its “carrier thread”) and frees that thread for another virtual thread. This makes it possible to have hundreds of thousands of virtual threads for just a few system threads. This is Java’s modern solution to the problem that other languages solve with [async] / [await].

These tools are everywhere today: the following chapters will explore them to access databases, write TCP servers that serve each client via a virtual thread, web clients using [java.net.http.HttpClient], and web services using Spring Boot.

All the examples in this chapter are compact source files ([Async01.java], [Async02.java]…) that are run using [java AsyncNN.java] in the [09-async] folder. Many of them measure execution times using [System.nanoTime()]: the milliseconds displayed vary from one run to another and from one machine to another (the examples were run on a dual-processor machine). It’s the orders of magnitude that matter: 1 second or 10 seconds, 300 ms or 0 ms.

docs.title: 9.1.1. Operations that wait
docs.text:
A program performs two types of work:

  • computational tasks, which occupy the processor: sorting a list, calculating a tax, analyzing a text;
  • input/output (I/O), which essentially consists of waiting for a peripheral device: reading a file from disk, sending a request to a web server and waiting for its response, executing a SQL query on a database server.

The orders of magnitude are very different. A processor executes a few billion instructions per second. A read operation on a disk (SSD) takes on the order of one-tenth of a millisecond; a round trip over a local network takes a fraction of a millisecond; a round trip to a server located on the other side of the country takes a few tens of milliseconds; and a somewhat complex SQL request can sometimes take several seconds. During these waits, the processor could have executed millions of instructions.

When a program reads a line over a network connection using a blocking method, the thread performing this read is blocked: it does nothing, but it still exists. A “classic” Java thread—now referred to as a “platform thread”—is an operating system thread: it occupies memory (its stack, on the order of a megabyte), it is recognized by the system, and, most importantly, it is no longer available to do anything else. This isn’t a problem in a small console program that does one thing at a time. It becomes much more of an issue in two situations:

  • in a server: each client served by a blocked thread ties up that thread. If the server’s thread pool has N threads and all N threads are performing a blocking operation, there are no threads left available for a new client. A modern server handles thousands of simultaneous requests: this is possible because its waiting operations do not tie up system threads;
  • in a graphical user interface: a single thread—the UI thread (Swing’s “Event Dispatch Thread,” the “JavaFX Application Thread”)—handles clicks and redraws windows. If it is blocked by a download, the window freezes.

Asynchrony involves initiating the I/O operation, freeing up the system thread while it is in progress (the hardware and operating system do not need it to transfer data), and then resuming work once the operation is complete, possibly on another system thread:

  • In [1], the platform thread T1 initiates the I/O and remains blocked until it finishes;
  • in [2], the virtual thread V1 initiates the I/O; JVM detaches it from its parent thread P1, which can then immediately execute other virtual threads. When the I/O completes, JVM reattaches V1 to a free carrier thread, P2 (which could also be P1), and V1 continues its execution immediately after the blocking instruction, as if nothing had happened.

The program [Async01.java] measures the difference over 100 operations, each of which waits for one second (the wait simulates I/O). It uses instructions that we will explain later in this chapter ([Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor], [CompletableFuture]): here, we are primarily interested in the results.

// Why asynchrony: 100 operations, each waiting one second
// (a wait simulates I/O: disk read, network request, SQL request…)
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;

final int nbOperations = 100;
long debut;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    IO.println(nbOperations + " opérations d'une seconde, "
            + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + " processeurs");

     // 1 - one platform thread per operation; each thread is blocked during the wait
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++) {
        threads.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> attendre(1000)));
    }
    afficher("1 - un thread de plate-forme par opération", threadsDeLaJvm());
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
    afficher("    fin", -1);

     // 2 - operations are assigned to a pool of 10 threads, but they block the pool
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)) {
        for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++) {
            pool.submit(() -> attendre(1000));
        }
        afficher("2 - pool de 10 threads, attentes bloquantes", threadsDeLaJvm());
    } // `close()` waits for all operations to complete
    afficher("    fin", -1);

     // 3 - one virtual thread per operation: it releases its host thread while waiting
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++) {
            executeur.submit(() -> attendre(1000));
        }
        afficher("3 - un thread virtuel par opération", threadsDeLaJvm());
    }
    afficher("    fin", -1);

     // 4 - Asynchronous waits: no thread waits; a timer completes each operation
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    var operations = new CompletableFuture<?>[nbOperations];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++) {
        operations[i] = new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, 1000, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    }
    afficher("4 - attentes asynchrones (CompletableFuture)", threadsDeLaJvm());
    CompletableFuture.allOf(operations).join();
    afficher("    fin", -1);
}

// a blocking wait of [ms] milliseconds
void attendre(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// number of platform threads for JVM, half a second after operations begin
int threadsDeLaJvm() {
    long ecoule = (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000;
    if (ecoule < 500) {
        attendre(500 - ecoule);
    }
    return ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().getThreadCount();
}

// displays the elapsed time and, if provided (>= 0), the number of threads
void afficher(String message, int nbThreads) {
    String infoThreads = nbThreads < 0 ? "" : String.format(", %3d threads dans la JVM", nbThreads);
    long ecoule = (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000;
    IO.println(String.format("%-44s : %5d ms%s", message, ecoule, infoThreads));
}

Results:

> java Async01.java
100 opérations d'une seconde, 2 processeurs
1 - un thread de plate-forme par opération   :   534 ms, 106 threads dans la JVM
    fin                                      :  1061 ms
2 - pool de 10 threads, attentes bloquantes  :   501 ms,  16 threads dans la JVM
    fin                                      : 10021 ms
3 - un thread virtuel par opération          :   501 ms,  10 threads dans la JVM
    fin                                      :  1091 ms
4 - attentes asynchrones (CompletableFuture) :   500 ms,  11 threads dans la JVM
    fin                                      :  1003 ms

Comments:

  • Lines 12–22: the simplest solution—one platform thread per operation. [Thread.ofPlatform().start(tâche)] (Java 21) creates and starts a thread, just like [new Thread(tâche).start()]. Each thread executes [Thread.sleep(1000)]: it is blocked for one second. The 100 waits occur simultaneously, and the entire process takes exactly one second (line 4 of the results), but at the cost of 100 additional system threads: JVM has 106 of them (line 3). With 10,000 operations, 10,000 system threads would be required;
  • Lines 24–32: The operations are assigned to a pool of 10 threads ([Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)]), a reasonable size for computations. But here, these threads aren’t computing—they’re idle. The operations wait for a free thread, in batches of 10, and the whole process takes… ten seconds (line 6). This is known as “thread pool starvation,” the most common flaw in servers that mix thread pools with blocking I/O. The method [close()] of an executor (Java 19), called upon exit from *[try]*, rejects new tasks and waits for the ones that have been submitted to finish;
  • Lines 34–42: One virtual thread per operation. [Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()] (Java 21) returns an executor that creates a new virtual thread for each submitted task. The task code is the same as in Step 1: a blocking [Thread.sleep(1000)]. However, a blocked virtual thread does not tie up a system thread: the JVM detaches it from its carrier thread. The 100 waits last a total of one second (line 8), and the JVM counts only 10 system threads (line 7): its service threads, and the two carrier threads—one per processor—that executed the 100 virtual threads. The virtual threads are not included in this count: they are objects of JVM, not system threads;
  • lines 44–52: the same wait with no threads waiting. [new CompletableFuture<Void>()] creates a “pending” operation, and [completeOnTimeout(valeur, délai, unité)] (Java 9) requests that it be completed with the specified value once the timeout expires. A single timer in JVM manages the 100 timeouts. [CompletableFuture.allOf(...)] returns an operation that completes when all others have finished, and [join()] waits for it to finish. The entire process takes one second (line 10), with only one additional thread compared to step 3—the timer thread (line 9);
  • lines 55–62: [Thread.sleep] can throw the controlled exception [InterruptedException] if the thread is interrupted while sleeping (we’ll discuss this further in the section on cancellation); the method [attendre] intercepts it so that the lambdas on lines 16, 28, and 38 do not have to handle it;
  • Lines 64–71: [ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().getThreadCount()] returns the number of live platform threads for JVM. The class [ManagementFactory] belongs to the module [java.management]: a compact source file automatically imports only the module [java.base], hence the import on line 3.

Let’s remember the lesson: to wait, you must not block any system threads. Asynchrony doesn’t make I/O faster; it allows you to handle a large number of I/O operations simultaneously using few system threads, while keeping the threads the application needs available. Java offers two approaches for this: creating [CompletableFuture] (Step 4), or writing ordinary blocking code executed by virtual threads (Step 3).

docs.title: 9.1.2. Several Successive Models
docs.text:
Java has offered several ways to write code that waits without blocking. The older ones are still found in existing code, so it’s useful to recognize them.

PatternIntroductionPrinciple[Future] and RuntimesJava 5 (2004)[ExecutorService.submit] assigns a task to a thread pool and returns a [Future<T>], which represents the upcoming result. But the only way to obtain this result is to wait, blocking, with [get()].Callback methods of NIO.2Java 7 (2011)Asynchronous channels ([AsynchronousSocketChannel], [AsynchronousFileChannel]) initiate an operation and receive a callback object ([CompletionHandler]) whose method [completed] or [failed] is called by a thread from a pool once the operation is complete.[CompletableFuture]Java 8 (2014)a [Future] that you can terminate yourself and whose sequence is composed of callback methods ([thenApply], [thenCompose], [exceptionally]…); reactive streams [java.util.concurrent.Flow] (Java 9) are an extension of this for sequences of values. Reactive libraries (Project Reactor, used by Spring WebFlux, RxJava) are based on the same concepts.virtual threadsJava 21 (2023)of ordinary blocking code, executed by virtual threads: JVM frees the system thread during waits. This is the recommended model today for new applications.structured concurrencyPreview of Java 21 through Java 25[StructuredTaskScope] organizes a group of subtasks executed by virtual threads as a single block of code, with shared error handling and cancellation (see the end of the chapter).

Callback methods have a drawback: the code is fragmented. What naturally reads as “connect, then read, then display” becomes a method that initiates the connection, a callback method that initiates the read operation, and another callback method that displays the result; variables must be shared among these methods, exceptions are caught at different locations, and a simple loop (“read as long as there is data”) becomes a callback method that recursively calls itself. [CompletableFuture] makes this fragmentation more readable by chaining the steps together; virtual threads make it disappear: asynchronous code takes the form of synchronous code, because it is synchronous code.

The program [Async02.java] implements the same client, TCP, using two extreme approaches: first, using the callback methods of NIO.2, and then using blocking code executed by a virtual thread. It also contains a small server, run by a thread, that responds to two clients (network programming will be covered in detail in Chapter 12; for now, it suffices to know that a client connects to the server and reads the message the server sends it).

// the same client, TCP, written using callback methods (NIO.2, Java 7), then with a virtual thread (Java 21)
final int port = 27500;
final InetAddress local = InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress();
final ByteBuffer tampon = ByteBuffer.allocate(1024);
final CountDownLatch fin = new CountDownLatch(1);

void main() throws IOException, InterruptedException {
     // a minimal server, run by a single thread: it serves two clients and then stops
    var ecoute = new ServerSocket(port, 10, local);
    Thread serveur = Thread.ofPlatform().name("serveur").start(() -> {
        try (ecoute) {
            for (int i = 1; i <= 2; i++) {
                try (Socket service = ecoute.accept()) {
                     // the server takes its time to respond
                    Thread.sleep(500);
                    byte[] message = ("Bonjour client n° " + i).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
                    service.getOutputStream().write(message);
                }
            }
        } catch (IOException | InterruptedException e) {
            afficher("serveur : " + e);
        }
    });
    afficher("début du programme");

     // 1 - the “callback methods” style: AsynchronousSocketChannel and CompletionHandler
    var client = AsynchronousSocketChannel.open();
     // The connection is initiated by specifying the object to be called back once the connection is established
    client.connect(new InetSocketAddress(local, port), client, new Connecte());
    afficher("rappels : connexion lancée, le programme continue");
     // The main thread has nothing left to do: it waits for the signal from the last callback method
    fin.await();

     // 2 - The blocking style, executed by a virtual thread: the code is read from top to bottom
    Thread virtuel = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
        try (var client2 = new Socket(local, port)) {
            afficher("thread virtuel : connecté, lecture lancée");
            byte[] octets = new byte[1024];
            int nbOctets = client2.getInputStream().read(octets);
            String message = new String(octets, 0, nbOctets, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            afficher("thread virtuel : reçu [" + message + "]");
        } catch (IOException e) {
            afficher("thread virtuel : " + e);
        }
    });
    virtuel.join();
    serveur.join();
}

// Callback method #1: the connection is established (or has failed)
class Connecte implements CompletionHandler<Void, AsynchronousSocketChannel> {
    @Override
    public void completed(Void rien, AsynchronousSocketChannel canal) {
        afficher("rappels : connecté, lecture lancée");
         // We start reading the server’s response using another callback object
        canal.read(tampon, canal, new Recu());
    }

    @Override
    public void failed(Throwable e, AsynchronousSocketChannel canal) {
        afficher("rappels : échec de la connexion : " + e);
        fin.countDown();
    }
}

// Callback method #2: data has arrived
class Recu implements CompletionHandler<Integer, AsynchronousSocketChannel> {
    @Override
    public void completed(Integer nbOctets, AsynchronousSocketChannel canal) {
        afficher("rappels : reçu [" + new String(tampon.array(), 0, nbOctets, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) + "]");
        try {
            canal.close();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            afficher("rappels : " + e);
        }
         // notifies the main thread
        fin.countDown();
    }

    @Override
    public void failed(Throwable e, AsynchronousSocketChannel canal) {
        afficher("rappels : échec de la lecture : " + e);
        fin.countDown();
    }
}

// display prefixed by the thread executing it
// (name of a platform thread, description of a virtual thread)
void afficher(String message) {
    Thread thread = Thread.currentThread();
    IO.println("[" + (thread.isVirtual() ? thread.toString() : thread.getName()) + "] " + message);
}

Results:

> java Async02.java
[main] début du programme
[main] rappels : connexion lancée, le programme continue
[InnocuousThread-4] rappels : connecté, lecture lancée
[InnocuousThread-2] rappels : reçu [Bonjour client n° 1]
[VirtualThread[#28]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1] virtual thread: connected, read initiated
[VirtualThread[#28]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2] virtual thread: received [Bonjour client n° 2]

Comments:

  • Lines 8–23: the server. It listens on port 27500 of the local machine ([InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()], i.e., 127.0.0.1), accepts two connections one after the other, and sends each client a welcome message after half a second. It is executed by a platform thread named [serveur]. The form [try (ecoute)] (Java 9) will close the [ServerSocket] declared on line 9 at the end of the block;
  • lines 26–32: the client writes using callback methods:
    • line 27: a *[AsynchronousSocketChannel]* is a TCP channel whose operations are asynchronous;
    • line 29: [connect] initiates the connection and immediately returns control (line 3 of the results). Its last two parameters are an arbitrary object that the callback method will receive (here, the channel itself) and the callback object, of type [Connecte];
    • line 32: the main thread has nothing left to do. To ensure the program does not terminate before the exchange is complete, it waits for a signal from the last callback method: a [CountDownLatch] initialized to 1 (line 5), whose [await] method blocks the calling thread until another thread calls its [countDown] method;
  • lines 50–64: the connection’s callback object implements the [CompletionHandler<V, A>] interface, where [V] is the result type of the operation ([Void] for a connection) and [A] is the type of the passed object. Its method [completed] is called if the operation succeeds, and its method [failed] is called if it fails. Once connected, reading is initiated with [read] by specifying a second callback object of type [Recu] (line 56);
  • lines 66–85: the read callback object receives the number of bytes read, displays the message, closes the channel, and releases the main thread. The classes [Connecte] and [Recu] are internal classes of the implicit class of the compact file: they have access to its fields [tampon] and [fin] and to its method [afficher];
  • the results show that the callback methods are executed by threads other than the main thread (threads from the JVM pool dedicated to asynchronous channels, named [InnocuousThread-N]);
  • lines 34–46: the same client, written using a standard [Socket] and blocking operations ([new Socket(...)] connects, [read] waits for data), executed by a virtual thread created by [Thread.ofVirtual().start(tâche)] (Java 21). The code reads from top to bottom like synchronous code; the variables are ordinary local variables; errors are handled by a single [try / catch]; there are no callback methods or signals to manage;
  • lines 87–92: Each display is prefixed with the thread that executes it. For a virtual thread, [toString()] returns a description in the form [VirtualThread[#28]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]: the virtual thread number, its state, and its current host thread. Lines 6 and 7 of the results show the same virtual thread No. 28, carried first by [worker-1] and then by [worker-2]: while waiting for the server’s response, it was detached from its first carrier and then reattached to another.

It is not necessary to retain the [CompletionHandler] interface. If you must use a API that only offers this model, convert it to [CompletableFuture] (we’ll do this in [Async17.java]), or use its blocking version on a virtual thread.

docs.title: 9.2. Upcoming tasks: Future and CompletableFuture
docs.text:
A [Future<T>] (interface of the [java.util.concurrent] package, Java 5) is an object that represents the result—of type [T]—of an ongoing or completed operation. We encountered it in the previous chapter: this is what the [submit] method of an executor returns. You can query it (has it finished? was it successful?), cancel it ([cancel]), and wait for its result ([get]), but nothing else: the only way to use the result is to block a thread until it is available.

The [CompletableFuture<T>] class (Java 8) implements [Future<T>] and adds two essential capabilities:

  • you can terminate it yourself, with a result ([complete]) or an exception ([completeExceptionally]);
  • you can attach a follow-up operation to it—a function that will be executed when the result is available ([thenApply], [thenAccept], [thenCompose]…), which produces a new [CompletableFuture]. In this way, chains of operations are constructed without any threads having to wait. These methods are declared by the [CompletionStage<T>] interface, which [CompletableFuture] also implements.

A [CompletableFuture] is not a thread. It may represent a process executed by a thread of an executor (as is the case with those created by [supplyAsync]), but many are not executed by any thread: the one in step 4 of [Async01.java] is simply “completed” by a timer after one second, and the one returned by [HttpClient.sendAsync] is completed when the server’s response arrives. It is a promise of a result.

The program [Async03.java] demonstrates the main ways to create, query, and wait for a [CompletableFuture]:

// CompletableFuture: creation, waiting, status, result, continuation
void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // 1 - supplyAsync assigns a task to an executor and returns a CompletableFuture<T>
    CompletableFuture<Long> f1 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
         // a calculation lasting a few tenths of a second
        long somme = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= 200_000_000; i++) {
            somme += i % 7;
        }
        return somme;
    });
    IO.println("f1 lancé, état : " + f1.state());
     // join() waits for the processing to finish, blocking the current thread, and returns its result
    long resultat = f1.join();
    IO.println("f1 terminé, état : " + f1.state() + ", résultat : " + resultat);

     // 2 - a CompletableFuture terminated by a timer after 300 ms, without occupying a thread
    CompletableFuture<Void> f2 = new CompletableFuture<Void>()
            .completeOnTimeout(null, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    IO.println("f2 lancé, état : " + f2.state());
    f2.join();
    IO.println("f2 terminé, état : " + f2.state());

     // 3 - CompletableFuture processes that have already completed, either successfully or with an error
    CompletableFuture<Integer> f3 = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(42);
    CompletableFuture<Integer> f4 = CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new IllegalStateException("panne"));
    IO.println("f3 : état " + f3.state() + ", résultat " + f3.resultNow()
            + " ; f4 : état " + f4.state() + ", exception " + f4.exceptionNow());

     // 4 - a failed operation: `join()` launches a `CompletionException` that wraps its exception
    CompletableFuture<Integer> f5 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Integer.parseInt("abc"));
    try {
        f5.join();
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        IO.println("f5 : état " + f5.state() + ", join() lance " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                + " contenant " + e.getCause());
    }

     // 5 - get(), inherited from the Future interface, wraps the exception in a ExecutionException
    try {
        f5.get();
    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
        IO.println("f5 : get() lance " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                + " contenant " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
    }

     // 6 - a continuation: what to do when the CompletableFuture is complete
    CompletableFuture<Integer> f6 = f2.thenApply(rien -> 2 * 21);
    CompletableFuture<Void> f7 = f6.thenAccept(valeur -> IO.println("f7 : la continuation a reçu " + valeur));
    f7.join();

     // 7 - isDone, isCompletedExceptionally, isCancelled
    IO.println("f1 : isDone=" + f1.isDone() + ", f5 : isDone=" + f5.isDone()
            + ", isCompletedExceptionally=" + f5.isCompletedExceptionally()
            + ", isCancelled=" + f5.isCancelled());
}

Results:

> java Async03.java
f1 lancé, état : RUNNING
f1 terminé, état : SUCCESS, résultat : 599999998
f2 lancé, état : RUNNING
f2 terminé, état : SUCCESS
f3 : état SUCCESS, résultat 42 ; f4 : état FAILED, exception java.lang.IllegalStateException: panne
f5 : état FAILED, join() lance CompletionException contenant java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "abc"
f5 : get() lance ExecutionException contenant NumberFormatException
f7 : la continuation a reçu 42
f1 : isDone=true, f5 : isDone=true, isCompletedExceptionally=true, isCancelled=false

Comments:

  • Lines 4–11: [CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(fournisseur)] passes a function with no parameters ([Supplier<T>]) to an executor and immediately returns a [CompletableFuture<T>] representing its execution. The function returns a [long], so we obtain a [CompletableFuture<Long>]. Without an explicit executor, the shared pool for JVM and [ForkJoinPool.commonPool()] executes the function; we’ll see later how to choose the executor. For a processing operation with no result ([Runnable]), we use [runAsync], which returns a [CompletableFuture<Void>];
  • Line 12: The method [state()] (Java 19) returns the status of the operation: [RUNNING] (in progress), [SUCCESS] (completed successfully), [FAILED] (terminated due to an exception), or [CANCELLED] (canceled). These are the constants of the [Future.State] enumeration; the last three are final states: a completed operation no longer changes state;
  • line 14: [join()] waits for the operation to finish and returns its result. Like [Thread.join] in the previous chapter, this is a blocking wait: the current thread is suspended (the main thread in this case, which is not a problem for a small console program);
  • Lines 17–22: A [CompletableFuture] created as "in progress" by its creator and terminated by a timer after 300 ms ([completeOnTimeout], Java 9). No thread is occupied during this time: this is the asynchronous equivalent of [Thread.sleep(300)]. Its type is [CompletableFuture<Void>]: it does not return a result ([Void] is the class corresponding to [void]; its only value is [null]);
  • Lines 25–28: [completedFuture(42)] returns a previously completed [CompletableFuture] with a result of 42, and [failedFuture(exception)] (Java 9) returns a [CompletableFuture] that has already failed. They are used when a method needs to return a *[CompletableFuture] but already has the result (a cached value, for example) or already knows that it will fail. [resultNow()] and [exceptionNow()] (Java 19) return the result or exception of a completed operation without waiting (they throw a [IllegalStateException]* if the operation is not in the desired state);
  • lines 31–37: An operation whose function throws an exception ends in the [FAILED] state. The exception is stored in [CompletableFuture], and [join()] triggers a [CompletionException] (an unhandled exception) whose cause ([getCause()]) is the original exception, in this case a [NumberFormatException];
  • lines 40–45: [get()], the method inherited from the [Future] interface also waits in a blocking state, but wraps the exception in a [ExecutionException]—a checked exception—and may also throw a [InterruptedException], which is also a checked exception: The call is therefore placed within a *[try / catch], which intercepts the first one, and the *[main] method declares the second one (line 2). [join()] is more convenient in code that manipulates [CompletableFuture]; [get()] is the only one available for a simple [Future], and there is a version with a delay, [get(délai, unité)];
  • Lines 48–50: a continuation. [f2.thenApply(fonction)] returns a new [CompletableFuture], which will be completed with the result of the function applied to the result of [f2] once [f2] is completed. Here, the function ignores its parameter ([null]) and returns 42: this results in a [CompletableFuture<Integer>]. [thenAccept] attaches a function that consumes the result without producing one ([Consumer<T>]) and returns a [CompletableFuture<Void>]. If the original operation fails, the continuation is not executed and the failure propagates along the chain;
  • lines 53–55: the Boolean methods [isDone()] (completed, regardless of how), [isCompletedExceptionally()] (completed with an exception or canceled), and [isCancelled()] (canceled).

There are numerous methods for [CompletableFuture] (more than fifty). The following table lists the ones we will use:

MethodRole[supplyAsync(f)], [runAsync(r)]Execute a function (with or without a result) using an executor[completedFuture(v)], [failedFuture(e)]Create an operation that has already been completed, whether successfully or unsuccessfully[complete(v)], [completeExceptionally(e)]complete a task on one's own[thenApply(f)]transform the result: [T → U][thenAccept(c)], [thenRun(r)]Use the result, or perform an action after the operation[thenCompose(f)]Chain another asynchronous operation: [T → CompletableFuture<U>][thenCombine(autre, f)]Combine the results of two operations performed in parallel[allOf(...)], [anyOf(...)]Wait for all operations to complete, or for the first one to finish[exceptionally(f)], [handle(f)], [whenComplete(c)]Handle or observe a failure[orTimeout(...)], [completeOnTimeout(...)]limit the duration of an operation[join()], [get()]Wait for the result by blocking the current thread

The methods [thenXxx], [handle], and [whenComplete] also exist in the [thenXxxAsync] version: we’ll see the difference in the section “Which thread executes the rest of the code?”

docs.title: 9.3.1. First method: returning a CompletableFuture
docs.text:
In Java, an asynchronous method is simply a method that initiates an operation and immediately returns, without waiting, a [CompletableFuture] that represents it:

  • [CompletableFuture<Void>] if the operation returns no result;
  • [CompletableFuture<T>] if it returns a result of type [T].

The language does not impose any naming conventions. Java libraries often suffix these methods with [Async] ([sendAsync], [supplyAsync]), but this is not a rule: the return type is sufficient to identify them.

The program [Async04.java] makes coffee and counts sugar cubes:

// methods that produce a CompletableFuture: The steps are composed of thenRun and thenCompose
final long debut = System.nanoTime();

void main() {
    afficher("appel de preparerCafe");
    CompletableFuture<Void> preparation = preparerCafe();
    afficher("preparerCafe a rendu la main : le programme continue");
    afficher("appel de compterSucres");
    CompletableFuture<Integer> comptage = compterSucres(3);
    afficher("compterSucres a rendu la main");
     // We combine the two operations, then wait for the result of the combination
    int nbSucres = preparation.thenCombine(comptage, (rien, nombre) -> nombre).join();
    afficher("café prêt, avec " + nbSucres + " sucre(s)");
}

// an operation that returns no result: it returns a CompletableFuture<Void>
CompletableFuture<Void> preparerCafe() {
    afficher("  café : la machine chauffe");
     // The method describes the sequence of steps, then immediately returns control
    return delai(1000)
            .thenRun(() -> afficher("  café : la machine coule le café"))
            .thenCompose(rien -> delai(500))
            .thenRun(() -> afficher("  café : terminé"));
}

// an operation that returns an integer: it returns a CompletableFuture<Integer>
CompletableFuture<Integer> compterSucres(int nombre) {
     // a sequence of steps that begins with a CompletableFuture that has already been completed
    CompletableFuture<Void> etapes = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
    for (int i = 1; i <= nombre; i++) {
         // a lambda can only use a local variable that is effectively final
        int numero = i;
        etapes = etapes.thenCompose(rien -> delai(200))
                .thenRun(() -> afficher("  sucre n° " + numero));
    }
     // at the end of the sequence, the result: the number of sugars
    return etapes.thenApply(rien -> nombre);
}

// the asynchronous equivalent of Thread.sleep: a CompletableFuture that completes after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delai(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// display showing the elapsed time since the start
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async04.java
    3 ms : appel de preparerCafe
   12 ms :   café : la machine chauffe
   15 ms : preparerCafe a rendu la main : le programme continue
   16 ms : appel de compterSucres
   17 ms : compterSucres a rendu la main
  217 ms :   sucre n° 1
  417 ms :   sucre n° 2
  618 ms :   sucre n° 3
 1014 ms :   café : la machine coule le café
 1515 ms :   café : terminé
 1516 ms : café prêt, avec 3 sucre(s)

Comments:

  • Lines 40–43: The [delai] method is the asynchronous equivalent of [Thread.sleep]: it returns a [CompletableFuture<Void>] that will complete after the timeout, without occupying a thread. We will use it in many examples to simulate I/O;
  • Lines 17–24: an operation with no result. The method displays an initial message, then describes the sequence of steps and immediately returns the final [CompletableFuture]: this is why line 4 of the results appears right after line 3, rather than a second and a half later. The steps will be executed later, each one once the previous one is complete:
    • line 21: [thenRun(action)] performs an action when the previous operation is complete;
    • line 22: [thenCompose(fonction)] triggers another asynchronous operation: the function itself returns a [CompletableFuture] (in this case, a new 500-ms delay), and the [CompletableFuture] returned by [thenCompose] will not be completed until this second operation is finished. With [thenApply], we would have obtained a [CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Void>>], which would have completed as soon as the second timeout began: [thenCompose] is to [thenApply] as [flatMap] is to [map] in the API stream;
  • Lines 27–38: An operation that returns an integer. A loop cannot “wait” on every iteration: it builds the sequence of steps, with each iteration adding a delay and a display to the existing sequence, starting from a pre-computed [CompletableFuture] (line 29). The entire string is constructed in a few microseconds and then unfolds as the delays occur. The variable [numero] (line 32) is necessary because a lambda can only use a local variable that is effectively final, which [i] is not. Finally, [thenApply] transforms the string into a [CompletableFuture<Integer>], the result of which is the number of sugars;
  • Lines 6–10: The main program calls both methods. It retrieves two [CompletableFuture] values and continues execution. The two operations then proceed “simultaneously”: the sugars are counted (lines 7–9 of the results) while the machine warms up;
  • line 12: [preparation.thenCombine(comptage, fonction)] returns a completed [CompletableFuture] when both operations are finished, along with the result of the function applied to their two results: in this case, the number of sugar cubes is retained. [join()] waits for this result. The coffee is ready after 1.5 seconds—the duration of the longer of the two operations—and not after 2.1 seconds (1.5 + 3 × 0.2).

We can see the strengths and limitations of this approach. No thread waits: the steps are executed by the timer thread as the time intervals elapse. But the code no longer reads like a sequence of instructions: the [compterSucres] loop doesn’t do what a loop usually does (it constructs a string instead of executing iterations), and a simple [if] or [try / catch] in the middle of the steps requires dedicated methods. That’s the price you pay when the language doesn’t offer keywords like [await].

docs.title: 9.3.2. Second approach: blocking code on virtual threads
docs.text:
Virtual threads allow you to write the same methods as ordinary, blocking methods. The program [Async05.java] makes the same cup of coffee:

// the same example with virtual threads: ordinary, blocking methods that are read from top to bottom
final long debut = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
     // an executor that creates a virtual thread for each task assigned to it
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        afficher("lancement de preparerCafe");
        Future<?> preparation = executeur.submit(this::preparerCafe);
        afficher("preparerCafe est lancé : le programme continue");
        afficher("lancement de compterSucres");
        Future<Integer> comptage = executeur.submit(() -> compterSucres(3));
        afficher("compterSucres est lancé");
         // Now we wait for both results
        preparation.get();
        int nbSucres = comptage.get();
        afficher("café prêt, avec " + nbSucres + " sucre(s)");
    }
}

// an ordinary method that does not return a result
void preparerCafe() {
    afficher("  café : la machine chauffe");
     // a blocking wait: on a virtual thread, it releases the carrying thread
    dormir(1000);
    afficher("  café : la machine coule le café");
    dormir(500);
    afficher("  café : terminé");
}

// an ordinary method that returns an integer
int compterSucres(int nombre) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= nombre; i++) {
        dormir(200);
        afficher("  sucre n° " + i);
    }
    return nombre;
}

// Thread.sleep without a controlled exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
         // the thread's interrupt flag is reset before the exception is thrown
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("attente interrompue");
    }
}

// display showing the elapsed time since the start
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async05.java
    3 ms : lancement de preparerCafe
   17 ms :   café : la machine chauffe
   18 ms : preparerCafe est lancé : le programme continue
   18 ms : lancement de compterSucres
   19 ms : compterSucres est lancé
  221 ms :   sucre n° 1
  422 ms :   sucre n° 2
  623 ms :   sucre n° 3
 1020 ms :   café : la machine coule le café
 1521 ms :   café : terminé
 1522 ms : café prêt, avec 3 sucre(s)

Comments:

  • Lines 20–37: Both operations are regular methods: [preparerCafe] returns nothing ([void]), and [compterSucres] returns a [int]. The expectations are blocking [Thread.sleep] calls; the loop is a true loop. Nothing in these methods indicates that they will be executed concurrently: they could be called directly;
  • lines 39–48: the method [dormir] calls [Thread.sleep] and converts any [InterruptedException] (controlled exception) into a [CancellationException] (uncontrolled exception), after resetting the thread’s interrupt flag: this is the rule when intercepting a [InterruptedException] without propagating it (we’ll return to this in the section on cancellation);
  • line 6: an executor that creates a virtual thread for each task. It is declared in a [try] with a resource: its [close()] method will wait for all tasks to complete;
  • Lines 8 and 11: [submit] delegates each method to a new virtual thread and returns a [Future]. The method reference [this::preparerCafe] is a [Runnable] (the method returns nothing), resulting in a [Future<?>]; the lambda [() -> compterSucres(3)] is a [Callable<Integer>], resulting in a [Future<Integer>];
  • Lines 14–15: The main program waits for both results using [get()]. This is a blocking wait by the main thread, which has no impact here;
  • the results are the same as with [Async04.java]: 1.5 seconds total, with the sugar counted while the machine warms up. During the waits, no system threads are blocked: the two virtual threads are detached from their carrier threads.

With virtual threads, asynchrony is no longer a matter of code writing but of execution: we write blocking code, and it is the executor’s choice (virtual threads rather than a platform thread pool) that determines whether the waits immobilize system threads. This is why existing Java libraries (JDBC, files, sockets, [HttpClient.send]…), all written in a blocking manner, take advantage of virtual threads without modification.

docs.title: 9.3.3. What JVM Does
docs.text:
How can a virtual thread be interrupted in the middle of a loop, release its host thread, and then resume later at the same point, with the same local variable values, possibly on a different host thread? A virtual thread is a Java object ([java.lang.VirtualThread], a class derived from [Thread]) that has its own call stack. To execute it, JVM “mounts” it onto a carrier thread—a platform thread of a [ForkJoinPool] reserved for this purpose, which by default has as many threads as there are processors. When the virtual thread calls a blocking operation ([Thread.sleep], reading from a socket; [BlockingQueue.take], waiting for a lock…), the classes in JVM—rewritten for this purpose in Java 21—do not block the containing thread:

  • they register the operation with the system (a timer for a delay, the system’s I/O notification mechanism—[epoll] on Linux—for a socket);
  • they “unmount” the virtual thread: its call stack frames are copied to the heap as an object called a continuation, and the carrier thread is returned to [ForkJoinPool], which assigns it another virtual thread ready to execute;
  • when the operation completes, the virtual thread becomes ready again: it will be remounted onto the first available carrier thread, its stack frames will be recopied, and execution will resume immediately after the blocking call.

This is the principle behind callback methods (“call me back when the operation is complete”), but it is the JVM that breaks down the execution, saves the variables, and restores the context at the call stack level, without the source code showing any trace of it. Other languages entrust this task to the compiler, which transforms each [async] method into a “state machine”; Java entrusts it to the JVM, which allows it to handle all existing code in the same way.

There are two limitations to be aware of:

  • certain operations cannot detach the virtual thread; it therefore remains “pinned” to its host thread, which is blocked while waiting. This occurs during the execution of a native method, and during most file reads and writes (the system does not provide a notification for files that can be used by the JVM); for the latter, the [ForkJoinPool] compensates by temporarily creating an additional carrier thread. Up to Java 23, this was also the case for a virtual thread waiting inside a [synchronized] block; since Java 24, this is no longer the case;
  • a virtual thread does not speed up a computation: a virtual thread performing a computation occupies its host thread for the entire duration of the computation. Virtual threads are intended for programs that do a lot of waiting, not those that do a lot of computation (for the latter, thread pools and parallel streams from the previous chapter are available).

docs.title: 9.3.4. Which thread executes the next section?
docs.text:
The program [Async06.java] displays the thread that executes each piece of code:

// Which thread is executing the next step of a process?
void main() throws InterruptedException {
    afficher("début du programme, parallélisme du pool commun : " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism());

     // 1 - The continuation of a CompletableFuture that has already completed is executed immediately by the caller
    CompletableFuture.completedFuture(42).thenAccept(valeur -> afficher("1 - thenAccept, résultat connu"));

     // 2 - Otherwise, it is executed by the thread that terminates the CompletableFuture
    delai(100).thenRun(() -> afficher("2 - thenRun après un délai")).join();
    CompletableFuture<String> commande = new CompletableFuture<>();
    commande.thenAccept(texte -> afficher("2 - thenAccept après complete(\"" + texte + "\")"));
    Thread.ofPlatform().name("livreur").start(() -> commande.complete("livrée")).join();
