     // 3 - the variants xxxAsync delegate the continuation to an executor
    delai(100).thenRunAsync(() -> afficher("3 - thenRunAsync, exécuteur par défaut")).join();
    ThreadFactory fabrique = Thread.ofPlatform().name("pool-", 1).factory();
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, fabrique)) {
        delai(100).thenRunAsync(() -> afficher("3 - thenRunAsync, exécuteur choisi"), pool).join();
        CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> afficher("3 - runAsync, exécuteur choisi"), pool).join();
    }
    try (ExecutorService virtuels = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> afficher("3 - runAsync, threads virtuels"), virtuels).join();
    }

     // 4 - a virtual thread can switch to a different carrier thread after each wait
    Thread a = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> travailler("A"));
    Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> travailler("B"));
    a.join();
    b.join();
    afficher("fin du programme");
}

void travailler(String nom) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
        afficher("  " + nom + i + " : avant l'attente");
        dormir(100);
    }
}

// a CompletableFuture that completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delai(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// Thread.sleep without a controlled exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("attente interrompue");
    }
}

// display prefixed by the thread executing it
// (name of a platform thread, description of a virtual thread)
void afficher(String message) {
    Thread thread = Thread.currentThread();
    IO.println("[" + (thread.isVirtual() ? thread.toString() : thread.getName()) + "] " + message);
}

Results:

> java Async06.java
[main] début du programme, parallélisme du pool commun : 1
[main] 1 - thenAccept, résultat connu
[ForkJoinPool.commonPool-delayScheduler] 2 - thenRun après un délai
[livreur] 2 - thenAccept après complete("livrée")
[ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1] 3 - thenRunAsync, exécuteur par défaut
[pool-1] 3 - thenRunAsync, exécuteur choisi
[pool-2] 3 - runAsync, exécuteur choisi
[VirtualThread[#28]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1] 3 - runAsync, virtual threads
[VirtualThread[#31]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]   A1: before the wait
[VirtualThread[#32]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2]   B1: before the wait
[VirtualThread[#32]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2]   B2: before the wait
[VirtualThread[#31]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]   A2: before the wait
[VirtualThread[#31]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2]   A3: before the wait
[VirtualThread[#32]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]   B3: before the wait
[main] fin du programme

Comments:

  • line 3: the shared pool ([ForkJoinPool.commonPool()]), the default executor for [CompletableFuture], has a parallelism equal to the number of processors minus one, which is 1 on our 2-processor machine (line 2 of the results);
  • Line 6: The continuation of a [CompletableFuture] that has already finished is executed immediately by the thread that attached it: thread [main] (line 3);
  • lines 9–12: if the operation is not complete, the continuation will be executed by the thread that will complete it: the timeout timer thread for [delai(100)] (line 4), the thread [livreur] that calls [complete] for the command (line 5). Therefore, the thread that executes a non-asynchronous continuation is not chosen; this is irrelevant for a brief action, but a long or blocking continuation would immobilize that thread (the timer thread, for example, which handles all the timeouts for [CompletableFuture]);
  • lines 15–23: the [xxxAsync] variants ([thenRunAsync], [thenApplyAsync]…) delegate the continuation to an executor: without additional parameters, to the shared pool (line 6 of the results); with an executor as the last parameter, to that executor. This allows one to choose platform threads (lines 7–8: a pool of two threads whose names are determined by a thread factory, [ThreadFactory], constructed by [Thread.ofPlatform().name("pool-", 1).factory()]), or virtual threads (line 9). [supplyAsync] and [runAsync] also accept an executor;
  • Lines 26–38: Two virtual threads that display a message and then sleep, three times in a row. The results show that they do not remain attached to a single host thread: virtual thread No. 31 (A) starts at [worker-1] and ends at [worker-2], while No. 32 (B) does the opposite. While one is sleeping, its carrier thread is free for the other. Therefore, in a virtual thread, one must never assume that the code following a wait is executed by the same carrier thread as the code preceding it; but it is always the same virtual thread, and that is what matters to the program ([Thread.currentThread()] returns the virtual thread; its variables, [ThreadLocal], are preserved).

This method of performing multiple operations simultaneously without increasing the number of system threads is called concurrency. It differs from parallelism, which involves executing multiple calculations at the same time across multiple processors (as discussed in the previous chapter: thread pools, parallel streams). Asynchrony facilitates I/O concurrency; it does not make calculations faster.

The choice of executor is therefore important:

  • the shared pool is suitable for brief continuations and short computations; blocking operations should not be executed there, as this risks the starvation described with [Async01.java] (it has only one thread on our machine);
  • for a blocking operation (I/O, calls to JDBC or [Thread.sleep]), use a virtual thread executor: [CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(fournisseur, executeurVirtuel)];
  • for a graphical user interface, we pass an executor that has the continuation executed by the UI thread, which allows the graphical components to be updated: with Swing, [thenAcceptAsync(action, SwingUtilities::invokeLater)] (the method reference [SwingUtilities::invokeLater] is a valid [Executor], since [Executor] is a functional interface whose sole method takes a [Runnable]); along with JavaFX and [Platform::runLater].

docs.title: 9.3.5. The Main Program
docs.text:
In other languages, the main method of an asynchronous program must be declared in a specific way. In Java, there is no such requirement: the method [main] is executed by the platform thread [main], and it is up to that method to wait for the operations it has initiated—using [join()] or [get()]—to complete. This is the only place where a blocking wait on a [CompletableFuture] is normal. The program [Async07.java] performs an asynchronous countdown:

// the main program waits for the asynchronous operations to complete and sets the exit code
void main(String[] args) {
     // The number of seconds is passed as an argument
    if (args.length != 1 || !args[0].matches("\\d+")) {
        IO.println("syntaxe : java Async07.java nbSecondes");
         // the program’s exit code: 0 for success, any other value for an error
        System.exit(1);
    }
    CompletableFuture<Void> compteARebours = compterARebours(Integer.parseInt(args[0]));
    IO.println("compte à rebours lancé");
     // Without this wait, `main` would terminate immediately, and the program along with it
    compteARebours.join();
    IO.println("terminé");
}

// An asynchronous loop is written using recursion: each step triggers the next
CompletableFuture<Void> compterARebours(int nbSecondes) {
    if (nbSecondes == 0) {
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
    }
    IO.println("encore " + nbSecondes + " s");
    return delai(1000).thenCompose(rien -> compterARebours(nbSecondes - 1));
}

// a CompletableFuture completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delai(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

Results, first with and then without an argument:

> java Async07.java 3
encore 3 s
compte à rebours lancé
encore 2 s
encore 1 s
terminé

> java Async07.java
syntaxe : java Async07.java nbSecondes
> echo $?
1

Comments:

  • line 2: the [args] parameter of [main] receives the command-line arguments, which are placed after the filename: [java Async07.java 3];
  • Lines 4–8: If the argument is missing or is not a positive integer (regular expression [\d+]: one or more digits), the program terminates with [System.exit(1)]. The integer passed to [System.exit] is the program’s exit code (0 for success, any other value for an error), which can be checked by a script: [echo $?] on Linux (second result), [echo %ERRORLEVEL%] on Windows. A program whose [main] method terminates normally returns code 0;
  • lines 16–23: an asynchronous countdown. An asynchronous loop is naturally implemented using recursion: each step displays a message and then, using [thenCompose], introduces a one-second delay followed by the next step. There is no call stack: the recursive call is made via the continuation, one second later;
  • lines 9–12: the method [compterARebours] displays its first message and then returns control (lines 2–3 of the results); the main program waits for the operation to finish with [join()]. Without this wait, [main] would terminate immediately, and the program along with it: JVM stops when only daemon threads remain, and the timer and shared pool threads are daemons. The same applies to virtual threads, which are always daemons: a program must wait for the virtual threads it has launched to finish (using [join], [get], or the [close] method of their executor).

docs.title: 9.4.1. allOf and invokeAll
docs.text:
The coffee example demonstrated this: the moment an asynchronous operation is initiated and the moment it is awaited can be different. Writing [methode().join()] initiates the operation and awaits it immediately; writing [var f = methode();] and then later [f.join();] allows other operations to be launched in between. The program [Async08.java] compares the two approaches using operations that take one second:

// sequential and concurrent execution of one-second operations
long debut = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // 1 - sequentially: each operation is waited for before starting the next one
    int a = lireTemperature("Angers").join();
    int b = lireTemperature("Brest").join();
    int c = lireTemperature("Colmar").join();
    IO.println("en séquence : " + a + ", " + b + ", " + c + " en " + ecoule() + " ms");

     // 2 - concurrently: all three operations are started, then they are waited for
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    CompletableFuture<Integer> fa = lireTemperature("Angers");
    CompletableFuture<Integer> fb = lireTemperature("Brest");
    CompletableFuture<Integer> fc = lireTemperature("Colmar");
    CompletableFuture.allOf(fa, fb, fc).join();
    IO.println("en concurrence : " + fa.resultNow() + ", " + fb.resultNow() + ", " + fc.resultNow()
            + " en " + ecoule() + " ms");

     // 3 - allOf on a list of CompletableFuture, then the list of results
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    List<String> villes = List.of("Angers", "Brest", "Colmar", "Dijon", "Évry", "Foix");
    List<CompletableFuture<Integer>> lectures = villes.stream().map(this::lireTemperature).toList();
    List<Integer> temperatures = CompletableFuture.allOf(lectures.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new))
            .thenApply(rien -> lectures.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList())
            .join();
    IO.println(villes.size() + " villes : " + temperatures + " en " + ecoule() + " ms");

     // 4 - the same thing with virtual threads and a blocking method
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        List<Callable<Integer>> taches = villes.stream()
                .map(ville -> (Callable<Integer>) () -> lireTemperatureBloquant(ville))
                .toList();
         // invokeAll launches all tasks and returns their Futures when they are all complete
        List<Integer> resultats = executeur.invokeAll(taches).stream().map(Future::resultNow).toList();
        IO.println(villes.size() + " villes (threads virtuels) : " + resultats + " en " + ecoule() + " ms");
    }
}

// simulates querying a remote service that responds in one second
CompletableFuture<Integer> lireTemperature(String ville) {
     // a “temperature” derived from the city’s name
    return delai(1000).thenApply(rien -> 10 + ville.length());
}

// the same operation, written as a blocking operation
int lireTemperatureBloquant(String ville) throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    return 10 + ville.length();
}

// a CompletableFuture completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delai(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// milliseconds elapsed since [debut]
long ecoule() {
    return (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000;
}

Results:

> java Async08.java
en séquence : 16, 15, 16 en 3007 ms
en concurrence : 16, 15, 16 en 1000 ms
6 villes : [16, 15, 16, 15, 14, 14] en 1006 ms
6 villes (threads virtuels) : [16, 15, 16, 15, 14, 14] en 1013 ms

Comments:

  • lines 41–45: the simulated operation: a one-second delay, followed by a “temperature” derived from the length of the city name;
  • lines 6–8: Each operation is started and then waited for before starting the next one. The three operations are performed one after the other: 3 seconds (line 2 of the results). This is the correct approach when one operation requires the result of the previous one (in which case, one would instead write a chain of [thenCompose]);
  • lines 13–15: The three operations are started without waiting for each other. They run simultaneously;
  • line 16: [CompletableFuture.allOf(...)] returns a [CompletableFuture<Void>], which completes once all the operations passed to it are finished. We wait for it with [join()]: 1 second instead of 3 (line 3);
  • lines 17–18: The three operations are complete, so [resultNow()] returns their result immediately;
  • lines 22–27: the case of a list of operations. [allOf] waits for an array ([CompletableFuture<?>...]): the [toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)] method in the list creates it. [allOf] does not return the results: they are collected in a continuation by calling [join()] on each operation, which does not block since they have all completed. We obtain the list of results in the order of the operations (not in the order in which they completed). The expression [villes.stream().map(this::lireTemperature).toList()] calls the method for each city and thus produces six operations launched simultaneously; all six together take one second (line 4);
  • lines 29–38: the same thing with a blocking method (lines 47–51) executed by virtual threads. The method [invokeAll] of an executor receives a collection of [Callable<T>], launches them all, and returns the list of their [Future<T>] when they are all complete: This is the blocking equivalent of [allOf]*. The type cast [(Callable<Integer>)] on line 33 tells the compiler the type of the lambda, which it cannot infer on its own in a *[map]. The six operations together take one second (line 5).

docs.title: 9.4.2. anyOf
docs.text:
[CompletableFuture.anyOf(...)] returns a [CompletableFuture<Object>] that terminates as soon as one of the operations passed to it is completed, with the result (or exception) of that operation. The program [Async09.java] uses it in two ways:

// anyOf: Respond to the first completed operation
long debut = System.nanoTime();

void main() {
     // 1 - query three mirror servers and keep the first response
    List<CompletableFuture<String>> requetes = List.of(
            interroger("miroir-paris", 800),
            interroger("miroir-lyon", 300),
            interroger("miroir-lille", 600));
     // anyOf returns a CompletableFuture<Object> that ends like the first completed operation
    Object premiere = CompletableFuture.anyOf(requetes.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
    afficher("première réponse : " + premiere);
     // The other requests continue: we wait for them here to see their responses
    CompletableFuture.allOf(requetes.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
    afficher("toutes les réponses : " + requetes.stream().map(CompletableFuture::resultNow).toList());

     // 2 - a time-limited operation: we’re “racing” against a time limit
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    CompletableFuture<String> lente = interroger("serveur-lent", 2000);
    CompletableFuture<Object> course = CompletableFuture.anyOf(lente, delai(500));
    course.join();
    if (lente.isDone()) {
        afficher("réponse obtenue à temps : " + lente.join());
    } else {
        afficher("le serveur lent n'a pas répondu dans le délai de 500 ms");
    }
}

// simulates a server that responds after [duree] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<String> interroger(String serveur, int duree) {
    return delai(duree).thenApply(rien -> serveur + " (" + duree + " ms)");
}

// A CompletableFuture completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delai(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// displays the elapsed time since [debut]
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async09.java
  309 ms : première réponse : miroir-lyon (300 ms)
  806 ms : toutes les réponses : [miroir-paris (800 ms), miroir-lyon (300 ms), miroir-lille (600 ms)]
  500 ms : le serveur lent n'a pas répondu dans le délai de 500 ms

Comments:

  • lines 6–9: Three mirror servers are queried; they all hold the same information and respond at varying speeds. The three operations are stored in a list;
  • line 11: [anyOf] returns a [CompletableFuture<Object>], whose result is that of the first completed operation. Its type is [Object] because the operations passed to [anyOf] may have different result types: it would need to be cast to be used as a string. The first response arrives after 300 ms (line 2 of the results);
  • line 14: the other requests are not terminated by [anyOf]; they continue until they finish. Here, we wait for them to display all the responses (line 3);
  • lines 19–26: a common use of [anyOf]: limiting the duration of a wait by setting up a “race” between the operation and a timeout. If the operation is not finished when the race is over, the timeout has won: the operation took too long (line 4). [CompletableFuture] offers a more direct way to write this case, the [orTimeout] method, which is presented later.

docs.title: 9.4.3. Processing Results as They Come In
docs.text:
We often want to process the results of multiple operations as they complete, without waiting for the slowest one. With [CompletableFuture], this is straightforward: simply attach a continuation to each operation. For tasks submitted to an executor, the [ExecutorCompletionService] class (Java 5) returns the [Future] objects in the order in which the tasks complete. The program [Async10.java] processes five “files,” each of which takes between 100 and 900 ms to process, in both ways:

// Process the results in the order in which the operations complete
long debut = System.nanoTime();
final int[] durees = {900, 300, 700, 100, 500};

void main() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
     // 1 - with CompletableFuture: one continuation per operation, executed as soon as it finishes
    List<CompletableFuture<Void>> affichages = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < durees.length; i++) {
        affichages.add(traiter("fichier" + i + ".txt", durees[i]).thenAccept(this::afficher));
    }
    CompletableFuture.allOf(affichages.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
    afficher("1 - tous les fichiers ont été traités");

     // 2 - with virtual threads: a CompletionService delivers the Futures in the order they complete
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        CompletionService<String> service = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(executeur);
        for (int i = 0; i < durees.length; i++) {
            String fichier = "fichier" + i + ".txt";
            int duree = durees[i];
            service.submit(() -> traiterBloquant(fichier, duree));
        }
         // take() waits (blocking) for the next completed task
        for (int i = 0; i < durees.length; i++) {
            afficher(service.take().get());
        }
    }
    afficher("2 - tous les fichiers ont été traités");
}

// simulates the processing of a file that takes [duree] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<String> traiter(String fichier, int duree) {
    return new CompletableFuture<String>()
            .completeOnTimeout(fichier + " traité en " + duree + " ms", duree, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// the same processing, written as a blocking operation
String traiterBloquant(String fichier, int duree) throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.sleep(duree);
    return fichier + " traité en " + duree + " ms";
}

// display showing the elapsed time since [debut]
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async10.java
  107 ms : fichier3.txt traité en 100 ms
  318 ms : fichier1.txt traité en 300 ms
  508 ms : fichier4.txt traité en 500 ms
  707 ms : fichier2.txt traité en 700 ms
  906 ms : fichier0.txt traité en 900 ms
  907 ms : 1 - tous les fichiers ont été traités
  115 ms : fichier3.txt traité en 100 ms
  314 ms : fichier1.txt traité en 300 ms
  514 ms : fichier4.txt traité en 500 ms
  714 ms : fichier2.txt traité en 700 ms
  914 ms : fichier0.txt traité en 900 ms
  915 ms : 2 - tous les fichiers ont été traités

Comments:

  • Lines 7–11: Each processing task receives its own continuation, [thenAccept(this::afficher)], which is executed as soon as it finishes: file 3 (100 ms) is displayed first, file 0 (900 ms) last (lines 2–6 of the results). The method [traiter] (lines 31–35) returns a completed [CompletableFuture<String>] after the specified duration with the desired message ([completeOnTimeout] directly receives the result value). The list of continuations is used to wait for all displays to finish with [allOf];
  • lines 16–27: a [CompletionService<T>] wraps an executor (in this case, a virtual thread executor). Its method [submit] launches a task; its method [take()] waits, blocking, for the next completed task and returns its [Future], whose result is immediately returned by [get()]. The loop in lines 24–26 therefore processes the files in the order in which they are completed (lines 8–12);
  • in both cases, the entire process takes 900 ms—the duration of the longest processing step—and each result is displayed as soon as possible.

docs.title: 9.5.1. Propagation, exceptionally, handle, whenComplete
docs.text:
An exception thrown by an asynchronous operation is not thrown back to the code that initiated the operation: it is stored in [CompletableFuture], which transitions to the [FAILED] state. It then propagates along the continuation chain until it reaches a method that handles it, or until it reaches [join()], which rethrows it wrapped in a [CompletionException]. The program [Async11.java] examines the different cases:

// exceptions in the asynchronous code
void main() {
     // 1 - `join()` throws a `CompletionException` that wraps the operation's exception
    try {
        int valeur = lireValeur("douze").join();
        IO.println("valeur = " + valeur);
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        IO.println("1 - join() lance " + nom(e) + ", de cause " + nom(e.getCause())
                + " : " + e.getCause().getMessage());
    }

     // 2 - `exceptionally` provides a fallback value in case of failure
    int valeur = lireValeur("treize").exceptionally(e -> -1).join();
    IO.println("2 - exceptionally : valeur de remplacement " + valeur);

     // 3 - `handle` receives the result or the exception; `whenComplete` observes them without changing anything
    for (String texte : List.of("14", "quinze")) {
        String bilan = lireValeur(texte)
                .whenComplete((v, e) -> IO.println("3 - whenComplete a vu : " + (e == null ? v : nom(e))))
                .handle((v, e) -> e == null ? "valeur " + v : "échec, " + nom(cause(e)))
                .join();
        IO.println("3 - handle a rendu : " + bilan);
    }

     // 4 - a method that returns a CompletableFuture can also throw an exception upon being called
    try {
        lireValeur(" ");
        IO.println("4 - l'appel n'a rien lancé");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        IO.println("4 - c'est l'appel lui-même qui lance " + nom(e) + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }

     // 5 - allOf with multiple failed operations
    List<CompletableFuture<Integer>> lectures = Stream.of("1", "deux", "3", "quatre")
            .map(this::lireValeur)
            .toList();
    try {
        CompletableFuture.allOf(lectures.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
         // join() rethrows only one of the exceptions…
        IO.println("5 - allOf échoue avec " + nom(e.getCause()) + " : " + e.getCause().getMessage());
         // … but each operation retained its own exception or result
        for (CompletableFuture<Integer> lecture : lectures) {
            switch (lecture.state()) {
                case SUCCESS -> IO.println("      réussite, résultat = " + lecture.resultNow());
                case FAILED -> IO.println("      échec, " + nom(lecture.exceptionNow())
                        + " : " + lecture.exceptionNow().getMessage());
                default -> IO.println("      état inattendu : " + lecture.state());
            }
        }
    }
}

// an asynchronous operation that fails if the string is not an integer
CompletableFuture<Integer> lireValeur(String texte) {
     // Immediate parameter validation before starting the operation
    if (texte == null || texte.isBlank()) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("le texte ne doit pas être vide");
    }
     // reading takes a little time
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>()
            .completeOnTimeout(null, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .thenApply(rien -> Integer.parseInt(texte));
}

// continuations often receive a CompletionException: trace back to its cause
Throwable cause(Throwable e) {
    return e instanceof CompletionException && e.getCause() != null ? e.getCause() : e;
}

// the simple name of an exception’s class
String nom(Throwable e) {
    return e.getClass().getSimpleName();
}

Results:

> java Async11.java
1 - join() lance CompletionException, de cause NumberFormatException : For input string: "douze"
2 - exceptionally : valeur de remplacement -1
3 - whenComplete a vu : 14
3 - handle a rendu : valeur 14
3 - whenComplete a vu : CompletionException
3 - handle a rendu : échec, NumberFormatException
4 - c'est l'appel lui-même qui lance IllegalArgumentException : le texte ne doit pas être vide
5 - allOf échoue avec NumberFormatException : For input string: "deux"
      réussite, résultat = 1
      échec, NumberFormatException : For input string: "deux"
      réussite, résultat = 3
      échec, NumberFormatException : For input string: "quatre"

Comments:

  • Lines 54–64: the method being tested. It first checks its parameter and launches a [IllegalArgumentException] if the string is [null] or empty. Otherwise, it returns an operation that waits 100 ms and then converts the entire string, which throws a [NumberFormatException] if the string is not a number;
  • lines 4–10: the standard case. The exception thrown by [Integer.parseInt] in the continuation of line 63 is caught by [CompletableFuture]; [join()] rethrows the exception wrapped in a [CompletionException], from which [getCause()] returns the original exception (line 2 of the results);
  • Line 13: [exceptionally(fonction)] returns a [CompletableFuture] that has the same result as the operation if it succeeds, and otherwise the result of the function applied to the exception: this is the [catch] from the world of [CompletableFuture]. Here, a failure is replaced with the value -1 (line 3);
  • lines 17–23: two other methods, applied to an operation that succeeds and then to one that fails:
    • [whenComplete(action)] receives the result and the exception (one of the two is [null]) and does not change anything: the [CompletableFuture] it returns has the same result or the same exception as the operation. It is used for observation (logging, freeing a resource): this is the [finally] of the [CompletableFuture] world;
    • [handle(fonction)] also receives the result and the exception, and returns a new value in both cases: it converts both a success and a failure into a result;
    • Lines 6 and 7 of the results reveal a pitfall: the exception received by the continuations is not [NumberFormatException] but a [CompletionException] that wraps it, because the failure occurred in a previous step of the chain (the continuation on line 63). The method [cause] (lines 66–69) traces back to the original exception: we’ll get into the habit of writing it out;
  • lines 26–31: an important difference from the [async] methods in other languages: a method that returns a [CompletableFuture] is an ordinary method, which can throw an exception as soon as it is called, before creating any [CompletableFuture]. This is the case here for an empty string (line 8 of the results). The calling code must therefore expect both types of errors, or the method must return an operation that has already failed ([return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new IllegalArgumentException(...));]), which is often preferable;
  • lines 34–38: We wait with [allOf] for four operations, two of which fail. The [CompletableFuture] from [allOf] fails in turn, but with only one of the exceptions (line 9 of the results);
  • lines 43–50: Each operation has retained its result or exception. We examine their status using a [switch]; [exceptionNow()] returns the original exception, without a wrapper. The failure of [allOf] does not prevent the other operations from succeeding (lines 10 and 12).

With virtual threads, the issue does not arise in the same way: the code executed by a virtual thread is ordinary code, where exceptions propagate as usual and are intercepted by [try / catch]. Only the boundary between two threads requires special attention: an exception from a task submitted to an executor is stored in its [Future], and [get()] rethrows it wrapped in a [ExecutionException].

docs.title: 9.5.2. Forgotten Operations
docs.text:
What happens to the exception from an operation that no one is waiting for? The program [Async12.java] demonstrates this:

// An operation that was started and then forgotten: its exception is lost
void main() {
     // the exception handler that no code in a thread has intercepted
    Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, e) ->
            IO.println("exception non interceptée dans [" + thread.getName() + "] : " + e.getMessage()));

     // 1 - an expected CompletableFuture: its exception is caught
    try {
        enregistrer("a").join();
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        IO.println("1 - CompletableFuture attendu : exception interceptée : " + e.getCause().getMessage());
    }

     // 2 - a forgotten CompletableFuture: its exception remains in the object; no one will see it
    enregistrer("b");
    IO.println("2 - CompletableFuture oublié : l'appel a rendu la main");

     // 3 - a task submitted to an executor and forgotten: its exception remains in the Future
    ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
    executeur.submit(() -> enregistrerBloquant("c"));
    IO.println("3 - Future oublié : la tâche est lancée");

     // 4 - a thread: an uncaught exception terminates the thread and reaches the handler
    Thread.ofVirtual().name("enregistreur").start(() -> enregistrerBloquant("d"));
    IO.println("4 - thread virtuel lancé");

     // 5 - run without waiting, but handle failure
    enregistrer("e").exceptionally(e -> {
        IO.println("5 - échec signalé par exceptionally : " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        return null;
    });

     // the program continues its work…
    for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
        dormir(100);
        IO.println("le programme travaille (" + i + ")");
    }
    executeur.close();
    IO.println("fin normale du programme");
}

// an asynchronous operation that fails after 200 ms
CompletableFuture<Void> enregistrer(String donnee) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>()
            .completeOnTimeout(null, 200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .thenRun(() -> {
                throw new IllegalStateException("échec de l'enregistrement de [" + donnee + "]");
            });
}

// the same operation, written as a blocking operation
void enregistrerBloquant(String donnee) {
    dormir(200);
    throw new IllegalStateException("échec de l'enregistrement de [" + donnee + "]");
}

// Thread.sleep without a controlled exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("attente interrompue");
    }
}

Results:

> java Async12.java
1 - CompletableFuture attendu : exception interceptée : échec de l'enregistrement de [a]
2 - CompletableFuture oublié : l'appel a rendu la main
3 - Future oublié : la tâche est lancée
4 - thread virtuel lancé
le programme travaille (1)
5 - échec signalé par exceptionally : échec de l'enregistrement de [e]
exception non interceptée dans [enregistreur] : échec de l'enregistrement de [d]
le programme travaille (2)
le programme travaille (3)
le programme travaille (4)
fin normale du programme

Comments:

  • lines 4–5: [Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler] sets up the handler that is called when an exception is not caught by any code in a thread, just before the end of that thread. Without it, JVM displays the exception’s stack trace in the error output;
  • lines 8–12: The operation is expected, and its exception is intercepted normally;
  • lines 14–16: the operation is launched and then forgotten. Its exception is stored in [CompletableFuture], which no one will consult: it is lost, without any message;
  • lines 18–21: The same applies to a task submitted by [submit] to an executor: its exception is stored in the returned [Future], which is ignored;
  • line 24: a thread launched directly has no [Future]: the exception it does not handle terminates the thread and reaches the uncaught exception handler (line 8 of the results). The program, however, continues;
  • lines 28–31: the correct way to start an operation without waiting for it: attach a continuation [exceptionally] (or [whenComplete]) to it that handles failure, in this case by printing a message (line 7);
  • Lines 33–39 show that, in all cases, the program continues running until its normal termination. This differs from some languages, where an uncaught exception can terminate the program; in Java, it goes unnoticed, which isn’t any better: a record error that no one sees means lost data.

The rule is therefore: an operation that has been initiated must be awaited ([join], [get], [allOf], or the [close] method of an executor, which waits for its tasks), or receive a continuation that handles its failure. Code analysis tools (SpotBugs, the analysis of IntelliJ and IDEA) may also flag the ignored result of a method that returns a [Future].

docs.title: 9.6.1. Future.cancel and thread termination
docs.text:
A long-running operation must be able to be canceled: the user clicked on [Annuler], a server client disconnected, the application shut down, or a timeout occurred. Java uses a cooperative mechanism for this—thread interruption:

  • a thread’s [interrupt()] method sets its interrupt flag; it does not stop the thread (the [Thread.stop] method, which forced a stop, has been deprecated since Java 20: it calls [UnsupportedOperationException]);
  • if the thread is blocked in an interruptible wait ([Thread.sleep], [Object.wait], [Thread.join], [BlockingQueue.take], [Future.get]…), the wait is immediately interrupted and triggers a [InterruptedException], clearing the flag;
  • a thread that performs calculations checks its own indicator regularly using [Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()] and terminates gracefully if it is set;
  • the [cancel(true)] method of a [Future] returned by an executor transitions the task to the [CANCELLED] state and interrupts the thread executing it ([cancel(false)] simply prevents the task from starting if it has not yet done so). After cancellation, [get()] launches a [CancellationException].

The mechanism is cooperative: no one forcibly stops an operation; the operation stops itself at a point where it can do so cleanly. This is why a method that intercepts a [InterruptedException] must not ignore it: it must either propagate it, terminate itself, or at the very least reset the flag with [Thread.currentThread().interrupt()] so that the calling code knows that an interruption has been requested (this is what our [dormir] method does).

The program [Async13.java] cancels a simulated download in several ways:

// cancel an operation: Future.cancel(true) and thread interruption
long debut = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
         // 1 - do not wait for the result for more than 1.2 seconds, then cancel the operation
        Future<?> telechargement1 = executeur.submit(() -> telecharger(10));
        try {
            telechargement1.get(1200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
             // cancel(true) interrupts the thread executing the task
            telechargement1.cancel(true);
            afficher("1 - " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", état : " + telechargement1.state());
        }

         // 2 - A calculation that periodically checks whether it has been interrupted
        debut = System.nanoTime();
        Future<Long> calcul = executeur.submit(this::calculer);
        Thread.sleep(300);
        calcul.cancel(true);
        try {
            afficher("2 - résultat : " + calcul.get());
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            afficher("2 - get() lance " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", état : " + calcul.state());
        }
        Thread.sleep(100);

         // 3 - The program requests cancellation after 700 ms
        debut = System.nanoTime();
        Future<?> telechargement3 = executeur.submit(() -> telecharger(10));
        Thread.sleep(700);
        afficher("3 - le programme demande l'annulation");
        telechargement3.cancel(true);
        afficher("3 - isCancelled=" + telechargement3.isCancelled());
        Thread.sleep(100);

         // 4 - calling `cancel()` on a `CompletableFuture` does not interrupt the operation it represents
        debut = System.nanoTime();
        CompletableFuture<Void> telechargement4 = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> telecharger(3), executeur);
        Thread.sleep(400);
        telechargement4.cancel(true);
        afficher("4 - CompletableFuture annulé : isCancelled=" + telechargement4.isCancelled()
                + ", mais l'opération continue");
    } // close() waits for all tasks to complete
}

// simulates the download of [nbBlocs] data blocks (one block every 300 ms)
void telecharger(int nbBlocs) {
    try {
        for (int i = 1; i <= nbBlocs; i++) {
             // A blocking wait is interrupted as soon as the thread is interrupted
            Thread.sleep(300);
            afficher("  bloc " + i + "/" + nbBlocs + " reçu");
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        afficher("  téléchargement interrompu");
    }
}

// a long calculation that checks its thread’s interrupt flag every 1,000,000 iterations
long calculer() {
    long somme = 0;
    for (long i = 0; i < 100_000_000_000L; i++) {
        if (i % 1_000_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            afficher("  calcul interrompu au tour " + i);
            return -1;
        }
        somme += i % 7;
    }
    return somme;
}

// display showing the elapsed time since [debut]
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async13.java
  318 ms :   bloc 1/10 reçu
  638 ms :   bloc 2/10 reçu
  939 ms :   bloc 3/10 reçu
 1212 ms :   téléchargement interrompu
 1214 ms : 1 - TimeoutException, état : CANCELLED
  301 ms : 2 - get() lance CancellationException, état : CANCELLED
  303 ms :   calcul interrompu au tour 131000000
  302 ms :   bloc 1/10 reçu
  603 ms :   bloc 2/10 reçu
  701 ms : 3 - le programme demande l'annulation
  702 ms :   téléchargement interrompu
  702 ms : 3 - isCancelled=true
  309 ms :   bloc 1/3 reçu
  404 ms : 4 - CompletableFuture annulé : isCancelled=true, mais l'opération continue
  609 ms :   bloc 2/3 reçu
  910 ms :   bloc 3/3 reçu

Comments:

  • Lines 47–58: The simulated download receives a block every 300 ms. It is executed by a virtual thread and uses a blocking wait, [Thread.sleep], which terminates as soon as the thread is interrupted: [InterruptedException] exits the loop, and the download stops by signaling this. It requires no special parameters to be cancelable: the waits in [java.util.concurrent] react in the same way to interruption, as do, in a virtual thread, the blocking I/O operations on sockets (the socket is then closed, and the operation initiates a [SocketException]);
  • Lines 6–14: [get(1200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)] waits for the result for at most 1.2 seconds, then launches a [TimeoutException]. The wait is abandoned but not the operation: it is explicitly canceled with [cancel(true)], which interrupts the download’s virtual thread. The thread has received three blocks and stops at 1,200 ms (lines 2–6 of the results);
  • lines 16–26: a cancelable calculation (not a wait). The [calculer] method (lines 60–71) checks its thread’s interrupt flag every million cycles and stops if it is set. The program aborts it after 300 ms: [get()] immediately launches a [CancellationException] (line 7), and the calculation stops on its own shortly thereafter (line 8);
  • lines 28–35: The program requests cancellation after 700 ms. It takes effect immediately: the wait for the third block is interrupted (lines 11–13);
  • Lines 37–43: A pitfall to be aware of. The method *[cancel] of a *[CompletableFuture] terminates the latter in the state *[CANCELLED], but does not interrupt anything: a [CompletableFuture] does not know which thread, if any, is working for it (its [mayInterruptIfRunning] parameter is ignored). The download continues until completion (lines 16–17); only its result will be ignored. For a [CompletableFuture] to be able to stop the operation it represents, that operation must monitor the state of the [CompletableFuture] ([isCancelled()]), or the [Future]* or the task’s thread must be retained to interrupt it;
  • Line 44: The executor’s [close()] method waits for all tasks to complete, including the one in step 4.

docs.title: 9.6.2. Multiple processes, multiple outcomes
docs.text:
The program [Async14.java] launches five processes lasting 1 to 5 seconds: process #3 throws an exception, and process #4 is canceled. It processes each process as soon as it finishes, regardless of how it ended, and always knows which process it is:

// Five processes lasting 1 to 5 seconds executed by virtual threads:
// No. 3 throws an exception; No. 4 is canceled
long debut;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
         ScheduledExecutorService planificateur = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()) {
         // CompletionService will deliver each task as soon as it is completed
        CompletionService<Resultat> service = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(executeur);
        List<Future<Resultat>> taches = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            int numero = i;
            taches.add(service.submit(() -> dormir(numero, numero + 1)));
        }
         // Process No. 4 is canceled after 2.5 seconds
        planificateur.schedule(() -> taches.get(4).cancel(true), 2500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        afficher("les " + taches.size() + " traitements sont lancés");

         // Each process is processed as soon as it is completed, regardless of how it ends
        for (int i = 0; i < taches.size(); i++) {
            Future<Resultat> tache = service.take();
            int numero = taches.indexOf(tache);
            String bilan = switch (tache.state()) {
                case SUCCESS -> String.format("terminé : durée programmée %d s, durée effective %.1f s",
                        tache.resultNow().duree(), tache.resultNow().dureeEffective());
                case FAILED -> "a rencontré l'erreur suivante : " + tache.exceptionNow().getMessage();
                case CANCELLED -> "annulé";
                case RUNNING -> "toujours en cours ?";
            };
            afficher("traitement " + numero + " " + bilan);
        }
    }
}

// the process: sleep for [duree] seconds, in one-second increments
Resultat dormir(int numero, int duree) throws InterruptedException {
    long debutTraitement = System.nanoTime();
     // Exception for process No. 3
    if (numero == 3) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("test....");
    }
    for (int i = 1; i <= duree; i++) {
        Thread.sleep(1000);
    }
     // the result returned to the caller
    return new Resultat(duree, (System.nanoTime() - debutTraitement) / 1e9);
}

// the result of a processing operation
record Resultat(int duree, double dureeEffective) {
}

// display showing the elapsed time since the start, in seconds
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%4.1f s : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1e9, message));
}

Results:

> java Async14.java
 0,0 s : les 5 traitements sont lancés
 0,0 s : traitement 3 a rencontré l'erreur suivante : test....
 1,0 s : traitement 0 terminé : durée programmée 1 s, durée effective 1,0 s
 2,0 s : traitement 1 terminé : durée programmée 2 s, durée effective 2,0 s
 2,5 s : traitement 4 annulé
 3,0 s : traitement 2 terminé : durée programmée 3 s, durée effective 3,0 s

Comments:

  • Lines 36–48: the process. No. 3 throws an exception; the others “sleep” for [duree] seconds in one-second increments, with an interruptible [Thread.sleep], and return a result—a [record]—that contains the programmed duration and the actual duration. The method declares [InterruptedException]: it is called by a [Callable], whose method [call] can throw controlled exceptions;
  • lines 7–8: two executors declared within the same [try]: the virtual thread executor, and a [ScheduledExecutorService], an executor capable of executing a task after a delay (we’ll revisit this in the section on time);
  • lines 10–15: the five processes are submitted to the [CompletionService] already encountered in [Async10.java], and their [Future] instances are stored in a list;
  • line 17: [ScheduledExecutorService] will cancel process No. 4 after 2.5 seconds, even though it still has 2.5 seconds left to run;
  • lines 21–32: [take()] delivers each process as soon as it is completed, regardless of how it ended: even a canceled [Future] is delivered. We do not call [get()], which would throw an exception, but instead examine the status of [Future] using a [switch] expression that covers the four constants of [Future.State] (the compiler verifies that none are missing). The process number is determined by the position of its [Future] in the list ([indexOf]);
  • the results show that No. 3 fails immediately, that Nos. 0, 1, and 2 complete after 1, 2, and 3 seconds, respectively, and that No. 4 is canceled at 2.5 seconds.

docs.title: 9.6.3. Limiting the Duration of a Wait
docs.text:
The program [Async15.java] provides tools for limiting the duration of a wait: the methods [orTimeout] and [completeOnTimeout] from [CompletableFuture] (Java 9), and the method [get] with a delay from [Future]. It also shows how to combine two stop causes.

// limit the duration of a wait: orTimeout, completeOnTimeout, get(delay)
long debut = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
         // 1 - orTimeout: the wait does not exceed one second
        CompletableFuture<String> lente = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
                () -> interrogerBloquant("serveur-lent", 3000), executeur);
        try {
            afficher("1 - réponse : " + lente.orTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).join());
        } catch (CompletionException e) {
            afficher("1 - " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName() + ", état : " + lente.state());
        }
         // The operation itself continues: let it finish
        Thread.sleep(2200);

         // 2 - completeOnTimeout: if it takes longer than one second, we settle for a default response
        debut = System.nanoTime();
        String reponse = interroger("serveur-lent", 3000)
                .completeOnTimeout("réponse par défaut", 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
                .join();
        afficher("2 - " + reponse);

         // 3 - To truly stop the operation, we terminate the thread executing it
        debut = System.nanoTime();
        Future<String> lente3 = executeur.submit(() -> interrogerBloquant("serveur-lent", 3000));
        try {
            afficher("3 - réponse : " + lente3.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            lente3.cancel(true);
            afficher("3 - délai d'une seconde dépassé, opération annulée, état : " + lente3.state());
        }
    }

     // 4 - Two causes of termination: the processing time specific to each operation and a general termination
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    CompletableFuture<Void> arretGeneral = new CompletableFuture<>();
    CompletableFuture<Void> tous = CompletableFuture.allOf(
            traiterAvecDelai("rapide", 500, 1000, arretGeneral),
            traiterAvecDelai("lent", 3000, 1000, arretGeneral),
            traiterAvecDelai("moyen", 1500, 2000, arretGeneral));
     // The caller requests a general shutdown after 1,200 ms
    Thread.sleep(1200);
    afficher("4 - arrêt général demandé");
    arretGeneral.complete(null);
    tous.join();
}

// A process limited to [delai] milliseconds, which can also be terminated by the caller
CompletableFuture<Void> traiterAvecDelai(String nom, int duree, int delai, CompletableFuture<Void> arret) {
    CompletableFuture<String> reponse = interroger(nom, duree).orTimeout(delai, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
     // A general stop cancels the wait for a response
    arret.thenRun(() -> reponse.cancel(false));
     // we examine how the wait ended
    return reponse.handle((texte, e) -> switch (e) {
        case null -> texte;
        case TimeoutException _ -> nom + " : délai de " + delai + " ms dépassé";
        case CancellationException _ -> nom + " : arrêté à la demande de l'appelant";
        default -> nom + " : " + e;
    }).thenAccept(message -> afficher("4 - " + message));
}

// simulates a server that responds after [duree] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<String> interroger(String serveur, int duree) {
    return new CompletableFuture<String>()
            .completeOnTimeout(serveur + " a répondu en " + duree + " ms", duree, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// The same operation, written as a blocking operation
String interrogerBloquant(String serveur, int duree) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(duree);
        afficher("  " + serveur + " a fini son travail");
        return serveur + " a répondu en " + duree + " ms";
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        afficher("  " + serveur + " a été interrompu");
        throw new CancellationException("opération interrompue");
    }
}

// Display the elapsed time since [debut]
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async15.java
 1028 ms : 1 - TimeoutException, état : FAILED
 3025 ms :   serveur-lent a fini son travail
 1001 ms : 2 - réponse par défaut
 1003 ms :   serveur-lent a été interrompu
 1004 ms : 3 - délai d'une seconde dépassé, opération annulée, état : CANCELLED
  501 ms : 4 - rapide a répondu en 500 ms
 1005 ms : 4 - lent : délai de 1000 ms dépassé
 1206 ms : 4 - arrêt général demandé
 1207 ms : 4 - moyen : arrêté à la demande de l'appelant

Comments:

  • lines 7–8: the slow operation is a blocking method (lines 69–79), executed by a virtual thread using [supplyAsync] with an executor;
  • Line 10: [orTimeout(délai, unité)] terminates [CompletableFuture] with a [TimeoutException] if it is not completed within the time limit. This is the direct write of the “run” with [anyOf] from the [Async09.java] program. [orTimeout] does not create a new [CompletableFuture]: it modifies the one to which it applies (and returns it); which is why the state of [lente] is [FAILED] (line 2 of the results);
  • Lines 14–15: [orTimeout] aborts the wait, not the operation: the virtual thread continues to run and completes its work after 3 seconds (line 3), to no avail. This is the same issue seen earlier with [cancel]: a [CompletableFuture] cannot interrupt the operation it represents;
  • lines 17–22: [completeOnTimeout(valeur, délai, unité)] terminates [CompletableFuture] with a default value if it is not completed within the time limit: after one second, a “default response” is returned (line 4);
  • lines 24–32: To truly stop the operation, it is submitted to the executor; we wait for its [Future] for at most one second, then cancel it with [cancel(true)], which interrupts its thread: the operation stops after 1 second (lines 5–6). This is the preferred solution when the operation is blocking and interruptible;
  • lines 49–61: a process may be stopped for several reasons; here, its own timeout and a general stop request from the caller:
    • line 51: the process’s own timeout is set with [orTimeout];
    • line 53: the general termination is itself a [CompletableFuture<Void>], which the caller will terminate; a continuation is attached to it that cancels the wait for the response;
    • lines 55–60: Regardless of the cause, the wait ends in failure; [handle] examines the exception with a [switch] on the types (Java 21): [case null] for success, [case TimeoutException _] for timeout, [case CancellationException _] for general termination. The character [_] (Java 22) is an anonymous variable: the type is checked without needing to name the object;
  • lines 36–46: three processes and a general shutdown requested at 1,200 ms by terminating [CompletableFuture] and [arretGeneral]. Process [rapide] completes normally; process [lent] exceeds its one-second time limit; process [moyen], which was allotted two seconds, is terminated by the general shutdown (lines 7–10).

docs.title: 9.7. Reporting Progress
docs.text:
A long-running operation often needs to report its progress (a progress bar, a percentage). The simplest approach is to pass it a callback function that receives progress reports: a *[Consumer<T>], the functional interface from Chapter 7 whose sole method, *[accept(T)], takes a value. The operation calls [accept] at each step; it is unaware of how the progress reports will be displayed.

In a graphical user interface, the reports—generated by the thread executing the operation—cannot directly update the graphical components: [Consumer] must delegate the update to the UI thread ([SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> barre.setValue(pourcentage))] with Swing, [Platform.runLater] with JavaFX). In a console program, it can display the output directly. The program [Async16.java] simulates a file copy that the user can cancel by typing [Entrée]:

// report the progress of an operation using a Consumer; the user can cancel it
void main() throws InterruptedException {
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        IO.println("Copie en cours, tapez [Entrée] pour l'annuler");
         // The copy is performed by a virtual thread; the display method shows its progress reports
        Future<Integer> copie = executeur.submit(() -> copier(8, this::afficher));
         // Another virtual thread waits for the user to type [Entrée] to cancel the copy
        Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
             // `readln` returns `null` if standard input is closed: nothing is canceled
            if (IO.readln() != null) {
                copie.cancel(true);
            }
        });
        try {
            IO.println("Copie terminée : " + copie.get() + " fichiers copiés");
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            IO.println("Copie annulée par l'utilisateur");
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            IO.println("Échec de la copie : " + e.getCause());
        }
    }
}

// The operation does not know how its progress is displayed: it only reports it
int copier(int nbFichiers, Consumer<Avancement> progression) throws InterruptedException {
    for (int i = 1; i <= nbFichiers; i++) {
         // Copying a file
        Thread.sleep(300);
         // the progress report (the caller may not want it: progress is then set to null)
        if (progression != null) {
            progression.accept(new Avancement(100 * i / nbFichiers, "fichier" + i + ".dat"));
        }
    }
    return nbFichiers;
}

// a progress report
record Avancement(int pourcentage, String fichier) {
}

// display of progress reports in the console: a 20-character bar
void afficher(Avancement avancement) {
    int nbDieses = avancement.pourcentage() / 5;
    String barre = "#".repeat(nbDieses) + ".".repeat(20 - nbDieses);
    IO.println(String.format("[%s] %3d %% %s", barre, avancement.pourcentage(), avancement.fichier()));
}

Results without cancellation:

> java Async16.java
Copie en cours, tapez [Entrée] pour l'annuler
[##..................]  12% fichier1.dat
[#####...............]  25% fichier2.dat
[#######.............]  37% fichier3.dat
[##########..........]  50% fichier4.dat
[############........]  62% fichier5.dat
[###############.....]  75% fichier6.dat
[#################...]  87% fichier7.dat
[####################] 100% fichier8.dat
Copie terminée : 8 fichiers copiés

Results when the user types [Entrée] during the copy operation, after about one and a half seconds:

> java Async16.java
Copie en cours, tapez [Entrée] pour l'annuler
[##..................]  12% fichier1.dat
[#####...............]  25% fichier2.dat
[#######.............]  37% fichier3.dat
[##########..........]  50% fichier4.dat
[############........]  62% fichier5.dat
Copie annulée par l'utilisateur

Comments:

  • Lines 24–35: The operation receives a [Consumer<Avancement>]. After each file, it reports its progress using a [Avancement] object (a [record] containing the percentage and the file name). A caller who does not want reports passes [null], hence the check on line 30;
  • lines 41–46: displaying a report: a 20-character bar constructed using [String.repeat] (Java 11). The method reference [this::afficher] (line 6) is the [Consumer<Avancement>] passed to the operation;
  • line 6: the copy is performed by a virtual thread;
  • lines 8–13: another virtual thread waits for the user to type [Entrée] ([IO.readln()] is a blocking read, which is why this thread: it is this thread that is blocked, not the program), then cancels the copy with [cancel(true)], which interrupts the [Thread.sleep] on line 28. The program does not wait for it: it is a daemon thread, abandoned at the end of the program if the user has not entered anything;
  • lines 14–20: the program waits for the copy to finish. A cancellation results in a [CancellationException], while a copy failure results in a [ExecutionException].

docs.title: 9.8.1. Files
docs.text:
I/O is the very reason for asynchronous processing. Java provides two families of classes for files:

  • the “classic,” blocking classes: [Files] ([readAllLines], [readString], [lines], [writeString], [newBufferedReader], [newBufferedWriter]…), [BufferedReader], [BufferedWriter]. These are currently executed on a virtual thread when you do not want to block an important thread;
  • the [AsynchronousFileChannel] class (Java 7), whose operations return a [Future] or call a [CompletionHandler]. It is rarely used: on Linux, it actually performs blocking reads on a thread pool internal to JVM, and its interface is cumbersome.

The program [Async17.java] displays both categories by reading the tax bracket file from the main program, [DataImpot.txt], located in the program’s directory:

4962:0:0
8382:0.068:291.09
14753:0.191:1322.92
23888:0.283:2668.39
38868:0.374:4846.98
47932:0.426:6883.66
0:0.481:9505.54

Each line contains the bracket threshold, the coefficient [coeffR] and the coefficient [coeffN], separated by the character [:] and written with a decimal point (the tax scale is the 2004 scale for 2003 income, retained as-is for this fiscal year). The program runs in the [09-async] folder and searches for its files in the current folder.

// file I/O: AsynchronousFileChannel, followed by blocking I/O on a virtual thread
final Path donnees = Path.of("DataImpot.txt");
final Path rapport = Path.of("rapport-17.txt");

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // 1 - AsynchronousFileChannel (Java 7): an asynchronous read, rendered as a CompletableFuture
    String contenu = lireAsynchrone(donnees).join();
    IO.println("1 - AsynchronousFileChannel : " + contenu.lines().count() + " lignes");

     // 2 through 7 - ordinary blocking I/O, executed by a virtual thread
    Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
        try {
            traiterFichiers();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            IO.println("erreur : " + e);
        }
    }).join();
}

// reads an entire (small) file using a AsynchronousFileChannel
CompletableFuture<String> lireAsynchrone(Path fichier) {
    CompletableFuture<String> resultat = new CompletableFuture<>();
    try {
        AsynchronousFileChannel canal = AsynchronousFileChannel.open(fichier, StandardOpenOption.READ);
        ByteBuffer tampon = ByteBuffer.allocate((int) canal.size());
         // Reading begins; the callback object will terminate the CompletableFuture
        canal.read(tampon, 0, tampon, new CompletionHandler<Integer, ByteBuffer>() {
            @Override
            public void completed(Integer nbOctets, ByteBuffer lus) {
                resultat.complete(new String(lus.array(), 0, nbOctets, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            }

            @Override
            public void failed(Throwable e, ByteBuffer lus) {
                resultat.completeExceptionally(e);
            }
        });
         // the channel will be closed when reading is complete, regardless of the outcome
        resultat.whenComplete((texte, e) -> fermer(canal));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        resultat.completeExceptionally(e);
    }
    return resultat;
}

void traiterFichiers() throws IOException {
     // 2 - Read the entire file in a single operation
    List<String> lignes = Files.readAllLines(donnees);
    IO.println("2 - Files.readAllLines : " + lignes.size() + " lignes");

     // 3 - read line by line with a BufferedReader
    List<TrancheImpot> tranches = new ArrayList<>();
    try (BufferedReader lecteur = Files.newBufferedReader(donnees)) {
        String ligne;
         // readLine returns null at the end of the file
        while ((ligne = lecteur.readLine()) != null) {
            tranches.add(TrancheImpot.parse(ligne));
        }
    }
    IO.println("3 - BufferedReader.readLine : " + tranches.size() + " tranches, 2e : " + tranches.get(1));

     // 4 - Files.lines returns a stream of lines, read on demand
    try (Stream<String> flux = Files.lines(donnees)) {
        IO.println("4 - Files.lines : " + flux.count() + " lignes");
    }

     // 5 - Writing with a BufferedWriter
    try (BufferedWriter ecrivain = Files.newBufferedWriter(rapport)) {
        ecrivain.write("Tranches du barème (exercice : barème 2004 sur les revenus 2003)");
        ecrivain.newLine();
        for (int i = 0; i < tranches.size(); i++) {
            TrancheImpot tranche = tranches.get(i);
            String limite = tranche.limite().signum() == 0 ? "au-delà"
                    : String.format("jusqu'à %,d €", tranche.limite().intValue());
            ecrivain.write(String.format("tranche %d : %-18s taux %.1f %%",
                    i + 1, limite, tranche.coeffR().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(100))));
            ecrivain.newLine();
        }
    }

     // 6 - reads the entire file as a string
    String texte = Files.readString(rapport);
    IO.print("5 et 6 - contenu de [" + rapport + "] :\n" + texte);

     // 7 - Append to the end of the file, then delete
    Files.writeString(rapport, "fin du rapport\n", StandardOpenOption.APPEND);
    IO.println("7 - dernière ligne : " + Files.readAllLines(rapport).getLast());
    Files.delete(rapport);
}

// closes a channel without a controlled exception
void fermer(Channel canal) {
    try {
        canal.close();
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("erreur à la fermeture : " + e);
    }
}

// a tax bracket; the file uses a decimal point, which BigDecimal understands
record TrancheImpot(BigDecimal limite, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
    static TrancheImpot parse(String ligne) {
        String[] champs = ligne.split(":");
        return new TrancheImpot(new BigDecimal(champs[0]), new BigDecimal(champs[1]),
                new BigDecimal(champs[2]));
    }
}

Results:

> java Async17.java
1 - AsynchronousFileChannel : 7 lignes
2 - Files.readAllLines : 7 lignes
3 - BufferedReader.readLine : 7 tranches, 2e : TrancheImpot[limite=8382, coeffR=0.068, coeffN=291.09]
4 - Files.lines : 7 lignes
5 et 6 - contenu de [rapport-17.txt] :
Tranches du barème (exercice : barème 2004 sur les revenus 2003)
tranche 1 : jusqu'à 4 962 €    taux 0,0 %
tranche 2 : jusqu'à 8 382 €    taux 6,8 %
tranche 3 : jusqu'à 14 753 €   taux 19,1 %
tranche 4 : jusqu'à 23 888 €   taux 28,3 %
tranche 5 : jusqu'à 38 868 €   taux 37,4 %
tranche 6 : jusqu'à 47 932 €   taux 42,6 %
tranche 7 : au-delà            taux 48,1 %
7 - dernière ligne : fin du rapport

Comments:

  • Lines 20–44: Reading with a [AsynchronousFileChannel], presented in the form of a [CompletableFuture<String>]. This is the general technique for converting a API with callback methods into a [CompletableFuture]: we create a “draft” [CompletableFuture] (line 22), return it immediately (line 43), and the callback methods complete it, with the result ([complete], line 30) or the exception ([completeExceptionally], line 35). The callback object is an anonymous class that implements [CompletionHandler<Integer, ByteBuffer>]: the result of a read operation is the number of bytes read, and the object passed here is the buffer itself. A single read operation is sufficient for a small file; a large file would require successive read operations, which the callback methods would need to chain together;
  • line 39: [whenComplete] closes the channel when the read operation is complete, whether it was successful or not;
  • Lines 11–17: The other operations are ordinary blocking I/O operations, grouped within the [traiterFichiers] method and executed by a virtual thread. The lambda of a [Runnable] cannot throw a controlled exception: the [IOException] is intercepted within the lambda;
  • line 48: [Files.readAllLines] reads the entire file and returns a list of its lines (in UTF-8 by default, like all methods of [Files]);
  • lines 52–59: line-by-line reading using [BufferedReader]; [readLine()] returns [null] at the end of the file. Each line is converted to [TrancheImpot] by the record’s [parse] method (lines 100–107); the numbers are [BigDecimal], whose constructor expects a decimal point regardless of the machine’s language. The representation of a record produced by its [toString] method appears on line 4 of the results;
  • lines 63–65: [Files.lines] returns a [Stream<String>] consisting of lines read on demand: unlike [readAllLines], it does not load the entire file into memory. This is the preferred method for large files. The stream keeps the file open: it must be closed, hence the [try] with a resource;
  • Lines 68–79: Writing with a [BufferedWriter], which is closed (and thus flushed to disk) upon exit from the [try]. The [%,d] format inserts the thousands separator for the machine’s language (a thin non-breaking space in French);
  • Lines 82–88: [Files.readString] (Java 11) re-reads the written file; [Files.writeString], using the [StandardOpenOption.APPEND] option, adds a line to it; [getLast()] (Java 21) returns the last element of the list, then the file is deleted.

Recall the limitation mentioned above: file reads and writes pin the virtual thread to its carrier thread during the operation, and JVM compensates by adding a carrier thread. For local files, this is rarely noticeable; for network operations, virtual threads actually release their carriers during waits.

docs.title: 9.8.2. Network: HttpClient
docs.text:
The Java client HTTP, [java.net.http.HttpClient] (Java 11), offers both approaches: [send], which is blocking and returns the response, and [sendAsync], which immediately returns a [CompletableFuture] containing the response. Chapter 12 will examine this in detail; the program [Async18.java] simply compares the two methods by querying a small local server, HTTP, which takes one second to return the “temperature” of a city:

// HttpClient: asynchronous (sendAsync) or blocking (send) requests to a small local server
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;

final int port = 27510;
final List<String> villes = List.of("Angers", "Brest", "Colmar", "Dijon", "Évry", "Foix");
long debut;

void main() throws IOException, InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
     // a server HTTP that takes one second to return a city’s “temperature”
    HttpServer serveur = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port), 0);
    serveur.createContext("/temperature", echange -> {
         // the request is in the form /temperature?city=xxx
        String parametre = echange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery().substring("ville=".length());
        String ville = URLDecoder.decode(parametre, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        dormir(1000);
        byte[] reponse = (ville + " : " + (10 + ville.length()) + " °C").getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        echange.sendResponseHeaders(200, reponse.length);
        try (OutputStream flux = echange.getResponseBody()) {
            flux.write(reponse);
        }
    });
     // Each request received is processed by a virtual thread
    serveur.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
    serveur.start();

    try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).build()) {
         // A first request, so that JVM loads the client classes before the measurements
        client.send(requete("Paris"), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding());

         // 1 - sendAsync immediately returns a CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>
        debut = System.nanoTime();
        List<CompletableFuture<String>> reponses = villes.stream()
                .map(ville -> client.sendAsync(requete(ville), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
                        .thenApply(HttpResponse::body))
                .toList();
        CompletableFuture.allOf(reponses.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
        afficher("1 - sendAsync : " + reponses.stream().map(CompletableFuture::resultNow).toList());

         // 2 - `send` is blocking: it is called from virtual threads
        debut = System.nanoTime();
        try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Future<String>> reponses2 = new ArrayList<>();
            for (String ville : villes) {
                reponses2.add(executeur.submit(
                        () -> client.send(requete(ville), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body()));
            }
            List<String> textes = new ArrayList<>();
            for (Future<String> reponse : reponses2) {
                textes.add(reponse.get());
            }
            afficher("2 - send sur des threads virtuels : " + textes);
        }
    } finally {
        serveur.stop(0);
    }
}

// the request GET, which retrieves a city’s temperature
HttpRequest requete(String ville) {
    String parametre = URLEncoder.encode(ville, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    URI adresse = URI.create("http://localhost:" + port + "/temperature?ville=" + parametre);
    return HttpRequest.newBuilder(adresse).build();
}

// Thread.sleep without a controlled exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("attente interrompue");
    }
}

// display showing the elapsed time since [debut]
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async18.java
 1033 ms : 1 - sendAsync : [Angers : 16 °C, Brest : 15 °C, Colmar : 16 °C, Dijon : 15 °C, Évry : 14 °C, Foix : 14 °C]
 1023 ms : 2 - send sur des threads virtuels : [Angers : 16 °C, Brest : 15 °C, Colmar : 16 °C, Dijon : 15 °C, Évry : 14 °C, Foix : 14 °C]

Comments:

  • lines 12–27: the server. The JVM file contains a small HTTP server, the class [HttpServer] from the module [jdk.httpserver], imported on line 2 (a compact file automatically imports only the module [java.base]; the client classes, from the [java.net.http] module, are imported on lines 3–5). [createContext] associates a handler with the [/temperature] path—a lambda that receives the HTTP exchange: it decodes the [ville] parameter from the requested address, waits one second, and then sends the response. Line 26 has each request processed by a virtual thread: a server configured this way can serve thousands of waiting clients;
  • Lines 29–31: The client is created by a constructor ([newBuilder]) that sets the protocol version here. Since Java 21, it implements [AutoCloseable] and declares itself in a [try] with a resource. An initial request is used to “warm up” the JVM: the first time a client is used, it loads numerous classes, which would skew the subsequent measurement by a few hundred milliseconds;
  • lines 33–40: [sendAsync(requête, gestionnaire)] sends the request and immediately returns a [CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>]; the body handler [BodyHandlers.ofString()] specifies that the response body must be read as a string. [thenApply(HttpResponse::body)] retains only the body. The six requests are sent simultaneously, and their responses arrive together after one second (line 2 of the results). While waiting, no thread waits for the response: the client monitors its connections using a “selector” thread;
  • Lines 42–55: [send] is blocking; it is being called from six virtual threads. The result is the same: one second for all six requests (line 3), and no system threads are blocked;
  • lines 61–66: the request GET. [URLEncoder.encode] encodes characters that cannot appear as-is in an address (the [É] from Évry), and the server decodes them using [URLDecoder.decode] (line 17).

docs.title: 9.9. Asynchronous Value Streams
docs.text:
An asynchronous operation returns a result after a certain amount of time. A stream ([Stream]) or an iterator returns a sequence of values, produced on demand. Sometimes it is necessary to combine the two: a sequence of values where each one requires a wait before being produced. This is the case for lines in a large file, the rows in the result of a SQL query, messages arriving over a network connection, sensor readings, and so on. Other languages have a dedicated type for this; Java offers two models:

  • the “pull” model: the consumer requests the next value and waits for it to be available. With virtual threads, this is simply a [Iterator] or a [Stream] where the production of each value blocks, read by a virtual thread;
  • the “push” model: the producer sends values to its subscribers as they are produced, and the subscribers control the throughput. This is the reactive stream model, standardized by the [java.util.concurrent.Flow] interfaces (Java 9).

docs.title: 9.9.1. The pull model: a Stream read by a virtual thread
docs.text:
The program [Async19.java] produces measurements—one every 200 ms—in the form of a [Stream<Mesure>]:

// a sequence of values produced with waits: a “blocking” stream read by a virtual thread
long debut;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // all work is done by a virtual thread: its waits do not block any carrier threads
    Thread.ofVirtual().start(this::consommer).join();
}

void consommer() {
    debut = System.nanoTime();
     // 1 - each value is processed as soon as it is produced
    try (Stream<Mesure> mesures = lireMesures("capteur-1", 4)) {
        mesures.forEach(mesure -> afficher("1 - reçu " + mesure));
    }

     // 2 - the loop can be exited before completion: the producer does not produce the subsequent values
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    try (Stream<Mesure> mesures = lireMesures("capteur-2", 100)) {
        Iterator<Mesure> iterateur = mesures.iterator();
        while (iterateur.hasNext()) {
            Mesure mesure = iterateur.next();
            afficher("2 - reçu " + mesure);
            if (mesure.valeur() >= 22) {
                break;
            }
        }
    }

     // 3 - Abortion: another thread interrupts the thread reading the stream
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    Thread lecteur = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
        try (Stream<Mesure> mesures = lireMesures("capteur-3", 100)) {
            mesures.forEach(mesure -> afficher("3 - reçu " + mesure));
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            afficher("3 - lecture annulée");
        }
    });
    attendreFin(lecteur, 700);

     // 4 - all operations of the API Stream apply to the stream
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    String fortes;
    try (Stream<Mesure> mesures = lireMesures("capteur-4", 6)) {
        fortes = mesures
                .filter(mesure -> mesure.valeur() > 21)
                .map(mesure -> NumberFormat.getInstance().format(mesure.valeur()))
                .collect(Collectors.joining(" ; ", "[", "]"));
    }
    afficher("4 - mesures supérieures à 21 : " + fortes);
}

// a producer: one measurement every 200 ms, produced only when the consumer requests it
Stream<Mesure> lireMesures(String capteur, int nombre) {
    return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, nombre)
            .mapToObj(i -> {
                 // waiting for the next measurement
                dormir(200);
                return new Mesure(capteur, i, 19.5 + i * 0.75);
            })
