             // Executed by close(): at normal termination, after a break, or upon cancellation
            .onClose(() -> IO.println("          " + capteur + " : fin de la production"));
}

// waits [delai] ms for a thread to finish, then interrupts it and waits for it to finish
void attendreFin(Thread thread, long delai) {
    try {
        thread.join(delai);
        thread.interrupt();
        thread.join();
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// Thread.sleep without a controlled exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("attente interrompue");
    }
}

// display showing the elapsed time since [debut]
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

// a measurement
record Mesure(String capteur, int numero, double valeur) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return capteur + " n° " + numero + " : " + NumberFormat.getInstance().format(valeur) + " °C";
    }
}

> java Async19.java

  455 ms : 1 - reçu capteur-1 n° 2 : 21 °C
  656 ms : 1 - reçu capteur-1 n° 3 : 21,75 °C
  857 ms : 1 - reçu capteur-1 n° 4 : 22,5 °C
          capteur-1 : fin de la production
  200 ms : 2 - reçu capteur-2 n° 1 : 20,25 °C
  401 ms : 2 - reçu capteur-2 n° 2 : 21 °C
  603 ms : 2 - reçu capteur-2 n° 3 : 21,75 °C
  804 ms : 2 - reçu capteur-2 n° 4 : 22,5 °C
          capteur-2 : fin de la production
  201 ms : 3 - reçu capteur-3 n° 1 : 20,25 °C
  402 ms : 3 - reçu capteur-3 n° 2 : 21 °C

Comments:

  • Lines 52–62: the producer. It returns a *[Stream<Mesure>] constructed from the integers 1 through *[nombre]*; the *[mapToObj]* function waits 200 ms and then returns a measurement. Since a stream is lazy, this function is called only when the consumer requests the next value, and each measurement is processed before the next one is produced. [onClose] records an action executed when the stream is closed, regardless of the reason: this is the producer’s [finally]*;
  • line 6: all the work is done by a virtual thread: the 200 ms wait for each measurement does not block any system threads;
  • Lines 11–14: Each measurement is processed as soon as it is produced: one every 200 ms (lines 2–5 of the results). The stream is declared in a [try] with a resource: closing it triggers the [onClose] action (line 6);
  • lines 16–27: To exit the loop before it ends, the stream is traversed using its iterator. After the [break], the producer does not produce the remaining 96 measurements, and the stream is closed upon exiting the [try] (line 11). The methods [takeWhile] (Java 9) or [limit] also allow you to stop a stream;
  • lines 29–38: cancellation. The stream is read by another virtual thread, which the [attendreFin] method (lines 64–73) interrupts after 700 ms. The wait for the fourth measurement is interrupted: the [dormir] method launches a [CancellationException], which traverses the stream; the [try] with a resource closes the stream (line 15 of the results), then the [catch] reports the cancellation (line 16);
  • lines 40–49: everything the API Stream can do is applied to the stream: filtering, transformation, collection. The result is only available at the end of the stream, after 6 × 200 ms;
  • lines 90–96: The [toString] method of the [Mesure] record is redefined for a more compact display; [NumberFormat.getInstance()] formats the real number according to the machine’s language, without unnecessary decimal places ([21], [21,75]).

The same pattern applies to a [BufferedReader] (its lines are read on demand, and its method [lines()] returns a [Stream<String>]), to a [ResultSet], JDBC, or to a socket’s incoming stream: on a virtual thread, a blocking stream is an asynchronous stream.

docs.title: 9.9.2. The push model: Flow and SubmissionPublisher
docs.text:
The [java.util.concurrent.Flow] interface (Java 9) groups together four internal interfaces that standardize reactive streams:

  • [Flow.Publisher<T>], the publisher, produces values; its method [subscribe] adds a subscriber to it;
  • [Flow.Subscriber<T>], the subscriber, receives values via its method [onNext], the end of the stream via [onComplete], an error via [onError], and at the beginning, the object [Flow.Subscription], which links it to the publisher via [onSubscribe];
  • [Flow.Subscription], the subscription: [request(n)] requests additional values from [n], and [cancel()] terminates the subscription. The publisher never sends more values than the subscriber has requested: this is “backpressure,” which prevents a fast publisher from overwhelming a slow subscriber;
  • [Flow.Processor<T, R>] is both a subscriber and a publisher (a transformation node).

Java provides an implementation of the publisher, [SubmissionPublisher<T>], which delivers values to each subscriber via an executor and a buffer specific to that subscriber. Reactive libraries (Project Reactor, RxJava) implement these same interfaces and add dozens of operators to them. The program [Async20.java] publishes six measurements to two subscribers: a fast display that unsubscribes when the temperature exceeds 22 °C, and a slow archive:

// the “push” model: java.util.concurrent.Flow and SubmissionPublisher (Java 9)
final long debut = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    Abonne ecran = new Abonne("écran", 0, 22);
    Abonne archive = new Abonne("archive", 500, Double.MAX_VALUE);
     // the publisher delegates the delivery of values to an executor and maintains a buffer of 2 values per subscriber
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        var editeur = new SubmissionPublisher<Mesure>(executeur, 2);
        editeur.subscribe(ecran);
        editeur.subscribe(archive);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
            dormir(200);
             // `submit` waits if there is no more space in a subscriber’s buffer; it returns the estimated delay
            int retard = editeur.submit(new Mesure("capteur-1", i, 19.5 + i * 0.75));
            afficher("éditeur : mesure n° " + i + " publiée, retard estimé : " + retard);
        }
         // `close()` signals the end of the stream to subscribers: their `onComplete` method will be called
        afficher("éditeur : fin de la publication");
        editeur.close();
         // we wait for the archive to finish processing everything
        archive.fin.await();
    }
}

// A subscriber who processes each measurement in [duree] ms and unsubscribes after [seuil]
class Abonne implements Flow.Subscriber<Mesure> {
    private final String nom;
    private final long duree;
    private final double seuil;
    private Flow.Subscription abonnement;
    final CountDownLatch fin = new CountDownLatch(1);

    Abonne(String nom, long duree, double seuil) {
        this.nom = nom;
        this.duree = duree;
        this.seuil = seuil;
    }

    @Override
    public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription abonnement) {
        this.abonnement = abonnement;
         // The subscriber requests the values one by one: the subscriber controls the data rate
        abonnement.request(1);
    }

    @Override
    public void onNext(Mesure mesure) {
        afficher("  " + nom + " : reçu " + mesure);
        dormir(duree);
        if (mesure.valeur() >= seuil) {
            afficher("  " + nom + " : seuil atteint, désabonnement");
            abonnement.cancel();
        } else {
            abonnement.request(1);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(Throwable e) {
        afficher("  " + nom + " : erreur " + e);
        fin.countDown();
    }

    @Override
    public void onComplete() {
        afficher("  " + nom + " : fin du flux");
        fin.countDown();
    }
}

// Thread.sleep without controlled interruption: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("attente interrompue");
    }
}

// display showing the elapsed time since the start
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

// a measurement
record Mesure(String capteur, int numero, double valeur) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return capteur + " n° " + numero + " : " + NumberFormat.getInstance().format(valeur) + " °C";
    }
}

> java Async20.java
  221 ms : éditeur : mesure n° 1 publiée, retard estimé : 1
  269 ms :   archive : reçu capteur-1 n° 1 : 20,25 °C
  274 ms :   écran : reçu capteur-1 n° 1 : 20,25 °C
  466 ms : éditeur : mesure n° 2 publiée, retard estimé : 2
  466 ms :   écran : reçu capteur-1 n° 2 : 21 °C
  667 ms :   écran : reçu capteur-1 n° 3 : 21,75 °C
  667 ms : éditeur : mesure n° 3 publiée, retard estimé : 3
  770 ms :   archive : reçu capteur-1 n° 2 : 21 °C
  867 ms : éditeur : mesure n° 4 publiée, retard estimé : 3
  868 ms :   écran : reçu capteur-1 n° 4 : 22,5 °C
  868 ms :   écran : seuil atteint, désabonnement
 1271 ms :   archive : reçu capteur-1 n° 3 : 21,75 °C
 1271 ms : éditeur : mesure n° 5 publiée, retard estimé : 3
 1771 ms :   archive : reçu capteur-1 n° 4 : 22,5 °C
 1772 ms : éditeur : mesure n° 6 publiée, retard estimé : 3
 1772 ms : éditeur : fin de la publication
 2274 ms :   archive : reçu capteur-1 n° 5 : 23,25 °C
 2775 ms :   archive : reçu capteur-1 n° 6 : 24 °C
 3276 ms :   archive : fin du flux

Comments:

  • lines 26–70: the subscriber, which processes each measurement in [duree] milliseconds and unsubscribes when the measurement reaches [seuil]:
    • lines 40–45: [onSubscribe] receives the subscription and requests an initial value;
    • lines 47–57: [onNext] processes a value and then either requests another one ([request(1)]) or terminates the subscription ([cancel()]). By requesting values one at a time, the subscriber controls the data rate themselves;
    • lines 59–69: [onError] and [onComplete] signal the end of the stream, either due to an error or normally. [CountDownLatch] allows the main program to wait for this end;
  • line 9: The publisher delivers the values to each subscriber via a task of the specified executor—in this case, virtual threads (without an executor, it would use the shared pool, where waiting for the archive would block one of its few threads)—and maintains a buffer of up to 2 values for each subscriber;
  • lines 12–17: the publisher publishes a measurement every 200 ms using [submit], which returns an estimate of the delay: the largest number of values published but not yet consumed by a subscriber. When a subscriber’s buffer is full, [submit] waits for a slot to become available: measurement #5, ready at around 1,070 ms, is not published until 1,271 ms (line 14 of the results), when the archive has processed measurement #3. This is backpressure: the publisher is slowed down to the pace of the slowest subscriber. ([SubmissionPublisher] also offers [offer], which allows a value to be discarded instead of waiting);
  • the results show that the screen, which is fast, processes each measurement as soon as it is published and unsubscribes at measurement No. 4 (22.5 °C, lines 11–12), while the archive, which takes 500 ms per measurement, falls behind and receives all six measurements;
  • lines 18–22: [close()] signals the end of the stream: each subscriber still subscribed will receive [onComplete] after processing the values in its buffer (line 20). The program waits for the archive to end with the message [CountDownLatch].

The push model is suitable for sources that produce data at their own pace (sensors, events, messages) and for reactive processing chains; the pull model, which is simpler to write and read, is suitable for reading from a source on demand. With virtual threads, the pull model is usually sufficient.

docs.title: 9.10. Cache, switch back to the correct thread, and finish the operation yourself
9.10.1. A cache for asynchronous operations
docs.text:
A [CompletableFuture] is an object: each call to a method that returns one allocates at least one object on the heap, which the garbage collector must reclaim. This is negligible for I/O that lasts milliseconds, and the current garbage collectors in JVM handle short-lived objects very efficiently: Java does not have a “lightweight” variant of [CompletableFuture] (other languages do have one, for asynchronous methods called millions of times that most often already have their result).

For an asynchronous method that often already has the result, best practice is to cache the [CompletableFuture] objects themselves: a value that is already known is returned by a [CompletableFuture] that has already completed, without a new allocation, and multiple concurrent requests for the same value share the same ongoing operation. The [Async21.java] program applies this to an exchange rate service:

// a cache of CompletableFuture: an asynchronous operation that, in most cases, already has the result
void main() {
    var service = new ServiceTaux();
     // 1 - successive reads: only the first read of a currency queries the server
    for (String code : List.of("EUR", "USD", "EUR", "EUR", "USD", "GBP", "EUR")) {
        long debutLecture = System.nanoTime();
        BigDecimal taux = service.lireTaux(code).join();
        IO.println(String.format("%s : %6s lu en %3d ms", code, NumberFormat.getInstance().format(taux),
                (System.nanoTime() - debutLecture) / 1_000_000));
    }
    IO.println("1 - accès au serveur : " + service.nbAccesServeur() + ", lectures : " + service.nbLectures());

     // 2 - three simultaneous reads of the same currency: they share the same operation
    List<CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> lectures = List.of(
            service.lireTaux("CHF"), service.lireTaux("CHF"), service.lireTaux("CHF"));
    IO.println("2 - même objet : " + (lectures.get(0) == lectures.get(2))
            + ", taux : " + NumberFormat.getInstance().format(lectures.get(0).join())
            + ", accès au serveur : " + service.nbAccesServeur() + ", lectures : " + service.nbLectures());

     // 3 - a failed operation is not kept in the cache
    try {
        service.lireTaux("XYZ").join();
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        IO.println("3 - " + e.getCause().getMessage() + ", devises en cache : " + service.devisesEnCache());
    }
}

class ServiceTaux {
     // The cache contains the CompletableFuture themselves, whether completed or in progress
    private final Map<String, CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final AtomicInteger nbAccesServeur = new AtomicInteger();
    private final AtomicInteger nbLectures = new AtomicInteger();

    CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> lireTaux(String code) {
        nbLectures.incrementAndGet();
         // If the currency is in the cache, the existing CompletableFuture is returned: no object is created
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(code, this::lireTauxServeur);
    }

    private CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> lireTauxServeur(String code) {
        nbAccesServeur.incrementAndGet();
         // simulates a query to a remote server (300 ms)
        CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> lecture = new CompletableFuture<Void>()
                .completeOnTimeout(null, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
                .thenApply(rien -> switch (code) {
                    case "EUR" -> BigDecimal.ONE;
                    case "USD" -> new BigDecimal("1.17");
                    case "GBP" -> new BigDecimal("0.87");
                    case "CHF" -> new BigDecimal("0.94");
                    default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("devise inconnue : " + code);
                });
         // If the operation fails, it is removed from the cache so that a subsequent read can be retried
        return lecture.whenComplete((taux, e) -> {
            if (e != null) {
                cache.remove(code);
            }
        });
    }

    int nbAccesServeur() {
        return nbAccesServeur.get();
    }

    int nbLectures() {
        return nbLectures.get();
    }

    Set<String> devisesEnCache() {
        return new TreeSet<>(cache.keySet());
    }
}

> java Async21.java
EUR :      1 lu en 363 ms
USD :   1,17 lu en 300 ms
EUR :      1 lu en   0 ms
EUR :      1 lu en   0 ms
USD :   1,17 lu en   0 ms
GBP :   0,87 lu en 300 ms
EUR :      1 lu en   0 ms
1 - accès au serveur : 3, lectures : 7
2 - même objet : true, taux : 0,94, accès au serveur : 4, lectures : 10
3 - devise inconnue : XYZ, devises en cache : [CHF, EUR, GBP, USD]

Comments:

  • line 30: The cache associates each currency code with the [CompletableFuture] for its exchange rate, whether completed or still in progress. This is a [ConcurrentHashMap] (Chapter 8), because it can be used by multiple threads at the same time (the main thread, the timer thread that completes the reads);
  • Lines 34–38: [computeIfAbsent(clé, fonction)] returns the value associated with the key if it exists; otherwise, it calls the function, stores its result in the dictionary, and returns it. For a [ConcurrentHashMap], this operation is atomic: two threads that simultaneously request a currency that is not present trigger only a single access to the server;
  • lines 40–58: the simulated server query (300 ms). The continuation [thenApply] contains a [switch] expression on a string, whose branch [default] throws an exception for an unknown currency;
  • lines 52–57: In case of failure, the operation is removed from the cache so that a subsequent request for the same currency will query the server again instead of indefinitely returning the same failure. It is the [CompletableFuture] returned by [whenComplete] that is stored in the cache: it does not complete until after the action has been executed, which guarantees the caller that the cache is up to date when they receive the result;
  • lines 5–11: For the caller, nothing changes: it waits for the result with [join()]. The results show the three server accesses (300 ms each; slightly longer for the first one, during which JVM loads the necessary classes) and the four immediate responses from the cache;
  • lines 13–18: Three simultaneous requests for the Swiss franc exchange rate retrieve the same object and result in only one server access (line 10 of the results);
  • lines 20–25: the unknown currency resulted in a failure and is no longer in the cache (line 11).

docs.title: 9.10.2. Return to the GUI thread
docs.text:
The program [Async06.java] demonstrated that a continuation is executed, depending on the case, either by the thread that completes the operation or by a thread of the selected executor. In a graphical application (Swing, JavaFX), this matters: a graphical component can only be manipulated by the UI thread. Java has no mechanism that automatically returns the rest of the code to this thread; it is up to the program to request this, either by passing the correct executor to the continuation or by using the tools of the graphics library:

  • with Swing, *[SwingUtilities.invokeLater(action)] causes the action to be executed by the interface thread; the method reference [SwingUtilities::invokeLater] can serve as an executor for a continuation: [telechargement.thenAcceptAsync(page -> zoneTexte.setText(page), SwingUtilities::invokeLater)]. The [SwingWorker] class also provides a method, [doInBackground], which is executed by a background thread, and methods [process] and [done]*, which are executed by the interface’s thread;
  • along with JavaFX, [Platform.runLater(action)] serves the same purpose, and the classes [Task] and [Service] of [javafx.concurrent] encapsulate a background process along with its progress.

In all cases, the rule is the same: the UI thread must never wait ([join()], [get()], blocking I/O), otherwise the window freezes. The long-running task is executed by another thread (a virtual thread, for example), and only the final update of the components is handled by the interface thread.

docs.title: 9.10.3. Terminating a CompletableFuture Manually
docs.text:
Sometimes you may need to use a API that signals its events via listeners (Chapter 7), while the rest of the code is written using [CompletableFuture]. We saw the technique with [Async17.java]: create a “pending” [CompletableFuture] using its constructor, return it immediately, and terminate it yourself when needed:

  • [complete(valeur)] completes it successfully;
  • [completeExceptionally(exception)] terminates it unsuccessfully;
  • [cancel(false)] cancels it.

These three methods have no effect if [CompletableFuture] has already been completed ([complete] and [completeExceptionally] then produce [false]): the first one to complete it wins, which naturally resolves contention situations (such as a result and a timeout arriving at the same time). The program [Async22.java] waits for a thermometer—which notifies its listeners with each measurement—to reach a certain temperature:

// a CompletableFuture terminated “manually”: convert a API based on listeners into an asynchronous operation
final long debut = System.nanoTime();

void main() {
    var thermometre = new Thermometre();
    thermometre.demarrer();

     // 1 - wait for the first reading greater than or equal to 21 °C
    double mesure = attendreTemperature(thermometre, 21).join();
    afficher("1 - température atteinte : " + format(mesure) + " °C");

     // 2 - the same wait, limited to one second
    try {
        mesure = attendreTemperature(thermometre, 30).orTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).join();
        afficher("2 - température atteinte : " + format(mesure) + " °C");
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        afficher("2 - 30 °C non atteints en une seconde : " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
    thermometre.arreter();
}

// converts the thermometer’s notifications into a CompletableFuture
CompletableFuture<Double> attendreTemperature(Thermometre thermometre, double seuil) {
     // a CompletableFuture that you will terminate yourself
    CompletableFuture<Double> resultat = new CompletableFuture<>();
     // the listener terminates the QZXW2HTMLCQ9tcGxldGFibGVGdXR1cmUZQX when the threshold is reached
    DoubleConsumer ecouteur = temperature -> {
        if (temperature >= seuil) {
            resultat.complete(temperature);
        }
    };
    thermometre.ajouterEcouteur(ecouteur);
     // regardless of how it ends (threshold, timeout, cancellation), the listener is removed
    resultat.whenComplete((temperature, e) -> thermometre.retirerEcouteur(ecouteur));
     // The CompletableFuture is returned immediately; it will be terminated later
    return resultat;
}

// a thermometer that notifies its listeners every 200 ms (an “old-school” API)
class Thermometre {
    private final List<DoubleConsumer> ecouteurs = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    private final ScheduledExecutorService minuterie = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();
    private double temperature = 19;

    void ajouterEcouteur(DoubleConsumer ecouteur) {
        ecouteurs.add(ecouteur);
    }

    void retirerEcouteur(DoubleConsumer ecouteur) {
        ecouteurs.remove(ecouteur);
    }

    void demarrer() {
        minuterie.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {
            temperature += 0.5;
            IO.println("          mesure : " + format(temperature) + " °C");
            ecouteurs.forEach(ecouteur -> ecouteur.accept(temperature));
        }, 200, 200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    }

    void arreter() {
        minuterie.shutdown();
    }
}

// a real number in French format, without unnecessary decimal places
String format(double valeur) {
    return NumberFormat.getInstance().format(valeur);
}

// display showing the elapsed time since the start
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async22.java
          mesure : 19,5 °C
          mesure : 20 °C
          mesure : 20,5 °C
          mesure : 21 °C
  807 ms : 1 - température atteinte : 21 °C
          mesure : 21,5 °C
          mesure : 22 °C
          mesure : 22,5 °C
          mesure : 23 °C
          mesure : 23,5 °C
 1809 ms : 2 - 30 °C non atteints en une seconde : TimeoutException

Comments:

  • Lines 39–64: The thermometer, an “old-school” class: a [ScheduledExecutorService] increases the temperature by 0.5 °C every 200 ms and transmits it to its listeners, of type [DoubleConsumer] (a [Consumer] specialized for the [double] type). The list of listeners is a [CopyOnWriteArrayList], a list that can be modified by one thread (adding or removing a listener) while another thread iterates through it;
  • lines 22–37: the method that converts notifications into a [CompletableFuture]. It creates a temporary [CompletableFuture<Double>], registers a listener with the thermometer, and immediately returns the [CompletableFuture], which is not yet complete;
  • lines 27–31: With each measurement, the listener checks the threshold. When it is reached, it terminates the [CompletableFuture] with the temperature as the result. Subsequent measurements continue to call [complete], to no effect, until the listener is removed;
  • line 34: Regardless of how [CompletableFuture] ends (threshold reached, timeout, cancellation by the caller), [whenComplete] removes the listener. Without this, a listener whose threshold is never reached would remain registered indefinitely;
  • Lines 8–18: For the caller, waiting for a temperature is an asynchronous operation like any other: it waits for it with [join()] and sets a time limit on it with [orTimeout]. Since [orTimeout] terminates [CompletableFuture] itself (and not a copy), the action [whenComplete] on line 34 is executed, and the listener is removed.

A note of caution: the continuations attached to [CompletableFuture] are executed by the thread that calls [complete]—in this case, the thermometer thread—in the middle of its listener notification. If these continuations are lengthy, they should be written using the [xxxAsync] variants and an executor, or [CompletableFuture] should be terminated with [completeAsync(() -> valeur, executeur)] (Java 9), which causes the executor to call [complete].

docs.title: 9.11.1. Virtual threads and semaphores
docs.text:
[allOf] and one virtual thread per operation launch all operations simultaneously. This is not always desirable: to download 10,000 web pages, you don’t want to open 10,000 simultaneous connections to the same server. With platform threads, concurrency was limited by the size of the thread pool. With virtual threads, threads are not pooled (they are so inexpensive that one is created per task): access to the scarce resource is limited using a [Semaphore] (Chapter 8), whose permissions represent the number of concurrent operations allowed. The program [Async23.java] downloads nine pages, no more than three at a time:

// Processing a collection with a limited number of concurrent operations: virtual threads and semaphores
final AtomicInteger enCours = new AtomicInteger();

long debut;

void main() {
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    List<String> pages = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 9).mapToObj(i -> "page" + i + ".html").toList();
     // No more than 3 downloads at the same time: a semaphore with 3 permissions
    var autorisations = new Semaphore(3);
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
         // One virtual thread per page: they are inexpensive, so you can create as many as there are pages
        for (String page : pages) {
            executeur.submit(() -> {
                 // the thread waits for permission (without blocking the parent thread)
                autorisations.acquire();
                try {
                    telecharger(page);
                } finally {
                    autorisations.release();
                }
                return null;
            });
        }
    } // close() waits for all downloads to finish
    afficher("les " + pages.size() + " pages sont téléchargées");
}

void telecharger(String page) throws InterruptedException {
     // counter shared by concurrent operations: it is modified atomically
    int n = enCours.incrementAndGet();
    afficher("début de " + page + " (" + n + " en cours)");
     // Simulated download of a page
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    enCours.decrementAndGet();
    afficher("fin de " + page);
}

// display showing the elapsed time since the start and the thread executing the display
void afficher(String message) {
    Thread thread = Thread.currentThread();
    String nom = thread.isVirtual() ? "virtuel #" + thread.threadId() : thread.getName();
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms [%-11s] : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, nom, message));
}

Results:

> java Async23.java
   13 ms [virtuel #25]: Start of page2.html (2 in progress)
   13 ms [virtuel #27]: Start of page3.html (3 in progress)
   13 ms [virtuel #23]: Start of page1.html (1 in progress)
 1026 ms [virtuel #25]: end of page2.html
 1026 ms [virtuel #27]: end of page3.html
 1026 ms [virtuel #23]: end of page1.html
 1026 ms [virtuel #28]: Start of page4.html (1 in progress)
 1027 ms [virtuel #29]: start of page5.html (2 in progress)
 1027 ms [virtuel #30]: Start of page6.html (3 in progress)
 2027 ms [virtuel #29]: end of page5.html
 2027 ms [virtuel #30]: end of page6.html
 2028 ms [virtuel #31]: start of page7.html (1 in progress)
 2028 ms [virtuel #32]: start of page8.html (2 in progress)
 2027 ms [virtuel #28]: end of page4.html
 2028 ms [virtuel #33]: start of page9.html (3 in progress)
 3028 ms [virtuel #31]: end of page7.html
 3028 ms [virtuel #32]: end of page8.html
 3029 ms [virtuel #33]: end of page9.html
 3030 ms [main       ] : les 9 pages sont téléchargées

Comments:

  • line 10: a semaphore with 3 permissions;
  • lines 13–24: one virtual thread per page. The task is a lambda that ends with [return null;]: this is therefore a [Callable], whose method can throw controlled exceptions, which avoids having to handle the [InterruptedException] from [acquire] and [Thread.sleep] here;
  • Lines 16–21: Each thread waits for a permit ([acquire]), downloads its page, and then returns the permit ([release]) in a [finally], so that it is returned even if the download fails. A virtual thread waiting for authorization is detached from its host thread, just as during an I/O operation;
  • Lines 29–37: The counter [enCours], shared by the threads, is a [AtomicInteger] that has been atomically modified;
  • The results show three waves of three pages: as soon as one page is finished, another begins, and the number of downloads in progress never exceeds 3. The entire process takes 3 seconds instead of 9. When two threads write at nearly the same time, the order of the lines may vary from one execution to another, and a displayed time may even be slightly earlier than that of the previous line;
  • Each page has its own virtual thread (nos. 23 through 33; the numbers are shared by all threads in JVM, including the carrier threads, hence the gaps), but these nine virtual threads were executed by the machine’s only two carrier threads.

docs.title: 9.11.2. Producers / Consumers: BlockingQueue
docs.text:
The previous chapter introduced the producer/consumer model: producers place items into a queue, and consumers remove them. The [BlockingQueue<E>] interface is the tool for this: [put] places an item in the queue and waits—if the queue is bounded and full—for a slot to become available; [take] removes an element and waits—if the queue is empty—for one to arrive; [offer] and [poll] attempt the same thing without waiting (or with a delay). These waits are blocking; when executed by virtual threads, they do not block any system threads, and the blocking queue becomes the communication tool between asynchronous operations.

The program [Async24.java] has commands—generated every 50 ms—processed by two consumers, each of which takes 400 ms to process a command:

// producer/consumer with a blocking queue, executed by virtual threads
// the value that signals to consumers that there will be no more orders
static final int FIN = -1;
// a bounded queue: it contains at most 2 commands waiting to be processed
final BlockingQueue<Integer> file = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);
long debut;

void main() {
    debut = System.nanoTime();
     // the producer and two consumers work simultaneously
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        executeur.submit(() -> produire(8));
        executeur.submit(() -> consommer("C1"));
        executeur.submit(() -> consommer("C2"));
    }
    afficher("toutes les commandes ont été traitées");
}

// the producer: one order every 50 ms
Void produire(int nbCommandes) throws InterruptedException {
    for (int i = 1; i <= nbCommandes; i++) {
        Thread.sleep(50);
         // The producer places the order immediately if there is space in the queue
        if (file.offer(i)) {
            afficher("P  : commande " + i + " déposée");
        } else {
             // Queue full: the producer waits until a spot becomes available
            afficher("P  : file pleine, la commande " + i + " attend");
            file.put(i);
            afficher("P  : commande " + i + " déposée");
        }
    }
     // nothing more will be produced: the end token is placed
    file.put(FIN);
    afficher("P  : fin de la production");
    return null;
}

// A consumer: processing an order takes 400 ms
Void consommer(String nom) throws InterruptedException {
    while (true) {
         // take waits until there is an order in the queue
        int commande = file.take();
        if (commande == FIN) {
             // The end marker is placed back in the queue for the other consumer
            file.put(FIN);
            break;
        }
        afficher(nom + " : traitement de la commande " + commande);
        Thread.sleep(400);
    }
    afficher(nom + " : plus de commandes");
    return null;
}

// display showing the time elapsed since the start
void afficher(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async24.java
   58 ms : P  : commande 1 déposée
   62 ms : C1 : traitement de la commande 1
  118 ms : C2 : traitement de la commande 2
  119 ms : P  : commande 2 déposée
  169 ms : P  : commande 3 déposée
  220 ms : P  : commande 4 déposée
  271 ms : P  : file pleine, la commande 5 attend
  469 ms : P  : commande 5 déposée
  469 ms : C1 : traitement de la commande 3
  519 ms : C2 : traitement de la commande 4
  519 ms : P  : commande 6 déposée
  570 ms : P  : file pleine, la commande 7 attend
  870 ms : C1 : traitement de la commande 5
  870 ms : P  : commande 7 déposée
  920 ms : C2 : traitement de la commande 6
  920 ms : P  : commande 8 déposée
 1270 ms : C1 : traitement de la commande 7
 1271 ms : P  : fin de la production
 1320 ms : C2 : traitement de la commande 8
 1672 ms : C1 : plus de commandes
 1721 ms : C2 : plus de commandes
 1721 ms : toutes les commandes ont été traitées

Comments:

  • line 5: a [ArrayBlockingQueue] with capacity 2: it contains at most 2 pending commands;
  • Lines 11–15: The producer and the two consumers are executed by three virtual threads; the program waits for all three to finish using the executor’s [close()] method. The methods [produire] and [consommer] return [Void] and end with [return null;]: the lambdas on lines 12–14 are therefore [Callable], and the methods can declare [InterruptedException];
  • Lines 19–37: The producer attempts to submit each order using [offer]. If the queue is full, it signals this and waits for space using [put]: the producer is throttled to the consumers’ pace (lines 8–9 of the results). This is the benefit of a bounded queue: a producer that is too fast cannot fill up memory;
  • line 34: production is complete; the producer places a specific value, the end marker [FIN] (line 3), which the consumers will recognize. A blocking queue, in fact, has no way of signaling that it is “closed”;
  • Lines 39–54: Each consumer retrieves orders with [take]. An order is delivered to only one consumer: orders are distributed between C1 and C2 based on their availability. The consumer that receives the end token places it back in the queue for the other consumer, then stops;
  • as in the previous example, two lines displayed at nearly the same time may appear out of order.

docs.title: 9.12. Time: ScheduledExecutorService and Clock
docs.text:
Two tools complement those related to time:

  • a [ScheduledExecutorService] (Java 5) is an executor capable of running a task after a delay ([schedule]) or periodically ([scheduleAtFixedRate], at fixed intervals measured from the start of one execution to the next; [scheduleWithFixedDelay], with a fixed delay between the end of one execution and the start of the next). A periodic task is never executed twice at the same time: if an execution takes longer than the period, the next one is delayed. A single-threaded executor is obtained with [Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()];
  • the abstract class [java.time.Clock] (Java 8) represents the clock: it provides the current time and time zone. [Clock.systemDefaultZone()] is the system clock in the machine’s time zone. All [now()] methods of API, [java.time] ([LocalDateTime.now(horloge)], [Instant.now(horloge)]…) accept a clock. A class that depends on the time receives a [Clock] instead of calling [LocalDateTime.now()]: it can then be tested with a controlled clock.

The program [Async25.java] uses both:

// Time: ScheduledExecutorService and Clock
void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // 1 - one action every 500 ms, stopped after 2.2 seconds
    long debut = System.nanoTime();
    AtomicInteger nbTops = new AtomicInteger();
    try (ScheduledExecutorService planificateur = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()) {
         // scheduleAtFixedRate: first tick in 500 ms, then one tick every 500 ms
        ScheduledFuture<?> tops = planificateur.scheduleAtFixedRate(
                () -> IO.println(String.format("%6d ms : top n° %d",
                        (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, nbTops.incrementAndGet())),
                500, 500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
         // schedule: a single action, in 2.2 seconds, that stops the ticks
        ScheduledFuture<?> arret = planificateur.schedule(
                () -> tops.cancel(false), 2200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        arret.get();
        IO.println(String.format("%6d ms : minuterie arrêtée après %d tops",
                (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000, nbTops.get()));
    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
        IO.println("erreur : " + e.getCause());
    }

     // 2 - Clock: a class that depends on the time receives its clock instead of calling LocalDateTime.now()
    Clock matin = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-10-03T09:30:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    Clock soir = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-10-03T19:45:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    IO.println(new Accueil(matin).saluer("Pierre"));
    IO.println(new Accueil(soir).saluer("Pierre"));
    IO.println(new Accueil(Clock.systemDefaultZone()).saluer("Pierre") + " (horloge du système)");
}

// A class that depends on the current time
record Accueil(Clock horloge) {
    String saluer(String nom) {
        LocalDateTime maintenant = LocalDateTime.now(horloge);
        String formule = maintenant.getHour() < 18 ? "Bonjour" : "Bonsoir";
        String date = maintenant.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm"));
        return "[" + date + "] " + formule + " " + nom;
    }
}

Results:

> java Async25.java
   504 ms : top n° 1
  1003 ms : top n° 2
  1503 ms : top n° 3
  2003 ms : top n° 4
  2204 ms : minuterie arrêtée après 4 tops
[03/10/2026 09:30] Bonjour Pierre
[03/10/2026 19:45] Bonsoir Pierre
[03/10/2026 19:18] Bonsoir Pierre (horloge du système)

Comments:

  • Lines 8–11: [scheduleAtFixedRate(tâche, délai initial, période, unité)] runs the task for the first time after 500 ms, and then every 500 ms. It returns a [ScheduledFuture] and a [Future], which, among other things, allows future executions to be canceled. The top counter is a [AtomicInteger]: a lambda cannot modify a local variable;
  • Lines 13–15: [schedule(tâche, délai, unité)] executes a single task after 2.2 seconds: it cancels the tops. [arret.get()] waits for this task to finish. The beeps occurred at 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2 seconds, and the timer stops at 2.2 seconds, after 4 beeps;
  • lines 30–38: the record [Accueil] says “Good morning” or “Good evening” depending on the time. It receives its clock from its constructor instead of calling [LocalDateTime.now()]: this is an injected dependency, just as the [dao] layer is injected into the [metier] layer in Chapter 6;
  • Lines 23–27: [Clock.fixed(instant, fuseau)] returns a stopped clock, which always shows the same time: this allows us to verify the behavior of [Accueil] in the morning and evening without having to wait until evening. The last line uses the system clock (so the result depends on the execution time). For more sophisticated tests, you can write your own class derived from [Clock], which you can advance as desired. The [InstantSource] interface (Java 17), which returns only the current time, is an even lighter dependency when the time zone is irrelevant.

To measure a duration, do not use the clock (which can be adjusted during the measurement, for example, by synchronizing the system time) but use [System.nanoTime()], as shown in the examples in this chapter.

docs.title: 9.13. Structured Concurrency (Overview)
docs.text:
In the previous examples, the operations launched by a program run independently of it: if one fails, the others continue; if the code that launched them is interrupted, they continue as well; and nothing forces that code to wait for them to finish. Structured concurrency proposes treating a group of subtasks as a single unit: they are launched within a scope, the scope waits for them to complete, and if one fails, the others are canceled. The [StructuredTaskScope] class implements this idea using virtual threads. It has been available since Java 21 but is still in “preview” status in Java 25: its API may still change, and a program that uses it must be compiled and run with the [--enable-preview] option. It is therefore not included in the course exercises; the following code (file [apercu/ConcurrenceStructuree.txt], to be copied into a file named [ConcurrenceStructuree.java] to test it) gives an idea of how it works:

// Structured concurrency: API in preview in Java 25
// Execution: java --enable-preview ConcurrenceStructuree.java
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner;
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Subtask;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // 1 - two subtasks that must both succeed
    try (var portee = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
        Subtask<Integer> angers = portee.fork(() -> lireTemperature("Angers", 1000));
        Subtask<Integer> brest = portee.fork(() -> lireTemperature("Brest", 500));
         // join waits for the subtasks to finish; if one fails, the other is aborted
         // and `join` throws an exception
        portee.join();
        IO.println("Angers : " + angers.get() + ", Brest : " + brest.get());
    }
     // 2 - the first response is sufficient: the other subtasks are canceled
    try (var portee = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Integer>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow())) {
        portee.fork(() -> lireTemperature("miroir-paris", 800));
        portee.fork(() -> lireTemperature("miroir-lyon", 300));
        IO.println("première réponse : " + portee.join());
    }
}

int lireTemperature(String ville, long duree) throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.sleep(duree);
    return 10 + ville.length();
}

Results:

> java --enable-preview ConcurrenceStructuree.java
Angers : 16, Brest : 15
première réponse : 21

Comments:

  • line 8: [StructuredTaskScope.open()] opens a scope, declared in a [try] with a resource; closing it ensures that no subtasks survive it;
  • Lines 9–10: [fork] launches a subtask in a new virtual thread and returns a [Subtask];
  • line 13: [join()] waits for all subtasks to finish. Under the default policy, if a subtask fails, the others are canceled (aborted) and [join()] throws an exception;
  • line 14: the results of the subtasks, all of which have completed;
  • Lines 17–21: Another policy, provided by [Joiner]: the first successful subtask returns the result of [join()], and the others are canceled. This is the structured equivalent of [anyOf], but the losing requests are actually terminated.

docs.title: 9.14. Application: Tax Calculation with Virtual Threads
docs.text:
The program [Async26.java] brings together several tools from this chapter related to the tax calculation in the main thread. It reads the tax brackets from the file [DataImpot.txt], which has already been used, and reads a list of taxpayers from the file [contribuables.txt]:

o 2 60000
o 3 60000
n 0 60000
n 2 25000
o 5 120000
x 1 20000
o 1 -5

(each line contains: married [o/n], number of children, annual salary), calculates each person’s tax, and writes the results to the file [resultats.txt]. Both reads are performed concurrently by virtual threads, and the entire process is limited to 10 seconds.

// Application: tax calculation, with input/output performed by virtual threads
// - tax brackets are read from [DataImpot.txt], taxpayers from [contribuables.txt]
// - the results are written to [resultats.txt]
// a valid taxpayer record: married (y/n), number of children, annual salary
static final Pattern CONTRIBUABLE = Pattern.compile("([on])\\s+(\\d+)\\s+(\\d+)");

void main() {
    Path resultats = Path.of("resultats.txt");
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
         // Both input files are read simultaneously by two virtual threads
        Future<List<TrancheImpot>> lectureTranches = executeur.submit(
                () -> chargerTranches(Path.of("DataImpot.txt")));
        Future<List<String>> lectureContribuables = executeur.submit(
                () -> Files.readAllLines(Path.of("contribuables.txt")));
         // the calculation waits for both files to be read, then writes the results
        Future<Integer> traitement = executeur.submit(
                () -> calculerImpots(lectureTranches.get(), lectureContribuables.get(), resultats));
        try {
             // The entire process is limited to 10 seconds
            int nbResultats = traitement.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            IO.println(nbResultats + " lignes écrites dans [" + resultats + "] :");
            IO.print(Files.readString(resultats));
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            traitement.cancel(true);
            IO.println("traitement abandonné : délai dépassé");
        }
    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
         // An error in one read operation is wrapped twice: by the read operation itself and by the calculation that was waiting for it
        Throwable cause = e.getCause();
        while (cause instanceof ExecutionException) {
            cause = cause.getCause();
        }
        IO.println("erreur : " + cause.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + cause.getMessage());
    } catch (IOException | InterruptedException e) {
        IO.println("erreur : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

// reads the tax brackets (range: coeffR:coeffN, decimal point)
List<TrancheImpot> chargerTranches(Path fichier) throws IOException {
    try (Stream<String> lignes = Files.lines(fichier)) {
        return lignes.filter(ligne -> !ligne.isBlank()).map(TrancheImpot::parse).toList();
    }
}

// calculates the tax for each taxpayer and writes the results
int calculerImpots(List<TrancheImpot> tranches, List<String> contribuables, Path sortie) throws IOException {
    try (BufferedWriter ecrivain = Files.newBufferedWriter(sortie)) {
        for (String ligne : contribuables) {
            Matcher champs = CONTRIBUABLE.matcher(ligne.trim());
            String resultat = champs.matches()
                    ? "impôt = " + calculerImpot(tranches, champs.group(1).equals("o"),
                            Integer.parseInt(champs.group(2)), Integer.parseInt(champs.group(3))) + " €"
                    : "ligne incorrecte";
            ecrivain.write(String.format("%-12s : %s", ligne, resultat));
            ecrivain.newLine();
        }
    }
    return contribuables.size();
}

// tax calculation (2004 tax schedule based on 2003 income, retained for the fiscal year)
int calculerImpot(List<TrancheImpot> tranches, boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire) {
    BigDecimal nbParts = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbEnfants).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
            .add(BigDecimal.valueOf(marie ? 2 : 1));
    if (nbEnfants >= 3) {
        nbParts = nbParts.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
    }
    BigDecimal revenu = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salaire));
    BigDecimal quotient = revenu.divide(nbParts, MathContext.DECIMAL64);
     // the first tax bracket whose threshold exceeds the family quotient, otherwise the last one
    TrancheImpot tranche = tranches.stream()
            .filter(t -> quotient.compareTo(t.limite()) <= 0)
            .findFirst()
            .orElse(tranches.getLast());
    return tranche.coeffR().multiply(revenu).subtract(tranche.coeffN().multiply(nbParts)).intValue();
}

// a tax bracket
record TrancheImpot(BigDecimal limite, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
    static TrancheImpot parse(String ligne) {
        String[] champs = ligne.split(":");
        return new TrancheImpot(new BigDecimal(champs[0]), new BigDecimal(champs[1]),
                new BigDecimal(champs[2]));
    }
}

Results:

> java Async26.java
7 lignes écrites dans [resultats.txt] :
o 2 60000    : impôt = 4282 €
o 3 60000    : impôt = 2959 €
n 0 60000    : impôt = 11519 €
n 2 25000    : impôt = 792 €
o 5 120000   : impôt = 11109 €
x 1 20000    : ligne incorrecte
o 1 -5       : ligne incorrecte

The same program, run in a folder where the file [DataImpot.txt] is missing:

> java Async26.java
erreur : NoSuchFileException : DataImpot.txt

Comments:

  • lines 11–14: The two input files are read simultaneously by two virtual threads using standard blocking read methods ([Files.lines], [Files.readAllLines]);
  • lines 16–17: The calculation is a third task, which begins by waiting for the two reads using [get()]. These waits block a virtual thread, which incurs no cost;
  • lines 18–26: The main program waits for the result for up to 10 seconds. After that, it aborts the process (which terminates its virtual thread) and reports the error;
  • lines 27–36: Errors are handled in a single location within the main program. A read error (missing file, incorrect number) is stored in the [Future] associated with the read operation; the [get()] from the calculation rethrows it into a [ExecutionException], which in turn becomes the exception from the calculation, rethrown by the [get] from the main program into a second [ExecutionException]. The loop in lines 30–32 traces back to the original cause (second result). This is the drawback of dependent tasks; structured concurrency, as described in the previous paragraph, will eliminate this issue;
  • lines 39–44: reading the brackets, using a [Stream] that skips empty lines;
  • lines 46–60: processing taxpayers. Each line is validated by the regular expression in line 5: a [o] or a [n], followed by two positive integers separated by spaces ([\s+]). The parentheses define three groups, which [group(1)], [group(2)], and [group(3)] return once [matches()] has verified that the entire line matches the expression. An incorrect line ([x] instead of [o/n], negative salary) is flagged as such;
  • Lines 62–77: tax calculation, in [BigDecimal]. Dividing the income by the number of shares may not be exact: this is done with a precision of 16 significant digits ([MathContext.DECIMAL64]). The first tax bracket whose threshold is greater than or equal to the family quotient is determined by a flow; [orElse(tranches.getLast())] returns the last bracket if none of the others apply. [intValue()] rounds the tax down to the nearest euro;
  • the results provide the control values for the red thread: €4,282 for a married couple with 2 children and a salary of €60,000, €2,959 with 3 children, and €11,519 for a single person without children.

The calculation itself is synchronous: it performs no I/O and takes a few microseconds. It would be pointless—and even harmful—to offload it to another thread. Only tasks that involve waiting are made asynchronous.

docs.title: 9.15. The Golden Rules
docs.text:
Let’s summarize the rules of asynchronous programming in Java:

  • to wait, do not block a system thread: a wait (I/O, timeout, or other operation) is performed either in a virtual thread or by attaching a continuation to a [CompletableFuture];
  • for new code, prefer virtual threads: write blocking, sequential, and readable code (loops, [try / catch], ordinary local variables), executed by [Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()]; one virtual thread per task, never use a pool of virtual threads;
  • Use [CompletableFuture] to compose operations, or to use a API that returns [CompletableFuture] ([HttpClient.sendAsync], reactive libraries); We then choose the continuation executor ([xxxAsync(..., executeur)]) and never execute a blocking operation in the shared pool;
  • no [join()] or [get()] in a continuation or in a GUI thread: these waits block the thread executing them. They belong in the main program or in a virtual thread;
  • Virtual threads are used for waits, not computations: for computations, use a platform-specific thread pool sized according to the number of processors, or parallel streams;
  • Limit access to scarce resources using a [Semaphore], not by the size of a thread pool;
  • Cancellation is cooperative: a task is canceled via [Future.cancel(true)], which interrupts its thread; an interrupted task terminates gracefully; a [InterruptedException] is never masked (it is either propagated or the interrupt flag is reset). And remember that [CompletableFuture.cancel] does not interrupt anything;
  • limit wait times: [orTimeout], [completeOnTimeout], [get(délai, unité)]; and terminate the operation itself if the wait is abandoned;
  • start first, then wait: to run multiple independent operations simultaneously, start them all and then wait for them ([allOf], [invokeAll], the executor’s [close] method);
  • A launched operation must be waited on or monitored: a forgotten operation hides its exceptions ([exceptionally], [whenComplete] to handle them); by tracing back a [CompletionException] or a [ExecutionException], we seek the root cause.

The following table summarizes the equivalences between the world of platform threads and blocking waits (previous chapter), that of [CompletableFuture], and that of virtual threads:

Platform threads, blocking waitsCompletableFutureVirtual threads[Thread.sleep(1000)] (blocks the thread)[new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, 1, SECONDS)][Thread.sleep(1000)] (releases the carrier)[thread.start()] followed by [thread.join()][supplyAsync(...)] followed by [join()] or a continuation[executeur.submit(...)] followed by [get()]Wait for multiple threads ([join] in a loop)[allOf(...)], [anyOf(...)][invokeAll(...)], [ExecutorCompletionService], [close()]Recall methods ([CompletionHandler])[thenApply], [thenCompose], [thenCombine]The code following the blocking call[try / catch] around [get()] ([ExecutionException])[exceptionally], [handle], [whenComplete][try / catch] (regular)[thread.interrupt()][cancel(...)] (does not interrupt anything)[future.cancel(true)] (interrupts the thread)[future.get(délai, unité)][orTimeout(...)], [completeOnTimeout(...)][future.get(délai, unité)]fixed-size thread poolcontinuation executor [xxxAsync][Semaphore][BlockingQueue] (blocks the thread)[Flow], [SubmissionPublisher][BlockingQueue] (releases the carrier)[ScheduledExecutorService][completeOnTimeout], [delayedExecutor][Thread.sleep] in a loop

The following chapters will apply these rules: database access using JDBC (Chapter 10) and Hibernate (Chapter 11), whose API threads are blocking and work naturally with virtual threads, the TCP server, which serves each client via a virtual thread, and the [HttpClient] client (Chapter 12); Spring Boot web services, where the Tomcat server can process each request via a virtual thread; and their clients (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 4.1.1. Overview
docs.text:
We will now explore object-oriented programming through examples. An object is an entity that contains data defining its state (referred to as fields, attributes, etc.) and functions (referred to as methods). An object is created based on a template called a class. For example, a class named [C1] declares two fields, [Type1 p1;] and [Type2 p2;], and two methods, [Type3 m3(...) { ... }] and [Type4 m4(...) { ... }], all enclosed within the curly braces of the declaration [public class C1 { ... }].

Starting with class [C1], you can create many objects such as [o1], [o2], … All of them will have the fields [p1], [p2], … and the methods [m3], [m4], … However, they will have different values for their [pi] fields, thus each having its own unique state. If [o1] is an object of type [C1], [o1.p1] refers to the [p1] field of [o1], and [o1.m3(...)] refers to thecall to the [m3] method of [o1].

Let’s consider an initial object model: the class [Personne].

docs.title: 4.1.2. A program consisting of multiple files
docs.text:
In the examples from the previous chapter, a program fit into a single source file. From now on, a program can consist of multiple source files: one class per file, plus the main program. In Java, a public class must be placed in a file that bears its name: the public class [Personne] is in the file [Personne.java]. We store the files for a single program in a folder—in this case, the [Personnes] folder within the [04-classes] folder:

Personnes/
  Personne.java     la classe Personne
  Main.java         le programme principal

Starting with Java 22, the source code launcher—which we already used in the previous chapter—can run a program consisting of multiple files: the command [java Main.java], entered in the [Personnes] folder, compiles the file [Main.java] in memory, then, on demand, the other files in the folder that it needs—in this case, [Personne.java]—and runs the program. No compiled files are written to disk. You can also explicitly compile the files using the [javac] compiler, which writes a [.class] file (intermediate code, or “bytecode”) per class, and then run the program with the command [java], specifying where to find the compiled classes (option [-cp], the “classpath”):

> javac -d classes *.java
> ls classes
Main.class
Personne.class
> java -cp classes Main
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

The multi-file launcher is sufficient for the programs in this chapter, which use only the classes from JDK. When a program requires external libraries, we will use a Maven project, as introduced in Chapter 2: Maven downloads the libraries, compiles the project, and runs it. The files in this chapter can be opened as-is in IntelliJ, IDEA, or VS Code.

docs.title: 4.1.3. Definition of the Person Class
docs.text:
The definition of the [Personne] class in the source file [Personne.java] will be as follows:

public class Personne {
     // attributes (fields)
    private String prenom = "";
    private String nom = "";
    private int age;

     // method
    public void initialise(String p, String n, int age) {
        this.prenom = p;
        this.nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // method
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • line 1: the class is public ([public]): it can be used by all other classes. It does not belong to any package, or more precisely, it belongs to the unnamed package; packages are described at the end of the chapter;
  • Lines 3–5: the class’s three fields. The two strings are initialized with the empty string: otherwise, they would be [null] when the object is created (an uninitialized object-type field is [null], a numeric field is 0, and a Boolean field is [false]);
  • lines 8–12: a method that sets the object’s state;
  • lines 15–17: a method that displays the object’s state. [IO] is the Java 25 console I/O class we used in the previous chapter.

Here we have the definition of a class—that is, a data type. When we create variables of this type, we call them objects or class instances. A class is therefore a template from which objects are constructed. By convention, a class name begins with a capital letter ([Personne]), while a field or method name begins with a lowercase letter ([prenom], [initialise]).

The members of a class can be data (fields) or methods (functions). These members can be accompanied by one of the following keywords:

KeywordAccess[private]A private member is accessible only by the class’s internal methods(none)If no keyword is specified, the member is accessible via any method of a class in the same package. This is the default access, known as “package access.”[protected]A protected member is accessible by methods of classes in the same package and by methods of derived classes (see the concept of inheritance below).[public]A public member is accessible by any method, whether or not it is defined within the class

In general, a class’s data is declared private, while its methods are declared public. This means that the user of an object (the programmer):

  • will not have direct access to the object’s private data;
  • can call the object’s public methods, including those that provide access to its private data.

The order in which the members [private], [protected], and [public] are declared is arbitrary. Note that the default access is not private: a field declared without a keyword is visible to all classes in the package. Therefore, you must remember to write [private].

docs.title: 4.1.4. The method initializes
docs.text:
What is the role of the method [initialise]? Because [nom], [prenom], and [age] are private members of the [Personne] class, a statement like [p1.prenom = "Jean";], written in the main program, is invalid. The compiler rejects it:

> java Main.java
Main.java:4: error: prenom has private access in Personne
    p1.prenom = "Jean";
      ^
1 error
error: compilation failed

The compiler message is in English: JDK has no French translation for its messages. It specifies the file and line number of the error, then marks it with a circumflex accent. We need to initialize an object of type [Personne] via a public method. This is the role of the [initialise] method. We will write [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);]. This syntax is valid because [initialise] is publicly accessible.

docs.title: 4.1.5. The new operator
docs.text:
However, something is still missing. The declaration [Personne p1;] declares [p1] as a reference to an object of type *[Personne]*. This object does not yet exist, so *[p1] is not initialized. When we then write [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], we call the method [initialise] of the object referenced by [p1]. However, this object does not exist, and the compiler reports the error: the local variable [p1]* has not been assigned a value.

> java Main.java
Main.java:4: error: variable p1 might not have been initialized
    p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    ^
1 error
error: compilation failed

If we write [Personne p1 = null;] followed by [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], we explicitly indicate with the keyword [null] that the variable [p1] does not yet reference any object. The compiler accepts the program, but at runtime, the method call triggers a [NullPointerException] exception:

> java Main.java
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "Personne.initialise(String, String, int)" because "<local1>" is null
    at Main.main(Main.java:4)

Starting with Java 14, the exception message specifies the operation that failed; [<local1>] refers to the local variable [p1], whose name was not retained by the in-memory compilation. For [p1] to reference an object, you must write [Personne p1 = new Personne();].

This creates an object of type [Personne] that has not yet been initialized: its fields have their default values—in this case, the empty string for [nom] and [prenom], and 0 for [age]. Now that [p1] references an object, the initialization statement for this object, [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], is valid.

docs.title: 4.1.6. The this keyword
docs.text:
Let’s look at the code for the [initialise] method:

    public void initialise(String p, String n, int age) {
        this.prenom = p;
        this.nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

The statement [this.prenom = p;] means that the field [prenom] of the current object ([this]) is assigned the value [p]. The keyword [this] refers to the current object—the one on which the method is executed. How do we know this? Let’s look at how the object referenced by [p1] is initialized in the calling program: [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);]. It is the method [initialise] of the object [p1] that is called. When, within this method, the object [this] is referenced, it actually refers to the object [p1].

When a method of an object references a field [a] of that object, the notation [this.a] is implied: the method [initialise] could have written [prenom = p;] and [nom = n;]. You must use [this] explicitly when there is a conflict of identifiers. This is the case with the statement [this.age = age;] (line 11), where [age] refers to both a field of the current object and the parameter [age] received by the method. In the method, the name [age] alone refers to the parameter; the field must be referred to as [this.age].

docs.title: 4.1.7. A Test Program
docs.text:
Here is a short test program. It is written in the source file [Main.java]:

// the main program
void main() {
     // a Person object
    Personne p1 = new Personne();
    p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    p1.identifie();
}
  • Line 2: The method [main] is the program’s entry point. As in the previous chapter, it is written without an enclosing class: the file [Main.java] is a compact source file (see the following paragraph);
  • line 4: creation of a [Personne] object referenced by [p1]. Since the [Personne] class belongs to the same package (the unnamed package), it is recognized without an import statement;
  • Line 5: Initialization of the object;
  • line 6: display of its status.

Results:

> java Main.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.8. Compact source files
docs.text:
For a short example, a folder containing multiple files is unnecessarily large. As in the previous chapter, we will therefore write a compact source file (Java 25): a file that contains the method [void main()], possibly other methods and fields, and the classes the program needs. We run it using the source code launcher: [java Classes01.java].

It is important to understand how the compiler processes such a file. It wraps it in an implicit class, which bears the file’s name ([Classes01]): the file’s methods and fields become members of this class, and the classes declared in the file become nested classes of this implicit class. The explicit compilation of the file demonstrates this:

> javac -d classes Classes01.java
> ls classes
Classes01$Personne.class
Classes01.class

The full name of the class [Personne] in the file [Classes01.java] is therefore [Classes01$Personne]. This has two consequences that we will encounter in the examples:

  • a class and the classes it contains share their private members: the method [main] in a compact file has access to the private fields of the classes in that file. To ensure that a private field is inaccessible from outside its class, you must, as in the file [Personnes], place the class in its own file;
  • An ordinary nested class is an internal class: its objects are bound to an object of the enclosing class. This is not apparent as long as the objects are created by methods in the file, but a static method (see the section on class members) cannot create them. We then declare the nested class [static]. Records and interfaces, discussed later, are always static.

Finally, a compact file automatically imports all public classes from the [java.base] module: [List], [ArrayList], [BigDecimal], [Objects]… can be used there without the [import] clause. This is not the case for a regular file such as [Personne.java], as we will see.

docs.title: 4.1.9. Another method is initialized: overloading
docs.text:
Let’s continue to consider the class [Personne] and add a second method to it: [initialise]. The program [Classes01.java] is as follows:

// overload of the initialize method
void main() {
    Personne p1 = new Personne();
    p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    p1.identifie();
    Personne p2 = new Personne();
    p2.initialise(p1);
    p2.identifie();
}

// the Person class is declared after the main method
class Personne {
     // attributes
    private String prenom = "";
    private String nom = "";
    private int age;

     // initialization using three values
    public void initialise(String p, String n, int age) {
        prenom = p;
        nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // initialization from another person
    public void initialise(Personne p) {
        prenom = p.prenom;
        nom = p.nom;
        age = p.age;
    }

     // the person's identity
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • lines 2–9: the main program;
  • line 12: the class [Personne] is declared after the method [main]. It is not public: in a compact file, this is unnecessary;
  • lines 19–23: the [initialise] method from the previous paragraph;
  • lines 26–30: a second method, [initialise].

We now have two methods named [initialise]: this is valid as long as they accept different parameters (in number or type). The method [initialise] is said to be overloaded. The compiler chooses which method to call based on the actual parameters: [p1.initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] (line 4) calls the first one, and [p2.initialise(p1)] (line 7) calls the second one. The return type alone is not sufficient to distinguish between two methods: two methods with the same name and the same parameters that differ only in their return type would be rejected.

The parameter of the second method is a reference ([p]) to a person. The fields of the person ([p]) are then assigned to the current object ([this]). Note that the method [initialise] has direct access to the fields of the object [p] even though they are private (lines 27–29). This is always true: a method of a class [C] has access to the private members of all objects of the same class [C].

Results:

> java Classes01.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.10. Constructors of the Person class
docs.text:
A constructor is a method that bears the name of the class and is called when the object is created. It is generally used to initialize the object. It is a method that can accept parameters but does not return a value. Its declaration is not preceded by any type (not even [void]).

If a class [C] has a constructor that accepts n parameters, the declaration and initialization of an object of this class can be done in the form [C objet = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);], or in two steps: [C objet;], followed later by [objet = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);].

When a class [C] has one or more constructors, one of these constructors must be used to create an object of that class. If a class [C] has no constructors, it has a default constructor with no parameters that does nothing. The object’s fields then retain their initial values. This is what happened in the previous programs, where we had written [new Personne()].

The program [Classes02.java] provides three constructors for the class [Personne]:

// constructors of the Person class
void main() {
    Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    p1.identifie();
    Personne p2 = new Personne(p1);
    p2.identifie();
    Personne p3 = new Personne();
    p3.identifie();
}

class Personne {
     // attributes
    private String prenom;
    private String nom;
    private int age;

     // main constructor
    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // copy constructor: it calls the primary constructor
    public Personne(Personne p) {
        this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age);
    }

     // parameterless constructor: it also calls the primary constructor
    public Personne() {
        this("?", "?", 0);
    }

     // person's identity
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • lines 18–22: the “main” constructor initializes the three fields. Since its parameters have the same names as the fields, the fields are distinguished using [this];
  • lines 25–27: the copy constructor. The statement [this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age);] calls the constructor of the same class, which accepts three parameters: [String], [String], and [int]. This is referred to as chained constructors. As a result, the initialization code is written only once;
  • Lines 30–32: the parameterless constructor, which is also chained to the main constructor. Since the class has declared constructors, it no longer has a default constructor: if you want to be able to write [new Personne()], you must declare it;
  • Lines 13–15: The fields are no longer initialized when they are declared; all constructors—either directly or through chaining—assign a value to them.

The call [this(...)] to another constructor can only be made within a constructor. Up to Java 24, it had to be the first statement; since Java 25, statements that do not use the object being constructed (to verify or prepare parameters, for example) may precede it. We could also have constructors call a method such as [initialise]; however, chaining is preferable: the initialization code is in a single location, and a constructor should not call a method that a derived class might override—we’ll see why.

Results:

> java Classes02.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[?, ?, 0]

docs.title: 4.1.11. Object References
docs.text:
We use the [Personne] class from the previous program, omitting its parameterless constructor but including the [initialise(String, String, int)] method from the beginning of the chapter. The test program becomes the following [Classes03.java]:

// object references
void main() {
     // p1
    Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    IO.print("p1="); p1.identifie();
     // p2 refers to the same object as p1
    Personne p2 = p1;
    IO.print("p2="); p2.identifie();
     // p3 refers to an object that is a copy of the object referred to by p1
    Personne p3 = new Personne(p1);
    IO.print("p3="); p3.identifie();
     // The state of the object referenced by p1 is changed
    p1.initialise("Micheline", "Benoît", 67);
    IO.print("p1="); p1.identifie();
     // Since p2 = p1, the object referenced by p2 has changed state
    IO.print("p2="); p2.identifie();
     // p3 does not reference the same object as p1: the object referenced by p3 has not changed
    IO.print("p3="); p3.identifie();
     // Are p1 and p2 the same reference? What about p1 and p3?
    IO.println("p1 == p2 : " + (p1 == p2) + ", p1 == p3 : " + (p1 == p3));
}

class Personne {
     // attributes
    private String prenom;
    private String nom;
    private int age;

     // constructors
    public Personne(String prenom, String nom, int age) {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public Personne(Personne p) {
        this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age);
    }

     // initialization
    public void initialise(String p, String n, int age) {
        prenom = p;
        nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // person’s identity
    public void identifie() {
        IO.println("[" + prenom + ", " + nom + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}

The [IO.print] method (lines 5, 8, …) writes its parameter without wrapping to the next line. Results:

> java Classes03.java
p1=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p2=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p2=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1 == p2 : true, p1 == p3 : false

When the variable [p1] is declared via [Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);] (line 4), [p1] references the object [Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] but is not the object itself. In C, this would be referred to as a pointer—that is, the address of the created object. If we then write [p1 = null;], it is not the object [Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] that is modified; rather, it is the reference [p1] that changes its value. The object will be “lost” if it is not referenced by any other variable: the memory it occupies will later be reclaimed by the Java virtual machine’s garbage collector.

When we write [Personne p2 = p1;] (line 7), we initialize the reference [p2]: it “points” to the same object (it refers to the same object) as the reference [p1]. Thus, if the object “pointed to” (or referenced) by [p1] is modified, the object referenced by [p2] is also modified (lines 5–6 of the results).

When [Personne p3 = new Personne(p1);] is written (line 10), a new object, [Personne], is created. This new object will be referenced by [p3]. If you modify the object referenced by [p1], you do not modify the one referenced by [p3] (line 7 of the results).

Finally, on line 20, the operator [==], applied to two object references, indicates whether they refer to the same object: [p1] and [p2] refer to the same object, while [p1] and [p3] refer to two different objects, although they have the same content (line 8 of the results). We will see later how to compare the contents of two objects using the [equals] method.

docs.title: 4.1.12. Passing Object Reference Parameters
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we saw that Java passes method parameters by value: the method receives a copy of the actual parameter’s value. Let’s see what this means when the parameter is an object reference. To do this, we’ll use the [StringBuilder] class from JDK. A [String] object cannot be modified: an operation such as [s.toUpperCase()] returns a new [String] object. An object of type [StringBuilder], on the other hand, is a mutable string: its method [append] adds characters to the string without creating a new object.

The program [Classes04.java] is as follows:

// passing parameters of the object reference type
void main() {
    StringBuilder sb0 = new StringBuilder("essai0"), sb1 = new StringBuilder("essai1");
    IO.println("Dans fonction appelante avant appel : sb0=" + sb0 + ", sb1=" + sb1);
    StringBuilder sb2 = changeStringBuilder(sb0, sb1);
    IO.println("Dans fonction appelante après appel : sb0=" + sb0 + ", sb1=" + sb1 + ", sb2=" + sb2);
}

// the called function
StringBuilder changeStringBuilder(StringBuilder sbf0, StringBuilder sbf1) {
    IO.println("Début fonction appelée : sbf0=" + sbf0 + ", sbf1=" + sbf1);
