Pattern filtering is well-suited for data hierarchies (records) on which one wishes to write processing logic external to that data.

docs.title: 4.14. Handling the null value
docs.text:
Any reference-type variable can have the value [null], and using a null reference causes the [NullPointerException] exception, the most common runtime error in Java. Unlike other languages such as C# or Kotlin, the Java compiler does not distinguish between types that can be [null] and those that cannot. However, the JDK and libraries provide several tools to mitigate this risk:

  • the [Optional<T>] class (Java 8), the return type of a method that may return nothing;
  • the methods of the [Objects] class: [requireNonNull] to reject [null] at the entry point of a method or constructor, and [requireNonNullElse] to provide a default value;
  • annotations that document intent and are verified by certain analysis tools. The most recent ones, proposed by a group of vendors (Google, JetBrains, Spring…), are those from the JSpecify library: [@Nullable] on a type that can be [null], and [@NullMarked] on a class or package to indicate that other types cannot be. Spring Framework 7, which we will be using, employs them. They require a library, so we will not use them in this chapter.

The program [Classes26.java] demonstrates the first two:

// null handling: Optional, Objects.requireNonNull...
void main() {
    Personne jean = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont");
    jean.setSecondPrenom("Marie");
    Personne[] personnes = { jean, new Personne("Paul", "Martin") };
    for (Personne p : personnes) {
         // a default value when the reference is null
        String second = Objects.requireNonNullElse(p.getSecondPrenom(), "(aucun)");
         // an explicit check
        String longueur = p.getSecondPrenom() == null ? "null" : String.valueOf(p.getSecondPrenom().length());
        IO.println(p.getPrenom() + " : second prénom=" + second + ", longueur=" + longueur);
    }

     // a method that may return nothing: it returns an Optional<Person>
    Optional<Personne> trouvee = chercher(personnes, "Durand");
    IO.println("Durand trouvé : " + trouvee.isPresent());
    IO.println(trouvee.map(Personne::getPrenom).orElse("Durand : personne non trouvée"));
     // we check for the presence of a value before using it
    trouvee = chercher(personnes, "Martin");
    if (trouvee.isPresent()) {
        IO.println("Martin : " + trouvee.get().getPrenom());
    }
     // ifPresent: the action is performed only if a value is present
    chercher(personnes, "Dupont").ifPresent(p -> p.setSecondPrenom("Louise"));
    chercher(personnes, "Durand").ifPresent(p -> p.setSecondPrenom("Louise"));
    IO.println(jean.getSecondPrenom());
     // orElseThrow: we assert that the value is present; otherwise, an exception is thrown
    Personne martin = chercher(personnes, "Martin").orElseThrow();
    IO.println(martin.getPrenom());

     // Objects.requireNonNull: a required parameter
    try {
        new Personne(null, "Morel");
    } catch (NullPointerException ex) {
        IO.println("Erreur : " + ex.getMessage());
    }
     // the exception NullPointerException and its detailed message (Java 14)
    try {
        Personne lise = new Personne("Lise", "Morel");
        IO.println(lise.getSecondPrenom().length());
    } catch (NullPointerException ex) {
        IO.println("Erreur : " + ex.getMessage());
    }
}

// Searching for a person by name
Optional<Personne> chercher(Personne[] personnes, String nom) {
    for (Personne p : personnes) {
        if (p.getNom().equals(nom)) {
            return Optional.of(p);
        }
    }
    return Optional.empty();
}

class Personne {
     // Required fields: they must never be null
    private final String prenom;
    private final String nom;
     // Optional field: `null` means “no middle name”
    private String secondPrenom;

    public Personne(String prenom, String nom) {
        this.prenom = Objects.requireNonNull(prenom, "le prénom est obligatoire");
        this.nom = Objects.requireNonNull(nom, "le nom est obligatoire");
    }

    public String getPrenom() {
        return prenom;
    }

    public String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    public String getSecondPrenom() {
        return secondPrenom;
    }

    public void setSecondPrenom(String secondPrenom) {
        this.secondPrenom = secondPrenom;
    }
}
  • lines 56–83: The [Personne] class has two required fields, initialized by the constructor, and one optional field, [secondPrenom]: [null] means “no middle name.” The constructor rejects a first name or last name of [null] when paired with [Objects.requireNonNull] (lines 64–65): the error is detected when the object is created rather than much later, when the field is used;
  • line 8: [Objects.requireNonNullElse(valeur, défaut)] (Java 9) returns [valeur] if it is not equal to [null]; otherwise, it returns [défaut];
  • line 10: An explicit check is often the simplest approach;
  • lines 47–54: The method [chercher] returns the person being searched for wrapped in a [Optional] object, or an empty [Optional]: its return type, [Optional<Personne>], warns the caller that the result may be missing, and requires the caller to handle this case to retrieve the person. [Optional.of(p)] creates a [Optional] containing [p], [Optional.empty()], and an empty [Optional];
  • line 16: [isPresent] indicates whether [Optional] contains a value;
  • line 17: [map(Personne::getPrenom)] converts any person present into their first name; [orElse(valeur)] returns the present value or, if none exists, the specified value. The expression [Personne::getPrenom] is a method reference, which we will examine in Chapter 7; here, it refers to “the person’s [getPrenom] method”;
  • lines 20–22: [get] returns the present value; it is called only after verifying its presence;
  • lines 24–25: [ifPresent] executes the specified action only if a value is present. The action is a lambda (Chapter 7): [p -> p.setSecondPrenom("Louise")] reads “for person p, set their middle name.” Dupont exists and is assigned a new middle name; Durand does not exist, and the statement does nothing;
  • Line 28: [orElseThrow] returns the value if it is present, or throws a [NoSuchElementException] exception if [Optional] is empty. This is used when you are certain the value is present;
  • lines 32–36: A person without a first name is rejected by the constructor;
  • lines 38–43: Using a null reference throws the [NullPointerException] exception. Since Java 14, its message specifically identifies the null expression.

Results:

> java Classes26.java
Jean : second prénom=Marie, longueur=5
Paul : second prénom=(aucun), longueur=null
Durand trouvé : false
Durand : personne non trouvée
Martin : Paul
Louise
Paul
Erreur : le prénom est obligatoire
Erreur : Cannot invoke "String.length()" because the return value of "Classes26$Personne.getSecondPrenom()" is null

[Optional] is intended for method return values; it is not used for fields or parameters. In this course, we document whether a value is optional, verify required parameters using [Objects.requireNonNull], and prefer objects that are always complete (constructed with all their required values) over objects that are populated incrementally.

docs.title: 4.15. Example Application - V2
docs.text:
We’ll revisit the tax calculation already covered in the previous chapter (version 1) and now implement it using classes and interfaces. Let’s review the problem. We aim to write a program to calculate a taxpayer’s tax. We’ll consider the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only their salary to report (the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, used as-is: this is an exercise):

  • we calculate the employee’s number of tax brackets: nbParts = nbEnfants / 2 + 1 if they are unmarried, nbEnfants / 2 + 2 if he is married, where nbEnfants is the number of his children;
  • if he has at least three children, he receives an additional half-share;
  • his taxable income R is calculated as R = 0.72 × S, where S is his annual salary;
  • his family quotient is calculated as QF = R / nbParts;
  • his tax I is calculated using the following table:
thresholdcoeffRcoeffN49620083820.068291.0914,7530.1911,322.9223,8880.2832,668.3938,8680.3744,846.9847,9320.4266,883.6600.4819,505.54

Each row has three fields. To calculate tax I, find the first row where QF ≤ the limit. For example, if QF = 5,000, the row (8,382; 0.068; 291.09) will be found. Tax I is then equal to 0.068 × R - 291.09 × nbParts. If QF is such that the condition QF ≤ limit is never satisfied, then the coefficients of the last row are used, resulting in tax I = 0.481 × R - 9,505.54 × nbParts.

The application generates the file [ImpotsV2]. The calculation classes are organized into a package named [impots]:

ImpotsV2/
  Main.java                 le programme de dialogue avec l'utilisateur
  impots/
    TrancheImpot.java       une tranche du barème
    IImpot.java             l'interface du calcul de l'impôt
    AbstractImpot.java      une classe abstraite implémentant IImpot
    HardwiredImpot.java     une classe dérivée, avec des données écrites en dur

First, we define a type capable of encapsulating a row from the previous array [TrancheImpot.java]:

package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

// a tax bracket
public record TrancheImpot(BigDecimal limite, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
}

We use a record:

  • because a slice is a small piece of data without an identity, defined solely by its value, and there is no reason for it to be modified once created: a record is immutable;
  • because the compiler generates the constructor, the accessors, [toString], and the equality operator from a single line.

The components are of type [BigDecimal] (package [java.math], hence the import on line 3). The types [float] and [double] represent numbers in binary: a decimal number such as 0.068 has no exact representation in them, and calculations accumulate small rounding errors. The [BigDecimal] class represents decimal numbers exactly: this is the type to use for amounts. Its drawback is the lack of operators: we write [a.add(b)], [a.multiply(b)], [a.compareTo(b)].

Next, we define an interface [IImpot] capable of calculating the tax [IImpot.java]:

package impots;

public interface IImpot {
     // Calculation of a taxpayer’s tax
    int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire);
}
  • Line 5: The method for calculating the tax based on three pieces of data: the taxpayer’s marital status, the number of children, and annual salary. It rounds the tax down to the nearest euro.

Next, we define an abstract class that implements this interface [AbstractImpot.java]:

package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.MathContext;
import java.util.List;

public abstract class AbstractImpot implements IImpot {
     // The tax brackets required for the calculation come from an external source
     // known only to derived classes
    protected abstract List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot();

     // tax calculation
    @Override
    public int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire) {
         // Calculation of the number of shares
        BigDecimal nbParts = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbEnfants).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
                .add(BigDecimal.valueOf(marie ? 2 : 1));
        if (nbEnfants >= 3) {
            nbParts = nbParts.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
        }
         // Calculation of taxable income and the family quotient
        BigDecimal revenu = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salaire));
        BigDecimal quotient = revenu.divide(nbParts, MathContext.DECIMAL128);
         // Determination of the tax bracket: the last one is used if no other limit applies
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = getTranchesImpot();
        TrancheImpot tranche = tranches.getLast();
        for (int i = 0; i < tranches.size() - 1; i++) {
            if (quotient.compareTo(tranches.get(i).limite()) <= 0) {
                tranche = tranches.get(i);
                break;
            }
        }
         // tax calculation
        return revenu.multiply(tranche.coeffR()).subtract(nbParts.multiply(tranche.coeffN())).intValue();
    }
}
  • Line 1: The class belongs to the [impots] package; its file is therefore in the [impots] folder;
  • Line 7: The class [AbstractImpot] implements the interface [IImpot];
  • Line 10: The scale data, provided by a protected abstract method. The [AbstractImpot] class does not know where this data comes from (written in the code, read from a file, a database, etc.). It leaves this up to the derived classes. This is why it is declared abstract, which prevents it from being instantiated. The abstract method requires derived classes to provide the brackets; the compiler verifies this;
  • lines 13–35: the implementation of the [calculer] method of the [IImpot] interface. Derived classes will not need to rewrite this method. The [AbstractImpot] class thus serves as a factorization class for the derived classes: it contains what is common to all of them;
  • lines 16–17: the number of shares. [BigDecimal.valueOf(n)] converts an integer to [BigDecimal]; division by [BigDecimal.TWO] is exact (3 / 2 = 1.5), unlike integer division by [nbEnfants / 2] (3 / 2 = 1). The expression [marie ? 2 : 1] equals 2 for a married taxpayer, 1 otherwise;
  • lines 18–20: the additional half-share. A [BigDecimal] is immutable: [add] returns a new object, which must be assigned to the variable;
  • lines 22–23: taxable income and the family quotient. Decimal constants are created from strings ([new BigDecimal("0.72")]) to ensure they are exact. The division of a [BigDecimal] can result in an infinite number of decimal places (1 / 3): we specify the desired precision, in this case [MathContext.DECIMAL128] (34 significant digits);
  • lines 25–32: searching for the bracket. By default, this is the last bracket ([tranches.getLast()], line 26). The loop iterates through all brackets except the last one and stops ([break]) at the first bracket whose limit is greater than or equal to the family quotient, as tested by [compareTo(...) <= 0];
  • line 34: the tax calculation. The method [intValue] truncates the result to its integer part.

A class that implements the [IImpot] interface can be created by deriving it from the [AbstractImpot] class. This is what we are now doing with [HardwiredImpot.java]:

package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class HardwiredImpot extends AbstractImpot {
     // tax calculation data (2004 tax schedule for 2003 income), hard-coded
    private static final double[] LIMITES = { 4962, 8382, 14753, 23888, 38868, 47932, 0 };
    private static final double[] COEFF_R = { 0, 0.068, 0.191, 0.283, 0.374, 0.426, 0.481 };
    private static final double[] COEFF_N = { 0, 291.09, 1322.92, 2668.39, 4846.98, 6883.66, 9505.54 };

     // Tax brackets
    private final List<TrancheImpot> tranchesImpot;

     // generator
    public HardwiredImpot() {
         // Creation and population of the tax bracket list
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < LIMITES.length; i++) {
            tranches.add(new TrancheImpot(BigDecimal.valueOf(LIMITES[i]),
                    BigDecimal.valueOf(COEFF_R[i]), BigDecimal.valueOf(COEFF_N[i])));
        }
         // The stored list cannot be modified
        tranchesImpot = List.copyOf(tranches);
    }

     // Implementation of the parent class's abstract method
    @Override
    protected List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }
}
  • Lines 9–11: The class [HardwiredImpot] hardcodes the data needed to calculate the tax. These are class fields ([static]) [final]: they are shared by all instances and cannot be replaced by other arrays. By convention, the names of the constants ([static final]) are written in uppercase;
  • lines 17–26: the constructor uses this data to build the list of tax brackets. [BigDecimal.valueOf(double)] (lines 21–22) converts a [double] to a [BigDecimal] via its shortest decimal representation: [BigDecimal.valueOf(0.068)] is exactly 0.068. Do not use the constructor [new BigDecimal(0.068)], which reproduces all the decimal places of the approximated binary value (0.068000000000000004884981308350688…);
  • line 25: [List.copyOf] returns a read-only copy of the list: no class will be able to modify the scale;
  • lines 29–32: The abstract method of the parent class is implemented: it returns the list of brackets.

The next chapter will add other classes derived from [AbstractImpot], which will read the brackets from a text file or from JSON: they will only need to provide the [getTranchesImpot] method.

A test program might look like the following [Main.java]:

// Interactive tax calculation program
// The user enters three pieces of data via the keyboard: married nbEnfants salary
// The program then displays the tax due
import impots.HardwiredImpot;
import impots.IImpot;

static final String SYNTAXE = """
        syntaxe : Marié NbEnfants Salaire
        Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié
        NbEnfants : nombre d'enfants
        Salaire : salaire annuel en euros""";

void main() {
     // creation of an object IImpot
    IImpot impot = new HardwiredImpot();

     // input loop
    while (true) {
         // The program prompts for the tax calculation parameters
        String parametres = IO.readln("Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : "
                + "Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : ");
         // End of standard input or empty line: the program stops
        if (parametres == null || parametres.isBlank()) {
            break;
        }
         // Check the number of fields in the entered line
        String[] champs = parametres.strip().split("\\s+");
        if (champs.length != 3) {
            IO.println(SYNTAXE);
            continue;
        }
         // Checking the validity of the parameters
         // married
        String marie = champs[0].toLowerCase();
        if (!marie.equals("o") && !marie.equals("n")) {
            IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument marié incorrect : tapez o ou n");
            continue;
        }
         // nbEnfants
        int nbEnfants = entierPositif(champs[1]);
        if (nbEnfants < 0) {
            IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument NbEnfants incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
            continue;
        }
         // salary
        int salaire = entierPositif(champs[2]);
        if (salaire < 0) {
            IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument salaire incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
            continue;
        }
         // Parameters are correct: calculate tax
        IO.println("Impôt=" + impot.calculer(marie.equals("o"), nbEnfants, salaire) + " euros");
    }
}

// returns the positive integer or zero represented by the string; returns -1 if the string does not represent one
int entierPositif(String chaine) {
    try {
        int valeur = Integer.parseInt(chaine);
        return valeur >= 0 ? valeur : -1;
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        return -1;
    }
}

The program above allows the user to perform repeated tax calculation simulations.

  • Lines 4–5: The main program is in the unnamed package; it imports the two types it needs from the [impots] package. These types must be public;
  • Lines 7–11: The help message is a constant of the implicit class, written as a text block (Java 15) delimited by three quotation marks: the string can span multiple lines, and the common indentation of the lines is removed. Since the closing quotation mark is placed at the end of the last line, the string does not end with a line break;
  • line 15: creation of a [impot] object that implements the [IImpot] interface. This object is obtained by instantiating a type [HardwiredImpot], a type that implements the interface [IImpot]. Note that the variable [impot] was not assigned the type [HardwiredImpot] but rather the type [IImpot]. By writing this, we indicate that we are only interested in the [calculer] method of the [impot] object and not in the rest. To use data from a file, simply change this single line;
  • lines 18–53: the loop for tax calculation simulations;
  • lines 20–21: the three parameters required for the [calculer] method are requested in a single line entered via the keyboard. [IO.readln(message)] displays the message and then reads a line; it returns [null] if standard input is closed: the check on line 23 then terminates the program, just as it would for an empty line;
  • line 27: the [split] method splits the line—with leading and trailing spaces removed—into words separated by one or more space characters (regular expression ["\\s+"]);
  • Lines 40 and 46: The method [entierPositif] (lines 57–64) verifies that the last two fields are positive integers or zero. [Integer.parseInt] throws a [NumberFormatException] exception if the string does not represent an integer: the method catches it and returns -1, which indicates an error;
  • line 52: call to the [calculer] method of the [impot] object implementing the [IImpot] interface.

Compared to Version 1, the calculation is now encapsulated in classes behind an interface: the dialog program only recognizes the [IImpot] interface. Subsequent versions will take advantage of this separation: Version 3 (next chapter) will change the data source by deriving new classes from [AbstractImpot], and then the application will be organized into layers (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 5. Commonly Used Java Classes
docs.text:
Here we present a few frequently used classes from the Java platform: strings, arrays, collections, files, and regular expressions. We also include the API Stream (Java 8), which is currently the most common way to search, sort, group, or transform elements in a Java collection. Before that, we’ll show you how to find information about the thousands of available classes. This resource is indispensable for any Java developer, even experienced ones.

With the exception of two (the JSON example and the sample application at the end), the examples in this chapter are compact source files executed by the source code launcher: [java Fichier.java]. They are located in the [05-classes-java] folder of the course code and run, like the entire course, in French (locale fr-FR). Note that a compact source file automatically imports all public classes from the [java.base] module: [java.util], [java.io], [java.nio.file], [java.util.regex], [java.util.stream], [java.time]… This is why the following programs do not contain any [import] statements.

docs.title: 5.1. Seeking Help with Java Classes
docs.text: The Java Standard Library (the API Java SE) includes more than 4,000 public classes. No one knows them all: Java developers constantly consult their documentation. This documentation is available online, free of charge, and published for each version of Java.

docs.title: 5.1.1. Online Documentation
docs.text:
The starting point is Oracle’s website at docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25. There you’ll find:

  • the Java 25 reference: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/. It describes, module by module and package by package, all Java classes and interfaces: their constructors, fields, and methods;
  • a search box at the top of each page of the reference, where you can type the name of a class or method ([StringBuilder], [Matcher.find]…): the list of results populates as you type;
  • the Java language specification (JLS) and topic-specific guides (JDK tools, security, regular expressions…);
  • a “New Features” page that describes what’s new in each version. The new features themselves are described in JEP (JDK Enhancement Proposals), available on openjdk.org/jeps: For example, JEP 512 describes the compact source files used in this chapter.

A class page, such as java.lang.String, provides:

  • the class’s module and package;
  • its declaration, its parent classes, and the interfaces it implements;
  • a general description, often lengthy and detailed, with examples;
  • a summary list of its fields, constructors, and methods, followed by details for each: parameters, return value, possible exceptions, and the Java version in which it was introduced (under the “Since” heading).

The documentation is in English. A search on a search engine using the class’s full name and version (“java.lang.StringBuilder 25”) usually leads directly to the correct page.

docs.title: 5.1.2. Javadoc and the editor’s help
docs.text:
This documentation is generated by the [javadoc] tool from the JDK tool based on documentation comments written in the source code of the classes. Such a comment begins with [/**] and is placed immediately before a class, field, or method. For example, here is the tax calculation method from the sample application in this chapter, documented as follows:

    /**
     * Calcule l'impôt d'un contribuable.
     *
     * @param marie     vrai si le contribuable est marié
     * @param nbEnfants nombre d'enfants
     * @param salaire   salaire annuel en euros
     * @return le montant de l'impôt, en euros
     */
    int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire);

The comment begins with a summary sentence; the [@param] tags describe the parameters, and [@return] describes the returned value ([@throws] would describe an exception). You can document your own code in this way; the command [javadoc] (or [mvn javadoc:javadoc] in a Maven project) generates HTML pages similar to those in Java. Starting with Java 23, documentation comments can also be written in Markdown, with lines beginning with [///].

The code editor (IntelliJ IDEA, Visual Studio Code with the Extension Pack for Java) leverages these comments and provides immediate assistance without leaving the code:

  • autocompletion: after typing [uneChaine.], the editor displays a list of the object’s methods, along with their parameters and return types;
  • Quick documentation: Hovering over a class or method name (or pressing Ctrl+Q in IntelliJ IDEA) displays its Javadoc;
  • Parameter help: When you type the opening parenthesis of a call (or press Ctrl+P in IntelliJ IDEA), the editor displays the different overloads of the method and the role of each parameter;
  • Go to Definition (Ctrl+B in IntelliJ, IDEA, F12 in VS Code): displays the source code for the class or method. JDK comes with the source code for its entire library (file [lib/src.zip]): This allows you to read the code for [ArrayList] or [HashMap], written by top Java experts, which is very educational.

Finally, the [jshell] tool from JDK lets you test a method without writing a program: you enter an expression, and it displays its value. For example, ["abc".repeat(3)] displays ["abcabcabc"]. The [/help] command from [jshell] lists its options.

docs.title: 5.2.1. The String class
docs.text:
The [String] type ([java.lang] package) represents character strings. It offers numerous methods. Here are a few of them:

Methodrole[int length()]number of characters in the string[char charAt(int index)]Character No. [index]; the first character is No. 0[boolean startsWith(String prefix)]returns [true] if the string begins with [prefix][boolean endsWith(String suffix)]returns [true] if the string ends with [suffix][boolean contains(CharSequence s)]returns [true] if the string contains [s][boolean equals(Object autre)]returns [true] if the string has the same content as [autre]; [equalsIgnoreCase] is case-insensitive[int indexOf(String str)]the first occurrence of [str] in the string, or -1. Another overload starts the search at position [fromIndex][int indexOf(int ch)]same for the character [ch][int lastIndexOf(int ch)]same as [indexOf] but returns the last position instead of the first[static String join(CharSequence delimiter, CharSequence... elements)]Class method: concatenates the elements, separating them with [delimiter][String replace(char oldChar, char newChar)]returns a copy of the string where the character [oldChar] has been replaced by [newChar]; an overload replaces one string with another[String[] split(String regex)]the string is treated as a sequence of fields separated by a separator described by the regular expression [regex]; the result is an array of these fields[String substring(int beginIndex, int endIndex)]substring consisting of the characters from position [beginIndex] (inclusive) to position [endIndex] (exclusive)[String toLowerCase()], [String toUpperCase()]converts the string to lowercase, uppercase[String strip()]removes leading and trailing spaces from the string (Java 11; [stripLeading], [stripTrailing]: on one side only)[String repeat(int count)]repeats the string [count] times (Java 11)[boolean isEmpty()], [boolean isBlank()]returns [true] if the string is empty, or if it contains only spaces (Java 11)[Stream<String> lines()]returns the lines of the string as a stream (Java 11; see API Stream below)[String formatted(Object... args)]returns the string, used as a template, in which the placeholders [%s], [%d]… have been replaced by the arguments (Java 15)

It is important to note that a string of type [String] is immutable; it cannot be modified after it is created. When a method returns a string, that string is different from the string on which the method was applied. Thus, [s1.strip()] returns the string [s2], and [s1] and [s2] are two different strings: [s1] has not changed.

Unlike in other languages, a Java string is not an array: you do not write [c[i]] but [c.charAt(i)], and the number of characters is obtained using the [c.length()] method (with parentheses, whereas the length of an array is the [tableau.length] field, without parentheses).

The program [Chaines01.java] is as follows:

// some methods of the String class
void main() {
    String uneChaine = "l'oiseau vole au-dessus des nuages";
    affiche("uneChaine=" + uneChaine);
    affiche("uneChaine.length()=" + uneChaine.length());
    affiche("uneChaine.charAt(10)=" + uneChaine.charAt(10));
    affiche("uneChaine.indexOf(\"vole\")=" + uneChaine.indexOf("vole"));
    affiche("uneChaine.indexOf(\"x\")=" + uneChaine.indexOf("x"));
    affiche("uneChaine.lastIndexOf('a')=" + uneChaine.lastIndexOf('a'));
    affiche("uneChaine.lastIndexOf('x')=" + uneChaine.lastIndexOf('x'));
    affiche("uneChaine.substring(4, 11)=" + uneChaine.substring(4, 11));
    affiche("uneChaine.toUpperCase()=" + uneChaine.toUpperCase());
    affiche("uneChaine.toLowerCase()=" + uneChaine.toLowerCase());
    affiche("uneChaine.replace('a', 'A')=" + uneChaine.replace('a', 'A'));
     // No insert method: concatenate two substrings
    affiche("insertion de \"ne \" en position 9=" + uneChaine.substring(0, 9) + "ne "
            + uneChaine.substring(9));
     // Splits the string into words (separator: a sequence of spaces)
    String[] champs = uneChaine.split("\\s+");
    for (int i = 0; i < champs.length; i++) {
        affiche("champs[" + i + "]=[" + champs[i] + "]");
    }
    affiche("String.join(\":\", champs)=" + String.join(":", champs));
    affiche("\"  abc  \".strip()=[" + "  abc  ".strip() + "]");
     // the original string has not been modified
    affiche("uneChaine=" + uneChaine);
}

// a display method
void affiche(String msg) {
    IO.println(msg);
}

Results:

> java Chaines01.java
uneChaine=l'oiseau vole au-dessus des nuages
uneChaine.length()=34
uneChaine.charAt(10)=o
uneChaine.indexOf("vole")=9
uneChaine.indexOf("x")=-1
uneChaine.lastIndexOf('a')=30
uneChaine.lastIndexOf('x')=-1
uneChaine.substring(4, 11)=seau vo
uneChaine.toUpperCase()=L'OISEAU VOLE AU-DESSUS DES NUAGES
uneChaine.toLowerCase()=l'oiseau vole au-dessus des nuages
uneChaine.replace('a', 'A')=l'oiseAu vole Au-dessus des nuAges
insertion de "ne " en position 9=l'oiseau ne vole au-dessus des nuages
champs[0]=[l'oiseau]
champs[1]=[vole]
champs[2]=[au-dessus]
champs[3]=[des]
champs[4]=[nuages]
String.join(":", champs)=l'oiseau:vole:au-dessus:des:nuages
"  abc  ".strip()=[abc]
uneChaine=l'oiseau vole au-dessus des nuages

Comments:

  • line 6: character #10, i.e., the 11th character in the string;
  • Lines 8, 10: An unsuccessful search returns -1;
  • Line 11: The two parameters of [substring] are the positions of the first protected character and the first unprotected character: this yields the 7 characters at positions 4 through 10. This is the general Java convention for specifying an index range (start included, end excluded): it appears in many methods;
  • Lines 16–17: The [String] class does not have an insertion method: we concatenate the beginning of the string, the inserted text, and the end of the string. We’ll see that the [StringBuilder] class has a [insert] method;
  • Line 19: [split] splits the string into fields. Its parameter is not a single character but a regular expression, which we’ll examine at the end of the chapter: ["\\s+"] denotes a sequence of one or more whitespace characters (space, tab, line break, etc.). The character [\] must be doubled in a Java string, hence the notation [\\s];
  • line 23: the static method [join] does the opposite of [split];
  • line 24: [strip] (Java 11) removes leading and trailing spaces. There is also the older method [trim], which recognizes only the spaces in the code for ASCII; [strip] recognizes all Unicode spaces and should be preferred;
  • line 26: all of the previous methods returned new strings: [uneChaine] remained unchanged (line 21 of the results);
  • Lines 30–32: a method from the compact source file, called by the method [main] as in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 5.2.2. The split and join methods
docs.text:
The program [Chaines02.java] performs a more detailed split of a string into fields:

// split and join
void main() {
    String ligne = "un:deux::trois:";
     // splitting using the ':' separator
    String[] champs = ligne.split(":");
    for (int i = 0; i < champs.length; i++) {
        IO.println("champs[" + i + "]=[" + champs[i] + "]");
    }
     // The reverse operation does not restore the original string: the final empty field is missing
    IO.println("join=[" + String.join(":", champs) + "]");

     // With a negative limit, split preserves the empty fields at the end
    champs = ligne.split(":", -1);
    IO.println("split(\":\", -1) : " + champs.length + " champs, join=[" + String.join(":", champs) + "]");

     // The separator is a regular expression: ":+" matches a sequence of ':'
    champs = ligne.split(":+");
    IO.println("split(\":+\") : " + champs.length + " champs [" + String.join("|", champs) + "]");

     // multiple delimiters and removal of spaces around fields
    String personne = " dupont , jean ;  45 ";
    champs = personne.strip().split("\\s*[,;]\\s*");
    IO.println("split(\"\\\\s*[,;]\\\\s*\") : " + champs.length + " champs ["
            + String.join("|", champs) + "]");

     // removes spaces and empty fields, field by field
    String liste = "  rouge ,, vert ,  , bleu ";
    List<String> couleurs = new ArrayList<>();
    for (String champ : liste.split(",")) {
        String couleur = champ.strip();
        if (!couleur.isEmpty()) {
            couleurs.add(couleur);
        }
    }
    IO.println("strip + isEmpty : " + couleurs.size() + " champs [" + String.join("|", couleurs) + "]");

     // a separator containing special characters from regular expressions
    String texte = "pomme | poire | abricot";
    champs = texte.split(Pattern.quote(" | "));
    IO.println("Pattern.quote : [" + String.join(", ", champs) + "]");

     // join accepts only strings: integers must first be converted
    int[] nombres = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    String[] textes = new String[nombres.length];
    for (int i = 0; i < nombres.length; i++) {
        textes[i] = String.valueOf(nombres[i]);
    }
    IO.println("join sur des entiers : " + String.join(" + ", textes));
}

Results:

> java Chaines02.java
champs[0]=[un]
champs[1]=[deux]
champs[2]=[]
champs[3]=[trois]
join=[un:deux::trois]
split(":", -1) : 5 champs, join=[un:deux::trois:]
split(":+") : 3 champs [un|deux|trois]
split("\\s*[,;]\\s*") : 3 champs [dupont|jean|45]
strip + isEmpty : 3 champs [rouge|vert|bleu]
Pattern.quote : [pomme, poire, abricot]
join sur des entiers : 1 + 2 + 3 + 4

Comments:

  • Line 5: The fields are separated by the character [:]. Two consecutive [:] characters delimit an empty field (line 4 of the results). But be careful: [split] removes empty fields from the end. The final [:] in the string delimits a fifth, empty field that has been removed: only 4 fields are obtained, and [join] does not reconstruct the original string (line 6 of the results). This is a common pitfall;
  • line 13: the second parameter of [split] is a limit. A negative limit instructs the program to keep all fields, including the empty fields at the end: we do indeed get 5 fields, and [join] reconstructs the original string;
  • line 17: Since the separator is a regular expression, we can define complex separators: [":+"] denotes one or more consecutive [:] characters. The two consecutive [:]s form a single separator, and the empty field is removed;
  • Line 22: The pattern [\\s*[,;]\\s*] matches a comma or semicolon, preceded and followed by any number of spaces: the spaces surrounding the separators are removed along with them. Those at the beginning and end of the string are removed beforehand by [strip]. This produces the three “cleaned up” fields in a single statement;
  • Lines 27–35: To remove both the spaces around the fields and the empty fields, we can also process the fields one by one: the field consisting of two spaces between two commas becomes empty after [strip] and is not retained. The list [ArrayList] used here to store the retained fields will be discussed a little later. We will also see that the API stream allows this processing to be written in a single instruction;
  • line 39: the [" | "] separator contains the character [|], which has a special meaning in a regular expression (“or”). The [Pattern.quote] method converts any string into a regular expression that literally matches it. We’ll use it whenever a separator contains one of the characters [\ ^ $ . | ? * + ( ) [ ] { }];
  • Lines 43–48: [join] accepts only strings (more precisely, [CharSequence] objects, an interface implemented by [String] and [StringBuilder]): an array of integers must first be converted to an array of strings. We will see that with the API Stream, [Arrays.stream(nombres).mapToObj(String::valueOf).collect(Collectors.joining(" + "))] does the same thing in a single instruction.

docs.title: 5.2.3. Searching for and Comparing Strings
docs.text:
String comparison is more subtle than it seems: should uppercase and lowercase letters be distinguished? How should “student” be compared to “essay”? And most importantly, in Java, what does the [==] operator compare? The program [Chaines03.java] demonstrates the search and comparison methods:

// search for and compare strings
void main() {
    String titre = "Apprentissage du langage Java 25";

     // contains, startsWith, endsWith: exact comparison
    IO.println("contains(\"langage\") : " + titre.contains("langage"));
    IO.println("contains(\"LANGAGE\") : " + titre.contains("LANGAGE"));
    IO.println("startsWith(\"Apprentissage\") : " + titre.startsWith("Apprentissage"));
    IO.println("endsWith(\"25\") : " + titre.endsWith("25"));

     // case-insensitive: strings are compared in lowercase
    String cherche = "LANGAGE";
    IO.println("toLowerCase().contains(cherche.toLowerCase()) : "
            + titre.toLowerCase().contains(cherche.toLowerCase()));
     // regionMatches (ignoreCase, start, other, start in other, length)
    IO.println("regionMatches(true, 0, \"apprentissage\", 0, 13) : "
            + titre.regionMatches(true, 0, "apprentissage", 0, 13));

     // equality: `equals` compares contents, `==` compares references
    String reponse = "OUI";
    String oui = new StringBuilder("ou").append('i').toString();
    IO.println("oui.equals(\"oui\") : " + oui.equals("oui"));
    IO.println("oui == \"oui\" : " + (oui == "oui"));
    IO.println("reponse.equals(\"oui\") : " + reponse.equals("oui"));
    IO.println("reponse.equalsIgnoreCase(\"oui\") : " + reponse.equalsIgnoreCase("oui"));

     // alphabetical order: by character codes or by language
    String a = "élève", b = "essai";
    IO.println("\"" + a + "\".compareTo(\"" + b + "\") : " + a.compareTo(b));
    Collator collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    IO.println("collator.compare(\"" + a + "\", \"" + b + "\") : " + collator.compare(a, b));

     // empty or blank strings
    String vide = "";
    String blanche = "   ";
    String absente = null;
    IO.println("\"\".isEmpty() : " + vide.isEmpty());
    IO.println("\"   \".isEmpty() : " + blanche.isEmpty());
    IO.println("\"   \".isBlank() : " + blanche.isBlank());
    IO.println("absente == null || absente.isBlank() : " + (absente == null || absente.isBlank()));

     // alignment and repetition
    IO.println("[" + String.format("%8s", "abc") + "] [" + String.format("%-8s", "abc") + "] ["
            + "-".repeat(8) + "]");
}

Results:

> java Chaines03.java
contains("langage") : true
contains("LANGAGE") : false
startsWith("Apprentissage") : true
endsWith("25") : true
toLowerCase().contains(cherche.toLowerCase()) : true
regionMatches(true, 0, "apprentissage", 0, 13) : true
oui.equals("oui") : true
oui == "oui" : false
reponse.equals("oui") : false
reponse.equalsIgnoreCase("oui") : true
"élève".compareTo("essai") : 132
collator.compare("élève", "essai") : -1
"".isEmpty() : true
"   ".isEmpty() : false
"   ".isBlank() : true
absente == null || absente.isBlank() : true
[     abc] [abc     ] [--------]

Comments:

  • lines 6–9: [contains], [startsWith], and [endsWith] perform an exact, character-by-character comparison: “LANGAGE” is not found;
  • lines 12–14: These methods do not have a case-insensitive variant. The simplest way to perform a case-insensitive search is to convert both strings to lowercase;
  • lines 16–17: The [regionMatches] method compares a portion of one string to a portion of another string. Its first parameter specifies whether to ignore case; the subsequent parameters are the starting position in the string, the other string, the starting position in the other string, and the number of characters to compare;
  • lines 20–25: the most important part of this program. A variable of type [String] contains a reference to a string object (Chapter 4). The operator [] compares the references: it returns [true] if the two variables refer to the same object, and not to two objects with the same content. The variable [oui] (line 21) refers to a string “yes” constructed at runtime: this is a different object from the program’s literal string “yes,” and [oui == "oui"] evaluates to [false] (line 9 of the results) even though the two strings have the same content. To compare contents, always use the [equals] method, or [equalsIgnoreCase] to ignore case—which is the correct way to test a “yes” response entered from the keyboard in uppercase or lowercase. The comparison using [] “works” sometimes, when both strings are program literals, of which Java stores only a single instance: this is what makes the error difficult to detect;
  • lines 28–31: The method [compareTo] returns a negative, zero, or positive integer depending on whether the string precedes, equals, or follows the parameter string. It compares the character codes: “élève” comes after “essai” because the code for the character é (233) is greater than that for the character e (101); here, it returns the difference between the two codes, 132. To sort words according to the rules of a language, use a [java.text.Collator] object: in French, the character “é” is grouped with “e,” and “élève” comes before “essai” (line 13 of the results). We’ll use the order defined by a [Collator] to sort words intended for a user, and [compareTo] to compare technical identifiers (file names, keys, etc.);
  • lines 34–40: [isEmpty] checks for an empty string, while [isBlank] (Java 11) checks for an empty string or one containing only spaces. A variable of type [String] can also be [null] (no string): calling a method on [null] throws a [NullPointerException] exception. Therefore, we first test for [absente == null]; thanks to the short-circuit behavior of the [||] operator, [absente.isBlank()] is not evaluated when [absente] is [null];
  • Lines 43–44: [String.format("%8s", ...)] pads a string with spaces up to a length of 8 characters, either on the left or on the right, using the format [%-8s]; [repeat] repeats a string.

docs.title: 5.2.4. Formats and Text Blocks
docs.text:
So far, we have built the strings to be displayed using concatenation with the [+] operator. To align values in columns, set the number of decimal places for a number, or display a date, use the [String.format] method or the [formatted] instance method (Java 15), which does the same thing. The first parameter is a format: a string in which [%[-][largeur][.précision]conversion] specifiers indicate where and how to insert the following parameters. The [Chaines04.java] program provides examples of this, as well as the Java 15 text blocks:

// formats, text blocks
void main() {
    String nom = "dupont";
    int age = 45;
    double salaire = 2345.678;
    double taux = 0.0525;
    LocalDateTime date = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 10, 3, 14, 5, 9);

     // simple concatenation
    IO.println(nom + " a " + age + " ans");
     // %[-]width: width > 0 right-aligned, the minus sign left-aligned
    IO.println(String.format("[%10s] [%-10s] [%5d]", nom, nom, age));
    IO.println(String.format("[%12.2f] [%-12.1f] [%,.2f]", salaire, salaire, salaire));
    IO.println(String.format("[%05d] [%X] [%,d] [%e]", age, age, 1234567, salaire));
     // the `formatted` instance method (Java 15): same result
    IO.println("%s est %s".formatted(nom, age >= 18 ? "majeur" : "mineur"));

     // currency and percentage: the NumberFormat class
    NumberFormat monnaie = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    NumberFormat pourcentage = NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    pourcentage.setMinimumFractionDigits(2);
    IO.println("[" + monnaie.format(salaire) + "] [" + pourcentage.format(taux) + "]");

     // dates: the DateTimeFormatter class
    IO.println("[" + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy")) + "] ["
            + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss")) + "] ["
            + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy")) + "]");

     // an aligned table
    String[] produits = {"pomme", "poire", "abricot"};
    double[] prix = {2.5, 3.15, 12};
    for (int i = 0; i < produits.length; i++) {
        IO.println("%-10s|%8.2f €".formatted(produits[i], prix[i]));
    }

     // the \ character must be doubled in a string
    String chemin = "C:\\data\\cours\\infos.txt";
    IO.println(chemin);

     // text block (Java 15): delimited by """, across multiple lines
    String json = """
        {
          "nom": "dupont",
          "chemin": "C:\\data"
        }
        """;
    IO.print(json);
     // a block of text with %s and %d placeholders filled in by formatted
    String json2 = """
        { "nom": "%s", "age": %d }""".formatted(nom, age);
    IO.println(json2);
}

Results:

> java Chaines04.java
dupont a 45 ans
[    dupont] [dupont    ] [   45]
[     2345,68] [2345,7      ] [2 345,68]
[00045] [2D] [1 234 567] [2,345678e+03]
dupont est majeur
[2 345,68 €] [5,25 %]
[03/10/2026] [14:05:09] [samedi 3 octobre 2026]
pomme     |    2,50 €
poire     |    3,15 €
abricot   |   12,00 €
C:\data\cours\infos.txt
{
  "nom": "dupont",
  "chemin": "C:\data"
}
{ "nom": "dupont", "age": 45 }

Comments:

  • line 12: a width aligns the value to the right within a 10-character field; when preceded by the [-] symbol, it aligns it to the left;
  • Lines 12–14: The most common conversions:
specifierMeaningexample (fr-FR)[%s]string; any object is converted using its [toString] methoddupont[%d], [%5d]integer, possibly 5 characters long45[%05d]integer with at least 5 digits, padded with zeros00045[%X]hexadecimal integer ([%x]: in lowercase)2D[%.2f], [%12.2f]real number with 2 decimal places, possibly 12 characters long2345.68[%,.2f], [%,d]same as above, with a thousands separator2,345.68[%e]real number in scientific notation2.345678e+03[%n]system line break [%%]the % character%
  • Numbers are formatted according to the current language, in this case French: decimal point, space as a thousands separator. This is a thin non-breaking space (character U+202F), which looks like a regular space but prevents a line break in the middle of a number; Similarly, a non-breaking space (U+00A0) precedes the € symbol and the % symbol. This will be taken into account when comparing these texts to strings written with regular spaces;
  • line 16: ["...".formatted(...)] is equivalent to [String.format("...", ...)]. A conditional expression can provide a parameter;
  • lines 19–22: Monetary amounts and percentages are formatted using [java.text.NumberFormat] objects, which are derived for a given language and country ([Locale.FRANCE]). The percentage format multiplies the value by 100;
  • lines 25–27: the dates from API and [java.time] (Java 8) are formatted using a [DateTimeFormatter] object constructed from a template: [dd] day, [MM] month, [yyyy] year, [HH] hour, [mm] minutes, [ss] seconds, [EEEE] day of the week spelled out, [MMMM] month spelled out. Be careful with case: [MM] is the month, [mm] is the minutes. The names of the days and months are those used in everyday language;
  • lines 30–34: the column widths allow data to be displayed in columns;
  • Line 37: In a string, the character [\] introduces an escape sequence ([\n], [\t], [\"]…); to obtain the character [\] itself, you must double it. Java does not have “raw” strings where [\] would be a regular character, which makes writing Windows paths and regular expressions a bit cumbersome;
  • Lines 41–46: A text block (Java 15) is delimited by three quotation marks; the text begins on the line following the opening quotation marks. It can span multiple lines and contain unescaped quotation marks. The indentation common to all lines (that of the least-indented line, counting from the closing quotation marks) is removed: the text JSON is displayed without the code margin. Escape sequences remain active here: “[\]” must still be doubled (line 44). Since the closing quotation marks are on their own line, the text ends with a line break: hence the use of [IO.print] on line 47 ([IO.println] would add a blank line after the closing curly brace);
  • lines 49–50: Java does not support string interpolation—that is, expressions written directly within the text, such as [${nom}] in other languages (a proposal, “String Templates,” was tested as a preview in Java 21 and 22, then removed). With a block of text, placeholders such as [%s], [%d]… are used, filled in by [formatted]. Placing the closing quotation marks at the end of the text prevents a final line break.

There is also the class [java.text.MessageFormat], whose formats refer to parameters by their numbers: [MessageFormat.format("{0} a {1} ans", nom, age)]. It is used for messages translated into multiple languages, where the order of parameters may vary from one language to another.

docs.title: 5.2.5. The StringBuilder class
docs.text:
We mentioned that the methods of the [String] class that are applied to a [s1] string return another [s2] string. The [java.lang.StringBuilder] class allows you to modify a string without creating a new string for each operation. This improves performance when constructing a string through many successive additions, by avoiding the proliferation of strings with very short lifespans.

The class supports various constructors:

constructorrole[StringBuilder()]creates an empty object with an initial capacity of 16 characters[StringBuilder(String str)]construct and initialize with [str]; the initial capacity is the length of [str] plus 16[StringBuilder(int capacity)]constructing an empty object with an initial capacity of [capacity] characters

A [StringBuilder] object stores its characters in an array whose size—its capacity—is automatically adjusted as the text grows. The program [Chaines05.java] illustrates this concept of capacity:

// size and capacity of a StringBuilder
void main() {
    StringBuilder str = new StringBuilder("test");
    IO.println("taille=" + str.length() + ", capacité=" + str.capacity());
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        str.append("test");
        IO.println("taille=" + str.length() + ", capacité=" + str.capacity());
    }
     // a StringBuilder with an initial capacity of 10
    StringBuilder str2 = new StringBuilder(10).append("test");
    IO.println("taille=" + str2.length() + ", capacité=" + str2.capacity());
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        str2.append("test");
        IO.println("taille=" + str2.length() + ", capacité=" + str2.capacity());
    }
}

Results:

> java Chaines05.java
taille=4, capacité=20
taille=8, capacité=20
taille=12, capacité=20
taille=16, capacité=20
taille=20, capacité=20
taille=24, capacité=42
taille=28, capacité=42
taille=32, capacité=42
taille=36, capacité=42
taille=40, capacité=42
taille=44, capacité=86
taille=4, capacité=10
taille=8, capacité=10
taille=12, capacité=22
taille=16, capacité=22
taille=20, capacité=22
taille=24, capacité=46
taille=28, capacité=46
taille=32, capacité=46
taille=36, capacité=46
taille=40, capacité=46
taille=44, capacité=46

Comments:

  • line 3: creation of a [StringBuilder] object containing “test”: its initial capacity is 4 + 16 = 20 characters;
  • line 4: [length] is the current number of characters; [capacity] is the number of characters the object can hold before it needs to expand its array;
  • line 6: [append] appends a string to the end of the text;
  • line 10: creation of an empty [StringBuilder] object with an initial capacity of 10, to which “test” is immediately added. The method [append] returns the object itself: it can be called directly on the result of the constructor.

The results show that when the capacity is insufficient, it is slightly more than doubled: the new capacity is the old one multiplied by 2, plus 2 (20, 42, 86 for the first object; 10, 22, 46 for the second). Each resize allocates a new array and copies the characters into it. If the approximate size of the text is known in advance, setting it at construction time avoids these successive resizes.

Here are some of the class’s methods:

methodrole[StringBuilder append(String str)]Add [str] to the end of the text. Overridden to accept the types [int], [double], [char], [boolean], [Object]…[StringBuilder insert(int offset, String str)]Inserts [str] at position [offset]; overwritten as [append][StringBuilder delete(int start, int end)]deletes characters from positions [start] (inclusive) to [end] (exclusive); [deleteCharAt] deletes one character[StringBuilder replace(int start, int end, String str)]replaces the characters at positions [start] (inclusive) through [end] (exclusive) with [str][StringBuilder reverse()]reverses the order of the characters[void setCharAt(int index, char ch)]replaces character No. [index] with [ch][int indexOf(String str)]position of [str] in the text, or -1[String toString()]converts the text into a string [String]

The program [Chaines06.java] uses them:

// The methods of StringBuilder return the StringBuilder object itself: they can be chained
void main() {
    StringBuilder str3 = new StringBuilder("test");
    IO.println(str3.append("abCD").insert(2, "xyZT").delete(0, 2).replace(0, 2, "XY"));
     // reverse reverses the order of the characters
    IO.println(new StringBuilder("élève").reverse());

     // builds a string piece by piece
    StringBuilder lignes = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
        lignes.append("ligne ").append(i).append('\n');
    }
     // String.join to add elements separated by commas
    lignes.append(String.join(", ", "a", "b", "c")).append('\n');
     // a formatted string
    int total = 42;
    lignes.append("total=%6.1f".formatted((double) total));
     // the final string
    String resultat = lignes.toString();
    IO.println(resultat);
    IO.println(resultat.length() + " caractères");

     // StringJoiner: separator, prefix, and suffix
    StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]");
    for (String couleur : new String[]{"rouge", "vert", "bleu"}) {
        joiner.add(couleur);
    }
    IO.println(joiner);
}

Results:

> java Chaines06.java
XYZTstabCD
evèlé
ligne 1
ligne 2
ligne 3
a, b, c
total=  42,0
44 caractères
[rouge, vert, bleu]

Comments:

  • Line 4: The modification methods return the [StringBuilder] object itself, which allows them to be chained together. Let’s follow the steps: “test” becomes “testabCD " ([append]), then “texyZTstabCD” ([insert] in position 2), then “xyZTstabCD " ([delete] for characters 0 and 1), and finally "XYZTstabCD" ([replace] for characters 0 and 1, replaced by "XY"). Note that, unlike the [replace] method of [String], the method of [StringBuilder] does not search for text: it replaces a range of positions. [IO.println] displays the object by calling its method [toString];
  • line 6: [reverse] reverses the text. Since [String] does not have a [reverse] method, this is the standard way to reverse a string;
  • lines 9–12: constructing a multi-line text through successive additions—this is the typical use of [StringBuilder]. The additions are chained together on a single line of code;
  • line 14: [StringBuilder] has no equivalent to [join]: the result of [String.join] is appended;
  • line 17: a formatted string is added. The conversion [%f] requires a real number: passing the integer [total] would throw a [IllegalFormatConversionException] exception at runtime, hence the conversion [(double) total];
  • line 19: the final text is obtained as a string [String];
  • lines 24–28: the class [java.util.StringJoiner] constructs a string consisting of elements separated by a separator, with an optional prefix and suffix. [String.join] performs the same function, without a prefix or suffix.

For a few concatenations, the operator [+] is sufficient: the compiler optimizes them. [StringBuilder] is necessary when the number of additions is large or unknown, typically within a loop: the [s = s + ...] concatenation in a loop with n iterations creates n strings and copies the entire previously constructed string in each iteration. In older code, you’ll find the [StringBuffer] class, which has the same methods as [StringBuilder] but makes them usable simultaneously by multiple threads, at the cost of some performance overhead: today, [StringBuilder] is preferred over it.

docs.title: 5.2.6. Parsing a string without copying it
docs.text:
Each call to [substring] creates a new string in memory. In performance-critical code (such as parsing large files or network requests), you may want to avoid these creations. Java does not have a “view of a string segment” type built into the language, but several methods operate on a portion of a string without copying it. The program [Chaines07.java] compares the two ways of parsing a line in the format “last name:first name:age”:

// parse a string without creating substrings
void main() {
    String ligne = "dupont:jean:45";

     // with substring: each field is a new string allocated in memory
    int p1 = ligne.indexOf(':');
    int p2 = ligne.lastIndexOf(':');
    String nom = ligne.substring(0, p1);
    int age = Integer.parseInt(ligne.substring(p2 + 1));
    IO.println("substring : nom=" + nom + ", âge=" + age);

     // parseInt on a portion of the string (Java 9): no intermediate string
    age = Integer.parseInt(ligne, p2 + 1, ligne.length(), 10);
     // regionMatches compares a portion of the string to another string, without copying
    boolean du = ligne.regionMatches(0, "du", 0, 2);
    IO.println("parseInt(ligne, début, fin, base) : âge=" + age + ", le nom commence par \"du\" : " + du);

     // a view of a substring: CharBuffer.wrap does not copy characters
    CharSequence vueNom = CharBuffer.wrap(ligne, 0, p1);
    IO.println("vue : nom=" + vueNom + ", longueur de la vue=" + vueNom.length()
            + ", vueNom.charAt(0)=" + vueNom.charAt(0));

     // indexOf with a search range (Java 21): the ':' is searched for between p1+1 and the end
    IO.println("indexOf(':', p1 + 1, ligne.length())=" + ligne.indexOf(':', p1 + 1, ligne.length()));

     // a string is created only if it is truly needed
    String prenom = ligne.substring(p1 + 1, p2);
    IO.println("prénom=" + prenom);
}

Results:

> java Chaines07.java
substring : nom=dupont, âge=45
parseInt(ligne, début, fin, base) : âge=45, le nom commence par "du" : true
vue : nom=dupont, longueur de la vue=6, vueNom.charAt(0)=d
indexOf(':', p1 + 1, ligne.length())=11
prénom=jean

Comments:

  • lines 8–9: Each call to [substring] creates a new string, even if, as with the age, it is only used for a moment;
  • line 13: an overloaded version of [Integer.parseInt] (Java 9) parses the characters between two positions in the string, starting from the specified base (here 10), without creating a substring;
  • line 15: [regionMatches], which we’ve already encountered, compares a portion of the string to another string without copying it;
  • line 19: [CharBuffer.wrap] (package [java.nio]) returns a view of the characters from 0 to [p1] - 1 in the string: an object that does not contain a copy of the characters, but provides a way to access them. It implements the [CharSequence] interface, just like [String] and [StringBuilder]: many Java methods accept a [CharSequence] ([String.join], [contains], [append], and regular expressions, for example);
  • line 24: an overloaded version of [indexOf] (Java 21) limits the search to a range of positions;
  • line 27: a string is created only if it is actually needed.

These techniques are optimization tools: for an ordinary program, [substring] works perfectly well. Since Java 9, the virtual machine has also been storing strings that contain only characters from the Latin-1 character set (as is the case with French text) at one byte per character instead of two (“compact strings”), which cuts the memory they occupy in half. We’ll only try to avoid copies in code that has been measured to be critical for performance.

docs.title: 5.3.1. The Arrays Class
docs.text:
Java arrays are objects, but they have no useful methods: aside from the [length] field, all operations on arrays are static methods of the utility class [java.util.Arrays]. These methods allow you to sort an array, search for an element in it, copy it, fill it, and so on… Almost all of them are overloaded: there is a version for each primitive type ([int[]], [double[]], [char[]]…) and a version for arrays of objects.

methodrole[static int binarySearch(int[] a, int key)]Returns the position of [key] in [a], which must be sorted; a negative number if [key] is missing[static int[] copyOf(int[] original, int newLength)]returns a new array of [newLength] elements containing the first elements of [original], padded with zeros as needed ([false] for booleans, [null] for references)[static int[] copyOfRange(int[] original, int from, int to)]returns a new array consisting of the elements from [from] (inclusive) to [to] (exclusive)[static boolean equals(int[] a, int[] a2)]Returns [true] if both arrays have the same elements in the same order[static void fill(int[] a, int val)]assigns [val] to all elements of [a]; an override fills only a range of indices[static void sort(int[] a)]sorts [a] according to the natural order of its elements; an overload sorts only a range of indices; for an array of objects, an overload receives a [Comparator] that defines the order (Chapter 4)[static String toString(int[] a)]returns the elements of the array as a string [[e1, e2, ...]]; [deepToString] does the same for an array of arrays[static <T> List<T> asList(T... a)]returns a list that is a view of the array of objects [a][static IntStream stream(int[] array)]returns a stream of the array’s elements (see the API Stream section below)

In addition, there is the method [System.arraycopy(source, debutSource, destination, debutDestination, nombre)], which copies elements from one array into another existing array.

The program [Tableaux01.java] illustrates the use of certain methods of the [Arrays] class:

// The Arrays class: resizing, sorting, searching
void main() {
     // Reading array elements entered via the keyboard
    double[] elements = saisie();
     // Displaying the unsorted array
    affiche("Tableau non trié", elements);
     // Linear search in an unsorted array
    recherche(elements, TypeRecherche.LINEAIRE);
     // Sorting the array
    Arrays.sort(elements);
     // Displaying the sorted array
    affiche("Tableau trié", elements);
     // binary search in the sorted array
    recherche(elements, TypeRecherche.DICHOTOMIQUE);
}

// Entering array values: returns the created array
double[] saisie() {
     // Initially, the table is empty
    double[] elements = {};
     // loop for entering array elements
    while (true) {
        String reponse = lire("Elément (réel) " + elements.length + " du tableau (rien pour terminer) : ");
         // End of entry if string is empty
        if (reponse.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
         // check the input
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(reponse);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Saisie incorrecte, recommencez");
            continue;
        }
         // One more element: expand the array by one slot
        elements = Arrays.copyOf(elements, elements.length + 1);
         // and add the new element to it
        elements[elements.length - 1] = element;
    }
    return elements;
}

// display array elements
void affiche(String texte, double[] elements) {
    IO.println(texte + "-".repeat(50 - texte.length()));
    for (double element : elements) {
        IO.println(element);
    }
}

// searching the array for elements entered via the keyboard
void recherche(double[] elements, TypeRecherche type) {
    while (true) {
        String reponse = lire("Elément cherché (rien pour arrêter) : ");
         // Done?
        if (reponse.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
         // verification
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(reponse);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Erreur, recommencez...");
            continue;
        }
         // Searching for the element in the array
        int i = type == TypeRecherche.DICHOTOMIQUE
                ? Arrays.binarySearch(elements, element)     // sorted array
                : indexOf(elements, element);                 // arbitrary array
         // displaying the answer
        IO.println(i >= 0 ? "Trouvé en position " + i : "Pas dans le tableau (" + i + ")");
    }
}

// linear search: the Arrays class does not have a method indexOf
int indexOf(double[] elements, double element) {
    for (int i = 0; i < elements.length; i++) {
        if (elements[i] == element) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

// reading a line from the keyboard, without the surrounding spaces; "" at the end of the stream
String lire(String invite) {
    String ligne = IO.readln(invite);
    return ligne == null ? "" : ligne.strip();
}

// search type
enum TypeRecherche { LINEAIRE, DICHOTOMIQUE }

Comments:

  • Lines 18–42: The [saisie] method enters array elements typed from the keyboard. Since the number of elements is not known in advance, the program starts with an empty array (line 20) and expands it by one element for each new entry (line 37). The size of a Java array is fixed at creation: [Arrays.copyOf] actually creates a new array, one element larger, and copies the elements from the old one into it. A more efficient algorithm would allocate space in groups of N elements. An array is not designed to be expanded: this scenario is better handled with a list [ArrayList], as we will see shortly;
  • line 39: the last element of an array has the index [length - 1];
  • lines 30–35: the conversion of the entered string to a real number by [Double.parseDouble], which throws a [NumberFormatException] exception if the string is not a number. [Double.parseDouble] is not dependent on the system’s language: it always expects a decimal point and rejects the input “3,6” (line 5 of the results);
  • lines 53–75: The method [recherche] searches the array for the characters typed on the keyboard. For an unsorted array, a linear search is performed (line 71), which examines the elements one by one. The class [Arrays] does not have a method named [indexOf]: we write it (lines 78–85). For a sorted array, we perform a binary search using [Arrays.binarySearch] (line 70), which halves the search range at each step: it finds an element among one million in about twenty comparisons;
  • line 10: we sort the array. Here we use a variant of [sort] that has only one parameter: the array to be sorted. The ordering relation used to compare the array elements is then the implicit one for those elements: in this case, the natural order of numbers;
  • Lines 45–50: Displaying an array. [IO.println] displays a [double] with a decimal point, regardless of the machine’s language, and always with at least one decimal place: -7 is displayed as -7.0;
  • lines 88–91: [IO.readln] (Java 25) displays a prompt, then reads a line typed on the keyboard; it returns [null] if standard input is exhausted, for example when it comes from a file;
  • line 94: an enumeration, declared in the compact source file just like methods.
