[après ajout de 20] grands=[5, 6, 10, 20], instantane=[5, 6, 10]
[findFirst sur un flux]
  filter examine 1
  filter examine 2
  filter examine 3
  premier=3
[sorted]
  avant sorted : 3
  avant sorted : 1
  avant sorted : 2
  après sorted : 1
  après sorted : 2
  après sorted : 3
[IntStream] somme des carrés des nombres pairs de 1 à 10 = 220
[IntStream] boxed : [5, 3, 8], asDoubleStream().average() : 5.333333333333333

Comments:

  • lines 7–15: a stream that keeps even numbers and then calculates their squares. The lambdas here are written with a body enclosed in curly braces, which displays a message before returning its value with [return];
  • Line 3 of the results: After defining the flow, nothing was displayed: neither [filter] nor [map] has yet processed a single element. [carresPairs] does not contain results, but rather a description of a calculation;
  • Lines 4–16 of the results: The calculation runs during the terminal operation [forEach], element by element: each number passes through [filter], then [map] if it is even, and then enters [forEach] before the next number is examined. No intermediate list is constructed;
  • lines 23–26: Since a stream can only be traversed once, we instead store the means to create it: a parameterless lambda [() -> nombres.stream().filter(...)], of type [Supplier<Stream<Integer>>], whose method [get] creates a new stream on each call. The flow created after adding 10 takes this new element into account;
  • lines 29–31: [toList] executes the processing and stores its results: [instantane] is a list that does not see the addition of 20;
  • lines 35–42: [findFirst] stops iterating as soon as it finds an element: the numbers following 3 are never examined. [anyMatch], [limit], [takeWhile]… likewise stop the iteration as early as possible; this is what allows for processing infinite streams;
  • Lines 46–49: Some intermediate operations cannot process elements one by one: [sorted] must know all the elements in order to transmit the smallest one. The operation [peek], which executes a lambda on each element as it passes through without modifying it, shows that the three elements are received by [sorted] before it transmits a single one;
  • lines 52–55: the primitive streams [IntStream], [LongStream], and [DoubleStream] prevent the creation of objects [Integer], [Long], and [Double]. [IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)] generates the integers from 1 to 10 (including 10). [boxed] converts a [IntStream] to [Stream<Integer>], and a [asDoubleStream] to [DoubleStream]. A [double] concatenated with a string is displayed with all its decimal places and a decimal point; to limit the number of decimal places, you would use [formatted].

Lazy evaluation has two practical consequences:

  • a stream can only be traversed once. If the result of a calculation is needed multiple times, it is stored in a list using [toList];
  • operations can be chained together at no cost: chaining [filter], [map], and [limit] creates no intermediate collection, and only the necessary elements are computed.

Finally, note that the [parallelStream] method of a collection returns a stream whose elements are processed simultaneously by multiple threads (Chapter 8). It only speeds up time-consuming operations on large volumes of data and requires lambdas with no side effects: it should only be used after assessing its benefits. We will encounter the API stream throughout the course, and in Chapter 7 we will see how the functional interfaces it uses are constructed.

docs.title: 5.6. Text files
docs.text:
Java has two API packages for files: the [java.io] package, which has been available since Java 1.0 ([File], [FileReader], [FileInputStream]…), and the [java.nio.file] package, introduced with Java 7 ([Path], [Files]…). The latter is more comprehensive and provides better error reporting: it is the one you should use today. It relies on the read and write classes of [java.io] ([BufferedReader], [BufferedWriter]…), which are obtained through methods of the [Files] class.

A file is represented by a [java.nio.file.Path] object, created by [Path.of("infos.txt")] (Java 11). A relative path, such as this one, is supplemented by the program’s current directory—the one from which it was launched.

Since Java 18 (JEP 400), the default encoding for text files is UTF-8, regardless of the operating system. Previously, it depended on the system (often Windows-1252 on French-language Windows), and the same program could interpret the same file differently depending on the machine. The methods of the [Files] class had already been using UTF-8 by default since Java 8.

docs.title: 5.6.1. The BufferedReader class
docs.text:
The [java.io.BufferedReader] class allows you to read the contents of a text file line by line. It is actually capable of processing streams that are not files (a network connection, for example). It reads the file in blocks, which it stores in a buffer: most reading is done in memory, without accessing the disk.

Methodrole[static BufferedReader Files.newBufferedReader(Path path)]opens the file [path] for reading as UTF-8; an overload allows you to specify the encoding: [Files.newBufferedReader(path, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1)][String readLine()]returns the next line of the stream, without the end-of-line marker, or [null] if at the end of the stream[int read()]returns the next character in the stream, or -1 at the end of the stream[Stream<String> lines()]returns the remaining lines as a stream from the API stream[void close()]closes the stream and releases the resources allocated for its management. This must be done after processing the stream, which is handled by the [try] instruction with resources

The program [Fichiers01.java] is as follows:

// reading a text file with BufferedReader
void main(String[] args) {
     // the current directory: this is where files specified by a relative path are searched for
    IO.println("Dossier courant : " + Path.of("").toAbsolutePath().getFileName());
     // The file name can be passed as an argument; otherwise, infos.txt
    Path fichier = Path.of(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "infos.txt");
    try {
         // Read mode 1: line by line
        IO.println("Lecture 1----------------");
        try (BufferedReader lecteur = Files.newBufferedReader(fichier)) {
            String ligne;
             // readLine sets the value to null at the end of the file
            while ((ligne = lecteur.readLine()) != null) {
                IO.println(ligne);
            }
        } // Here, the stream is closed

         // Read 2: the entire file at once
        IO.println("Lecture 2----------------");
        IO.print(Files.readString(fichier));
    } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
         // e.getFile() is the path to the file that cannot be found
        IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : le fichier [" + e.getFile() + "] n'existe pas");
    } catch (IOException e) {
         // other I/O errors
        IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 2: the [main] method receives the command-line arguments here, in the [args] array;
  • Line 4: Displays the name of the current folder, the one from which the [java] command was launched. [Path.of("")] refers to the current folder; [toAbsolutePath] converts it to a full path, of which [getFileName] retains only the last element, so as not to clutter the results with a full path;
  • line 6: The file being read is [infos.txt] or the one passed as an argument. Since this is a relative path, it is searched for in the current directory;
  • line 10: the [try (déclaration de ressource) { ... }] statement, known as a “try-with-resources” block (Java 7), ensures that the stream is closed upon exiting the block, even if an exception occurs within the block. It eliminates the need to explicitly call the [close] method. It applies to any object that implements the [AutoCloseable] interface—that is, any object with a [close] method that releases resources (file, network connection, database connection, etc.). Prior to Java 7, the stream had to be closed in a [finally] clause after verifying that it had indeed been opened;
  • lines 13–15: the file is read line by line. The assignment [ligne = lecteur.readLine()] is an expression whose value is that of [ligne]: it is compared to [null], which indicates the end of the file;
  • Line 20: [Files.readString] (Java 11) reads the entire file at once and closes it;
  • Lines 21–27: Input/output errors are signaled by exceptions derived from [java.io.IOException]. These are controlled exceptions (Chapter 4): the compiler requires that they be caught or declared. A missing file triggers a [NoSuchFileException], which is derived from it; therefore, it must be caught first. Its [getFile] method returns the path of the file being searched for. The older classes of [java.io] report the same error as a [FileNotFoundException].

The [infos.txt] file is as follows:

12620:0:0
13190:0,05:631
15640:0,1:1290,5

It is located in the [05-classes-java] folder, from which the program is run:

> java Fichiers01.java
Dossier courant : 05-classes-java
Lecture 1----------------
12620:0:0
13190:0,05:631
15640:0,1:1290,5
Lecture 2----------------
12620:0:0
13190:0,05:631
15640:0,1:1290,5

With a file that does not exist:

> java Fichiers01.java xx.txt
Dossier courant : 05-classes-java
Lecture 1----------------
NoSuchFileException : le fichier [xx.txt] n'existe pas

When a folder is used instead of a file, the read operation triggers another exception, [IOException], whose message is provided by the operating system:

> java Fichiers01.java .
Dossier courant : 05-classes-java
Lecture 1----------------
IOException : Is a directory

Choosing the current directory to locate data files is natural for a compact source file that is run from its own directory. For a Maven project, the [mvn exec:java] command runs in the project directory: that is where we will place the data files for the example application.

docs.title: 5.6.2. The BufferedWriter class
docs.text:
The [java.io.BufferedWriter] class allows you to write to a text file. Like [BufferedReader], it uses a buffer and is capable of processing streams that are not files.

MethodRole[static BufferedWriter Files.newBufferedWriter(Path path)]Opens the file [path] for writing as UTF-8. The file is created, or cleared if it already exists. Optional parameters allow you to specify the encoding and the opening mode: [Files.newBufferedWriter(path, StandardOpenOption.APPEND)] appends the writes to the end of the existing file[void write(String str)]writes [str] to the file[void newLine()]writes a line-end character: the system’s default, “\r\n” on Windows, “\n” on Linux, and macOS[void flush()]writes the contents of the buffer to the file without waiting for it to be full[void close()]closes the stream after writing the buffer’s contents to the file. This must be done after processing the stream

Writes to a [BufferedWriter] are not immediate: the text is first written to the buffer, then to the file when the buffer is full, when it is explicitly flushed using the [flush] method, or when the stream is closed. This is the most efficient mode for files because it minimizes disk access. It is not suitable for all data streams, particularly network streams: in a dialogue between two partners, what one writes must be read immediately by the other, and the buffer must be flushed after each message. The [java.io.PrintWriter] class, which we will use later, adds the methods [print], [println], and [printf], and can automatically clear its buffer after each call to [println] (constructor [new PrintWriter(writer, true)]).

The program [Fichiers02.java] is as follows:

// Writing a text file with BufferedWriter
void main() {
    Path fichier = Path.of("infos2.txt");
    try {
         // creating the text file (if it already exists, it is overwritten)
        try (BufferedWriter ecrivain = Files.newBufferedWriter(fichier)) {
            IO.println("encodage par défaut : " + Charset.defaultCharset());
             // Loop as long as the entered line is not empty
            while (true) {
                String saisie = IO.readln("ligne (rien pour arrêter) : ");
                String ligne = saisie == null ? "" : saisie.strip();
                if (ligne.isEmpty()) {
                    break;
                }
                 // Write the line to the text file, followed by a newline
                ecrivain.write(ligne);
                ecrivain.newLine();
            }
        } // close the stream: the buffer is written to the file

         // Verification: Reads the created file
        IO.println("Contenu de " + fichier + " (" + Files.size(fichier) + " octets) :");
        IO.print(Files.readString(fichier));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : " + e);
    }
}

Results:

> java Fichiers02.java
encodage par défaut : UTF-8
ligne (rien pour arrêter) : 1ère ligne
ligne (rien pour arrêter) : 2ième ligne
ligne (rien pour arrêter) : 
Contenu de infos2.txt (25 octets) :
1ère ligne
2ième ligne

Comments:

  • line 6: once again, we use the [try] statement with resources so that we don’t have to explicitly close the stream. This closure occurs automatically at the end of the block (closing curly brace on line 19). It is this closure that writes the text remaining in the buffer to the file; without it, the file might remain incomplete;
  • line 7: the default encoding, UTF-8;
  • lines 16–17: writes a line to the text file, followed by a line break;
  • line 22: the [Files.size] method returns the size of a file in bytes. The 25 bytes break down as follows: 21 characters, plus 1 additional byte for each of the two [è] (which take up 2 bytes in UTF-8), plus two one-byte line breaks ("\n" on Linux, where the tests were run; on Windows, each "\r\n" line break would take up 2 bytes);
  • Line 24: Why [try / catch]? We could use a filename in the form [rep1/rep2/fichier] with a folder named [rep1/rep2] that does not exist, making it impossible to create the file. A [NoSuchFileException] exception, derived from [IOException], would then be thrown. There are other possible exception scenarios (disk full, insufficient permissions, etc.). In any case, the compiler requires that the controlled exceptions [IOException] thrown by [newBufferedWriter], [write], or [size] be handled.

docs.title: 5.6.3. The Files and Path Classes
docs.text:
For common operations, the utility class [Files] eliminates the need to handle streams: a single method opens the file, reads or writes it in its entirety, and then closes it. It also allows you to create, copy, move, and delete files and folders. The [Path] interface handles paths.

Methodrole[Files.readString(path)]returns the file’s contents as a string (Java 11)[Files.readAllLines(path)]returns the lines of the file in a list [List<String>][Files.lines(path)]Returns the lines of the file as a stream [Stream<String>] that is read on demand and must be closed after use[Files.writeString(path, texte, options...)]creates (or overwrites) the file and writes [texte] (Java 11) to it; with the [StandardOpenOption.APPEND] option, appends the text to the end of the file[Files.write(path, lignes, options...)]writes a collection of lines, each followed by a line break[Files.readAllBytes(path)], [Files.write(path, octets)]reads and writes the file as a byte array[Files.exists(path)], [Files.size(path)], [Files.delete(path)], [Files.copy(source, cible)], [Files.move(source, cible)]checks if a file exists, returns its size, deletes it, copies it, moves it[Files.createDirectories(path)]creates the folder and its parent folders if they do not exist[Files.list(dossier)], [Files.walk(dossier)]the elements of the folder and its entire tree structure, in the form of a stream [Stream<Path>][path.resolve(autre)]constructs a path by appending [autre] to [path], using the system separator[path.getFileName()], [path.getParent()], [path.toAbsolutePath()]the file name, its folder, and its full path

The program [Fichiers03.java] uses them:

// The Path and Files classes
void main() throws IOException {
     // resolve constructs a path using the system separator (\ on Windows, / on Linux)
    Path dossier = Path.of("donnees");
    Path chemin = dossier.resolve("villes.txt");
    String nom = chemin.getFileName().toString();
    IO.println("chemin=" + chemin + ", nom=" + nom + ", dossier=" + chemin.getParent()
            + ", sans extension=" + nom.substring(0, nom.lastIndexOf('.')));

     // createDirectories creates the folder (and its parent folders) if it does not exist
    Files.createDirectories(dossier);

     // writeString: creates (or overwrites) a file with the given text, in UTF-8
    Files.writeString(chemin, "Angers\nNantes\n");
     // write with the option APPEND: adds lines to the end of the file
    Files.write(chemin, List.of("Paris", "Lyon"), StandardOpenOption.APPEND);
     // readAllLines: all lines in a list
    List<String> lignes = Files.readAllLines(chemin);
    IO.println("readAllLines : " + lignes.size() + " lignes " + lignes);
     // readString: the entire file in a string
    IO.println("readString : " + Files.readString(chemin).length() + " caractères");
     // lines: a stream of lines read on demand; close after use
    try (Stream<String> flux = Files.lines(chemin)) {
        flux.filter(l -> l.startsWith("N") || l.startsWith("L"))
                .forEach(ville -> IO.println("lines + filter : " + ville));
    }

     // encoding: UTF-8 by default; another encoding can be specified
    String texte = "élève";
    Files.writeString(dossier.resolve("utf8.txt"), texte);
    Files.writeString(dossier.resolve("utf8bom.txt"), "\uFEFF" + texte);
    Files.writeString(dossier.resolve("latin1.txt"), texte, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1);
    HexFormat hex = HexFormat.of().withUpperCase();
    for (String fichier : List.of("utf8.txt", "utf8bom.txt", "latin1.txt")) {
        byte[] octets = Files.readAllBytes(dossier.resolve(fichier));
        IO.println("%-12s: %2d octets : %s".formatted(fichier, octets.length, hex.formatHex(octets)));
    }
     // a Latin-1 file re-read in UTF-8: readString rejects invalid bytes
    Path latin1 = dossier.resolve("latin1.txt");
    try {
        IO.println(Files.readString(latin1));
    } catch (MalformedInputException e) {
        IO.println("latin1.txt lu en UTF-8 : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
     // new String(bytes, UTF_8) replaces each invalid byte with the character �
    IO.println("latin1.txt décodé en UTF-8 : "
            + new String(Files.readAllBytes(latin1), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    IO.println("latin1.txt lu en Latin-1 : " + Files.readString(latin1, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1));
     // the BOM is not removed during reading: it is an extra character
    IO.println("utf8bom.txt : " + Files.readString(dossier.resolve("utf8bom.txt")).length() + " caractères");

     // exists, list
    IO.println("exists(villes.txt)=" + Files.exists(chemin) + ", exists(xx.txt)="
            + Files.exists(dossier.resolve("xx.txt")));
    try (Stream<Path> fichiers = Files.list(dossier)) {
        for (Path fichier : fichiers.sorted().toList()) {
            IO.println("  %-12s %3d octets".formatted(fichier.getFileName(), Files.size(fichier)));
        }
    }

     // cleanup: a folder must be empty to be deleted; its contents are deleted first
    try (Stream<Path> arbre = Files.walk(dossier)) {
        for (Path p : arbre.sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).toList()) {
            Files.delete(p);
        }
    }
    IO.println("après suppression : exists(donnees)=" + Files.exists(dossier));
}

Results:

> java Fichiers03.java
chemin=donnees/villes.txt, nom=villes.txt, dossier=donnees, sans extension=villes
readAllLines : 4 lignes [Angers, Nantes, Paris, Lyon]
readString : 25 caractères
lines + filter : Nantes
lines + filter : Lyon
utf8.txt    :  7 octets : C3A96CC3A87665
utf8bom.txt : 10 octets : EFBBBFC3A96CC3A87665
latin1.txt  :  5 octets : E96CE87665
latin1.txt lu en UTF-8 : MalformedInputException : Input length = 3
latin1.txt décodé en UTF-8 : �l�ve
latin1.txt lu en Latin-1 : élève
utf8bom.txt : 6 caractères
exists(villes.txt)=true, exists(xx.txt)=false
  latin1.txt     5 octets
  utf8.txt       7 octets
  utf8bom.txt   10 octets
  villes.txt    25 octets
après suppression : exists(donnees)=false

Comments:

  • Line 2: The methods of [Files] call [IOException]. To keep this demo program lightweight, the [main] method declares them using the [throws IOException] clause instead of intercepting them: an error would terminate the program and display the exception;
  • Lines 4–8: [resolve] uses the system’s path separator. The course runs were performed on Linux: the resulting path is [donnees/villes.txt]; on Windows, it would be [donnees\villes.txt]. Building paths using [resolve] (or [Path.of("donnees", "villes.txt")]) rather than concatenating strings makes the code portable. Since [Path] does not have a method that returns a file extension, we separate it from the name using [lastIndexOf];
  • Line 11: Creating the folder [donnees] does not cause an error if it already exists;
  • Lines 14–21: writing, adding, and reading, each in a single statement;
  • Lines 23–26: [Files.lines] returns a stream: the lines are read one by one as the stream is processed. You can apply the API stream to it, thereby processing a file several gigabytes in size without loading it into memory—which is what [readAllLines] would do. The stream keeps the file open: it must be closed, hence the [try] instruction with resources ([Stream] implements [AutoCloseable]);
  • lines 29–37: the same text “élève” is written using three encodings, then the bytes in the files are displayed in hexadecimal using the [HexFormat] class (Java 17):
    • In UTF-8, Java’s default encoding, accented characters take up 2 bytes (é = C3 A9) and the others 1 byte: 7 bytes for 5 characters;
    • in UTF-8 with BOM (Byte Order Mark), the file begins with the 3 bytes EF BB BF, which indicate to software that the file is encoded in UTF-8. Java never writes BOM on its own: it is obtained by writing the character U+FEFF at the beginning of the text, denoted as ["\uFEFF"];
    • in Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1), the traditional encoding for Western European texts, each character occupies one byte (é = E9);
  • lines 39–44: Reading a file using an encoding different from the one used to write it alters accented characters: the byte sequence E9 6C E8 is invalid in UTF-8. [Files.readString] and [Files.readAllLines] reject such a file by throwing a [MalformedInputException] exception (derived from [IOException]);
  • Lines 46–47: The conversion of a byte array to a string by the [new String(octets, encodage)] constructor is less strict: each invalid byte is replaced by the character �. A [InputStreamReader] behaves the same way; in contrast, the [BufferedReader] returned by [Files.newBufferedReader] is strict, like [Files.readString], and also invokes a [MalformedInputException];
  • line 48: when read with the correct encoding, the file is correct;
  • line 50: upon reading, Java does not recognize the BOM: it is read as an invisible character at the beginning of the text, which has 6 characters instead of 5. If you need to read UTF-8 files generated with a BOM (by certain Windows software), you must remove this character yourself. Today, the rule is simple: write and read text files in UTF-8, without BOM;
  • lines 53–59: the files in the folder. [Files.list] returns a stream that must be closed, just like the one for [Files.lines], and does not guarantee the order of the names: [sorted] sorts them;
  • lines 62–67: deleting the folder. [Files.delete] refuses to delete a non-empty folder: we traverse the entire directory tree using [Files.walk], and sort the paths in reverse order ([Comparator.reverseOrder()]) to delete a folder’s contents before the folder itself.

The methods of [Files] block the thread that calls them until the operation is complete. In Chapter 9, which covers asynchronous programming, we’ll see how to avoid blocking a program during a long I/O operation.

docs.title: 5.7.1. The DataOutputStream and DataInputStream classes
docs.text:
The classes [java.io.DataOutputStream] and [java.io.DataInputStream] are used to write to and read from binary files. In such a file, data is not written as text but in its internal form: a [int] always occupies 4 bytes, regardless of its value. These are byte streams: they are derived from the classes [OutputStream] and [InputStream], whereas text streams are derived from [Writer] and [Reader].

Consider the following application:

// syntax: Java Fichiers04.java binary text logs
// A text file (text) is read, and its contents are written to a binary file (binary)
// The text file contains lines in the form "name: age," which are written in the form (String, int)
// (logs) is a text log file

The text file [personnes1.txt] has the following content:

paul : 10
helene : 15

jacques : 11
sylvain : 12
xx : -1

xx: yy : zz
xx : yy

The program [Fichiers04.java] is as follows:

// syntax: java Fichiers04.java binary text logs
// a text file (text) is read, and its contents are written to a binary file (binary)
// The text file contains lines in the form "name: age," which are written as (String, int)
// (logs) is a text file containing logs
void main(String[] args) {
     // Three arguments are required
    if (args.length != 3) {
        IO.println("syntaxe : java Fichiers04.java texte binaire logs");
        System.exit(1);
    }
     // Opening the three files; they will be closed at the end of the `try` block, in reverse order
    try (BufferedReader input = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of(args[0]));
         DataOutputStream output = new DataOutputStream(
                 new BufferedOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(Path.of(args[1]))));
         PrintWriter logs = new PrintWriter(Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of(args[2])))) {
         // Processing the text file
        String ligne;
        int numLigne = 0, nbPersonnes = 0;
        while ((ligne = input.readLine()) != null) {
             // one more line
            numLigne++;
             // Empty line? Ignore it
            if (ligne.isBlank()) {
                continue;
            }
             // a line containing name: age
            String[] champs = ligne.strip().split("\\s*:\\s*");
             // We need 2 fields
            if (champs.length != 2) {
                logs.println("La ligne n° [" + numLigne + "] du fichier [" + args[0]
                        + "] a un nombre de champs incorrect");
                continue;
            }
             // The first field must not be empty
            boolean erreur = false;
            String nom = champs[0];
            if (nom.isEmpty()) {
                logs.println("La ligne n° [" + numLigne + "] du fichier [" + args[0] + "] a un nom vide");
                erreur = true;
            }
             // The second field must be an integer >= 0
            int age = entier(champs[1]);
            if (age < 0) {
                logs.println("La ligne n° [" + numLigne + "] du fichier [" + args[0] + "] a un âge ["
                        + champs[1] + "] incorrect");
                erreur = true;
            }
             // If there are no errors, write the data to the binary file
            if (!erreur) {
                output.writeUTF(nom);
                output.writeInt(age);
                nbPersonnes++;
            }
        }
        IO.println(numLigne + " lignes lues, " + nbPersonnes + " personnes écrites dans [" + args[1]
                + "], erreurs dans [" + args[2] + "]");
    } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
        IO.println("Le fichier [" + e.getFile() + "] n'existe pas");
        System.exit(2);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : " + e);
        System.exit(3);
    }
}

// a positive integer or zero; -1 if the string is not an integer
int entier(String champ) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(champ);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return -1;
    }
}

Let’s take a closer look at the operations related to class [DataOutputStream]:

  • Lines 13–14: The [DataOutputStream] object is built around another byte stream, following the principle of nested streams (the “decorator” design pattern):
    • [Files.newOutputStream(Path.of(args[1]))] writes a byte stream to the file, which is created or flushed if it already exists;
    • [BufferedOutputStream] adds a buffer to it, so as not to access the disk with every write;
    • [DataOutputStream] adds methods for writing basic data types;
  • Lines 50–51: the write operations. The class [DataOutputStream] has one method per simple data type: [writeInt], [writeDouble], [writeLong], [writeBoolean], [writeUTF] for a string…;
  • Lines 12–15: The three streams are opened in a single [try] statement with resources, with their declarations separated by semicolons. They will be closed at the end of the [try] block, in the reverse order in which they were opened. Closing the outer stream ([DataOutputStream]) closes the streams it contains. The log file is written via a [PrintWriter], to make use of the [println] method;
  • line 27: the separator is the character [:], surrounded by any spaces, which are removed along with it;
  • Lines 42–47: The age must be a positive integer or zero. Java does not have a method that converts a string to an integer without throwing an exception in case of an error: the method [entier] (lines 67–73) catches the exception [NumberFormatException] and returns -1, which is an invalid value for an age;
  • lines 9, 59, 62: [System.exit(n)] terminates the program with exit code n, which a script can check (0: success; this is the exit code of a program whose [main] method terminates normally).

The program’s three arguments are passed after the source file name in the [java] command. The results are as follows:

> java Fichiers04.java personnes1.txt personnes1.bin logs.txt
9 lignes lues, 4 personnes écrites dans [personnes1.bin], erreurs dans [logs.txt]

The [logs.txt] log file contains the following:

> cat logs.txt
La ligne n° [6] du fichier [personnes1.txt] a un âge [-1] incorrect
La ligne n° [8] du fichier [personnes1.txt] a un nombre de champs incorrect
La ligne n° [9] du fichier [personnes1.txt] a un âge [yy] incorrect

The contents of the binary file [personnes1.bin] can be displayed in hexadecimal using the Linux command [od] (on Windows, the command PowerShell [Format-Hex] produces a similar display):

> od -A d -t x1z personnes1.bin
0000000 00 04 70 61 75 6c 00 00 00 0a 00 06 68 65 6c 65  >..paul......hele<
0000016 6e 65 00 00 00 0f 00 07 6a 61 63 71 75 65 73 00  >ne......jacques.<
0000032 00 00 0b 00 07 73 79 6c 76 61 69 6e 00 00 00 0c  >.....sylvain....<
0000048

This shows how [DataOutputStream] writes the data:

  • a string is written by [writeUTF], preceded by its length in bytes, on 2 bytes: 00 04, followed by the 4 bytes of “paul” (70 61 75 6c). The characters are encoded using a variant of UTF-8;
  • an integer [int] is written over 4 bytes, with the most significant byte first (known as “big-endian” order, used in network protocols): 10 is written as 00 00 00 0a. This format is the same on all machines: a file written by [DataOutputStream] on Windows can be read on Linux;
  • the data is written consecutively, without any separators or line breaks: the file is 48 bytes long (line 5: with the [-A d] option, [od] displays the positions in decimal).

To read this file, you must therefore know the exact order and type of the written data. For each method [writeXX] of [DataOutputStream], the class [DataInputStream] has a corresponding method [readXX]: [readUTF], [readInt], [readDouble]… However, it cannot indicate how many bytes remain to be read: a file read by [DataInputStream] must begin with the number of records it contains, or be read until the [EOFException] exception occurs, which signals the end of the stream. But an exception must remain exceptional, and the end of a file is not.

docs.title: 5.7.2. The RandomAccessFile class
docs.text:
The [java.io.RandomAccessFile] class reads from and writes to a file using direct access: you can position the read/write head at any location in the file before reading or writing. It has the same read and write methods as [DataInputStream] and [DataOutputStream] (it implements the same interfaces as [DataInput] and [DataOutput]), and in addition:

methodrole[RandomAccessFile(String name, String mode)]opens the file for reading ([mode] "r") or for reading and writing ("rw")[long length()]the file size, in bytes[long getFilePointer()]the current position in the file[void seek(long pos)]moves to position [pos] in the file

The program [Fichiers05.java] performs the reverse operation of the previous program: it reads the binary file to create a text file. If the resulting text file contains the correct data from the original file, we will know that the text → binary → text conversion was successful.

// syntax: java Fichiers05.java binary text
// Reads a binary file (binary) and stores its contents in a text file (text)
// the binary file contains (String, int) pairs
// The text file will contain lines in the form name:age
void main(String[] args) {
     // Two arguments are required
    if (args.length != 2) {
        IO.println("syntaxe : java Fichiers05.java binaire texte");
        System.exit(1);
    }
     // Open the binary file for reading ("r") and the text file for writing
    try (RandomAccessFile input = new RandomAccessFile(args[0], "r");
         PrintWriter output = new PrintWriter(Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of(args[1])))) {
         // Process the binary file until the end of the file is reached
        int nbPersonnes = 0;
        while (input.getFilePointer() < input.length()) {
             // Read "name," then "age": in the order they were written
            String nom = input.readUTF();
            int age = input.readInt();
             // Write to the text file
            output.println(nom + ":" + age);
            nbPersonnes++;
        }
        IO.println(nbPersonnes + " personnes lues dans [" + args[0] + "] et écrites dans [" + args[1] + "]");
         // direct access: return to the beginning of the file and reread the first person
        input.seek(0);
        IO.println("première personne : " + input.readUTF() + ", " + input.readInt() + " ans");
    } catch (EOFException e) {
         // the file ends in the middle of a record
        IO.println("Le fichier [" + args[0] + "] est tronqué");
        System.exit(2);
    } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
         // RandomAccessFile indicates a missing file with a FileNotFoundException
        IO.println(e.getMessage());
        System.exit(3);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : " + e);
        System.exit(4);
    }
}

Let’s take a closer look at the operations involving the [RandomAccessFile] class:

  • line 12: the [RandomAccessFile] object is opened in read-only mode (“r” mode);
  • lines 18–19: the read operations, [readUTF] and [readInt]. They must be called in the order of the writes;
  • line 16: reading continues until the current position in the file reaches the end of the file;
  • lines 26–27: direct access: [seek] resets the position to the beginning of the file, and the first record is read again. If all records were the same size, we could read the nth record directly by moving to position n × size: this is the principle behind direct-access files, the precursors to databases;
  • line 28: the exception [EOFException] now signals a true anomaly: a file that ends in the middle of a record;
  • line 32: [RandomAccessFile], a class of [java.io], signals a missing file via a [FileNotFoundException], whose message—provided by the system—contains the file name.

Let’s run the program on the [personnes1.bin] file generated earlier:

> java Fichiers05.java personnes1.bin personnes2.txt
4 personnes lues dans [personnes1.bin] et écrites dans [personnes2.txt]
première personne : paul, 10 ans

The contents of [personnes2.txt] are as follows:

> cat personnes2.txt
paul:10
helene:15
jacques:11
sylvain:12

We find the 4 valid people from the file [personnes1.txt]. With a file [tronque.bin] consisting of the first 33 bytes of [personnes1.bin], reading Jacques’s age fails:

> java Fichiers05.java tronque.bin tronque.txt
Le fichier [tronque.bin] est tronqué

And with a nonexistent file:

> java Fichiers05.java xx.bin xx.txt
xx.bin (No such file or directory)

Java also has a mechanism for binary serialization of objects: the classes *[ObjectOutputStream] and [ObjectInputStream] write and read entire objects, provided that their class implements the *[java.io.Serializable] interface. This mechanism is now deprecated: deserializing data from an untrusted source has enabled numerous attacks, as deserialization can execute code chosen by the attacker. A text-based format such as JSON is preferred instead. However, the [Serializable] interface is still found in many classes, particularly exceptions, which inherit it from the [Throwable] class: which is why the compiler, with the [-Xlint:all] option, requires that they declare a [serialVersionUID] field, as we will see in the sample application.

docs.title: 5.7.3. JSON Serialization with Jackson
docs.text:
Writing to and reading from a binary file one data point at a time is tedious, and even the slightest discrepancy between writing and reading produces incorrect results. It is generally preferable to serialize objects: automatically converting them into a sequence of characters, then deserializing them to reconstruct them.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text-based, human-readable, and universal format: it is the exchange format for web services (Chapter 13) and many configuration files. An object is written within curly braces as pairs of "property": value, or as an array enclosed in square brackets.

The Java standard library cannot read or write JSON. An external library is used; the most common one is Jackson, which Spring Boot uses by default. Version 3 (2025) has changed packages: [tools.jackson.*] instead of [com.fasterxml.jackson.*] for version 2, which is still commonly encountered; its annotations remain in the [com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation] package. An external library is obtained using Maven (Chapter 2): the program is therefore a Maven project, [Fichiers06], with the following directory structure:

05-classes-java/
  Fichiers06/
    pom.xml
    src/main/java/json/
      Fichiers06.java

The file [pom.xml] declares the dependency on Jackson:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>exemples.classes</groupId>
    <artifactId>fichiers06</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
         <!-- Jackson 3: serialization JSON -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>tools.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>3.1.5</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.15.0</version>
                <configuration>
                    <parameters>true</parameters>
                    <compilerArgs>
                        <arg>-Xlint:all</arg>
                    </compilerArgs>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
             <!-- `mvn exec:java` executes the main class -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.5.1</version>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>json.Fichiers06</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

Comments:

  • lines 7–9: the project details;
  • lines 11–14: the Java version and the encoding of the source files;
  • lines 16–23: the dependency on the [jackson-databind] library. Maven downloads it from the central repository (Maven Central), along with the libraries on which it itself depends ([jackson-core] and [jackson-annotations]);
  • lines 27–37: the compiler, configured as in all projects in the course: warnings enabled ([-Xlint:all]) and parameter names preserved in the compiled code;
  • lines 39–46: the plugin [exec-maven-plugin], which executes the main class using the command [mvn exec:java].

The central object in Jackson is [JsonMapper], which has two main methods:

methodrole[String writeValueAsString(Object value)]returns the text JSON representing the object [value][<T> T readValue(String content, Class<T> valueType)]reconstructs an object of type [T] from the text JSON [content]; throws a [JacksonException] if the text is incorrect. An overload receives a [TypeReference] instead of a [Class]

The program [Fichiers06.java] uses them:

package json;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import tools.jackson.core.JacksonException;
import tools.jackson.core.json.JsonWriteFeature;
import tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference;
import tools.jackson.databind.MapperFeature;
import tools.jackson.databind.SerializationFeature;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

// Serialization JSON with Jackson 3
public class Fichiers06 {

     // a person: a record, whose components become the properties JSON
    record Personne(String nom, int age, List<String> loisirs) {
    }

     // an article: the @JsonProperty annotation sets the property name JSON
    record Article(@JsonProperty("reference") String code, BigDecimal prix) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        List<Personne> personnes = List.of(
                new Personne("paul", 10, List.of("football")),
                new Personne("hélène", 15, List.of("piano", "tennis")),
                new Personne("jacques", 11, List.of()));

         // 1 - a JsonMapper with the default configuration: a single line
        JsonMapper mapper = JsonMapper.builder().build();
        String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(personnes.get(1));
        IO.println("[par défaut] " + json);
         // Non-ASCII characters can be escaped
        JsonMapper ascii = JsonMapper.builder().enable(JsonWriteFeature.ESCAPE_NON_ASCII).build();
        IO.println("[ESCAPE_NON_ASCII] " + ascii.writeValueAsString(personnes.get(1)));

         // 2 - an option: indentation
        JsonMapper indente = JsonMapper.builder().enable(SerializationFeature.INDENT_OUTPUT).build();
        json = indente.writeValueAsString(personnes);
         // writing to a text file
        Path fichier = Path.of("personnes.json");
        Files.writeString(fichier, json);
        IO.println("[personnes.json]");
        IO.println(Files.readString(fichier));

         // 3 - deserialization: from JSON text to objects
        String texte = Files.readString(fichier);
         // TypeReference passes the full type `List<Person>` to Jackson
        List<Personne> relues = mapper.readValue(texte, new TypeReference<List<Personne>>() {
        });
        IO.println("[relues] " + relues.size() + " personnes");
        for (Personne p : relues) {
            IO.println("  " + p.nom() + ", " + p.age() + " ans, loisirs : " + p.loisirs());
        }

         // 4 - a property name specified by an annotation
        String jsonArticle = mapper.writeValueAsString(new Article("A12", new BigDecimal("12.5")));
        IO.println("[@JsonProperty] " + jsonArticle);
         // Parsing can ignore case in property names
        JsonMapper casse = JsonMapper.builder()
                .enable(MapperFeature.ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES)
                .build();
        Article article = casse.readValue("""
                { "REFERENCE": "B7", "Prix": 3 }""", Article.class);
        IO.println("[ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES] " + article);

         // 5 - an invalid JSON document causes a JacksonException
        try {
            mapper.readValue("""
                    { "nom": "x", "age": "douze" }""", Personne.class);
        } catch (JacksonException e) {
            IO.println("[erreur] " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getOriginalMessage());
            IO.println("[erreur] ligne " + e.getLocation().getLineNr() + ", colonne "
                    + e.getLocation().getColumnNr() + ", chemin : " + e.getPathReference());
        }
    }
}

It is run in the project folder using the [mvn compile exec:java] command, or from the IDE file. We do not reproduce the Maven messages, but only the program’s output:

> mvn compile exec:java
[par défaut] {"nom":"hélène","age":15,"loisirs":["piano","tennis"]}
[ESCAPE_NON_ASCII] {"nom":"h\u00E9l\u00E8ne","age":15,"loisirs":["piano","tennis"]}
[personnes.json]
[ {
  "nom" : "paul",
  "age" : 10,
  "loisirs" : [ "football" ]
}, {
  "nom" : "hélène",
  "age" : 15,
  "loisirs" : [ "piano", "tennis" ]
}, {
  "nom" : "jacques",
  "age" : 11,
  "loisirs" : [ ]
} ]
[relues] 3 personnes
  paul, 10 ans, loisirs : [football]
  hélène, 15 ans, loisirs : [piano, tennis]
  jacques, 11 ans, loisirs : []
[@JsonProperty] {"reference":"A12","prix":12.5}
[ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES] Article[code=B7, prix=3]
[erreur] InvalidFormatException : Cannot deserialize value of type `int` from String "douze": not a valid `int` value
[erreur] ligne 1, colonne 22, chemin : json.Fichiers06$Personne["age"]

Comments:

  • line 1: In a Maven project, classes are organized into packages: the class [Fichiers06] from the package [json] is located in the file [src/main/java/json/Fichiers06.java];
  • Lines 3–14: Unlike a compact source file, a regular class must import the classes it uses, including those from the standard library;
  • lines 20–21: the [Personne] record to be serialized, declared in the [Fichiers06] class. Jackson 3 can serialize a record: each component becomes a JSON property with the same name;
  • lines 24–25: the annotation [@JsonProperty] sets the name of a component’s property JSON to [reference] instead of [code];
  • line 27: the method [main] is a static method of a class. It declares the exception [IOException], which can be thrown by methods of [Files];
  • Lines 34–36: A [JsonMapper] is created by an object builder: [JsonMapper.builder()] returns an object to which the desired options are passed, and then [build] creates the [JsonMapper]. With the default options, the text is written on a single line, and accented characters are written as-is (line 2 of the results);
  • Lines 38–39: The [ESCAPE_NON_ASCII] option instructs the system to write non-ASCII characters as escape sequences: [é] becomes [\u00E9]. The text remains correct, but it is difficult to read; this is useful when the text JSON must pass through a system that only recognizes ASCII;
  • lines 42–43: The option [INDENT_OUTPUT] produces indented text spread across multiple lines. A list is serialized into an array JSON;
  • lines 45–48: the text JSON is written to a text file and then read back to be displayed: this is how binary serialization is replaced today;
  • lines 53–54: deserialization reconstructs the list. Jackson creates the objects [Personne] by calling the record’s constructor, whose parameters are associated with the JSON properties of the same name. For a list, you must specify the type of its elements to Jackson. However, the expression [List<Personne>.class] does not exist: Java generics are erased at compile time (“type erasure”), and at runtime there is only a class [List], without any type parameters. The trick with [TypeReference] is to create an anonymous class ([new TypeReference<List<Personne>>() { }]***) derived from [TypeReference<List<Personne>>]***: the parent type of a class is preserved in the compiled code, and Jackson can read it. For an array, which is simpler, we write [Personne[].class];
  • lines 61–62: serialization of a [Article]: the property [reference] has the name specified by the annotation. A [BigDecimal] is written as a number JSON;
  • lines 64–69: With the [ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES] option, Jackson ignores case in property names during parsing: [REFERENCE] and [Prix] are accepted;
  • lines 72–79: An invalid JSON document—in this case, a string where a number is expected—triggers an exception derived from [JacksonException], in this instance [InvalidFormatException]. In Jackson 3, these exceptions are unchecked (they are derived from [RuntimeException]), whereas in Jackson 2 they were derived from [IOException]. [getOriginalMessage] returns the message without the location information, which [getLocation] and [getPathReference] provide separately: row 1, column 22, property [age] of record [Personne].

A [JsonMapper] is costly to create, but once created, it is reusable and can be shared among multiple threads: a program typically creates only one, which is stored in a constant. We will use JSON in the following example application and throughout the course.

docs.title: 5.8. Regular Expressions
docs.text:
The [java.util.regex] package supports the use of regular expressions. These allow you to validate the format of a string. For example, you can verify that a string representing a date is indeed in the dd/mm/yy format. To do this, you use a pattern and compare the string to that pattern. In this example, d, m, and y must be digits. The pattern for a valid date format is therefore [\d\d/\d\d/\d\d], where the symbol [\d] represents a digit. The symbols that can be used in a pattern are as follows:

characterdescription[\]marks the following character as a special character or literal. For example, [n] corresponds to the character n, [ ] corresponds to a newline character, [\] corresponds to \, and [\(] corresponds to ([^]corresponds to the beginning of the string[$]corresponds to the end of the string[*]matches the preceding element zero or more times. Thus, [zo*] matches z or zoo[+]matches the previous element once or more times. Thus, [zo+] matches "zoo," but not "z"[?]matches the preceding element zero or one time. For example, [a?ve?] matches "ve" in "lever"[.]matches any single character, except for a newline character[(modèle)]searches for the pattern and stores the match (a group). The matching substring can be extracted from the result using the [group] method. To find matches with characters in parentheses, use [\(] or [\)][x|y]matches either x or y. For example, [z|foot] matches z or foot; [(z|f)oo] matches zoo or foo[{n}]n is a non-negative integer. Corresponds exactly n times to the previous element. For example, [o{2}] does not correspond to o in Bob, but to the first two o’s in fooooot[{n,}]matches the previous element at least n times. For example, [o{2,}] does not match the 'o' in 'Bob', but matches all the 'o's in 'fooooot'. [o{1,}] is equivalent to [o+], and [o{0,}] is equivalent to [o*][{n,m}]matches the previous element at least n times and at most m times. For example, [o{1,3}] matches the first three “o”s in “foooooot”; [o{0,1}] is equivalent to [o?][[xyz]]character set: matches one of the specified characters. For example, [[abc]] matches the letter "a" in "plat"[[^xyz]]negative character set: matches any character not listed. For example, [[^abc]] matches "p" in "plat"[[a-z]]Character range: matches any character in the specified range, in this case a lowercase unaccented letter[[^m-z]]negative character range: matches any character not between 'm' and 'z'[ ]matches a word boundary, that is, the position between a word character and a non-word character. For example, [er ] matches "er" in "lever," but not "er" in "verb"[\B]corresponds to a position that is not a word boundary. [en*t\B] corresponds to “ent” in “bien entendu”[\d]matches a digit; is equivalent to [[0-9]][\D]corresponds to a character that is not a digit[ ], [ ], [ ], [ ]correspond to the characters page break, new line, carriage return, and tab, respectively[\s]corresponds to any whitespace: space, tab, page break, line break… Equivalent to [[ \x0B ]][\S]matches any character that is not a whitespace character[\w]matches any word character: by default in Java, this is an unaccented letter, a digit, or an underscore; equivalent to [[a-zA-Z_0-9]]. With the [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS] option (see below), it also recognizes accented letters[\W]matches any character that is not a word character[ um]num is a positive integer: refers to group number num. For example, [(.)\1] corresponds to two consecutive identical characters[\xnn], [\unnnn]corresponds to the hexadecimal character nn (2 digits) or nnnn (4 digits). For example, [\x41] corresponds to A

An element in a template can appear once or multiple times. Let’s look at a few examples using the symbol [\d], which represents a single digit:

templateMeaning[\d]one digit[\d?]0 or 1 digit[\d*]0 or more digits[\d+]1 or more digits[\d{2}]2 digits[\d{3,}]At least 3 digits[\d{5,7}]between 5 and 7 digits

Now let’s imagine a model capable of describing the expected format for a string:

target stringpatterna date in dd/mm/yy format[\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}]a time in the hh:mm:ss format[\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}]an unsigned integer[\d+]a sequence of spaces, which may be empty[\s*]an unsigned integer that may be preceded or followed by spaces[\s*\d+\s*]an integer that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces[\s*[+-]?\s*\d+\s*]an unsigned real number that may be preceded or followed by spaces[\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]a real number that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces[\s*[+-]?\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]a string containing the word "just"[ juste ]

Note that within square brackets, the character [|] has no special meaning: the [[+|-]] pattern, which is sometimes used for the sign, also accepts the character | before a number. Similarly, the decimal point must be escaped, [\.]: an unescaped period matches any character.

You can specify where to search for the pattern in the string:

patternmeaning[^modèle]the pattern starts the string[modèle$]Model ends the string[^modèle$]The pattern starts and ends the string[modèle]The pattern is searched for anywhere in the string, starting from the beginning of the string search stringpatterna string ending with an exclamation point[!$]a string ending with a period[\.$]a string beginning with the sequence //[^//]a string consisting of a single word, possibly preceded or followed by spaces[^\s*\w+\s*$]a string consisting of exactly two words, possibly preceded or followed by spaces[^\s*\w+\s+\w+\s*$]a string containing the word "secret"[ secret ]

Sub sets of a pattern can be “extracted.” Thus, not only can we verify that a string matches a particular pattern, but we can also extract from that string the elements corresponding to the pattern’s sub sets that have been enclosed in parentheses. For example, if we parse a string containing a date in the format dd/mm/yy and also want to extract the elements dd, mm, and yy from that date, we would use the pattern [(\d\d)/(\d\d)/(\d\d)].

In Java code, a pattern is written as a regular string: each character [\] in the pattern must be duplicated. The pattern [\d+] is written as ["\d+"], and the pattern [\], which represents the \ character, is written as ["\\"]. Text blocks do not change this: [\] is also an escape character here. The editor makes it easier to read: IntelliJ IDEA recognizes the strings passed to [Pattern.compile], highlights them as regular expressions, and allows you to test them.

docs.title: 5.8.1. Check whether a string matches a given pattern
docs.text:
A template is first compiled into a [java.util.regex.Pattern] object, which then provides [Matcher] objects responsible for searching within a given string:

methodrole[static Pattern compile(String regex)]compiles the [regex] template; throws a [PatternSyntaxException] exception if the template is invalid[static Pattern compile(String regex, int flags)]same as above, with options (see below)[Matcher matcher(CharSequence input)]returns a [Matcher] object that looks up the template in [input][boolean find()] (class [Matcher])searches for the next occurrence of the pattern in the string; returns [true] if one is found[boolean matches()] (class [Matcher])returns [true] if the entire string matches the pattern[static boolean matches(String regex, CharSequence input)]compiles the pattern and checks whether the entire string matches it

The program [Regex01.java] is as follows:

// Check that a string matches a pattern
void main() {
    String modele1 = "^\\s*\\d+\\s*$";
    Pattern regex1 = Pattern.compile(modele1);
     // compare instances to the template
    for (String exemplaire : List.of("  123  ", "  123a  ", "4567")) {
        if (regex1.matcher(exemplaire).find()) {
            IO.println("[" + exemplaire + "] correspond au modèle [" + modele1 + "]");
        } else {
            IO.println("[" + exemplaire + "] ne correspond pas au modèle [" + modele1 + "]");
        }
    }
     // `find` searches for the pattern in the string; `matches` requires the entire string to match
    Pattern nombre = Pattern.compile("\\d+");
    IO.println("find(\"abc 123\") : " + nombre.matcher("abc 123").find()
            + ", matches(\"abc 123\") : " + nombre.matcher("abc 123").matches());
     // the static method Pattern.matches and the String.matches method: the entire string
    IO.println("Pattern.matches(date, \"18/05/97\") : "
            + Pattern.matches("\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{2}", "18/05/97"));
    IO.println("\"5/1/01\".matches(date) : " + "5/1/01".matches("\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{2}"));
}

Results:

> java Regex01.java
[  123  ] correspond au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[  123a  ] ne correspond pas au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[4567] correspond au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$]
find("abc 123") : true, matches("abc 123") : false
Pattern.matches(date, "18/05/97") : true
"5/1/01".matches(date) : false

Comments:

  • line 3: the pattern for an unsigned integer, possibly surrounded by spaces, which occupies the entire string (anchors [^] and [$]). The [\] entries are duplicated;
  • line 4: the template compilation;
  • line 7: [find] searches for the pattern in the string. The string “123a,” surrounded by spaces, does not match the pattern: the character “a” cannot be a digit or a space. Without the anchors [^] and [$], the string would match, since it contains a number;
  • lines 14–16: the difference between [find], which searches for the pattern within the string, and [matches], which requires that the entire string match the pattern, as if it were bounded by [^] and [$];
  • Lines 18–20: The static method [Pattern.matches] and the method [matches] of the class [String] also test the entire string. They compile the pattern on every call: while useful for a standalone test, they should be avoided in a loop. The method [split] of [String], which we’ve already encountered, likewise compiles its pattern on every call, except for separators consisting of a single ordinary character, which it processes without a regular expression.

docs.title: 5.8.2. Finding all occurrences of a pattern in a string
docs.text:
The [find] method of a [Matcher] object can be called multiple times: each call searches for the next occurrence of the pattern. After a successful call, the [Matcher] object provides information about the occurrence found:

  • [group()]: the text of the occurrence, i.e., an element matching the pattern;
  • [start()]: the position where the element was found in the searched string; [end()]: the position following the element.

The program [Regex02.java] is as follows:

// find all occurrences of a pattern in a string
void main() {
    String modele2 = "\\d+";
    Pattern regex2 = Pattern.compile(modele2);
    String exemplaire3 = "  123  456  789 ";
    IO.println("Modèle=[" + modele2 + "], exemplaire=[" + exemplaire3 + "]");
     // `find` moves from one occurrence to the next
    Matcher matcher = regex2.matcher(exemplaire3);
    int nbOccurrences = 0;
    while (matcher.find()) {
        nbOccurrences++;
        IO.println("[" + matcher.group() + "] trouvé en position " + matcher.start());
    }
    IO.println("Il y a " + nbOccurrences + " occurrences du modèle dans l'exemplaire");
     // results (Java 9): the stream of occurrences, to which the API Stream is applied
    int somme = regex2.matcher(exemplaire3).results().mapToInt(m -> Integer.parseInt(m.group())).sum();
    IO.println("somme des nombres trouvés : " + somme);
    long voyelles = Pattern.compile("[aeiouy]").matcher("anticonstitutionnellement").results().count();
    IO.println("nombre de voyelles de \"anticonstitutionnellement\" : " + voyelles);
}

Results:

> java Regex02.java
Modèle=[\d+], exemplaire=[  123  456  789 ]
[123] trouvé en position 2
[456] trouvé en position 7
[789] trouvé en position 12
Il y a 3 occurrences du modèle dans l'exemplaire
somme des nombres trouvés : 1368
nombre de voyelles de "anticonstitutionnellement" : 10

Comments:

  • Line 3: The pattern being searched for is a sequence of digits;
  • line 5: the string in which this pattern is searched for;
  • lines 8–13: Each call to [find] finds the next occurrence; the loop stops when there are no more. Each occurrence and its position are displayed;
  • line 16: the [results] method (Java 9) returns a stream of occurrences in the form of [MatchResult] objects (which have the methods [group], [start], [end]): the API stream is applied to it. Here, the sum of the found numbers is calculated;
  • line 18: the number of occurrences of the pattern [[aeiouy]], which denotes a vowel, is the number of elements in the stream.

docs.title: 5.8.3. Retrieving Parts of a Pattern
docs.text:
As mentioned, the parts of a pattern enclosed in parentheses are stored: these are the groups. The program [Regex03.java] uses them:

// retrieve parts of a pattern: groups
void main() {
    String modele3 = "(\\d\\d):(\\d\\d):(\\d\\d)";
    Pattern regex3 = Pattern.compile(modele3);
    String exemplaire4 = "Il est 18:05:49";
     // find searches for the first occurrence of the pattern
    Matcher resultat = regex3.matcher(exemplaire4);
    if (resultat.find()) {
        IO.println("L'exemplaire [" + exemplaire4 + "] correspond au modèle [" + modele3 + "]");
         // Parentheses groups are displayed; group 0 is the entire occurrence
        for (int i = 0; i <= resultat.groupCount(); i++) {
            IO.println("groupes[" + i + "]=[" + resultat.group(i) + "] trouvé en position "
                    + resultat.start(i));
        }
    } else {
        IO.println("L'exemplaire [" + exemplaire4 + "] ne correspond pas au modèle [" + modele3 + "]");
    }

     // named groups: (?<name>...)
    Pattern regexDate = Pattern.compile("(?<jour>\\d{1,2})/(?<mois>\\d{1,2})/(?<annee>\\d{4})");
    String texte = "Rendez-vous le 3/10/2026, puis le 15/11/2026.";
    DateTimeFormatter format = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy");
    Matcher m = regexDate.matcher(texte);
    while (m.find()) {
         // A group is referred to by its name rather than its number
        int jour = Integer.parseInt(m.group("jour"));
        int mois = Integer.parseInt(m.group("mois"));
        int annee = Integer.parseInt(m.group("annee"));
        LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(annee, mois, jour);
        IO.println("[" + m.group() + "] : jour=" + jour + ", mois=" + mois + ", année=" + annee + " -> "
                + date.format(format));
    }

     // replaceAll: groups can be reused in the replacement string
    String inverse = regexDate.matcher(texte).replaceAll("${annee}-${mois}-${jour}");
    IO.println("replaceAll(chaîne) : " + inverse);
     // replaceAll with a function (Java 9): the replacement is calculated for each occurrence
    String iso = regexDate.matcher(texte).replaceAll(r -> LocalDate.of(Integer.parseInt(r.group(3)),
            Integer.parseInt(r.group(2)), Integer.parseInt(r.group(1))).toString());
    IO.println("replaceAll(fonction) : " + iso);
}

Results:

> java Regex03.java
L'exemplaire [Il est 18:05:49] correspond au modèle [(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)]
groupes[0]=[18:05:49] trouvé en position 7
groupes[1]=[18] trouvé en position 7
groupes[2]=[05] trouvé en position 10
groupes[3]=[49] trouvé en position 13
[3/10/2026] : jour=3, mois=10, année=2026 -> samedi 3 octobre 2026
[15/11/2026] : jour=15, mois=11, année=2026 -> dimanche 15 novembre 2026
replaceAll(chaîne) : Rendez-vous le 2026-10-3, puis le 2026-11-15.
replaceAll(fonction) : Rendez-vous le 2026-10-03, puis le 2026-11-15.

Comments:

  • lines 7–8: the string [exemplaire4] is compared to the pattern [regex3]; [find] searches for the first occurrence of the pattern. After a successful call, we use two new methods from [Matcher]:
    • [groupCount] (line 11): the number of parenthesis groups in the pattern;
    • [group(i)] (line 12): the text captured by group #i; [group(0)], or [group()], is the entire occurrence of the pattern. [start(i)] is the position of this text in the parsed string. The loop therefore runs from 0 to [groupCount], inclusive;
  • line 20: a group can be named using the syntax [(?<nom>...)]. Here, the pattern recognizes a date in the format d/m/yyyy, with a one- or two-digit day and month;
  • lines 26–28: A named group is referred to by its name rather than its number: the code is more readable and does not depend on the order of the parentheses;
  • lines 29–31: The class [LocalDate] (Java 8) represents a date without a time. It is displayed using the template [EEEE d MMMM yyyy]: the day of the week appears in French;
  • line 35: the [replaceAll] method replaces each occurrence of the template with a string in which [${nom}] (or [$1], [$2]… for numbered groups) denotes the value of a group. Dates are thus rewritten in year-month-day format;
  • lines 38–39: an overloaded version of *[replaceAll]* (Java 9) takes a function that calculates the replacement text from each occurrence, of type *[MatchResult]. Here, the date is constructed and replaced with its normalized form ISO 8601, which is returned by the [toString] method of [LocalDate]*: days and months are always two digits.

docs.title: 5.8.4. A Learning Program
docs.text:
Finding the regular expression that verifies whether a string matches a certain pattern can sometimes be a real challenge. The program [Regex04.java] allows you to practice. It takes a pattern and a string as input and indicates whether the string matches the pattern or not.

// A program for learning regular expressions
void main() {
    while (true) {
         // the pattern is requested
        String modele = lire("Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : ");
         // Done?
        if (modele.isBlank()) {
            break;
        }
         // Compiling the regular expression; an incorrect pattern causes an exception
        Pattern regex;
        try {
            regex = Pattern.compile(modele);
        } catch (PatternSyntaxException e) {
            IO.println("Erreur : " + e.getDescription() + " (position " + e.getIndex() + ")");
            continue;
        }
         // The examples to be compared against the pattern are requested
        while (true) {
            String chaine = lire("Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [" + modele
                    + "] ou rien pour arrêter : ");
             // Done?
            if (chaine.isBlank()) {
                break;
            }
            try {
                 // Performing the comparison, with a one-second time limit
                Matcher m = regex.matcher(new ChaineLimitee(chaine, Duration.ofSeconds(1)));
                boolean trouve = false;
                while (m.find()) {
                    trouve = true;
                     // The element matching the pattern is displayed
                    IO.println("J'ai trouvé la correspondance [" + m.group() + "] en position ["
                            + m.start() + "]");
                     // and its subelements (groups 1, 2, ...)
                    for (int j = 1; j <= m.groupCount(); j++) {
                        IO.println("    sous-élément [" + m.group(j) + "] en position ["
                                + m.start(j) + "]");
                    }
                }
                if (!trouve) {
                    IO.println("Je n'ai pas trouvé de correspondances");
                }
            } catch (DelaiDepasseException e) {
                IO.println("La recherche a été abandonnée : elle durait plus d'une seconde");
            }
        }
    }
}

// read a line from the keyboard; "" at the end of the stream
String lire(String invite) {
    String ligne = IO.readln(invite);
    return ligne == null ? "" : ligne;
}

// a string that cannot be read past a deadline
record ChaineLimitee(CharSequence texte, long limite) implements CharSequence {

    ChaineLimitee(CharSequence texte, Duration delai) {
        this(texte, System.nanoTime() + delai.toNanos());
    }

    @Override
    public char charAt(int index) {
         // the regular expression engine reads the string character by character
        if (System.nanoTime() > limite) {
            throw new DelaiDepasseException();
        }
        return texte.charAt(index);
    }

    @Override
    public int length() {
        return texte.length();
    }

    @Override
    public CharSequence subSequence(int debut, int fin) {
        return new ChaineLimitee(texte.subSequence(debut, fin), limite);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return texte.toString();
    }
}

// the exception thrown when the timeout is exceeded (static: usable in the record)
static class DelaiDepasseException extends RuntimeException {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
}

Comments:

  • line 13: compilation of the pattern entered via the keyboard. An incorrect pattern triggers an exception [PatternSyntaxException], for which [getDescription] returns the error description and [getIndex] returns its position in the pattern (line 15). Its full message, rendered by [getMessage], spans several lines and shows the template with a marker below the error;
  • line 28: the search is not performed directly on the typed string, but on an object [ChaineLimitee] (lines 58–87), which limits the search duration to one second: if the search takes longer, a [DelaiDepasseException] exception is thrown and then caught on line 44. We’ll see later why this is useful and how it works;
  • lines 36–39: for each match, groups #1 and subsequent groups are displayed, if any;
  • lines 52–55: Unlike previous programs, spaces are not removed from the entered line; they may be part of the pattern or the string to be tested.

Here is an example of the output:

> java Regex04.java
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : \d+
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [\d+] ou rien pour arrêter : 123 456 789
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [123] en position [0]
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [456] en position [4]
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [789] en position [8]
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [\d+] ou rien pour arrêter : 
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : (\d{2}):(\d\d)
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] ou rien pour arrêter : 14:15 abcd 17:18 xyzt
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [14:15] en position [0]
    sous-élément [14] en position [0]
    sous-élément [15] en position [3]
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [17:18] en position [11]
    sous-élément [17] en position [11]
    sous-élément [18] en position [14]
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] ou rien pour arrêter : 
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : ^\s*\d+\s*$
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter :    1456
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [   1456] en position [0]
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter :

Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter : 1456
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [1456] en position [0]
    sous-élément [1456] en position [0]
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter : abcd 1456
Je n'ai pas trouvé de correspondances
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter : 
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : ^(a+)+$
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^(a+)+$] ou rien pour arrêter : aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
Je n'ai pas trouvé de correspondances
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^(a+)+$] ou rien pour arrêter :

Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^(a+)+\1$] ou rien pour arrêter : aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
La recherche a été abandonnée : elle durait plus d'une seconde
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^(a+)+\1$] ou rien pour arrêter :
