Erreur : Unclosed group (position 4)
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter :

The templates [^\s*\d+\s*$] and [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] demonstrate the benefits of using groups: the first recognizes the string “1456” preceded by three spaces, including the spaces; the second also extracts the number without the spaces. The [^(a+)+$] and [^(a+)+\1$] templates are discussed below.

docs.title: 5.8.5. The split method
docs.text:
We have already encountered the [split] method of the [String] class, whose separator is a regular expression. The [Pattern] class has the same method, which uses the precompiled pattern:

methodrole[String[] split(CharSequence input)]The string [input] is split into fields, which are separated by a separator corresponding to the template[Stream<String> splitAsStream(CharSequence input)]same as above, but the fields are rendered as a stream

Suppose, for example, that a text file contains lines of the form field1, field2, ..., fieldn. The fields are separated by a comma, but this comma may be preceded or followed by spaces. The template [\s*,\s*] describes this separator exactly, as shown by the program [Regex05.java]:

// split: the separator is defined by a pattern
void main() {
    String ligne = "abc  , def  ,ghi ,   jkl";
     // a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces
    Pattern separateur = Pattern.compile("\\s*,\\s*");
    String[] champs = separateur.split(ligne);
    for (int i = 0; i < champs.length; i++) {
        IO.println("champs[" + i + "]=[" + champs[i] + "]");
    }
     // multiple possible separators: ; or | or a sequence of spaces
    String[] mots = "un;deux|trois   quatre".split("[;|]|\\s+");
    IO.println("mots=" + Arrays.toString(mots));
     // splitAsStream: fields in the form of a stream
    IO.println("splitAsStream : " + separateur.splitAsStream(ligne).map(String::toUpperCase).toList());
}

Results:

> java Regex05.java
champs[0]=[abc]
champs[1]=[def]
champs[2]=[ghi]
champs[3]=[jkl]
mots=[un, deux, trois, quatre]
splitAsStream : [ABC, DEF, GHI, JKL]

Comments:

  • line 5: the separator: a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces. The spaces are removed along with the separator. Once compiled, the template can split as many lines as desired without being recompiled: this is the method for splitting all the lines in a file;
  • line 11: a separator that can take several forms: a semicolon or a vertical bar ([[;|]]), or ([|]) a sequence of spaces ([\s+]);
  • line 14: [splitAsStream] renders the fields as a stream, to which the operation [map] is applied here.

docs.title: 5.8.6. Precompiled templates, options, and searches that take too long
docs.text:
Unlike other platforms, Java does not have a mechanism that generates the code for a regular expression search at program compile time: a pattern is always parsed at runtime by [Pattern.compile]. This compilation comes at a cost; therefore, best practice is to compile each known pattern once and for all in advance and store the [Pattern] object in a constant, as the program [Regex06.java] does. A [Pattern] object is immutable and can be used simultaneously by multiple threads; a [Matcher] object, which stores the state of a search, cannot.

// templates compiled once and for all, options, protection against overly long searches

// a time in hh:mm:ss format with named groups
static final Pattern HEURE = Pattern.compile("(?<h>\\d\\d):(?<m>\\d\\d):(?<s>\\d\\d)");
// yes, regardless of case
static final Pattern OUI = Pattern.compile("^\\s*oui\\s*$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);
// a problematic pattern: a repeated group followed by a backreference to that group
static final Pattern CATASTROPHE = Pattern.compile("^(a+)+\\1$");

void main() {
     // 1 - Patterns compiled once, stored in constants
    IO.println("HEURE.matcher(\"Il est 18:05:49\").find() : " + HEURE.matcher("Il est 18:05:49").find());
    Matcher m = HEURE.matcher("départ à 07:45:00");
    if (m.find()) {
        IO.println("heures=" + m.group("h") + ", minutes=" + m.group("m") + ", secondes=" + m.group("s"));
    }

     // 2 - options: here, CASE_INSENSITIVE, set when the pattern is compiled
    for (String reponse : List.of("oui", "OUI", "Oui", "non", "ouiii")) {
        IO.print(reponse + "=" + OUI.matcher(reponse).matches() + " ");
    }
    IO.println();
     // MULTILINE: ^ and $ correspond to the beginning and end of each line; \w only recognizes [a-zA-Z0-9_]
    String texte = "prix: 10\nquantité: 3\ntotal: 30";
    affiche(Pattern.compile("^(\\w+): (\\d+)$", Pattern.MULTILINE), texte);
     // UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS: \w also recognizes accented letters
    affiche(Pattern.compile("^(\\w+): (\\d+)$", Pattern.MULTILINE | Pattern.UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS), texte);
     // options can also be written in the pattern: (?i) for CASE_INSENSITIVE, (?m) for MULTILINE
    IO.println("(?i)oui sur \"OUI\" : " + "OUI".matches("(?i)oui"));

     // 3 - a pattern with catastrophic backtracking, first without and then with a time limit
    for (int n : new int[]{10, 15, 20}) {
        String chaine = "a".repeat(n) + "!";
        long debut = System.nanoTime();
        boolean trouve = CATASTROPHE.matcher(chaine).find();
        IO.println(n + " a : " + trouve + " en " + (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000 + " ms");
    }
    String chaine = "a".repeat(30) + "!";
    try {
        IO.println(CATASTROPHE.matcher(new ChaineLimitee(chaine, Duration.ofMillis(100))).find());
    } catch (DelaiDepasseException e) {
        IO.println("30 a : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : recherche abandonnée au bout de 100 ms");
    }
     // The Java engine recognizes the pattern (a+)+ without a backreference and responds immediately
    long debut = System.nanoTime();
    boolean trouve = Pattern.compile("^(a+)+$").matcher(chaine).find();
    IO.println("^(a+)+$ sur 30 a : " + trouve + ", réponse en moins d'une seconde : "
            + ((System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000 < 1000));
}

// display of name=value pairs found in a text
void affiche(Pattern modele, String texte) {
    Matcher ligne = modele.matcher(texte);
    while (ligne.find()) {
        IO.print("[" + ligne.group(1) + "=" + ligne.group(2) + "] ");
    }
    IO.println();
}

// A string that refuses to be read past a timeout
record ChaineLimitee(CharSequence texte, long limite) implements CharSequence {

    ChaineLimitee(CharSequence texte, Duration delai) {
        this(texte, System.nanoTime() + delai.toNanos());
    }

    @Override
    public char charAt(int index) {
        if (System.nanoTime() > limite) {
            throw new DelaiDepasseException();
        }
        return texte.charAt(index);
    }

    @Override
    public int length() {
        return texte.length();
    }

    @Override
    public CharSequence subSequence(int debut, int fin) {
        return new ChaineLimitee(texte.subSequence(debut, fin), limite);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return texte.toString();
    }
}

// The exception thrown when the time limit is exceeded
static class DelaiDepasseException extends RuntimeException {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
}

Results:

> java Regex06.java
HEURE.matcher("Il est 18:05:49").find() : true
heures=07, minutes=45, secondes=00
oui=true OUI=true Oui=true non=false ouiii=false 
[prix=10] [total=30] 
[prix=10] [quantité=3] [total=30] 
(?i)oui sur "OUI" : true
10 a : false en 0 ms
15 a : false en 2 ms
20 a : false en 39 ms
30 a : DelaiDepasseException : recherche abandonnée au bout de 100 ms
^(a+)+$ sur 30 a : false, réponse en moins d'une seconde : true

Comments:

  • lines 4–8: The program’s templates are compiled once and stored in [static final] constants (Chapter 4), written in uppercase as is customary. In a compact source file, these constants are fields of the implicit class that contains the file’s methods;
  • lines 12–16: The constants are used in the same way as the [Pattern] objects in the previous programs;
  • line 6: the second parameter of [compile] is a combination of options. [CASE_INSENSITIVE] is case-insensitive: “OUI” and “Yes” match the pattern (line 4 of the results);
  • Lines 23–27: The options are combined with the operator [|]. [MULTILINE] matches [^] and [$] at the beginning and end of each line in the string, rather than just at the beginning and end of the string itself. However, with the default options, [\w] recognizes only unaccented letters: the line “quantity: 3” is not recognized (line 5 of the results). The option [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS] (Java 7) assigns the correct Unicode meanings to [\w], [\d], [\s], and [\b]: accented letters are treated as word characters (line 6 of the results). This option should be used for all French text. Other useful options include: [DOTALL] ([.] also corresponds to a line break), [COMMENTS] (spaces in the template are ignored, allowing it to be written across multiple lines, with comments), [UNICODE_CASE] (along with [CASE_INSENSITIVE], also ignores the case of accented letters: É and é);
  • line 29: options can also be written at the beginning of the template: [(?i)] for [CASE_INSENSITIVE], [(?m)] for [MULTILINE], [(?U)] for [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS]…

The rest of the program addresses a security issue. Some patterns are pathological: when applied to certain strings, they force the regular expression engine to try an enormous number of ways to match the string to the pattern before reaching a conclusion. The Java engine uses a process called “backtracking”: when an attempt fails, it returns to the last choice made and tries another one. The pattern [^(a+)+\1$] on line 8 is an example of this: When applied to a sequence of “a”s ending with another character, it tries every possible way to distribute the “a”s among the repetitions of the group and its backreference [\1] before concluding that the match has failed, and the number of possibilities multiplies with each additional “a.” This is known as a catastrophic backtrack. When applied to user-entered strings, such a pattern constitutes a security vulnerability (known as ReDoS, “regular expression denial of service”): just a few requests are enough to bring a server to a standstill.

  • Lines 32–37: The search duration is measured for 10, 15, and 20 a. It increases very rapidly (lines 8–10 of the results; durations vary from one run to another and from one machine to another). Since the duration roughly doubles with each additional a, the search would take several minutes with 30 a;
  • lines 38–43: The [Pattern] class has no timeout option. A standard technique is used: the search is performed in an object of type [ChaineLimitee] (lines 61–89), which implements the [CharSequence] interface accepted by [matcher]. The regular expression engine reads the string character by character using the [charAt] method: this method checks the time and throws a [DelaiDepasseException] exception (lines 92–95) if the deadline—stored when the object was created—has been exceeded. The search is abandoned after 100 ms;
  • lines 61–65: The [ChaineLimitee] record has two components: the text and the deadline, expressed as the value of the [System.nanoTime] clock, which must not be exceeded. The additional constructor calculates this deadline based on a timeout, an object [java.time.Duration];
  • Line 92: The exception [DelaiDepasseException] is derived from [RuntimeException]: it is an unchecked exception that [charAt] can throw without declaring it. It is declared as [static] so that it can be created in the record, which is itself implicitly static. The field [serialVersionUID] prevents a compiler warning, since an exception is serializable;
  • lines 45–48: The Java runtime can recognize and efficiently handle simple cases of nested repetitions: the pattern [^(a+)+$], which is catastrophic with other runtimes, responds immediately here. It is the backward reference [\1] that prevents this optimization in the pattern on line 8.

It is important to note that you should be wary of patterns containing nested repetitions ([(a+)+], [(\w+\s?)*]…) and limit the duration of searches as soon as the pattern or string being searched for comes from outside the program. Java’s possessive quantifiers ([a++], [a*+]), which prevent backtracking within the element they repeat, also allow you to write safe patterns, provided you fully understand their meaning.

docs.title: 5.9. Example Application - V3
docs.text: We’ll revisit the application discussed in Chapter 3 (Version 1) and Chapter 4 (Version 2). Remember that this is an exercise: the tax scale used is the 2004 version (2003 income), which has remained unchanged since the original course.

docs.title: 5.9.1. Data in a File
docs.text:
In Version 2, the tax calculation was performed in the abstract class [AbstractImpot], which we are reusing here in the project’s [impots] package, with two minor differences: the tax brackets are now provided in the form of a table ([TrancheImpot[]]) rather than a list, and the division is performed with 16 significant digits instead of 34, which is more than sufficient:

package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.MathContext;

public abstract class AbstractImpot implements IImpot {

     // The tax brackets needed for the calculation come from an external source
     // known only to derived classes
    protected abstract TrancheImpot[] getTranchesImpot();

     // tax calculation
    @Override
    public int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire) {
         // Calculation of the number of shares
        BigDecimal nbParts = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbEnfants).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
                .add(marie ? BigDecimal.TWO : BigDecimal.ONE);
        if (nbEnfants >= 3) {
            nbParts = nbParts.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
        }
         // Calculation of taxable income and the family quotient
        BigDecimal revenu = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salaire));
        BigDecimal quotient = revenu.divide(nbParts, MathContext.DECIMAL64);
         // Determination of the tax bracket: the last one is used if no other limit applies
        TrancheImpot[] tranches = getTranchesImpot();
        TrancheImpot tranche = tranches[tranches.length - 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < tranches.length - 1; i++) {
            if (quotient.compareTo(tranches[i].limite()) <= 0) {
                tranche = tranches[i];
                break;
            }
        }
         // tax calculation
        return revenu.multiply(tranche.coeffR()).subtract(nbParts.multiply(tranche.coeffN())).intValue();
    }
}

The [calculer] method uses the tax brackets returned by the abstract method [getTranchesImpot] (line 10). The [AbstractImpot] class does not know where these brackets come from: it is up to the derived classes to provide them. In version 2, the derived class [HardwiredImpot] hard-coded them into its code. The calculations are performed using exact decimal numbers [java.math.BigDecimal] (Chapter 3): [BigDecimal.TWO] (Java 19) is the constant 2; the division of the revenue by the number of shares is performed with 16 significant digits ([MathContext.DECIMAL64]); and [intValue] returns the integer part of the result. A bracket is represented, as in version 2, by the record [TrancheImpot]:

package impots;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

// a tax bracket from the tax scale
public record TrancheImpot(BigDecimal limite, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
}

and the calculation is described by the [IImpot] interface, documented here by a Javadoc comment:

package impots;

/**
 * Le calcul de l'impôt.
 */
public interface IImpot {

    /**
     * Calcule l'impôt d'un contribuable.
     *
     * @param marie     vrai si le contribuable est marié
     * @param nbEnfants nombre d'enfants
     * @param salaire   salaire annuel en euros
     * @return le montant de l'impôt, en euros
     */
    int calculer(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire);
}

The new version stores the data in a file, which allows you to change the scale without recompiling the program. We write two new classes derived from [AbstractImpot]:

  • [FileImpot] reads the brackets from a text file [DataImpot.txt];
  • [JsonImpot] reads them from a file named JSON and [DataImpot.json].

The text file [DataImpot.txt] contains one segment per line, in the format limit:coeffR:coeffN:

4962:0:0
8382:0.068:291.09
14753:0.191:1322.92
23888:0.283:2668.39
38868:0.374:4846.98
47932:0.426:6883.66
0:0.481:9505.54

Numbers in the file are written with a decimal point. A data file must not depend on the language of the machine reading it: a file written with decimal commas and interpreted according to French rules ([NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE)]) would be rejected or, worse, misinterpreted on an English-language machine. The [new BigDecimal(String)] generator, like [Double.parseDouble], always expects a decimal point, regardless of the machine’s language. This is also the convention for JSON and most data formats.

The file [DataImpot.json] contains the same data, in the form of a JSON array of objects:

[
  { "limite": 4962, "coeffR": 0, "coeffN": 0 },
  { "limite": 8382, "coeffR": 0.068, "coeffN": 291.09 },
  { "limite": 14753, "coeffR": 0.191, "coeffN": 1322.92 },
  { "limite": 23888, "coeffR": 0.283, "coeffN": 2668.39 },
  { "limite": 38868, "coeffR": 0.374, "coeffN": 4846.98 },
  { "limite": 47932, "coeffR": 0.426, "coeffN": 6883.66 },
  { "limite": 0, "coeffR": 0.481, "coeffN": 9505.54 }
]

docs.title: 5.9.2. Errors
docs.text:
Processing these files may fail due to a missing file, a malformed line, an incorrect number, etc. We create a special exception class to report these errors, [ImpotException]. It will also be used for other data sources (the JSON file here, and databases later). It carries an error code:

package impots;

import java.io.Serial;

// Exception thrown by the classes that read the tax brackets
// It derives from RuntimeException: this is an unchecked exception
public class ImpotException extends RuntimeException {

     // the class version for serialization (an exception is serializable)
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

     // the error code (a combination of values CodeErreur)
    private final int code;

    public ImpotException(String message, int code) {
        super(message);
        this.code = code;
    }

    public ImpotException(String message, Throwable cause, int code) {
        super(message, cause);
        this.code = code;
    }

    public int getCode() {
        return code;
    }
}

Comments:

  • Line 7: The [ImpotException] class derives from the [RuntimeException] class: this is an unchecked exception (Chapter 4). The compiler will not require the code that creates a [FileImpot] or [JsonImpot] object to catch this exception; that code will catch it where it is able to handle it;
  • Lines 10–11: Every exception is serializable by inheriting from the [Throwable] class. A serializable class should declare a version number [serialVersionUID], which is used to verify that a serialized object is deserialized by the same version of the class; otherwise, the compiler, when using the [-Xlint:all] option, issues a warning. The [@Serial] annotation (Java 14) indicates that the field is part of the serialization mechanism;
  • line 14: the error code, set when the exception is created;
  • lines 16–24: two constructors. The first takes an error message and a code; the second also takes the exception that caused the error (the cause), which will be accessible via the [getCause] method. It is this form of exception, with an integer code, that subsequent versions of the application will use.

The possible error codes are described by an enumeration:

package impots;

import java.util.EnumSet;

// error codes: powers of 2, which can be combined
public enum CodeErreur {
    ACCES(1),       // The file cannot be read
    LIGNE(2),       // A row does not have three fields
    CHAMP1(4),      // Field 1 (limit) is incorrect
    CHAMP2(8),      // Field 2 (coeffR) is incorrect
    CHAMP3(16),     // Field 3 (coeffN) is incorrect
    JSON(32);       // The document JSON is incorrect

     // The integer value of the code
    private final int valeur;

    CodeErreur(int valeur) {
        this.valeur = valeur;
    }

    public int getValeur() {
        return valeur;
    }

     // the codes present in a code combination
    public static EnumSet<CodeErreur> decoder(int code) {
        EnumSet<CodeErreur> codes = EnumSet.noneOf(CodeErreur.class);
        for (CodeErreur c : values()) {
            if ((code & c.valeur) != 0) {
                codes.add(c);
            }
        }
        return codes;
    }
}

Comments:

  • Lines 7–12: Possible error codes:
    • [ACCES]: error accessing the data file;
    • [LIGNE]: row missing the three expected fields, or file containing no time periods;
    • [CHAMP1], [CHAMP2], [CHAMP3]: Field 1, 2, or 3 in a row is incorrect;
    • [JSON]: The document JSON is incorrect;
  • Lines 15–23: A Java enum is a class; it can have fields, a (private) constructor, and methods. Each constant is constructed with its integer value, enclosed in parentheses;
  • lines 26–34: Some errors can occur in combination: all three fields in a line may be incorrect. Therefore, the error code values are powers of 2: each corresponds to a bit of the integer. An error in fields 2 and 3 will result in the code 8 | 16 = 24. The static method [decoder] performs the inverse operation: it converts the set of codes into an integer by testing each bit with the operator [&]. The result is a *[EnumSet]*, a specialized set for the constants of an enumeration, which stores them as the bits of an integer: this is the Java way of handling combinations of options. Its [toString] method displays a combination in the form “[CHAMP2, CHAMP3]”.

docs.title: 5.9.3. The FileImpot class
docs.text:
The [FileImpot] class provides the segments read from a text file:

package impots;

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

// the tax brackets read from a text file of line limits:coeffR:coeffN
public class FileImpot extends AbstractImpot {

     // the field separator: the character : surrounded by optional spaces
    private static final Pattern SEPARATEUR = Pattern.compile("\\s*:\\s*");
     // a positive or zero number: digits, possibly followed by a period and digits
    private static final Pattern NOMBRE = Pattern.compile("\\d+(\\.\\d+)?");

     // the tax brackets read from the file
    private final TrancheImpot[] tranchesImpot;

     // Implementation of the parent class’s abstract method
    @Override
    protected TrancheImpot[] getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }

    public FileImpot(String nomFichier) {
         // the filename (without the path) for error messages
        Path chemin = Path.of(nomFichier);
        String nom = chemin.getFileName().toString();
         // the tax brackets read; their number is unknown in advance
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = new ArrayList<>();
        try (BufferedReader lecteur = Files.newBufferedReader(chemin)) {
            int numLigne = 0;
            String ligneLue;
            while ((ligneLue = lecteur.readLine()) != null) {
                numLigne++;
                String ligne = ligneLue.strip();
                 // empty lines are ignored
                if (ligne.isEmpty()) {
                    continue;
                }
                 // the line must have three fields
                String[] champs = SEPARATEUR.split(ligne);
                if (champs.length != 3) {
                    throw new ImpotException("Ligne n° " + numLigne + " incorrecte (" + ligne + ")",
                            CodeErreur.LIGNE.getValeur());
                }
                 // three positive or zero decimal numbers, written with a decimal point
                int code = 0;
                if (!NOMBRE.matcher(champs[0]).matches()) code |= CodeErreur.CHAMP1.getValeur();
                if (!NOMBRE.matcher(champs[1]).matches()) code |= CodeErreur.CHAMP2.getValeur();
                if (!NOMBRE.matcher(champs[2]).matches()) code |= CodeErreur.CHAMP3.getValeur();
                if (code != 0) {
                    throw new ImpotException("Ligne n° " + numLigne + " incorrecte (" + ligne + ")", code);
                }
                 // the new tax bracket is stored
                tranches.add(new TrancheImpot(new BigDecimal(champs[0]), new BigDecimal(champs[1]),
                        new BigDecimal(champs[2])));
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
             // File access error: wrap it in a ImpotException
            throw new ImpotException("Erreur lors de la lecture du fichier " + nom, e,
                    CodeErreur.ACCES.getValeur());
        }
         // At least one tax bracket is required
        if (tranches.isEmpty()) {
            throw new ImpotException("Le fichier " + nom + " ne contient aucune tranche",
                    CodeErreur.LIGNE.getValeur());
        }
         // Transfer the list to the tax bracket array
        tranchesImpot = tranches.toArray(TrancheImpot[]::new);
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 13: the class [FileImpot] is derived from the class [AbstractImpot], just as the class [HardwiredImpot] was in version 2;
  • Lines 16–18: Two regular expressions, compiled once and for all and stored as constants: the field separator for a boundary line:coeffR:coeffN (the character [:], preceded and followed by any number of spaces), and a positive or zero number, consisting of digits possibly followed by a period and more digits;
  • lines 21–27: the read segments, returned by the method [getTranchesImpot], which implements the abstract method [AbstractImpot];
  • line 29: the constructor receives the name of the text file containing the data. Its role is to populate the array [tranchesImpot];
  • line 32: the file name without its path, used in error messages. The constructor may indeed receive a full path, which does not need to be displayed to the user;
  • line 34: Reading a text file is sequential: the number of lines is not known until the entire file has been read. Therefore, the array cannot be sized in advance; the chunks are temporarily stored in a list;
  • lines 35–38: The file is read line by line using a [BufferedReader], opened by a [try] statement with resources;
  • lines 46–50: The line is split into fields using a regular expression; if there are not three fields, a [ImpotException] exception with code [LIGNE] is thrown immediately. The file is closed regardless: the [try] statement with resources closes [BufferedReader] regardless of how the block is exited—whether normally or via an exception;
  • Lines 52–58: validation of the three fields. Errors are accumulated in the variable [code] using the operator [|=], then reported collectively. The method [matches] requires that the integer field conform to the pattern [NOMBRE]: no sign, no spaces, and no decimal point. Negative numbers are thus rejected, which validates the data at the same time it is being checked;
  • lines 60–61: the fields, now validated, are converted to [BigDecimal], with a decimal point regardless of the machine’s language;
  • Lines 63–67: File access errors ([IOException] and its variants, such as [NoSuchFileException] for a missing file, [AccessDeniedException] for insufficient permissions, or [MalformedInputException] for a file that is not in UTF-8) are wrapped in a [ImpotException] with code [ACCES], with the original exception becoming its cause. The [ImpotException] exceptions thrown within the loop are not [IOException] exceptions: they are not intercepted by this [catch] clause and exit the constructor as-is;
  • lines 69–74: an empty file is rejected; otherwise, the list is transferred to the slice array, which was the purpose of the constructor.

Encapsulating low-level exceptions ([IOException]) within an application-specific exception ([ImpotException]) allows the calling code to handle only a single type of exception, regardless of the data source: a text file, a JSON file, and, later in the course, a database. This is also why [ImpotException] is unchecked: a checked exception would need to be declared by every method it passes through, which would tie the calling code to the details of the data source.

docs.title: 5.9.4. The JsonImpot class
docs.text:
The [JsonImpot] class provides the segments read from a JSON file:

package impots;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Arrays;
import tools.jackson.core.JacksonException;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

// the tax brackets read from a file JSON
public class JsonImpot extends AbstractImpot {

     // The JsonMapper is reusable and can be used by multiple threads: only one is created
    private static final JsonMapper MAPPER = JsonMapper.builder().build();

     // the tax brackets read from the file
    private final TrancheImpot[] tranchesImpot;

     // Implementation of the parent class’s abstract method
    @Override
    protected TrancheImpot[] getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }

    public JsonImpot(String nomFichier) {
         // the file name, without its path, for error messages
        Path chemin = Path.of(nomFichier);
        String nom = chemin.getFileName().toString();
        String json;
        try {
             // reading the file
            json = Files.readString(chemin);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new ImpotException("Erreur lors de la lecture du fichier " + nom, e,
                    CodeErreur.ACCES.getValeur());
        }
        TrancheImpot[] tranches;
        try {
             // deserialization of the tax bracket array
            tranches = MAPPER.readValue(json, TrancheImpot[].class);
        } catch (JacksonException e) {
            throw new ImpotException("Le fichier " + nom + " est incorrect : " + e.getOriginalMessage()
                    + " (ligne " + e.getLocation().getLineNr() + ", colonne " + e.getLocation().getColumnNr()
                    + ")", e, CodeErreur.JSON.getValeur());
        }
         // At least one slice is required; negative values are not allowed
        if (tranches == null || tranches.length == 0) {
            throw new ImpotException("Le fichier " + nom + " ne contient aucune tranche",
                    CodeErreur.JSON.getValeur());
        }
        if (Arrays.stream(tranches).anyMatch(t -> negatif(t.limite()) || negatif(t.coeffR())
                || negatif(t.coeffN()))) {
            throw new ImpotException("Le fichier " + nom + " contient une valeur négative ou absente",
                    CodeErreur.JSON.getValeur());
        }
        tranchesImpot = tranches;
    }

     // A missing (null) or negative value is invalid
    private static boolean negatif(BigDecimal valeur) {
        return valeur == null || valeur.signum() < 0;
    }
}

Comments:

  • Line 15: A single [JsonMapper], stored in a constant, is used for all [JsonImpot] objects. The properties JSON, [limite], [coeffR], and [coeffN] are named after the components of the [TrancheImpot] record: no annotation is necessary;
  • lines 31–37: reading the file; an access error is handled as in [FileImpot];
  • line 41: a single instruction converts the text JSON into an array of slices. Jackson constructs each record by calling its constructor and converts the numbers JSON to [BigDecimal] without any loss of precision;
  • lines 42–46: an invalid document causes a [JacksonException], encapsulated in a [ImpotException] with code [JSON]. The message indicates the location of the error, identified by [getLocation];
  • lines 48–56: deserialization checks the document’s format, not the validity of the data: it remains to be verified that there is at least one segment (the document [null] or [[]] is a valid JSON) and that no values are negative or missing. If a property is missing from a JSON object, the corresponding component is assigned the value [null]. The [anyMatch] operation of the API Stream performs this final check in a single statement, with [Arrays.stream(tranches)] returning the stream of array elements;
  • lines 61–63: the method that tests a value.

Comparing the two classes is instructive: with a structured data format and a library that understands it, parsing the file requires almost no code.

docs.title: 5.9.5. The main program
docs.text:
The Maven project [ImpotsV3] has the following directory structure:

05-classes-java/
  ImpotsV3/
    pom.xml
    DataImpot.json
    DataImpot.txt
    DataImpotInvalide.json
    DataImpotInvalide.txt
    src/main/java/impots/
      AbstractImpot.java
      CodeErreur.java
      FileImpot.java
      IImpot.java
      ImpotException.java
      JsonImpot.java
      Main.java
      TrancheImpot.java

The data files are located at the root of the project, next to the file [pom.xml]: this is the program’s current directory when it is run with the command [mvn exec:java] from the project directory. The file [pom.xml] corresponds to the project [Fichiers06], differing only in its coordinates and main class:

    <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
    <artifactId>impots-v3</artifactId>
    <version>3.0</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
         <!-- Jackson 3: reading the JSON file containing tax brackets -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>tools.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>3.1.5</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

The [groupId] and [exemples.impots] files will be used for all versions of the sample application. The main class, declared in the [exec-maven-plugin] plugin, is [impots.Main]:

package impots;

// Tax calculation, version 3: tax brackets are read from a file
// Syntax: mvn exec:java [-Dexec.args="fichier"]; file: DataImpot.txt by default, or a .json file
public class Main {

    private static final String SYNTAXE = """
            syntaxe : Marié NbEnfants Salaire
            Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié
            NbEnfants : nombre d'enfants
            Salaire : salaire annuel en euros""";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // the data file is searched for in the current folder
        String nomFichier = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "DataImpot.txt";
        IO.println("Tranches d'impôt lues dans [" + nomFichier + "]");

         // creation of a IImpot object; the class depends on the file extension
        IImpot impot;
        try {
            String extension = nomFichier.substring(nomFichier.lastIndexOf('.') + 1).toLowerCase();
            impot = switch (extension) {
                case "json" -> new JsonImpot(nomFichier);
                default -> new FileImpot(nomFichier);
            };
        } catch (ImpotException e) {
             // displaying the error; the code is displayed as a set of CodeErreur
            String origine = e.getCause() == null ? ""
                    : ", Exception d'origine : " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName();
            IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : [Code=" + CodeErreur.decoder(e.getCode())
                    + ", Message=" + e.getMessage() + origine + "]");
             // program termination
            System.exit(1);
            return;
        }

         // input loop
        while (true) {
             // Tax calculation parameters are requested
            String saisie = IO.readln("Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : "
                    + "Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : ");
            String parametres = saisie == null ? "" : saisie.strip();
             // Is there anything to do?
            if (parametres.isEmpty()) {
                break;
            }
             // Checking the number of fields in the entered row
            String[] champs = parametres.split("\\s+");
            if (champs.length != 3) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE);
                continue;
            }
             // Checking parameter validity
             // married
            String marie = champs[0].toLowerCase();
            if (!marie.equals("o") && !marie.equals("n")) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument marié incorrect : tapez o ou n");
                continue;
            }
             // nbEnfants
            int nbEnfants = entier(champs[1]);
            if (nbEnfants < 0) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument NbEnfants incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
                continue;
            }
             // salary
            int salaire = entier(champs[2]);
            if (salaire < 0) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument salaire incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
                continue;
            }
             // the parameters are correct: calculate the tax
            IO.println("Impôt=" + impot.calculer(marie.equals("o"), nbEnfants, salaire) + " euros");
        }
    }

     // a positive integer or zero; -1 if the string is not an integer
    private static int entier(String champ) {
        try {
            return Integer.parseInt(champ);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return -1;
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 7–11: the help text, in a text block stored in a constant;
  • Line 15: The name of the data file is passed as an argument; by default, it is [DataImpot.txt]. With Maven, the program’s arguments are passed via the property [exec.args]: [mvn exec:java -Dexec.args="DataImpot.json"];
  • Lines 21–25: An expression [switch] (Chapter 3) selects the class to instantiate based on the file extension, which is extracted from the filename using [lastIndexOf] and [substring]. The two branches return objects of different types, [JsonImpot] and [FileImpot], both of type [IImpot]. The rest of the program only recognizes the [IImpot] interface and is unaware of where the data comes from;
  • lines 26–35: Creating the object may trigger a [ImpotException], which is displayed before the program terminates. The code is decoded into a set of [CodeErreur] messages to be displayed in plain text; the original exception, if any, is indicated by its type. The [return] statement following [System.exit] is never executed, but the compiler—which does not know that [System.exit] does not yield control—requires it: without it, the variable [impot] would not be considered initialized on line 73;
  • Lines 38–74: The dialog loop is the one from version 2.

  { "limite": 4962, "coeffR": 0, "coeffN": 0 },

]

Jackson’s message specifically identifies the error: the string “0.068” cannot be converted to [BigDecimal]. Jackson accepts a string where a number is expected if it contains a valid number (“0.068”); it is the decimal point that is rejected. The error is located on line 3 of the document—since Jackson numbers lines starting at 1—and in column 31, immediately after the incorrect value.

docs.title: 5.10. Conclusion
docs.text:
This chapter has introduced the Java classes used in almost all programs:

  • the immutable strings [String], which are compared with [equals] and not with [==], and [StringBuilder] for constructing them piece by piece; the formats [String.format] and [formatted], the text blocks;
  • tables and the [Arrays] class;
  • the collections [List], [Map], [Set], [Deque], and their implementations [ArrayList], [HashMap], [LinkedHashMap], [TreeMap], [HashSet], [ArrayDeque], [PriorityQueue]; immutable collections ([List.of], [List.copyOf], [Collections.unmodifiableList]), Java 21 sequenced collections, and comparators ([Comparator]); Java 1.0 collections ([Vector], [Hashtable], [Stack]) are deprecated;
  • the API Stream, its intermediate and terminal operations, its collectors, and its lazy evaluation;
  • text files ([Files], [Path], [BufferedReader], [BufferedWriter]), still in UTF-8; binary files ([DataOutputStream], [DataInputStream], [RandomAccessFile]) and the JSON serialization using Jackson, which replaces the deprecated Java binary serialization;
  • regular expressions, compiled once and for all and protected against excessively long searches when processing external data.

The sample application now reads its data from a text file or JSON. The next chapter reorganizes it into layers: reading data, calculating taxes, and user interaction will become independent components.

docs.title: 8. Execution Threads
docs.text:
This chapter introduces the simultaneous execution of multiple pieces of code within a single program: threads (execution threads) and the tools used to synchronize them. About twenty years ago, most machines had only one processor, and parallelism was largely an illusion maintained by the operating system. Today, even the most basic laptop has multiple cores: multiple threads actually run at the same time, making the synchronization issues discussed here even more prevalent.

Java has supported threads since its very first version (1996): the [Thread] class, the [synchronized] keyword, and the [wait] / [notify] methods of the [Object] class. Java 5 (2004) added the [java.util.concurrent] package and its subpackages [java.util.concurrent.locks] and [java.util.concurrent.atomic]: locks, semaphores, concurrent collections, thread pools, etc. Java 7 added the [Fork/Join] framework, Java 8 introduced parallel streams, and Java 21 introduced virtual threads, which have profoundly changed the way servers are written. Java 25 finally introduces scope-bound values ([ScopedValue]). We will cover all of these tools in this chapter.

The examples are compact source files ([java Threads01.java]) located in the [08-threads] folder. Remember that a compact source file automatically imports the entire [java.base] module: the classes in the packages [java.util.concurrent], [java.util.concurrent.locks], [java.util.concurrent.atomic], and [java.time] can therefore be used without the [import] directive.

A word of caution before you begin: the results of a multithreaded program vary from one run to the next. The order in which threads are assigned the processor depends on the operating system, the number of processors, and the machine’s load. The results reproduced in this chapter were obtained on a dual-processor Linux machine, shared with other highly active programs. If you run the examples, you will obtain similar results, but they will rarely be identical. We will indicate in each case what is reproducible and what is not.

docs.title: 8.1. The Thread Class
docs.text:
When an application is launched, it runs in an execution flow called a thread. The Java class that models a thread is the [java.lang.Thread] class. Its main constructors and methods are as follows:

MemberRole[Thread(Runnable tâche)], [Thread(Runnable tâche, String nom)]Creates a thread that will execute the [run] method of [tâche]. [Runnable] is the functional interface for [void run()]: it is most often passed a lambda or a method reference[static Thread.Builder.OfPlatform ofPlatform()], [static Thread.Builder.OfVirtual ofVirtual()](Java 21) return a builder for platform threads or virtual threads, which you configure (name, daemon, etc.) before creating the thread[static Thread currentThread()]the thread that executes the code that called this method[String getName()], [void setName(String nom)]the thread’s name, useful for tracking[long threadId()](Java 19) a unique numeric identifier for the thread; it replaces [getId()], which is deprecated[boolean isDaemon()], [void setDaemon(boolean b)]Indicates (fixed) whether the thread is a daemon thread (see below)[int getPriority()], [void setPriority(int p)]the thread's priority, from 1 ([MIN_PRIORITY]) to 10 ([MAX_PRIORITY]), with 5 ([NORM_PRIORITY]) as the default[Thread.State getState()], [boolean isAlive()]thread status ([NEW], [RUNNABLE], [BLOCKED], [WAITING], [TIMED_WAITING], [TERMINATED]); [isAlive] indicates whether it has been started but not yet completed[boolean isVirtual()](Java 21) indicates whether the thread is a virtual thread[void start()]starts the thread's execution[void join()], [boolean join(Duration délai)]The thread T1, which is executing [T2.join()], is blocked until the thread T2 has finished. The second form (Java 19) limits the wait time and indicates whether T2 has finished[static void sleep(long ms)], [static void sleep(Duration d)]the thread executing the method is suspended for [ms] milliseconds (for the duration [d]). It loses the CPU, which is given to another thread[void interrupt()], [boolean isInterrupted()]asks the thread to suspend; checks whether a suspension has been requested (see below)

The methods [join] and [sleep] throw the controlled exception [InterruptedException] if the thread is interrupted while waiting: the compiler requires that it be handled or declared. We will discuss its meaning in the section on interruptions.

The [Thread] class also has a method, [stop], which forcibly terminated a thread. It has been deprecated since Java 1.2, and since Java 20, it simply throws the [UnsupportedOperationException] exception: abruptly stopping a thread could leave the data it was handling in an inconsistent state. Today, we ask a thread to stop cooperatively by interrupting it: we’ll look at this a little later.

Here is an initial application demonstrating the existence of a main execution thread—the one that executes the [main] method. The [Threads01.java] program is as follows:

// the main thread of a program

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // the thread that executes this code
    Thread principal = Thread.currentThread();
     // the Java launcher gave it a name
    IO.println("Nom du thread courant : [" + principal.getName() + "]");
     // you can change it
    principal.setName("Main");
    IO.println("Nom du thread courant : [" + principal.getName() + "]");
     // some properties
    IO.println("Identifiant (threadId) : " + principal.threadId());
    IO.println("Thread démon (isDaemon) : " + principal.isDaemon());
    IO.println("Thread virtuel (isVirtual) : " + principal.isVirtual());
    IO.println("Priorité (getPriority) : " + principal.getPriority());
    IO.println("État (getState) : " + principal.getState());
    IO.println("Représentation textuelle : " + principal);
    IO.println("Nombre de processeurs : " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());

     // a display update every second
    var format = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss");
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        IO.println(principal.getName() + " : " + LocalTime.now().format(format));
         // the thread is suspended for 1 second
        Thread.sleep(1000);
    }
}

Results:

> java Threads01.java
Nom du thread courant : [main]
Nom du thread courant : [Main]
Identifiant (threadId) : 3
Thread démon (isDaemon) : false
Thread virtuel (isVirtual) : false
Priorité (getPriority) : 5
État (getState) : RUNNABLE
Représentation textuelle : Thread[#3,Main,5,main]
Nombre de processeurs : 2
Main : 19:14:06
Main : 19:14:07
Main : 19:14:08
Main : 19:14:09
Main : 19:14:10

Comments:

  • line 5: a reference to the thread executing the program is retrieved;
  • lines 7–10: we display its name, modify it, and then display it again. Initially, the main thread is named [main] (line 2 of the results): the Java launcher assigned this name to it;
  • Lines 12–18: Some properties of the thread. In this execution, the main thread has ID 3: the virtual machine creates a few threads for its own purposes before executing [main], and this ID may vary from one version of Java to another. It is neither a daemon thread ([isDaemon()] equals [false]) nor a virtual thread (we will discuss these two concepts later); its priority is the normal priority of 5; it is currently running ([RUNNABLE]). The thread’s method [toString] (line 17) displays its ID, name, priority, and the name of its thread group ([main]);
  • line 18: the machine on which the example was run has 2 processors;
  • lines 21–26: a loop that displays output every second. [Thread.sleep(1000)] suspends the main thread for one second. Since [sleep] can throw the controlled exception [InterruptedException], the method [main] declares it in its [throws] clause (line 3). Note the format [HH:mm:ss] (hours from 0 to 23): the format [hh] would display hours from 1 to 12.

docs.title: 8.2. Creating Execution Threads
docs.text:
It is possible to have applications where pieces of code execute “simultaneously” in different execution threads. If the machine has fewer processors than there are threads ready to execute, the threads share the processors: each one has access to them in turn for a short moment (a few milliseconds). On a multiprocessor machine, multiple threads actually execute at the same time. The amount of time allocated to a thread depends on various factors, including its priority, which has a default value but can be set programmatically ([setPriority]); this is merely a guideline, which the operating system is free to ignore (Linux ignores it by default). A thread that has access to the processor may release it early:

  • by waiting for an event (completion of another thread using [join], waiting for a signal);
  • by entering a sleep state for a specified duration ([sleep]).

A thread T is first created, for example, by the constructor [new Thread(tâche, nom)], where [tâche] is an object that implements the functional interface [Runnable], whose only method is [void run()]. This object is most often a lambda or a method reference (functional interfaces were introduced in Chapter 7). In older code, you may also encounter classes derived from *[Thread]* that redefine its method *[run]*: this is not recommended, as it mixes the task to be performed with the means of executing it.

Creating a thread does not start it:

  • the execution of thread T is started by [T.start()]: the [run] method of the task passed to T’s constructor will then be executed by thread T. The code that executes the [T.start()] instruction does not wait for thread T to finish: it immediately moves on to the next instruction. We now have two threads running in parallel. They often need to communicate with each other to track the progress of the shared work: this is the problem of thread synchronization;
  • Once started, thread T runs autonomously. It stops when the method it is executing is complete;
  • we can wait for it to finish executing using [T.join()]. This is a blocking instruction: the thread executing it is blocked until thread T has finished its work. This is a basic method of synchronization.

The program [Threads02.java] is as follows:

// creation of execution threads

void main() {
     // the main thread is named
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");

     // creating 5 threads
    var taches = new Thread[5];
    for (int i = 0; i < taches.length; i++) {
         // Thread No. i will execute the display method; we name it "i"
        taches[i] = new Thread(this::affiche, String.valueOf(i));
         // Its execution is started (non-blocking operation)
        taches[i].start();
    }

     // End of the main thread
    IO.println("Fin du thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + " à " + heure());
}

// The method executed by the threads: it has the signature Runnable.run()
void affiche() {
     // the thread executing the method
    Thread courant = Thread.currentThread();
    IO.println("Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread " + courant.getName()
            + " (id " + courant.threadId() + ") : " + heure());
     // suspended for 1 s
    dormir(1000);
    IO.println("Fin d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread " + courant.getName()
            + " : " + heure());
}

// slept for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
         // Sleep was interrupted: the thread's interrupt flag is reset
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 5: we assign a name to the main thread;
  • lines 8–14: 5 threads are created and started. Their references are stored in an array so they can be retrieved later. Each thread executes the [affiche] method in lines 21–30;
  • Line 11: The method reference [this::affiche] is automatically converted to a [Runnable] object: the method [affiche] has no parameters and returns no result, just like [run]. We write [this::affiche] because, in a compact source file, methods declared outside any class are instance methods of the implicit class, whose name cannot be used in the code. The second parameter of the constructor is the thread name;
  • line 13: thread #i is launched. This operation is non-blocking: thread #i runs in parallel with the main thread that launched it;
  • line 17: the main thread reaches the end of the program;
  • Lines 21–30: The [affiche] method displays the name and ID of the thread executing it, as well as the start and end times (to the millisecond) of execution;
  • line 27: Any thread executing the [affiche] method pauses for 1 second. The processor is then handed over to another thread waiting for the processor. At the end of the 1-second pause, the paused thread becomes eligible for the processor again. It will obtain the processor when its turn comes;
  • lines 33–40: the method [dormir] wraps [Thread.sleep]. The method [run] of [Runnable] does not declare any checked exceptions: therefore, the [affiche] method cannot let the [InterruptedException] exception thrown by [sleep] escape. The method [dormir] intercepts it and resets the thread’s interrupt flag (line 38); we’ll explain this action in the section on interrupts. We’ll encounter this small method in most of the programs in this chapter;
  • lines 43–45: The method [heure] returns the current time in the format [HH:mm:ss.SSS] ([SSS]: milliseconds).

Results:

> java Threads02.java
Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 4 (id 26) : 19:14:13.727
Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 1 (id 23) : 19:14:13.728
Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 0 (id 22) : 19:14:13.729
Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 2 (id 24) : 19:14:13.732
Fin du thread Main à 19:14:13.725
Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 3 (id 25) : 19:14:13.732
Fin d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 2 : 19:14:14.744
Fin d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 3 : 19:14:14.746
Fin d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 1 : 19:14:14.746
Fin d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 4 : 19:14:14.747
Fin d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 0 : 19:14:14.747

These results are very informative:

  • First, we can see that launching a thread is non-blocking. The main thread launched 5 threads and reached the end of the program (line 6) even though thread 3 had not yet displayed its first message;
  • the execution order of the threads is unpredictable: in this run, thread 4 displayed its start message before thread 0. The operating system has 6 threads and 2 processors here; it allocates the processors to these threads according to its own rules;
  • We also note that the order of the displays does not always follow the order of the displayed times: the main thread displayed its end at 13.725, after messages dated from 13.727 to 13.732. The time is calculated before the output, and in the meantime, another thread may have written to the console. [IO.println] (like [System.out.println]) is thread-safe: two lines written by two threads do not get mixed up, but their order is not guaranteed;
  • the IDs of the created threads (22 through 26) show that the virtual machine had already created about twenty threads for its own purposes (garbage collection, just-in-time compiler, etc.);
  • each thread pauses for one second at [sleep], then completes execution of the [affiche] method;
  • Finally, the program did not stop when the main thread finished its work: the virtual machine waited for all five threads to complete. This is because these threads are not daemon threads: the Java virtual machine stops when all its non-daemon threads have finished.

Conversely, a thread can be declared a daemon thread by [setDaemon(true)] before it is launched. Daemon threads are service threads that do not prevent the virtual machine from stopping: when the last non-daemon thread terminates, they are stopped. The program [Threads03.java] is as follows:

// daemon threads

void main() {
     // the main thread is named
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");

     // A thread constructor: platform threads, daemons, named 0, 1, 2…
    Thread.Builder constructeur = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().name("", 0);
     // creation and launch of 5 daemon threads
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
         // `start` creates a thread and launches it immediately
        constructeur.start(this::affiche);
    }

     // allow the threads time to start up
    dormir(100);
     // End of the main thread, and thus of the program
    IO.println("Fin du thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + " à " + heure());
}

// the method executed by the threads
void affiche() {
    Thread courant = Thread.currentThread();
    IO.println("Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread " + courant.getName()
            + " : " + heure());
     // sleep for 1 s
    dormir(1000);
    IO.println("Fin d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread " + courant.getName()
            + " : " + heure());
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 8: Since Java 21, the [Thread.ofPlatform()] method returns a thread constructor of type [Thread.Builder], which is configured using chained calls: [daemon()] requests daemon threads; [name("", 0)] specifies that the threads be named with a prefix (in this case, the empty string) followed by a number that starts at 0 and increments by one for each thread created. Platform threads are the “classic” threads we’ve been using since the beginning of this chapter, as opposed to the virtual threads discussed later;
  • line 12: the constructor’s method [start(Runnable)] creates a thread and starts it immediately. Its method [unstarted(Runnable)] creates a thread without starting it;
  • line 16: the main thread waits 100 ms to give the threads time to start, then it terminates.

Results:

> java Threads03.java
Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 1 : 19:14:17.388
Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 0 : 19:14:17.424
Fin du thread Main à 19:14:17.425
Début d'exécution de la méthode affiche dans le thread 3 : 19:14:17.366

Three of the five threads began execution, then the main thread terminated (line 4). Thread 3 had calculated the time for its message before the main thread ended, but was only able to display it afterward (line 5), while the virtual machine was shutting down. The daemon threads were then terminated during their one-second sleep period: no end messages were displayed. Two threads did not even have time to display their start messages: since the machine was heavily loaded, 100 ms was not enough for them to acquire the CPU (another run will yield a different number of start messages, but never any end messages). The same effect is achieved by terminating [main] with [System.exit(0)], which shuts down the virtual machine—and thus all of the application’s threads, whether daemon threads or not. Virtual threads, which we will discuss later, are always daemon threads.

If the main thread wants to wait for the threads it has created to finish, it uses the [join] method. The program [Threads04.java] also demonstrates another way to specify the code a thread should execute: a lambda.

// Wait for a thread to finish using `join`—threads created with a lambda

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // the main thread is named
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");

     // creating 5 threads
    var taches = new Thread[5];
    for (int i = 0; i < taches.length; i++) {
         // local copy of i: a lambda uses only variables that are effectively final
        int numero = i;
         // The thread executes the lambda, which calls `affiche` with typed parameters
        taches[i] = new Thread(() -> affiche(numero, 1000 + 100 * numero), String.valueOf(i));
        taches[i].start();
    }

     // waiting for all threads to finish
    for (Thread tache : taches) {
         // The main thread is blocked until the end of thread [tache]
        tache.join();
    }
     // Main thread ends
    IO.println("Fin du thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + " à " + heure());
}

// the method executed by the threads
static void affiche(int numero, long duree) {
    String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
    IO.println("Début d'exécution de la tâche " + numero + " dans le thread " + nom + " : " + heure());
     // Sleeps for [duree] milliseconds
    dormir(duree);
    IO.println("Fin d'exécution de la tâche " + numero + " dans le thread " + nom + " : " + heure());
}

// slept for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • Line 13: The thread executes the lambda [() -> affiche(numero, 1000 + 100 * numero)]. A lambda with no parameters and no return value is compatible with the [Runnable] interface. This syntax allows calling a method with typed parameters (in this case, a [int] and a [long]), whereas [run] has none;
  • Line 11: The lambda uses a copy of the loop variable [i]. This is mandatory: a lambda can only use local variables that are truly final, meaning they are never modified after initialization. The variable [i] is modified by the loop ([i++]): if the lambda used it, the compiler would reject the program (“local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final”). The variable [numero], declared within the loop body, is, on the other hand, a new variable for each iteration and is never modified. This rule protects against a common pitfall: without it, a thread that starts late could read the value of [i] from a subsequent iteration, or even the final value 5;
  • Lines 18–21: The main thread waits for each of the threads. It is first blocked while waiting for thread 0, then for thread 1, and so on. When it exits the loop, the 5 threads it launched have all finished. Since [join] can launch [InterruptedException], [main] throws this exception (line 3);
  • line 31: task #i sleeps for 1,000 + 100 × i milliseconds, so that the threads terminate in a known order.

Results:

> java Threads04.java
Début d'exécution de la tâche 1 dans le thread 1 : 19:14:21.035
Début d'exécution de la tâche 2 dans le thread 2 : 19:14:21.035
Début d'exécution de la tâche 3 dans le thread 3 : 19:14:21.035
Début d'exécution de la tâche 4 dans le thread 4 : 19:14:21.032
Début d'exécution de la tâche 0 dans le thread 0 : 19:14:21.035
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 0 dans le thread 0 : 19:14:22.039
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 1 dans le thread 1 : 19:14:22.140
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 2 dans le thread 2 : 19:14:22.239
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 3 dans le thread 3 : 19:14:22.360
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 4 dans le thread 4 : 19:14:22.440
Fin du thread Main à 19:14:22.440

The start messages appear in any order, but the end messages appear in numerical order, since the sleep durations are in ascending order: this part of the result is reproducible. The last line shows that the main thread terminated after the threads it had launched, at the moment the last of them terminated.

docs.title: 8.3. Stopping a Thread: Interruption
docs.text:
How do you stop a thread before it finishes its work, for example, when the user cancels a long-running operation? Java does not allow you to kill a thread; instead, it provides a cooperative mechanism called interruption:

  • Each thread has an interruption flag, a boolean initially set to [false];
  • A thread T1 that wants to stop thread T2 calls [T2.interrupt()]. This sets the interruption flag of T2. This is a request to terminate: T2 is not terminated; it is up to it to decide when and how to terminate, so as to leave its data in a consistent state;
  • if T2 is blocked in a waiting method ([sleep], [join], [wait], and most of the blocking methods in [java.util.concurrent]), it is woken up: the method throws the [InterruptedException] exception, and the interrupt flag is reset to [false];
  • if T2 performs a calculation without ever waiting, it must check its own flag using [Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()] at regular intervals.

This is why blocking methods declare the controlled exception [InterruptedException]: the compiler requires the programmer to decide what to do with a stop request. There are two correct responses: let the exception propagate to the caller (by declaring it in the [throws] clause), or intercept it and cleanly finish the task. When neither option is possible, as in the [dormir] method of the previous program, the flag is reset using [Thread.currentThread().interrupt()] so that the calling code can still see the request. The only incorrect response is to ignore the exception. The program [Threads05.java] demonstrates all three cases:

// stop a thread: the interruption

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // 1 - a thread that sleeps most of the time
    Thread dormeur = Thread.ofPlatform().name("dormeur").start(() -> {
        int tour = 0;
        try {
            while (true) {
                tour++;
                IO.println(heure() + " : dormeur, tour " + tour);
                 // sleep calls InterruptedException if the thread is interrupted while sleeping
                Thread.sleep(400);
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
             // An interruption is a request to stop: the thread cleanly finishes its work
            IO.println(heure() + " : dormeur interrompu pendant son sommeil, il s'arrête");
        }
    });
     // 2 - a thread that performs calculations without ever sleeping
    Thread calculateur = Thread.ofPlatform().name("calculateur").start(() -> {
        long n = 0;
         // the thread regularly checks its interrupt flag
        while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            n++;
        }
        IO.println(heure() + " : calculateur interrompu après %,d itérations, il s'arrête".formatted(n));
    });
     // 3 - A thread that ignores interrupts (do not imitate)
    Thread sourd = Thread.ofPlatform().name("sourd").daemon().start(() -> {
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
            try {
                Thread.sleep(400);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                 // The exception is “swallowed”: the stop request is lost
                IO.println(heure() + " : sourd ignore l'interruption et continue");
            }
        }
    });

     // the threads are allowed to run for 1 s
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    IO.println(heure() + " : Main demande l'arrêt des trois threads");
    dormeur.interrupt();
    calculateur.interrupt();
    sourd.interrupt();
     // wait for each thread to finish, for no more than 1 s
    for (Thread thread : List.of(dormeur, calculateur, sourd)) {
        boolean termine = thread.join(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
        IO.println(heure() + " : thread " + thread.getName() + " terminé : " + termine);
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • Lines 5–18: The [dormeur] thread spends most of its time in [Thread.sleep]. The [while (true)] loop has no exit condition: it is the [InterruptedException] exception, thrown by [sleep] when the thread is interrupted, that causes the loop to exit (line 14). The lambda is an instruction [try] that encompasses all of the thread’s work: upon receiving the exception, the thread displays a message and then terminates;
  • lines 20–27: the thread [calculateur] never waits. It checks its interrupt flag on every loop iteration (line 23);
  • Lines 29–38: The thread [sourd] intercepts [InterruptedException] and continues as if nothing had happened. The request to stop is lost: this is the mistake you must avoid. It is a daemon thread, so that the program can terminate without waiting for it;
  • Line 41: The main thread lets the other threads run for one second;
  • lines 43–45: it requests that the three threads terminate;
  • lines 47–50: it waits for each thread to finish for at most one second. The method [join(Duration)] (Java 19) returns [true] if the thread has finished within that time, and [false] otherwise. [Duration.ofSeconds(1)] represents a duration of one second (class [java.time.Duration]).

Results:

> java Threads05.java
19:14:25.674 : dormeur, tour 1
19:14:26.228 : dormeur, tour 2
19:14:26.605 : Main demande l'arrêt des trois threads
19:14:26.606 : sourd ignore l'interruption et continue
19:14:26.615 : dormeur interrompu pendant son sommeil, il s'arrête
19:14:26.622 : thread dormeur terminé : true
19:14:26.642 : calculateur interrompu après 37 667 665 itérations, il s'arrête
19:14:26.742 : thread calculateur terminé : true
19:14:27.756 : thread sourd terminé : false

The threads [dormeur] and [calculateur] terminated a few milliseconds after the request; the thread [sourd] ignored it and had still not finished one second later ([false], last line). The number of iterations of the calculator varies greatly from one run to the next, depending on the share of CPU time it received; the rest of the result is reproducible.

Interruption is the mechanism for stopping the entire Java library: we will see later that the method [cancel] of a task ([Future]) and the abrupt termination of a thread pool ([shutdownNow]) interrupt the affected threads. The next chapter will present other ways to cancel asynchronous processing, such as timeouts.

docs.title: 8.4. Virtual threads
docs.text:
The threads we’ve created so far are platform threads: each one is a wrapper around an operating system thread, which it occupies for its entire lifetime. A system thread is a costly resource: creating it takes time, its stack reserves memory (on the order of a megabyte), and the system cannot efficiently manage more than a few thousand of them. However, a server that dedicates a thread to each client (see the diagram in the following paragraph) spends most of its time waiting: for a response from a database, for the client’s next request… During these waits, the system thread is blocked and unusable.

Java 21 introduced virtual threads (“virtual threads,” JEP 444). A virtual thread is an object [Thread] like any other, but it is managed by the Java Virtual Machine rather than by the operating system:

  • To execute, a virtual thread is mounted on a platform thread, called its “carrier thread.” Carrier threads form a small pool, whose size defaults to the number of processors;
  • when a virtual thread blocks ([sleep]—waiting for network I/O, a lock, a blocking queue, etc.), it is unmounted: its stack is set aside in the virtual machine’s memory, and the carrier thread is immediately available for another virtual thread. When the wait ends, the virtual thread is reattached to a host thread—not necessarily the same one;
  • a virtual thread takes up a few hundred bytes: millions can be created.

The program [Threads06.java] compares the launch of 10,000 platform threads and 10,000 virtual threads, each of which sleeps for one second:

// platform threads and virtual threads (Java 21)

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    final int nbThreads = 10_000;
     // two thread constructors
    mesurer("threads de plate-forme", Thread.ofPlatform(), nbThreads);
    mesurer("threads virtuels", Thread.ofVirtual(), nbThreads);

     // a virtual thread runs on a platform thread called the carrier thread
    Thread virtuel = Thread.ofVirtual().name("virtuel").start(() -> {
        IO.println("Avant sommeil : " + Thread.currentThread());
        dormir(100);
        IO.println("Après sommeil : " + Thread.currentThread());
    });
    virtuel.join();
    IO.println("isVirtual : " + virtuel.isVirtual() + ", isDaemon : " + virtuel.isDaemon());
}

// launches [nbThreads] threads that sleep for 1 second, waits for them to finish, and displays the total duration
static void mesurer(String nature, Thread.Builder constructeur, int nbThreads) throws InterruptedException {
    long debut = System.nanoTime();
    var threads = new ArrayList<Thread>(nbThreads);
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        threads.add(constructeur.start(() -> dormir(1000)));
    }
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
    long duree = (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000;
    IO.println("%,d %s ont dormi 1 s chacun : durée totale %,d ms".formatted(nbThreads, nature, duree));
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 6–7: the method [mesurer] is called twice, first with a platform thread constructor ([Thread.ofPlatform()]) and then with a virtual thread constructor ([Thread.ofVirtual()]). Both constructors share the common type [Thread.Builder]; the rest of the code is identical;
  • lines 20–31: the method [mesurer] launches [nbThreads] threads that sleep for one second, waits for them to finish, and displays the total duration. The method [System.nanoTime()] returns a time in nanoseconds, which is used only to measure durations;
  • lines 10–14: A virtual thread named [virtuel] displays its textual representation before and after a sleep;
  • line 16: a virtual thread is always a daemon thread.

Results:

> java Threads06.java
10 000 threads de plate-forme ont dormi 1 s chacun : durée totale 4 518 ms
10 000 threads virtuels ont dormi 1 s chacun : durée totale 1 222 ms
Avant sommeil : VirtualThread[#20026,virtual]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2
Après sommeil : VirtualThread[#20026,virtual]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2
isVirtual : true, isDaemon : true
  • 10,000 platform threads took several seconds to do what should have taken one second: creating the system threads and managing their stacks came at a high cost. With 100,000 threads, the program would likely fail due to a lack of memory or available system threads;
  • 10,000 virtual threads completed the same task in just over one second: while dormant, they did not occupy any system threads. The exact times vary from one run to another, but the difference between the two types of threads is reproducible;
  • The textual representation of a virtual thread ([VirtualThread[#…,virtuel]]) indicates, after the character [@], the host thread on which it is mounted: a thread from the [ForkJoinPool-1] pool, which we will revisit later. After being suspended, the virtual thread can resume execution on another carrier.

Virtual threads do not make computations faster: a computation that keeps the processor busy without ever waiting will not run any faster in a virtual thread than in a platform thread, and the number of concurrent computations remains limited by the number of processors. Their benefit lies in the ability to dedicate, without counting the cost, a thread to each task that spends most of its time waiting: this is the case for servers, the following paragraph, and Chapters 12 and 13. Everything we will cover regarding thread synchronization applies equally to both virtual threads and platform threads.

docs.title: 8.5. Benefits of Threads
docs.text:
Now that we’ve highlighted the existence of a default thread—the one that executes the [main] method—and we know how to create others, let’s consider the benefits of threads. They have two main uses:

  • to utilize all the machine’s processors for a time-consuming calculation: the work is divided into chunks assigned to different threads. We’ll do this using parallel streams and the [Fork/Join] framework at the end of this chapter;
  • to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, particularly when some of them primarily involve waiting (for a network response, a disk read, or user input). This is the case with client/server Internet applications, which we’ll cover in Chapter 12.

In a client-server Internet application, a server located on a machine S1 responds to requests from clients located on remote machines C1, C2, …, Cn:

We use Internet applications that follow this pattern every day: web services, email, file transfers, etc. In the diagram above, the server S1 must serve clients Ci simultaneously. If we take the example of a file server, we know that a transfer can sometimes take several minutes. It is out of the question for a single client to monopolize the server for such a long period of time. A common solution is for the server to create as many execution threads as there are clients. Each thread is then responsible for handling a specific client:

With platform threads, the server effectively uses a thread pool—discussed later—whose limited number of threads caps the number of clients served simultaneously. With virtual threads, the scheme above once again becomes the correct solution: one virtual thread per client, even if there are tens of thousands of clients, since a client that is waiting does not occupy any system threads. This is what modern Java web servers, such as Tomcat—which we will use in Chapter 13—enable today.

docs.title: 8.6. Information Exchange Between Threads
docs.text:
In the previous examples, the threads executed a method without parameters, or a lambda that called a method with parameters. Since the method [run]* in [Runnable] has neither parameters nor a return value, it is the lambda that passes information to the launched thread: it captures the variables it needs. If the captured variable refers to an object, the launched thread can also store results in it that the launching thread will read. The program [Threads07.java]* is as follows:

// information exchange between threads

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // This is called the main thread
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");

     // creation of 5 threads
    var taches = new Thread[5];
    var donnees = new Donnees[5];
    for (int i = 0; i < taches.length; i++) {
         // The object exchanged with the thread: the launching thread sets the start time and duration
        Donnees d = new Donnees(LocalTime.now(), i + 1);
        donnees[i] = d;
         // The launched thread receives the object via the lambda that captures it
