        taches[i] = new Thread(() -> dormir(d), String.valueOf(i));
        taches[i].start();
    }

     // We wait for the threads one after another
    var format = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss");
    for (int i = 0; i < taches.length; i++) {
         // Waiting for thread #i to finish
        taches[i].join();
         // Thread No. i has set the end time for its object
        Donnees d = donnees[i];
        double dureeEffective = Duration.between(d.getDebut(), d.getFin()).toMillis() / 1000.0;
        IO.println("Thread %s terminé : début %s, durée programmée %d s, fin %s, durée effective %.3f s"
                .formatted(taches[i].getName(), d.getDebut().format(format), d.getDuree(),
                        d.getFin().format(format), dureeEffective));
    }
     // End of the main thread
    IO.println("Fin du thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + " à " + LocalTime.now().format(format));
}

// The method executed by the threads
static void dormir(Donnees data) {
    try {
         // Suspended for [duree] seconds
        Thread.sleep(data.getDuree() * 1000L);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
     // the launched thread returns a result to the launching thread
    data.setFin(LocalTime.now());
}

// Information exchanged between the calling thread and the called thread
static class Donnees {
     // set by the calling thread
    private final LocalTime debut;
    private final int duree;
     // set by the called thread
    private LocalTime fin;

    Donnees(LocalTime debut, int duree) {
        this.debut = debut;
        this.duree = duree;
    }

    LocalTime getDebut() {
        return debut;
    }

    int getDuree() {
        return duree;
    }

    LocalTime getFin() {
        return fin;
    }

    void setFin(LocalTime fin) {
        this.fin = fin;
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 48–75: The information exchanged with each thread is a [Donnees] object. There is a two-way exchange of information between the launching thread and the launched thread. [debut] and [duree] are fields of [final]: they are set once and for all by the constructor:
    • [debut]: the thread’s execution start time, set by the launching thread;
    • [duree]: duration in seconds of the launched thread’s sleep, set by the launching thread;
    • [fin]: the end time of the thread’s execution, set by the launched thread;
  • line 12: a [Donnees] object is created and stored in the [donnees] array (line 13);
  • line 15: the lambda [() -> dormir(d)] captures the variable [d], which is effectively final: the launched thread will execute the method [dormir] in lines 36–45 with the object [d] as a parameter;
  • lines 21–30: the main thread waits for each of the threads it has launched to finish, then retrieves the object [donnees[i]] from thread #i and displays its contents. The actual duration is calculated by [Duration.between(début, fin)];
  • line 39: the [duree] field of the parameter sets the sleep duration;
  • line 44: the [fin] field of the parameter is populated.

Results:

> java Threads07.java
Thread 0 terminé : début 19:14:38, durée programmée 1 s, fin 19:14:39, durée effective 1,005 s
Thread 1 terminé : début 19:14:38, durée programmée 2 s, fin 19:14:40, durée effective 2,006 s
Thread 2 terminé : début 19:14:38, durée programmée 3 s, fin 19:14:41, durée effective 3,000 s
Thread 3 terminé : début 19:14:38, durée programmée 4 s, fin 19:14:42, durée effective 4,000 s
Thread 4 terminé : début 19:14:38, durée programmée 5 s, fin 19:14:43, durée effective 5,000 s
Fin du thread Main à 19:14:43

This example shows that two threads can exchange information:

  • the calling thread can control the execution of the called thread by providing it with information;
  • the launched thread can return results to the launching thread.

In order for the calling thread to know when the results it is waiting for are available, it must be notified when the called thread has finished. Here, it waited for the thread to finish using the [join] method. This isn’t just a matter of timing: as we’ll see in the section on the [volatile] keyword, a write operation performed by one thread isn’t necessarily visible to another. Java’s memory model guarantees that everything written by a thread is visible to the thread that waited for it to finish using [join], and that everything written by the launching thread before [start] is visible to the launched thread. We’ll explore other ways to synchronize later on.

Instead of a lambda, we could write a class that implements [Runnable] and whose fields contain the exchanged information. The lambda is more concise; it is the most common approach today. To retrieve the result of a processing operation, we’ll also look at the [Callable<V>] interface later on, whose [V call()] method returns a result.

docs.title: 8.7.1. Unsynchronized concurrent access
docs.text:
In the previous section, information was exchanged only between two threads and at very specific times: this was a classic example of parameter passing. There are other cases where information is shared by multiple threads that may want to read or update it at the same time. This raises the issue of the integrity of this information. Suppose the shared information is a structure S containing various pieces of information I1, I2, …, In:

  • A thread T1 begins updating structure S: it modifies field I1 and is interrupted before completing the full update of structure S;
  • a thread T2 that acquires the processor then reads structure S to make decisions. It reads a structure in an unstable state: some fields are up to date, others are not.

This situation is called concurrent access to a shared resource—in this case, structure S. It is often difficult to manage. Let’s consider the following example to illustrate the problems that can arise:

  • an application will generate n threads, where n is passed as a parameter;
  • the shared resource is a counter that must be incremented by each generated thread;
  • at the end of the application, the counter’s value is displayed. It should therefore equal n.

The program [Threads08.java] is as follows:

// Unsynchronized concurrent access to a shared resource

void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
     // Verification of the argument: the number of threads to create
    final int nbMaxThreads = 100;
    int nbThreads = args.length == 1 ? entier(args[0]) : -1;
    if (nbThreads < 1 || nbThreads > nbMaxThreads) {
        System.err.println("syntaxe : java Threads08.java nbThreads"
                + " (nbThreads entre 1 et " + nbMaxThreads + ")");
        System.exit(1);
    }

     // creation and launch of threads
    var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        threads[i] = new Thread(Compteur::incrementer, String.valueOf(i));
        threads[i].start();
    }
     // waiting for threads to finish
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
     // displaying the counter
    IO.println("Nombre de threads générés : " + Compteur.getValeur());
}

// the integer contained in [texte], -1 if invalid
static int entier(String texte) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(texte);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return -1;
    }
}

// the shared resource
static class Compteur {
     // the thread counter, shared by all threads
    private static int valeur;

    static int getValeur() {
        return valeur;
    }

     // the method executed by each thread
    static void incrementer() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
         // reading the counter
        int v = valeur;
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a lu la valeur du compteur : " + v);
         // wait: the thread yields the CPU
        dormir(1000);
         // incrementing the counter
        valeur = v + 1;
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a écrit la valeur du compteur : "
                + valeur);
    }
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • Lines 5–11: The number of threads is passed as an argument. The method [entier] (lines 28–34) returns the integer contained in a string, or -1 if the string contains none; the condition on line 7 therefore rejects both a missing or invalid argument and a number outside the range [1, 100]. In the event of an error, the program writes a message to the error output ([System.err]) and terminates with exit code 1 ([System.exit(1)]);
  • line 16: Each thread executes the static method [incrementer] of the class [Compteur]. The method reference [Compteur::incrementer] is valid here because [Compteur] is a named class;
  • lines 37–58: the shared resource is the static field [valeur] of the class [Compteur]. The counter is encapsulated in a static nested class, with the method [incrementer] executed by each thread;
  • line 49: the counter is read;
  • line 52: the thread pauses for 1 second. It therefore loses the CPU;
  • line 54: the counter is incremented.

The one-second pause is only there to force the thread to lose the CPU between reading and writing the counter. In practice, there is no guarantee that a thread will not be interrupted between these two moments, and on a multiprocessor machine, two threads may even read the counter at exactly the same time. The one-second sleep merely systematizes this risk.

Program arguments are placed after the source file name. Without arguments, an error message is displayed (the Linux shell command ***[echo $?]*** displays the exit code of the last program executed):

> java Threads08.java
syntaxe : java Threads08.java nbThreads (nbThreads entre 1 et 100)
> echo $?
1

With 5 threads:

> java Threads08.java 5
À 19:14:46.240, le thread 1 a lu la valeur du compteur : 0
À 19:14:46.244, le thread 3 a lu la valeur du compteur : 0
À 19:14:46.246, le thread 4 a lu la valeur du compteur : 0
À 19:14:46.247, le thread 0 a lu la valeur du compteur : 0
À 19:14:46.237, le thread 2 a lu la valeur du compteur : 0
À 19:14:47.244, le thread 1 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:14:47.245, le thread 3 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:14:47.247, le thread 4 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:14:47.247, le thread 0 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:14:47.252, le thread 2 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 1
Nombre de threads générés : 1

Looking at these results, it’s clear what’s happening:

  • A first thread reads the counter. It finds 0. It pauses for 1 second and thus loses the CPU;
  • a second thread also reads the counter value. It is still 0 since the previous thread has not yet incremented it. It also pauses for 1 second;
  • in less than a second, all 5 threads have time to read the value 0;
  • when they wake up, they increment the value 0 they read and all write the value 1 to the counter, as confirmed by the last line (line 12). This incorrect result is reproducible: only the order of the threads changes from one execution to the next.

One might object that the example is artificial. So let’s remove the sleep and use the operator [++], which gives the illusion of a single instruction. The program [Threads09.java] is as follows:

// Lost updates without sleep: counter++ is not atomic

void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
     // parameters: number of threads, number of increments per thread
    int nbThreads = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4;
    int nbIncrements = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 50_000_000;

     // We repeat the experiment three times
    for (int essai = 1; essai <= 3; essai++) {
        Compteur.valeur = 0;
         // Creating and launching threads
        var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
        for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
            threads[i] = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
                for (int j = 0; j < nbIncrements; j++) {
                     // read, increment, write: three operations
                    Compteur.valeur++;
                }
            });
        }
         // waiting for the threads to finish
        for (Thread thread : threads) {
            thread.join();
        }
         // Result
        int attendu = nbThreads * nbIncrements;
        IO.println("Essai %d : valeur attendue %,d, valeur obtenue %,d, mises à jour perdues %,d"
                .formatted(essai, attendu, Compteur.valeur, attendu - Compteur.valeur));
    }
}

// the shared resource
static class Compteur {
    static int valeur;
}

Comments:

  • lines 5–6: The number of threads (4 by default) and the number of increments performed by each thread (50 million by default) can be passed as arguments. The separator [_] makes the constant [50_000_000] readable;
  • line 14: The threads are created and launched by [Thread.ofPlatform().start(…)]; they do not need names;
  • Line 17: Each thread increments the shared counter without pausing;
  • line 27: In the format string, [%,d] displays an integer using the thousands separator for the current language (in this case, French: a thin, non-breaking space). The instance method [formatted(…)] (Java 15) for a string is equivalent to [String.format(chaîne, …)].

Results:

> java Threads09.java
Essai 1 : valeur attendue 200 000 000, valeur obtenue 132 308 591, mises à jour perdues 67 691 409
Essai 2 : valeur attendue 200 000 000, valeur obtenue 135 621 476, mises à jour perdues 64 378 524
Essai 3 : valeur attendue 200 000 000, valeur obtenue 50 000 635, mises à jour perdues 149 999 365

Tens of millions of updates have been lost, and their number varies from one test to another. The high-level operation [Compteur.valeur++] is in fact translated into several basic processor instructions: read the value from memory, increment it in a register, and write the result to memory. If two threads read the same value before one of them has written its own, an increment is lost, exactly as in the previous example.

Test 3 warrants an explanation: it lost almost exactly 150 million updates, representing the work of three out of four threads. After a few seconds of execution, the virtual machine’s just-in-time compiler (JIT) optimized the loop in lines 15–18: it determined that no other thread was supposed to see the counter during the loop (nothing in the code requires it to) and placed the counter in a processor register. Each thread then reads the counter once, adds 50 million to it in its register, and writes it back once at the end. If all four threads read the value 0 before any of them has written to it, three out of four results are lost; if, on the other hand, their work does not overlap, the result is correct. In other runs of this program, tests 2 and 3 actually yielded the exact value of 200,000,000. Only the first test, run before this optimization, consistently loses updates. This is what makes these errors so dangerous: a program can run for months and then fail on the very day the machine is under heavier load or running faster.

Where does the problem come from? One thread read an outdated value because another thread had been interrupted—or was working simultaneously on another processor—before it had finished its task of updating the counter. This brings us to the concepts of critical resources and critical sections in a program:

  • a critical resource is a resource that can be held by only one thread at a time. Here, the critical resource is the counter;
  • a critical section of a program is a sequence of instructions in a thread’s execution flow during which it accesses a critical resource. We must ensure that, during this critical section, the thread is the only one with access to the resource.

In the program [Threads08.java], the critical section is the code between reading the counter and writing its new value:

         // reading the counter
        int v = valeur;
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a lu la valeur du compteur : " + v);
         // wait: the thread loses the CPU
        dormir(1000);
         // incrementing the counter
        valeur = v + 1;

To execute this code, a thread must be guaranteed to be the only one running. It may be interrupted, but during that interruption, no other thread must be able to execute this same code. Java offers various tools to ensure single-threaded entry into critical sections of code. We’ll look at a few of them now.

docs.title: 8.7.2. The synchronized keyword
docs.text:
The block [synchronized] delimits a critical section as follows: [synchronized (verrou) { …section critique… }]***. [verrou]* is an object visible to all threads executing the critical section. In Java, every object has an internal lock, also known as a monitor. The block [synchronized] ensures that only one thread at a time holds the monitor of the object [verrou], meaning that only one thread at a time executes the critical section: a thread that encounters a monitor held by another thread is blocked until the monitor is released. The monitor is released upon exiting the block, whether the exit is normal or due to an exception.

The previous example is rewritten as follows in [Threads10.java]:

// critical section protected by a `synchronized` block

void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
     // checking the argument: the number of threads to create
    final int nbMaxThreads = 100;
    int nbThreads = args.length == 1 ? entier(args[0]) : -1;
    if (nbThreads < 1 || nbThreads > nbMaxThreads) {
        System.err.println("syntaxe : java Threads10.java nbThreads"
                + " (nbThreads entre 1 et " + nbMaxThreads + ")");
        System.exit(1);
    }

     // creation and launch of threads
    var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        threads[i] = new Thread(Compteur::incrementer, String.valueOf(i));
        threads[i].start();
    }
     // waiting for threads to finish, in the reverse order of their creation
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");
    for (int i = nbThreads - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread Main attend la fin du thread " + threads[i].getName());
        threads[i].join();
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread Main a été prévenu de la fin du thread "
                + threads[i].getName());
    }
     // displaying the counter
    IO.println("Nombre de threads générés : " + Compteur.getValeur());
}

// the integer contained in [texte], -1 if it is invalid
static int entier(String texte) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(texte);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return -1;
    }
}

// the shared resource
static class Compteur {
     // the thread counter
    private static int valeur;
     // the synchronization object, visible to all threads
    private static final Object verrou = new Object();

    static int getValeur() {
        synchronized (verrou) {
            return valeur;
        }
    }

     // the method executed by each thread
    static void incrementer() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom
                + " attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique");
         // only one thread at a time executes the following block
        synchronized (verrou) {
             // read the counter
            int v = valeur;
            IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a lu la valeur du compteur : " + v);
             // wait: the thread yields the CPU but retains the lock
            dormir(1000);
             // incrementing the counter
            valeur = v + 1;
            IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a écrit la valeur du compteur : "
                    + valeur);
        }
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a quitté la section critique");
    }
}

// sleeps for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 45: [verrou] is the object that will enable synchronization of all threads. It serves no other purpose: it is a simple [Object]. It is [final]: the reference must never change, otherwise two threads could lock two different objects;
  • lines 59–69: The critical section of the [incrementer] method is enclosed by the [synchronized] block. The thread holds the lock while it sleeps for one second: the other threads cannot enter;
  • lines 47–51: The main thread’s read of the counter is also protected by the lock. Here, this isn’t strictly necessary, since the main thread waited for the other threads to finish with [join]; but it’s good practice: data protected by a lock must be read and written under the protection of that lock;
  • lines 20–26: The main thread waits for the threads in the reverse order of their creation.

Results with 3 threads:

> java Threads10.java 3
À 19:14:50.140, le thread 2 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:14:50.147, le thread 2 a lu la valeur du compteur : 0
À 19:14:50.140, le thread 1 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:14:50.140, le thread 0 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:14:50.133, le thread Main attend la fin du thread 2
À 19:14:51.151, le thread 2 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:14:51.152, le thread 1 a lu la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:14:51.153, le thread 2 a quitté la section critique
À 19:14:51.153, le thread Main a été prévenu de la fin du thread 2
À 19:14:51.153, le thread Main attend la fin du thread 1
À 19:14:52.160, le thread 1 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 2
À 19:14:52.160, le thread 0 a lu la valeur du compteur : 2
À 19:14:52.160, le thread 1 a quitté la section critique
À 19:14:52.162, le thread Main a été prévenu de la fin du thread 1
À 19:14:52.162, le thread Main attend la fin du thread 0
À 19:14:53.160, le thread 0 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 3
À 19:14:53.160, le thread 0 a quitté la section critique
À 19:14:53.161, le thread Main a été prévenu de la fin du thread 0
Nombre de threads générés : 3
  • All three threads request to enter the critical section at nearly the same time;
  • only one enters it—in this case, thread 2 (the order of entry is not guaranteed: it is not necessarily the first to arrive that enters first). It reads the counter, sleeps for one second, writes the new value, and exits the critical section;
  • the other two threads are blocked until the first one exits the critical section, then proceed one after the other. Each reads the value written by the previous one. Note (lines 8–9) that Thread 1 read the counter before Thread 2 indicated that it had exited the critical section: Thread 2 did indeed release the lock, but it does not display its message until after the block [synchronized], and Thread 1 was faster;
  • the main thread was waiting for Thread 2 to finish. When notified that Thread 2 had finished, it waited for Thread 1 to finish, then for Thread 0 to finish;
  • The number of threads is correct (line 20). Regardless of the order in which the threads run, this result is reproducible.

The keyword [synchronized] can also apply to an entire method: [synchronized void m() {…}] is equivalent to a block [synchronized (this) {…}] that encompasses the entire body of the method, and [static synchronized void m() {…}] to a block [synchronized (Compteur.class) {…}], which locks the class object [Class]. This is the shortest notation, and it is commonly used. However, it has one drawback: the locked object ([this], or the object [Class]) is visible from the outside, and external code can acquire the same lock and block ours. Therefore, it is often preferable to lock a private object, as in the example. For the same reason, we never lock a string (identical string literals are a single object shared by the entire program) or, since Java 16, an object of a “value-based” class such as [Integer] or [LocalDate] (the compiler issues a warning in such cases).

A thread that already holds a monitor can re-enter a [synchronized] block on the same object without blocking itself: the lock is said to be reentrant. A [synchronized] method can thus call another [synchronized] method on the same object.

docs.title: 8.7.3. The ReentrantLock class
docs.text:
The [synchronized] lock is simple but rigid: a thread waiting on a monitor waits indefinitely, without being able to give up after a certain amount of time, and without being able to be interrupted. The [java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock] class (Java 5) is an explicit lock—which is also reentrant—that offers these capabilities. It implements the [Lock] interface. We will use the following constructors and methods:

MemberRole[ReentrantLock()], [ReentrantLock(boolean équitable)]creates a lock. A fair lock ([true]) is granted to threads in the order in which they requested it; a non-fair lock (the default) is faster, but a thread may cut in front of others[void lock()]The thread T1, which is executing [V.lock()], requests lock V. If V is not held by any thread, it is granted to T1. If a thread T2 then performs the same operation, it is blocked: a lock can belong to only one thread. T2 will be unblocked when T1 releases V. Thus, multiple threads may be blocked while waiting for V[boolean tryLock()], [boolean tryLock(long délai, TimeUnit unité)]requests the lock immediately, or while waiting for at most [délai]. The method returns [false] if the lock could not be obtained[void lockInterruptibly()]like [lock], but the wait can be interrupted ([InterruptedException])[void unlock()]The thread holding V releases it. One of the threads waiting for V then acquires it[boolean isHeldByCurrentThread()]indicates whether the current thread holds the lock[Condition newCondition()]creates a condition associated with the lock (see below)

Synchronization of a critical section always follows the same pattern: [V.lock(); try { …section critique… } finally { V.unlock(); }]. Do not forget to release the lock; otherwise, the threads waiting for it will remain blocked indefinitely: this is why the lock is released in a [finally] clause, which is executed regardless of whether an exception occurred or not. The [synchronized] block does this automatically; with a [ReentrantLock], it is up to the programmer to do so. The [Threads11.java] program continues the previous example with a [ReentrantLock]:

// critical section protected by a lock ReentrantLock

void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
     // checking the argument: the number of threads to create
    final int nbMaxThreads = 100;
    int nbThreads = args.length == 1 ? entier(args[0]) : -1;
    if (nbThreads < 1 || nbThreads > nbMaxThreads) {
        System.err.println("syntaxe : java Threads11.java nbThreads"
                + " (nbThreads entre 1 et " + nbMaxThreads + ")");
        System.exit(1);
    }

     // creating and launching threads
    var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        threads[i] = new Thread(Compteur::incrementer, String.valueOf(i));
        threads[i].start();
    }
     // waiting for threads to finish
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
     // displaying the counter
    IO.println("Nombre de threads générés : " + Compteur.getValeur());
}

// the integer contained in [texte], -1 if invalid
static int entier(String texte) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(texte);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return -1;
    }
}

// the shared resource
static class Compteur {
     // the thread counter
    private static int valeur;
     // the synchronization object: a fair lock (true)
    private static final ReentrantLock verrou = new ReentrantLock(true);

    static int getValeur() {
        verrou.lock();
        try {
            return valeur;
        } finally {
            verrou.unlock();
        }
    }

     // the method executed by each thread
    static void incrementer() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom
                + " attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique");
         // the lock is requested
        verrou.lock();
        try {
             // read the counter
            int v = valeur;
            IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a lu la valeur du compteur : " + v);
             // wait
            dormir(1000);
             // increment the counter
            valeur = v + 1;
            IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a écrit la valeur du compteur : "
                    + valeur);
        } finally {
             // release the lock, regardless of whether an exception occurred
            IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " quitte la section critique");
            verrou.unlock();
        }
    }
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

The main program is that of [Threads08.java]. Comments:

  • line 41: the thread synchronization object is now a fair lock, [ReentrantLock];
  • line 58: start of the critical section. The thread is blocked until the lock is released;
  • lines 59–73: Because a lock must always be released, regardless of whether an exception occurs, the critical section is placed within a [try], whose [finally] clause releases the lock (line 72);
  • Lines 43–50: The same pattern protects the meter reading. The instruction [return valeur;] is executed before the clause [finally]: the returned value is read while the lock is held.

Results:

> java Threads11.java 3
À 19:14:55.022, le thread 1 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:14:55.025, le thread 1 a lu la valeur du compteur : 0
À 19:14:55.020, le thread 2 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:14:55.020, le thread 0 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:14:56.027, le thread 1 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:14:56.027, le thread 1 quitte la section critique
À 19:14:56.027, le thread 2 a lu la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:14:57.028, le thread 2 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 2
À 19:14:57.028, le thread 2 quitte la section critique
À 19:14:57.028, le thread 0 a lu la valeur du compteur : 2
À 19:14:58.028, le thread 0 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 3
À 19:14:58.028, le thread 0 quitte la section critique
Nombre de threads générés : 3

The results are similar to the previous ones: the threads enter the critical section one by one, and the final counter value is correct. Since the lock is fair, the threads acquired it in the order in which they requested it: the order of their calls to [lock], which the times of the “waiting for permission” messages—calculated a little earlier—only approximate.

When should you use [ReentrantLock] instead of [synchronized]? When you need one of its additional features: timeout ([tryLock], which we’ll use to prevent deadlock), interruptible wait, fairness, or multiple conditions. Otherwise, the [synchronized] block—which is simpler and eliminates the risk of forgetting [unlock]—works very well. Since Java 24, it no longer causes any issues with virtual threads: previously, a virtual thread blocked in a [synchronized] block could not release its host thread, which made [ReentrantLock] the preferred choice.

docs.title: 8.7.4. Synchronizing Processes: The File Lock
docs.text:
The locks described above synchronize threads within the same virtual machine—that is, within the same process. Sometimes different processes need to share a resource, such as a file, or you may want to prevent two instances of the same application from being launched. Java does not provide a named synchronization object shared across processes; instead, a file lock managed by the operating system is used: the [java.nio.channels.FileLock] class. A lock is obtained on an open file in the form of a [FileChannel] channel:

  • [FileLock lock()]: waits for the lock to become available and acquires it;
  • [FileLock tryLock()]: attempts to acquire the lock without waiting, and returns [null] if it is held by another process;
  • [void release()]: releases the lock. The lock is also released when the channel is closed or when the process ends, even if terminated abruptly: a lock cannot remain “abandoned.”

The program [Threads12.java] is launched twice, in two different processes, which share a critical section:

// A file lock synchronizes different processes

void main(String[] args) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
     // the locked file is known to all processes that use it
    Path fichier = Path.of(System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir"), "cours-java-threads-12.lock");
     // the process name is passed as an argument
    String processus = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "P";

     // The file is opened (it is created if it does not yet exist)
    try (FileChannel canal = FileChannel.open(fichier, StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.WRITE)) {
        IO.println(heure() + " : le processus " + processus + " demande le verrou");
         // Non-blocking attempt: returns null if another process holds the lock
        FileLock verrou = canal.tryLock();
        if (verrou == null) {
            IO.println(heure() + " : le verrou est détenu par un autre processus, " + processus + " attend");
             // wait without a time limit
            verrou = canal.lock();
        }
        try {
             // critical section between processes
            IO.println(heure() + " : le processus " + processus + " a obtenu le verrou, il travaille 3 s");
            Thread.sleep(3000);
            IO.println(heure() + " : le processus " + processus + " libère le verrou");
        } finally {
            verrou.release();
        }
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 5: the file that serves as the lock. All processes that lock this file synchronize with one another. It is placed in the system’s temporary files folder, specified by the system property [java.io.tmpdir] ([/tmp] on Linux). Its contents are irrelevant: it can remain empty;
  • line 10: the file is opened for writing (an exclusive lock requires this), and created if it does not yet exist ([CREATE]). The [try] statement with the resource will close the channel at the end;
  • line 13: the process attempts to acquire the lock without waiting. If it fails, it reports the failure and then waits for the lock indefinitely (line 17);
  • Lines 19–26: the critical section, which lasts 3 seconds, followed by the release of the lock.

A file lock belongs to the entire process, not to a single thread: it is not used to synchronize threads within the same process (two lock requests on the same file within the same process cause the [OverlappingFileLockException] exception). We start process A, wait 1.5 seconds, then start process B in a second terminal. Results from Process A:

> java Threads12.java A
19:15:04.965 : le processus A demande le verrou
19:15:04.976 : le processus A a obtenu le verrou, il travaille 3 s
19:15:07.976 : le processus A libère le verrou

Results from Process B:

> java Threads12.java B
19:15:06.394 : le processus B demande le verrou
19:15:06.405 : le verrou est détenu par un autre processus, B attend
19:15:07.977 : le processus B a obtenu le verrou, il travaille 3 s
19:15:10.978 : le processus B libère le verrou

Process B detected the lock held by process A and waited. It acquired the lock the very moment A released it. A common use of this mechanism is to prevent the launch of two instances of the same application: the second instance, unable to acquire the lock with [tryLock], terminates immediately.

docs.title: 8.7.5. A Barrier: The Semaphore Class
docs.text:
A semaphore is a counter for permits (or slots). The [java.util.concurrent.Semaphore] class provides the following methods:

MemberRole[Semaphore(int permis)], [Semaphore(int permis, boolean équitable)]creates a semaphore with [permis] permits; the second parameter has the same meaning as for [ReentrantLock][void acquire()]acquires a permit. If there are no permits left, the thread is blocked until a permit is released. The wait can be interrupted ([InterruptedException])[void acquireUninterruptibly()]same as above, but the wait cannot be interrupted[boolean tryAcquire()], [boolean tryAcquire(long délai, TimeUnit unité)]Get a license immediately, or wait no longer than [délai]; return [false] if unsuccessful[void release()]returns (adds) a permit; one of the waiting threads can then take it[int availablePermits()]the number of available permits

Unlike a lock, a permit does not belong to any specific thread: any thread can call [release], even if it has never acquired a permit. A semaphore created with zero permits is therefore a closed barrier, at which threads calling [acquire] are blocked. Another thread will open it when the time comes, by calling [release]. This timing depends entirely on the problem being solved. The thread that acquired the single permit passed through the barrier, which closed behind it; by returning the permit, it opens the barrier for another thread. If, in the previous example, we replace the lock with such a barrier, the code becomes the following ([Threads13.java]):

// barrier-protected critical section: a semaphore with a single permit

void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
     // Argument check: the number of threads to create
    final int nbMaxThreads = 100;
    int nbThreads = args.length == 1 ? entier(args[0]) : -1;
    if (nbThreads < 1 || nbThreads > nbMaxThreads) {
        System.err.println("syntaxe : java Threads13.java nbThreads"
                + " (nbThreads entre 1 et " + nbMaxThreads + ")");
        System.exit(1);
    }

     // creation and launch of threads
    var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        threads[i] = new Thread(Compteur::incrementer, String.valueOf(i));
        threads[i].start();
    }
     // Allowing threads to reach the closed barrier
    Thread.sleep(500);
     // Open the barrier to the critical section
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");
    IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread Main ouvre la barrière de la section critique");
    Compteur.synchro.release();
     // Wait for the threads to finish
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
     // display the counter
    IO.println("Nombre de threads générés : " + Compteur.getValeur());
}

// the integer contained in [texte], -1 if it is invalid
static int entier(String texte) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(texte);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return -1;
    }
}

// the shared resource
static class Compteur {
     // the thread counter
    private static int valeur;
     // the barrier: a semaphore created without any permission, and therefore closed
    static final Semaphore synchro = new Semaphore(0);

    static int getValeur() {
        return valeur;
    }

     // the method executed by each thread
    static void incrementer() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom
                + " attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique");
         // passing the barrier: the thread takes the single permit; the barrier closes behind it
        synchro.acquireUninterruptibly();
        try {
             // reading the counter
            int v = valeur;
            IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a lu la valeur du compteur : " + v);
             // wait
            dormir(1000);
             // incrementing the counter
            valeur = v + 1;
            IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " a écrit la valeur du compteur : "
                    + valeur);
        } finally {
             // returning the permit: the barrier opens for another thread
            IO.println("À " + heure() + ", le thread " + nom + " quitte la section critique");
            synchro.release();
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 47: the barrier is created in a closed state. It will be opened by the main thread on line 24;
  • line 20: the main thread waits half a second to allow the threads to arrive at the barrier;
  • line 59: the thread responsible for incrementing the counter requests permission to enter the critical section. The various threads accumulate in front of the closed barrier. When the main thread opens it, one of the waiting threads passes through, and the barrier closes again. The method [acquireUninterruptibly] avoids having to handle the exception [InterruptedException] here;
  • line 73: when it has finished its work, the thread reopens the barrier, allowing another thread to enter.

Results:

> java Threads13.java 3
À 19:15:00.034, le thread 1 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:15:00.048, le thread 2 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:15:00.041, le thread 0 attend l'autorisation d'entrer dans la section critique
À 19:15:00.532, le thread Main ouvre la barrière de la section critique
À 19:15:00.533, le thread 1 a lu la valeur du compteur : 0
À 19:15:01.535, le thread 1 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:15:01.535, le thread 1 quitte la section critique
À 19:15:01.535, le thread 2 a lu la valeur du compteur : 1
À 19:15:02.536, le thread 2 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 2
À 19:15:02.536, le thread 2 quitte la section critique
À 19:15:02.536, le thread 0 a lu la valeur du compteur : 2
À 19:15:03.536, le thread 0 a écrit la valeur du compteur : 3
À 19:15:03.536, le thread 0 quitte la section critique
Nombre de threads générés : 3

The results are similar to the previous ones. We can see that the three threads wait at the barrier until the main thread opens it (line 5).

docs.title: 8.7.6. The CountDownLatch and Semaphore classes
docs.text:
Two additional uses of synchronization tools complement the previous examples.

A [java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch] object is a counter: it is created with an initial value N; each call to its [countDown] method decrements it; its [await] method blocks the calling thread until the counter reaches 0. Once it reaches 0, it remains there: the barrier is permanently open and allows all threads to pass. With N = 1, this serves as the “starting signal” for a race; with N = the number of tasks, it is a way to wait for the completion of N tasks, each of which calls [countDown] when it finishes. The program [Threads14.java] is as follows:

// CountDownLatch: a start signal that releases all waiting threads

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // the start signal: a countdown starting from 1
    var depart = new CountDownLatch(1);

     // creation and launch of 4 threads
    var threads = new Thread[4];
    for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) {
        threads[i] = Thread.ofPlatform().name(String.valueOf(i)).start(() -> {
            String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
            IO.println(heure() + " : le coureur " + nom + " attend le signal de départ");
            try {
                 // waiting for the countdown to reach 0
                depart.await();
                IO.println(heure() + " : le coureur " + nom + " est parti");
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                IO.println(heure() + " : le coureur " + nom + " a abandonné");
            }
        });
    }

     // The main thread waits 1 second, then sends the start signal
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    IO.println(heure() + " : signal de départ");
     // The countdown reaches 0: all waiting threads are released
    depart.countDown();
     // waiting for the threads to finish
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
    IO.println("Valeur du compte à rebours : " + depart.getCount());
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 5: the countdown starts at 1: the gate is closed;
  • line 15: each thread waits for the countdown to reach 0. The method [await] can launch [InterruptedException]; if the thread is interrupted while waiting, it drops out of the race (line 18);
  • line 27: The main thread decrements the countdown timer after one second; it becomes 0;
  • line 32: the [getCount] method returns the current value of the countdown.

Results:

> java Threads14.java
19:15:14.328 : le coureur 2 attend le signal de départ
19:15:14.328 : le coureur 0 attend le signal de départ
19:15:14.323 : le coureur 1 attend le signal de départ
19:15:14.329 : le coureur 3 attend le signal de départ
19:15:15.293 : signal de départ
19:15:15.294 : le coureur 0 est parti
19:15:15.296 : le coureur 1 est parti
19:15:15.296 : le coureur 3 est parti
19:15:15.296 : le coureur 2 est parti
Valeur du compte à rebours : 0

The four runners started together, within a few milliseconds of each other, after the starting signal. A [CountDownLatch] is used only once; the [CyclicBarrier] class provides a reusable rendezvous point (the N threads wait for each other, then set off together), and the [Phaser] class generalizes these two tools.

Let’s return to the semaphore in its most common use: an N-permit semaphore allows at most N threads to enter a code section at a time. This is useful for limiting access to a resource available in limited quantities (database connections, concurrent requests to a server, etc.). The program [Threads15.java] is as follows:

// Semaphore: at most N threads at a time in a code section

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // a semaphore with 2 permits (2 slots)
    var semaphore = new Semaphore(2);

     // Creating and launching 5 threads
    var threads = new Thread[5];
    for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) {
        threads[i] = Thread.ofPlatform().name(String.valueOf(i)).start(() -> {
            String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
            IO.println(heure() + " : le thread " + nom + " attend une place");
             // Requesting a slot: blocks if there are no slots left
            semaphore.acquireUninterruptibly();
            try {
                IO.println(heure() + " : le thread " + nom + " a obtenu une place (places libres : "
                        + semaphore.availablePermits() + ")");
                 // work
                dormir(1000);
            } finally {
                 // release the slot
                IO.println(heure() + " : le thread " + nom + " libère sa place");
                semaphore.release();
            }
        });
    }
     // waiting for threads to finish
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 5: the semaphore has 2 permits: 2 slots;
  • line 14: a thread requests a slot. If one is available, it takes it and continues; otherwise, it is blocked until a slot becomes available;
  • line 17: the number of slots still available;
  • line 23: the thread returns its slot, in a [finally] clause.

Results:

> java Threads15.java
19:15:16.772 : le thread 0 attend une place
19:15:16.773 : le thread 0 a obtenu une place (places libres : 1)
19:15:16.776 : le thread 3 attend une place
19:15:16.776 : le thread 3 a obtenu une place (places libres : 0)
19:15:16.770 : le thread 2 attend une place
19:15:16.768 : le thread 1 attend une place
19:15:16.767 : le thread 4 attend une place
19:15:17.774 : le thread 0 libère sa place
19:15:17.775 : le thread 2 a obtenu une place (places libres : 0)
19:15:17.776 : le thread 3 libère sa place
19:15:17.777 : le thread 1 a obtenu une place (places libres : 0)
19:15:18.775 : le thread 2 libère sa place
19:15:18.777 : le thread 4 a obtenu une place (places libres : 0)
19:15:18.777 : le thread 1 libère sa place
19:15:19.780 : le thread 4 libère sa place

All five threads request a slot; two obtain one immediately, while the other three wait. Each time a thread releases its slot, a waiting thread obtains it. There are never more than two threads in the code section. A single-permit semaphore acts as a lock, as in the program [Threads13.java]. With virtual threads, the semaphore is the natural tool for limiting concurrency: rather than limiting the number of threads, a virtual thread is created for each task, and a semaphore is used to limit the number of tasks simultaneously using the scarce resource.

docs.title: 8.7.7. Write Visibility: The volatile Keyword
docs.text:
Locks aren't just used to make a group of operations indivisible. They address a second, more insidious problem: the visibility of writes. To speed things up, the processor stores values in its registers and caches, and the compiler reorders or eliminates reads and writes on the fly, as we saw with the program [Threads09.java]. As a result, a value written by one thread may not be seen by another thread until later—or perhaps never at all.

The Java Memory Model precisely defines when a write is guaranteed to be visible: when there is a “happens-before” relationship between the write and the read. The main ones are as follows:

  • everything a thread has done before releasing a lock (end of a block [synchronized], [unlock]) is visible to the thread that subsequently acquires that lock;
  • what the calling thread did before [start] is visible to the called thread; what a thread did is visible to the thread that waited for it to finish via [join];
  • a write to a field [volatile] is visible to any subsequent read of that field;
  • the tools in [java.util.concurrent] provide similar guarantees: what a thread did before [release()], [countDown()], or the insertion of an element into a concurrent collection, is visible to the thread that subsequently executes [acquire()], [await()], or retrieves the element.

When none of these relationships exist, the program is said to contain a “data race,” and there are no guarantees. The program [Threads16.java] illustrates this with a common scenario: a flag that instructs a thread to stop.

// Visibility of writes between threads: the `volatile` keyword

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // 1 - the stop flag is a regular field
    Thread t1 = Thread.ofPlatform().name("T1").daemon().start(() -> {
        long tours = 0;
        while (!Drapeaux.arret) {
            tours++;
        }
        IO.println(heure() + " : T1 a vu la demande d'arrêt après %,d tours".formatted(tours));
    });
     // 2 - the stop flag is a volatile field
    Thread t2 = Thread.ofPlatform().name("T2").daemon().start(() -> {
        long tours = 0;
        while (!Drapeaux.arretVolatile) {
            tours++;
        }
        IO.println(heure() + " : T2 a vu la demande d'arrêt après %,d tours".formatted(tours));
    });

     // We let the threads run for one second
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    IO.println(heure() + " : Main demande l'arrêt de T1 et de T2");
    Drapeaux.arret = true;
    Drapeaux.arretVolatile = true;
     // Wait for both threads to finish, for up to 2 seconds each
    for (Thread thread : List.of(t2, t1)) {
        boolean termine = thread.join(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
        IO.println(heure() + " : " + thread.getName() + " terminé : " + termine);
    }
}

// The stop flags, shared by the threads
static class Drapeaux {
     // a regular field: a thread may never see the new value
    static boolean arret;
     // a volatile field: any write is visible to subsequent reads
    static volatile boolean arretVolatile;
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • lines 5–11: The thread T1 runs as long as the ordinary field [Drapeaux.arret] is equal to [false];
  • lines 13–19: The thread T2 does the same with the fields [volatile] and [Drapeaux.arretVolatile];
  • lines 24–25: After one second, the main thread passes both flags to [true];
  • lines 27–30: it waits for each of the two threads for up to 2 seconds. Both threads are daemons, so that the program can terminate even if one of them is still running;
  • lines 34–39: the two flags. The keyword [volatile] (line 38) specifies that any read operation on the field must read from memory, and that any write operation must be performed there immediately.

Results:

> java Threads16.java
19:15:23.635 : Main demande l'arrêt de T1 et de T2
19:15:23.677 : T2 a vu la demande d'arrêt après 315 278 741 tours
19:15:23.714 : T2 terminé : true
19:15:25.729 : T1 terminé : false

The thread T2 saw the stop request immediately. The thread T1, on the other hand, never saw it: it was still running two seconds later and only stopped when the virtual machine shut down. The just-in-time compiler, noting that the loop in lines 7–9 does not modify [arret] and that no synchronization requires it to be re-read, read this field only once, before the loop: the loop thus became an infinite loop. This behavior is reproducible with the HotSpot virtual machine used here, but it is not guaranteed: another virtual machine, or another version, might allow T1 to stop. That is precisely the problem: without an arrive-before relationship, the program’s behavior is undefined.

The keyword [volatile] guarantees visibility, but not atomicity: [valeur++] on a field [volatile] remains a read followed by a write, and two threads can still lose an update. [volatile] is therefore suitable for a flag written by one thread and read by others, but not for a shared counter. To stop a thread, the interruption described above is actually preferable to a flag: it also wakes up a thread that is blocked in a wait.

docs.title: 8.7.8. Atomic Classes
docs.text:
The [java.util.concurrent.atomic] package (Java 5) provides classes that make simple operations on a variable atomic: the operation is executed entirely by the thread, without any other thread being able to observe or modify the variable in the middle of the operation. The previous tools ([synchronized], [ReentrantLock], [Semaphore]) are all designed to make a group of operations atomic, at the cost of blocking other threads. For simple but frequent operations, atomic classes avoid this blocking by using special processor instructions. The main methods of the [AtomicInteger] class are as follows:

MethodRole[int get()], [void set(int v)]Reads and writes the value (using the semantics of a [volatile] field)[int incrementAndGet()], [int decrementAndGet()]increments (decrements) the value by 1 and returns the new value[int getAndIncrement()], [int getAndDecrement()]same as above, but returns the previous value (such as [x++] and [x--])[int addAndGet(int delta)]adds [delta] to the value and returns the new value[int getAndSet(int v)]assigns [v] and returns the old value[boolean compareAndSet(int attendu, int nouveau)]assigns [nouveau] only if the value is [attendu]; returns [true] if the assignment took place[int updateAndGet(IntUnaryOperator f)]replaces the value v with f(v) atomically and returns the new value

The package also offers [AtomicLong], [AtomicBoolean], [AtomicReference<V>] (an atomic reference to an object), and atomic arrays ([AtomicIntegerArray]…). The [LongAdder] class (Java 8) is a counter designed for very frequent updates by many threads: instead of a single variable that all threads compete for, it distributes the increments across multiple cells, which are only added together when the sum is requested ([sum]).

The program [Threads17.java] builds on the experiment from the program [Threads09.java] and compares five ways to increment the shared counter:

// Atomic classes: lock-free operations

// parameters: number of threads, number of increments per thread
int nbThreads;
int nbIncrements;

void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
    nbThreads = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4;
    nbIncrements = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 10_000_000;
    IO.println("%d threads, %,d incrémentations par thread, valeur attendue %,d"
            .formatted(nbThreads, nbIncrements, nbThreads * nbIncrements));

     // five ways to increment a shared counter
    mesurer("sans synchronisation", Compteur::sansSynchronisation, () -> Compteur.valeur);
    mesurer("avec synchronized", Compteur::avecSynchronized, () -> Compteur.valeur);
    mesurer("avec ReentrantLock", Compteur::avecReentrantLock, () -> Compteur.valeur);
    mesurer("avec AtomicInteger", Compteur::avecAtomicInteger, Compteur.atomique::get);
    mesurer("avec LongAdder", Compteur::avecLongAdder, Compteur.additionneur::sum);
}

// launches threads that each execute [incrementer] nbIncrements times, then displays [valeur]
void mesurer(String methode, Runnable incrementer, LongSupplier valeur) throws InterruptedException {
    Compteur.raz();
     // a start signal so that all threads begin at the same time
    var depart = new CountDownLatch(1);
    var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        threads[i] = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
            try {
                depart.await();
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                return;
            }
            for (int j = 0; j < nbIncrements; j++) {
                incrementer.run();
            }
        });
    }
     // Go!
    long debut = System.nanoTime();
    depart.countDown();
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
    long duree = (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000;
    IO.println("%-22s : valeur obtenue %,12d en %5d ms".formatted(methode, valeur.getAsLong(), duree));
}

// the shared resource
static class Compteur {
     // `volatile` guarantees the visibility of writes, not the atomicity of `value++`
    static volatile int valeur;
    private static final Object verrou = new Object();
    private static final ReentrantLock reentrantLock = new ReentrantLock();
    static final AtomicInteger atomique = new AtomicInteger();
    static final LongAdder additionneur = new LongAdder();

     // resetting counters
    static void raz() {
        valeur = 0;
        atomique.set(0);
        additionneur.reset();
    }

     // read, increment, write: non-atomic
    static void sansSynchronisation() {
        valeur++;
    }

     // critical section protected by `synchronized`
    static void avecSynchronized() {
        synchronized (verrou) {
            valeur++;
        }
    }

     // critical section protected by a ReentrantLock
    static void avecReentrantLock() {
        reentrantLock.lock();
        try {
            valeur++;
        } finally {
            reentrantLock.unlock();
        }
    }

     // atomic increment, without a lock
    static void avecAtomicInteger() {
        atomique.incrementAndGet();
    }

     // increment of a distributed adder, lock-free
    static void avecLongAdder() {
        additionneur.increment();
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 4–5: In a compact source file, fields can be declared outside any class; these are fields of the implicit class. They are used by the instance methods [main] and [mesurer];
  • lines 14–18: The method [mesurer] is called with five different increment methods, passed as [Runnable], and with a function that returns the resulting value, of type [LongSupplier] (a functional interface of type [long getAsLong()]). The method references [Compteur.atomique::get] and [Compteur.additionneur::sum] refer to methods of two specific objects;
  • lines 22–47: the method [mesurer] launches [nbThreads] threads, each of which calls the received method [nbIncrements] times, and measures the total time. The format [%,12d] right-aligns the value to 12 characters, with a thousands separator;
  • lines 25, 30, and 41: the threads all wait behind a [CountDownLatch], which is opened once they are all launched. They thus begin their work at the same time, making concurrent accesses much more likely than with threads launched one after another;
  • line 52: the counter is [volatile]. This prevents the compiler from performing on-the-fly the optimization we observed with [Threads09.java]: each increment actually reads from and writes to memory;
  • line 67: the unsynchronized increment;
  • lines 72–74 and 79–84: the increment within a critical section protected by [synchronized] or by a [ReentrantLock];
  • line 89: atomic increment;
  • line 94: incrementing a [LongAdder].

Results:

> java Threads17.java
4 threads, 10 000 000 incrémentations par thread, valeur attendue 40 000 000
sans synchronisation   : valeur obtenue   22 447 283 en   729 ms
avec synchronized      : valeur obtenue   40 000 000 en  3789 ms
avec ReentrantLock     : valeur obtenue   40 000 000 en  1145 ms
avec AtomicInteger     : valeur obtenue   40 000 000 en   739 ms
avec LongAdder         : valeur obtenue   40 000 000 en   293 ms
  • Without synchronization, the result is incorrect once again: the [volatile] field did not make [valeur++] atomic;
  • the other four methods return the correct result;
  • Atomic classes are significantly faster than locks in this execution. Locks are costly here because four threads are constantly competing for them over a tiny operation. The measured execution times depend heavily on the machine and its load: only their order of magnitude is significant. [LongAdder] was the fastest: its threads interfere with each other less than those competing for the single variable in a [AtomicInteger], and its performance advantage increases with the number of processors.

The [compareAndSet] method (“CAS”) is the building block of “lock-free” algorithms: we read the value, calculate the new one, and then write it only if the variable has not changed in the meantime; otherwise, we start over. This is what [updateAndGet] does, and the concurrent collections presented later make extensive use of it.

docs.title: 8.8. Concurrent Access to Multiple Shared Resources
8.8.1. Deadlock
docs.text:
In our previous examples, a single resource was shared among the different threads. The situation becomes more complicated if there are multiple resources and they are dependent on one another. In particular, a deadlock can occur: two threads are waiting for each other. Consider the following actions, which occur sequentially:

  • a thread T1 acquires the lock V1 to access a shared resource R1;
  • a thread T2 acquires the lock V2 to access a shared resource R2;
  • Thread T1 requests lock V2. It is blocked;
  • the thread T2 requests the lock V1. It is blocked.

The threads T1 and T2 are waiting for each other indefinitely. Several solutions are possible:

  • request both resources at the same time using a single lock. This isn’t always possible if it results in a long lock on a costly resource;
  • always acquire locks in the same order: if all threads acquire V1 before V2, deadlock is impossible. This is the most commonly used rule;
  • A thread holding V1 that cannot acquire V2 releases V1 to avoid deadlock.

The program [Threads18.java] causes a deadlock and implements the last solution, using the method [tryLock] from [ReentrantLock]:

// deadlock: two threads acquire two locks in a different order

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // the locks on the two shared resources
    var verrouR1 = new ReentrantLock();
    var verrouR2 = new ReentrantLock();

     // T1 acquires R1 and then requests R2; it aborts after 2 seconds
    var t1 = new Thread(() -> travailler(verrouR1, "R1", verrouR2, "R2", Duration.ofSeconds(2)), "T1");
     // T2 acquires R2 and then requests R1; it waits up to 5 seconds
    var t2 = new Thread(() -> travailler(verrouR2, "R2", verrouR1, "R1", Duration.ofSeconds(5)), "T2");
    t1.start();
    t2.start();
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    IO.println("Fin de Main");
}

// acquires the first resource, then attempts to acquire the second during [delai]
static void travailler(Lock premier, String nomPremier, Lock second, String nomSecond, Duration delai) {
    String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
    premier.lock();
    try {
        IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " a obtenu " + nomPremier);
         // allows the other thread time to acquire its first resource
        Thread.sleep(500);
        IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " demande " + nomSecond);
         // requests with a maximum wait time, instead of a lock() that would wait indefinitely
        if (second.tryLock(delai.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
            try {
                IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " a obtenu " + nomSecond
                        + " et travaille avec " + nomPremier + " et " + nomSecond);
            } finally {
                second.unlock();
            }
        } else {
            IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " n'a pas obtenu " + nomSecond + " en " + delai.toSeconds()
                    + " s : il relâche " + nomPremier + " et abandonne");
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    } finally {
        premier.unlock();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • lines 5–6: the locks on the two resources. These are local variables here, captured by the lambdas on lines 9 and 11;
  • Line 9: The thread T1 acquires R1 and then requests R2; it waits for a maximum of 2 seconds;
  • line 11: the thread T2 acquires R2 and then requests R1—that is, in reverse order; it waits for at most 5 seconds;
  • line 20: the method [travailler] acquires locks of the type defined by the interface [Lock], which is implemented by [ReentrantLock];
  • line 22: the thread acquires its first resource. The [finally] clause on line 42 will release it in any case;
  • line 26: it waits for half a second, which gives the other thread time to acquire its own first resource: deadlock is then certain;
  • line 29: instead of a *[lock], which would wait indefinitely, the thread requests the second lock with a maximum wait time. [tryLock] returns [true] if the lock was obtained, and [false] if the timeout expired. The timeout is expressed as a number and a unit ([TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS]); the method [toMillis()] converts the duration [delai]* to milliseconds;
  • line 34: a lock acquired by [tryLock] must be released by [unlock], within a [finally] clause;
  • lines 36–39: if the second lock could not be acquired, the thread aborts. Upon exiting the method, it releases its first resource (line 43);
  • lines 40–41: [sleep] and [tryLock] with a timeout can start [InterruptedException].

Results:

> java Threads18.java
19:15:36.043 : T1 a obtenu R1
19:15:36.033 : T2 a obtenu R2
19:15:36.553 : T2 demande R1
19:15:36.554 : T1 demande R2
19:15:38.554 : T1 n'a pas obtenu R2 en 2 s : il relâche R1 et abandonne
19:15:38.558 : T2 a obtenu R1 et travaille avec R2 et R1
Fin de Main

Each of the two threads obtained its first resource and then requested the second: they are in a deadlock. After 2 seconds, T1 gives up and releases R1; T2, which was still waiting, immediately obtains R1 and can do its work. Without a timeout, the program would never have finished. This sequence of events is reproducible; only the order of lines 2 and 3 and that of lines 4 and 5 can change. It would not be possible to write this program using [synchronized] blocks, since their wait time cannot be limited.

When a Java program appears to be frozen, the [jcmd <pid> Thread.print] command from JDK displays the call stack for each of its threads ([pid] is the process ID, which is returned by the [jcmd] command without any parameters); it detects deadlocks between locks and reports them with the message “Found one Java-level deadlock,” followed by the threads and locks involved.

docs.title: 8.8.2. An example: readers and writers
docs.text:
Consider the following example:

  • we have an array into which some threads write data (the writers) and others read it (the readers);
  • the writers are equal to one another but exclusive: only one writer at a time can write data to the array;
  • readers are equal to one another but exclusive: only one reader at a time can read the data stored in the array;
  • a reader can only read data from the array when a writer has placed some there, and a writer can only place new data in the array when the data already there has been read by a reader.

There are two types of shared resources:

  • the writable table: only one writer at a time may access it;
  • the read-only table: only one reader at a time may access it.

and an order for using these resources:

  • a reader must always follow a writer;
  • a writer must always follow a reader, except the first time.

Access to these two resources can be controlled using two barriers of type [Semaphore]:

  • The [peutEcrire] barrier controls writers’ access to the array;
  • the barrier [peutLire] controls readers’ access to the array;
  • The [peutEcrire] barrier is created open (one permit), allowing the first writer to pass and blocking all others;
  • The [peutLire] barrier is created in the closed state (no permission), blocking all readers;
  • When a writer has finished their work, they open barrier [peutLire] to let a reader in;
  • when a reader has finished their work, they open the barrier [peutEcrire] to let a writer in.

Here we see the benefit of a barrier that does not belong to any thread: the barrier [peutLire] is closed by a reader (who takes the permit) and opened by a writer (who returns it). This is impossible with a lock, which can only be released by the thread that holds it. The program [Threads19.java] illustrating this synchronization is as follows:

// Readers and writers synchronized by two semaphores

void main() {
     // the number of threads of each type
    final int nbThreads = 2;

     // creation and launch of reader threads
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        new Thread(Tableau::lire, "L" + i).start();
    }
     // creation and launch of writer threads
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        new Thread(Tableau::ecrire, "E" + i).start();
    }
     // End of the task: the other threads continue their work
    IO.println("Fin de Main...");
}

// the shared resource and its synchronization
static class Tableau {
     // the array shared between readers and writers
    private static final int[] data = new int[3];
     // indicates that the contents of `data` can be read: initially closed (no permission)
    private static final Semaphore peutLire = new Semaphore(0);
     // indicates that you can write to `data`: open by default (one permission)
    private static final Semaphore peutEcrire = new Semaphore(1);

     // read the table's contents
    static void lire() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("Méthode [lire] démarrée par le thread " + nom);
         // Waiting for read permission
        peutLire.acquireUninterruptibly();
         // reading the array
        for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
             // Waiting for 0.5 s: the thread yields the CPU
            dormir(500);
            IO.println(heure() + " : le lecteur " + nom + " a lu le nombre " + data[i]);
        }
         // A writer is granted permission
        peutEcrire.release();
        IO.println("Méthode [lire] terminée par le thread " + nom);
    }

     // writing to the array
    static void ecrire() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("Méthode [ecrire] démarrée par le thread " + nom);
         // waiting for write permission
        peutEcrire.acquireUninterruptibly();
         // writing to the array
        for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
             // Waiting for 0.5 s
            dormir(500);
             // ThreadLocalRandom: a random number generator specific to each thread
            data[i] = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(0, 1000);
            IO.println(heure() + " : l'écrivain " + nom + " a écrit le nombre " + data[i]);
        }
         // allowing a reader
        peutLire.release();
        IO.println("Méthode [ecrire] terminée par le thread " + nom);
    }
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • lines 8–14: creation and launch of two reader threads, followed by two writer threads. No references are kept to the threads: the main thread does not wait for them;
  • line 16: the main thread terminates immediately. The process continues until all four threads—which are not daemons—have finished;
  • line 22: the array [data] is the shared resource between the reader and writer threads;
  • line 24: The barrier [peutLire] notifies the readers that they can read the array. It is opened by the writer who has filled the array. It is created in a closed state: a writer must first fill the array;
  • line 26: The barrier [peutEcrire] notifies writers that they can write to the array. It is opened by the reader who has read the entire array. It is created open: the array is writable from the start;
  • line 33: a reader waits for a writer to signal that the array has been filled. When this signal arrives, only one of the waiting readers proceeds;
  • lines 35–39: the array is read, with a half-second pause at each element to force the thread to yield the CPU;
  • line 41: the reader notifies the writers that the array has been read and can be filled again;
  • the method [ecrire] is symmetric to the method [lire];
  • line 56: the written numbers are randomly generated. The [ThreadLocalRandom.current()] method (Java 7) returns a random number generator specific to the current thread: threads do not compete for a single generator. The [nextInt(0, 1000)] method returns an integer from the interval [0, 1000[;
  • the array [data] is not protected by any lock. However, there is no data race: the writer’s writes precede its [peutLire.release()] call, which precedes (earlier-than relation) the reader’s [peutLire.acquireUninterruptibly()] call, and thus its reads.

Results:

> java Threads19.java
Méthode [lire] démarrée par le thread L0
Méthode [lire] démarrée par le thread L1
Méthode [ecrire] démarrée par le thread E0
Fin de Main...
Méthode [ecrire] démarrée par le thread E1
19:15:41.498 : l'écrivain E0 a écrit le nombre 408
19:15:42.004 : l'écrivain E0 a écrit le nombre 58
19:15:42.505 : l'écrivain E0 a écrit le nombre 490
Méthode [ecrire] terminée par le thread E0
19:15:43.006 : le lecteur L0 a lu le nombre 408
19:15:43.507 : le lecteur L0 a lu le nombre 58
19:15:44.016 : le lecteur L0 a lu le nombre 490
Méthode [lire] terminée par le thread L0
19:15:44.520 : l'écrivain E1 a écrit le nombre 310
19:15:45.020 : l'écrivain E1 a écrit le nombre 964
19:15:45.520 : l'écrivain E1 a écrit le nombre 830
Méthode [ecrire] terminée par le thread E1
19:15:46.021 : le lecteur L1 a lu le nombre 310
19:15:46.521 : le lecteur L1 a lu le nombre 964
19:15:47.022 : le lecteur L1 a lu le nombre 830
Méthode [lire] terminée par le thread L1

The following points are worth noting:

  • there is only one reader at a time, although it loses the CPU in the critical section [lire];
  • there is only one writer at a time, although it loses the processor in the critical section [ecrire];
  • a reader reads only when there is something to read in the array;
  • a writer writes only when the array has been fully read;
  • On the other hand, we have no control over the order in which they appear: there was no reason why writer E0 should come before writer E1, nor why reader L0 should come before reader L1. A different execution may result in a different order.

docs.title: 8.8.3. The wait and notifyAll methods
docs.text:
In the previous example, when the writers are blocked on the instruction [peutEcrire.acquireUninterruptibly()], one of them—any one—is unblocked by the operation [peutEcrire.release()]. If you want to open the barrier for a specific writer, things become more complicated.

Consider the analogy of a public service office with service counters. When a customer arrives, they take a numbered ticket from the dispenser and then go sit down. Customers are called by their number over a loudspeaker. While waiting, the customer can do whatever they want: they can read or doze off. They are woken up every time the loudspeaker announces a number. If it’s their number, the customer gets up and goes to the counter; otherwise, they go back to what they were doing. We can operate in a similar way with threads. Let’s take the example of writers:

At the counterWith threadsseveral writers are waiting for the same countertheir threads are blockedthe counter becomes available and the next writer’s number is calledthe thread that was reading from the array notifies the writers that the array is available. Either that thread or another thread has determined which writer should proceedEach writer checks its number; only the one with the called number proceeds to the counter; the others return to the waiting queueEach thread checks to see if it is the one selected. If so, it passes through the barrier; otherwise, it returns to the waiting queue

Java allows you to implement this scenario using methods available to every object, since they are defined in the [Object] class:

MethodRole[void wait()]returns the object’s monitor and blocks the thread until another thread signals a change via [notify] or [notifyAll]; the thread must then reclaim the monitor before continuing. The wait can be interrupted ([InterruptedException])[void wait(long ms)]same as above, with a maximum wait time[void notify()]wakes up one of the threads blocked by [wait] on this object[void notifyAll()]wakes up all threads blocked by [wait] on this object

We will now describe a standard pattern—presented notably in the book by Brian Goetz et al., [Java Concurrency in Practice]—that can resolve barrier problems with entry conditions.

Threads that share a resource (the counter) access it via an object we’ll call a token: it’s a simple object ([new Object()]) whose monitor is used. To cross the barrier leading to the counter, you must have the token, and there is only one. The threads must therefore pass the token back and forth.
