To go to the counter, a thread first requests the token using a block [synchronized (jeton)]. If it obtains the token, it checks whether it meets the condition to proceed to the counter in a loop [while (!jeSuisCeluiQuiEstAttendu) { jeton.wait(); }], then proceeds to the counter, still within the block [synchronized]. If the thread is not the one expected at the counter, it yields its turn by returning the token via [jeton.wait()] and enters the blocked state. It will be woken up when another thread signals a change in the access condition; it will then retrieve the token and check the condition again. This is why the test is a loop ([while]) rather than a simple [if]. There is a second reason, specific to Java: the specification allows for “spurious wakeups,” where [wait] terminates without any thread having called [notify]; the loop renders these harmless. The operation [jeton.wait()] can only be performed by a thread that holds the token monitor; otherwise, a [IllegalMonitorStateException] exception is thrown. In this scheme, the token is released only after the transaction is completed.

The thread that modifies the condition for accessing the counter must also hold the token and notify the waiting threads: within a [synchronized (jeton)] block, it modifies the condition for accessing the counter, then wakes up the waiting threads using [jeton.notifyAll()].

Waking up the threads means that the waiting threads become candidates for the token; they do not receive it immediately. The token is only available at the end of the block [synchronized]. All the awakened threads will then receive the token in turn, in an indeterminate order, which gives them the opportunity to check the access condition again. The first one to satisfy the condition keeps the token and proceeds to the queue.

With this information, we can rewrite the reader/writer application by specifying the order in which readers and writers proceed to their respective counters ([Threads20.java]):

// readers and writers pass through the queue in a specified order: wait / notifyAll

void main() {
     // the number of threads of each type
    final int nbThreads = 3;

     // the order in which readers pass through: the reverse of the order of creation
    Tableau.ordreLecture = IntStream.range(0, nbThreads).mapToObj(i -> "L" + (nbThreads - 1 - i)).toList();
     // the order in which writers pass through: the order of creation
    Tableau.ordreEcriture = IntStream.range(0, nbThreads).mapToObj(i -> "E" + i).toList();
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        IO.println("Le lecteur " + Tableau.ordreLecture.get(i) + " est en position " + i
                + ", l'écrivain " + Tableau.ordreEcriture.get(i) + " est en position " + i);
    }

     // creation and launch of reader threads, followed by writer threads
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        new Thread(Tableau::lire, "L" + i).start();
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++) {
        new Thread(Tableau::ecrire, "E" + i).start();
    }

     // write permission
    Tableau.autoriserEcriture();
     // end of thread
    IO.println("Fin de Main...");
}

// The shared resource and its synchronization
static class Tableau {
     // The array shared between readers and writers
    private static final int[] data = new int[3];
     // Access tokens for read and write counters
    private static final Object peutLire = new Object();
    private static final Object peutEcrire = new Object();
     // Access conditions for the channels
    private static boolean lectureAutorisee = false;
    private static boolean ecritureAutorisee = false;
    private static int lecteurSuivant = 0;
    private static int ecrivainSuivant = 0;
     // the order of readers and writers
    static List<String> ordreLecture = List.of();
    static List<String> ordreEcriture = List.of();

     // opens the write port
    static void autoriserEcriture() {
        synchronized (peutEcrire) {
            ecritureAutorisee = true;
             // wakes up all writers waiting for a token
            peutEcrire.notifyAll();
        }
    }

     // read the contents of the array
    static void lire() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("Méthode [lire] démarrée par le thread " + nom);
         // request a token from the reading counter
        synchronized (peutLire) {
            try {
                 // as long as it’s not our turn, return the token and wait
                while (!lectureAutorisee || !ordreLecture.get(lecteurSuivant).equals(nom)) {
                    peutLire.wait();
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                return;
            }
             // At the counter: read the table
            for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
                dormir(500);
                IO.println(heure() + " : le lecteur " + nom + " a lu le nombre " + data[i]);
            }
             // Next reader
            lectureAutorisee = false;
            lecteurSuivant++;
             // Notify the writers that they can write
            synchronized (peutEcrire) {
                ecritureAutorisee = true;
                peutEcrire.notifyAll();
            }
            IO.println("Méthode [lire] terminée par le thread " + nom);
        }
    }

     // Write on the board
    static void ecrire() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("Méthode [ecrire] démarrée par le thread " + nom);
         // ask for the token from the writing counter
        synchronized (peutEcrire) {
            try {
                 // until it’s our turn, we return the token and wait
                while (!ecritureAutorisee || !ordreEcriture.get(ecrivainSuivant).equals(nom)) {
                    peutEcrire.wait();
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                return;
            }
             // turn at the counter: write to the array
            for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
                dormir(500);
                data[i] = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(0, 1000);
                IO.println(heure() + " : l'écrivain " + nom + " a écrit le nombre " + data[i]);
            }
             // Next writer
            ecritureAutorisee = false;
            ecrivainSuivant++;
             // Notify readers that they can read
            synchronized (peutLire) {
                lectureAutorisee = true;
                peutLire.notifyAll();
            }
            IO.println("Méthode [ecrire] terminée par le thread " + nom);
        }
    }
}

Access to the read counter is determined by the following:

  • line 35: the token [peutLire];
  • line 38: the Boolean value [lectureAutorisee];
  • Line 43: The sorted list of readers' names. Readers proceed to the reading station in the order listed here;
  • line 40: [lecteurSuivant] is the index in this list of the next reader authorized to proceed to the counter.

Access to the write counter is similarly controlled by the token [peutEcrire], the boolean [ecritureAutorisee], the list [ordreEcriture], and the index [ecrivainSuivant].

The main program:

  • lines 8–10: readers will proceed to the counter in reverse order of their creation (L2, L1, L0), and writers in the order they were created (E0, E1, E2). The lists are constructed using a pipeline: [IntStream.range(0, nbThreads)] generates the integers 0, 1, 2; [mapToObj] converts each of them into a thread name; and [toList()] (Java 16) collects the names into a read-only list;
  • Lines 17–22: creation and launch of the readers, followed by the writers. They will all be blocked, since neither reading nor writing is permitted;
  • line 25: writing is enabled, and the writers are notified that something has changed (method [autoriserEcriture], lines 47–53).

The [lire] method:

  • lines 60–83: the entire process at the reading station is controlled by the [synchronized] block on token [peutLire]. The reader who obtains it retains it throughout their time at the station;
  • lines 63–65: A reader who has acquired the token returns it if reading is not authorized or if it is not their turn. Names are compared by [equals];
  • lines 66–68: If the thread is interrupted while waiting, it aborts;
  • lines 70–73: processing at the counter (reading the table);
  • lines 75–76: the reader changes the access conditions for the read queue. It still holds the read token, and these changes prevent any reader from proceeding;
  • lines 78–81: the reader changes the access conditions for the write queue and notifies all waiting writers that something has changed. To do this, it takes the token [peutEcrire]: here we see that the thread holds two tokens at the same time. The writers do the same in reverse order (they hold [peutEcrire] and request [peutLire]), which is the deadlock situation described above. However, there is no risk here: a thread requests the second token only at the end of its visit to the counter; the two counters are never occupied at the same time; and the other threads hold a token only long enough to check the access condition, without requesting the other token.

The method [ecrire] is symmetric to the method [lire]. Note the use of [notifyAll] rather than [notify], which wakes up only a single thread: if that thread were not the expected writer, it would go back to sleep, and the expected writer might never be woken up. With an access condition that specifies a particular thread, you must use [notifyAll].

docs.title: 8.8.4. Conditions: The Condition Interface
docs.text:
The methods [wait] and [notifyAll] are associated with an object’s monitor, and thus with the blocks [synchronized]. For a lock [ReentrantLock], the equivalent is the interface [java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition]: A [Condition] object is created by the lock’s [newCondition()] method and provides the methods [await()] (the equivalent of [wait]), [await(long délai, TimeUnit unité)], [signal()] (the equivalent of [notify]), and [signalAll()] (the equivalent of [notifyAll]). Their usage follows the same rules: the thread must hold the lock, and the access condition is tested within a [while] loop.

The key advantage is that a single lock can have multiple conditions—that is, multiple distinct queues. In our problem, a single lock can protect both counters, with one condition for readers and one for writers: a reader who finishes wakes up the writers—and only the writers. There are no longer two tokens, so there is no longer any lock nesting to monitor. The program [Threads21.java] has the same main program as [Threads20.java]; its class [Tableau] is as follows:

// the shared resource and its synchronization
static class Tableau {
     // the array shared between readers and writers
    private static final int[] data = new int[3];
     // a single lock for both queues
    private static final ReentrantLock verrou = new ReentrantLock();
     // two conditions associated with this lock: two separate queues
    private static final Condition peutLire = verrou.newCondition();
    private static final Condition peutEcrire = verrou.newCondition();
     // the conditions for accessing the channels
    private static boolean lectureAutorisee = false;
    private static boolean ecritureAutorisee = false;
    private static int lecteurSuivant = 0;
    private static int ecrivainSuivant = 0;
     // the order in which readers and writers are served
    static List<String> ordreLecture = List.of();
    static List<String> ordreEcriture = List.of();

     // opens the write port
    static void autoriserEcriture() {
        verrou.lock();
        try {
            ecritureAutorisee = true;
             // wakes up all writers, and only them
            peutEcrire.signalAll();
        } finally {
            verrou.unlock();
        }
    }

     // read the contents of the table
    static void lire() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("Méthode [lire] démarrée par le thread " + nom);
        verrou.lock();
        try {
             // Until it’s our turn, return the lock and wait for a signal
            while (!lectureAutorisee || !ordreLecture.get(lecteurSuivant).equals(nom)) {
                peutLire.await();
            }
             // Go to the counter: read the table
            for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
                dormir(500);
                IO.println(heure() + " : le lecteur " + nom + " a lu le nombre " + data[i]);
            }
             // next reader
            lectureAutorisee = false;
            lecteurSuivant++;
             // We notify the writers that they can write
            ecritureAutorisee = true;
            peutEcrire.signalAll();
            IO.println("Méthode [lire] terminée par le thread " + nom);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        } finally {
            verrou.unlock();
        }
    }

     // Write on the board
    static void ecrire() {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println("Méthode [ecrire] démarrée par le thread " + nom);
        verrou.lock();
        try {
             // Until it’s our turn, return the lock and wait for a signal
            while (!ecritureAutorisee || !ordreEcriture.get(ecrivainSuivant).equals(nom)) {
                peutEcrire.await();
            }
             // Go to the counter: write to the table
            for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
                dormir(500);
                data[i] = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(0, 1000);
                IO.println(heure() + " : l'écrivain " + nom + " a écrit le nombre " + data[i]);
            }
             // next writer
            ecritureAutorisee = false;
            ecrivainSuivant++;
             // notify readers that they can read
            lectureAutorisee = true;
            peutLire.signalAll();
            IO.println("Méthode [ecrire] terminée par le thread " + nom);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        } finally {
            verrou.unlock();
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 35: a single, non-fair lock;
  • lines 37–38: two conditions created from this lock;
  • lines 49–58: to open the write channel, the lock is acquired, the access condition is modified, and the writers are woken up by [peutEcrire.signalAll()];
  • lines 64–86: switching to the read channel is done while holding the lock, according to the sequence [lock] / [try] / [finally] / [unlock];
  • lines 67–69: until it is its turn, the reader waits on the condition [peutLire]. The method [await] releases the lock while waiting and reacquires it before yielding control;
  • lines 79–80: the reader authorizes the write and wakes up the writers. It already holds the lock: it does not need to acquire a second token;
  • lines 82–83: if the thread is interrupted while waiting, it resets its interruption flag and terminates; the [finally] clause releases the lock.

docs.title: 8.8.5. Multiple Simultaneous Readers: ReadWriteLock
docs.text:
In the previous examples, readers were exclusive. In many applications, this is unnecessarily restrictive: multiple threads can read data at the same time that no one is modifying. Only writes must be exclusive: while a writer is modifying the data, neither a reader nor any other writer should be able to access it. This is the classic read-write problem, which is solved by the [java.util.concurrent.locks.ReadWriteLock] interface. A [ReadWriteLock] object provides two linked locks:

  • [readLock()]: the read lock, which can be held by multiple threads at the same time, as long as no thread holds the write lock;
  • [writeLock()]: the write lock, which is exclusive.

The program [Threads22.java] is as follows:

// Multiple simultaneous readers, a single writer: ReadWriteLock

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    var catalogue = new Catalogue();
    var threads = new ArrayList<Thread>();
     // Three readers check the keyboard price twice
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        threads.add(Thread.ofPlatform().name("L" + i).start(() -> {
            catalogue.lire("clavier");
            catalogue.lire("clavier");
        }));
    }
     // a writer, started 0.5 seconds later, changes that price
    Thread.sleep(500);
    threads.add(Thread.ofPlatform().name("E").start(() -> catalogue.modifier("clavier", 25)));
     // waiting for all threads to finish
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
}

// the shared resource: a price catalog
static class Catalogue {
    private final Map<String, Integer> prix = new HashMap<>(Map.of("clavier", 20, "souris", 10));
     // one lock for readers, one lock for writers
    private final ReadWriteLock verrou = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

     // Multiple threads can hold the read lock at the same time
    int lire(String article) {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        verrou.readLock().lock();
        try {
            IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " commence à lire le prix de " + article);
             // long read
            dormir(1000);
            int p = prix.get(article);
            IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " a lu le prix de " + article + " : " + p);
            return p;
        } finally {
            verrou.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

     // The write lock is exclusive: no readers or other writers
    void modifier(String article, int nouveauPrix) {
        String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " demande le verrou d'écriture");
        verrou.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " commence à modifier le prix de " + article);
             // Long write
            dormir(1000);
            prix.put(article, nouveauPrix);
            IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " a fixé le prix de " + article + " à " + nouveauPrix);
        } finally {
            verrou.writeLock().unlock();
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 23–59: the shared resource is a price catalog, stored in a dictionary [HashMap] (line 24);
  • line 26: the [ReentrantReadWriteLock] implementation of the [ReadWriteLock] interface;
  • lines 29–42: The method [lire] acquires a read lock for a read operation that lasts one second;
  • lines 45–58: the [modifier] method acquires the write lock during a modification that lasts one second;
  • lines 7–12: Three readers read the price from the keyboard twice in a row;
  • lines 14–15: a writer, started half a second later, modifies this price.

19:16:18.009 : L1 commence à lire le prix de clavier

19:16:19.010 : L1 a lu le prix de clavier : 25
19:16:19.011 : L0 a lu le prix de clavier : 25
  • the three readers read at the same time (lines 2–4 and 6–8): with a standard lock, the first series of reads would have taken three seconds instead of one;
  • the writer, who arrived while the reads were in progress, waited for them to finish. He then changed the price on his own;
  • the second set of reads, which began after the writer arrived, waited for the modification to finish and then read the new price. The lock [ReentrantReadWriteLock] thus prevents a continuous stream of readers from indefinitely blocking a writer from writing: a reader who arrives while a writer is waiting goes after the writer. This sequence is reproducible.

A read/write lock is only useful if reads are numerous and sufficiently long. For very short reads, the [StampedLock] class (Java 8) offers an “optimistic” read—without a lock—that is validated afterward. And for a collection that is read very often but modified rarely, the concurrent collections described in the following paragraph are often the best solution.

docs.title: 8.9. Concurrent Collections
docs.text:
The previous examples protected very simple shared data (a counter, an array, a small dictionary). When threads share a collection (list, dictionary, queue), one could protect each access with a lock. However, standard collections ([ArrayList], [HashMap], [ArrayDeque]) are not designed to be modified by multiple threads simultaneously: unprotected use can result in the loss of elements, trigger unexpected exceptions ([ConcurrentModificationException]), or even corrupt the collection’s internal structure. The methods [Collections.synchronizedList(…)], [Collections.synchronizedMap(…)]… wrap a regular collection in an object whose every method is [synchronized]: this is safe, but all threads compete for a single lock, and iterating over the collection still must be protected manually. Since Java 5, the [java.util.concurrent] package has offered collections designed to be shared among threads without an explicit lock:

CollectionRole[ConcurrentHashMap<K,V>]A dictionary whose operations, including conditional updates ([merge], [compute], [putIfAbsent]…), are safe and atomic. Multiple threads can read and modify it at the same time[ConcurrentSkipListMap<K,V>]a dictionary sorted by key[CopyOnWriteArrayList<E>]a list that copies its internal array with every modification: reads and traversals, which are very fast, are never affected by modifications. It is suitable for lists that are read frequently and modified rarely (playlists, for example)[ConcurrentLinkedQueue<E>], [ConcurrentLinkedDeque<E>]A queue (first-in, first-out), a double-ended queue[BlockingQueue<E>]a queue interface that blocks the consumer when the queue is empty and, if its capacity is limited, blocks the producer when it is full. Implementations: [ArrayBlockingQueue], [LinkedBlockingQueue], [PriorityBlockingQueue], [SynchronousQueue]…

docs.title: 8.9.1. ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList
docs.text:
In the program [Threads23.java], four threads generate random numbers and count the number of times each number appears in a shared dictionary:

// Concurrent collections: ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // the shared dictionary: code -> number of draws
    var tirages = new ConcurrentHashMap<Integer, Integer>();
     // the shared list of thread reports
    var comptesRendus = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<String>();

     // 4 threads each generate 100,000 random digits
    final int nbTirages = 100_000;
    var threads = new Thread[4];
    for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) {
        threads[i] = Thread.ofPlatform().name("T" + i).start(() -> {
            for (int j = 0; j < nbTirages; j++) {
                int chiffre = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(0, 10);
                 // Add a key with the value 1 or perform an atomic update of the existing value
                tirages.merge(chiffre, 1, Integer::sum);
            }
             // report added to the list
            comptesRendus.add("le thread %s a terminé ses %,d tirages"
                    .formatted(Thread.currentThread().getName(), nbTirages));
        });
    }
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }

     // The reports, in the order they were received
    for (String compteRendu : comptesRendus) {
        IO.println(compteRendu);
    }
     // draw results, in key order
    new TreeMap<>(tirages).forEach((chiffre, nombre) ->
            IO.println("chiffre %d : %,6d tirages".formatted(chiffre, nombre)));
    int total = tirages.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
    IO.println("total : %,d tirages (attendu : %,d)".formatted(total, threads.length * nbTirages));
     // computeIfAbsent: returns the value associated with the key, after calculating and adding it if necessary
    IO.println("computeIfAbsent(10, …) = " + tirages.computeIfAbsent(10, cle -> 0)
            + ", nombre de clés : " + tirages.size());
}

Comments:

  • line 5: the shared dictionary associates each digit with its number of occurrences;
  • line 7: a list where each thread stores a report at the end of its work;
  • line 17: the method [merge(clé, valeur, fonction)] adds the key [chiffre] with the value 1 if it does not exist, and otherwise replaces its value v with [fonction(v, 1)], which is the sum [Integer::sum] in this case. In a [ConcurrentHashMap], the operation is atomic. We could not write [tirages.put(chiffre, tirages.get(chiffre) + 1)]: this expression reads the value and then writes the new one, in two operations, and two threads could lose an update as in the example [Threads09.java];
  • line 20: each thread adds its report to the list;
  • lines 29–31: the main thread iterates over the list. The iteration over a [CopyOnWriteArrayList] is performed on a snapshot of the internal array: it never calls [ConcurrentModificationException], even if other threads modify the list during the iteration;
  • lines 33–34: the dictionary is copied into a sorted dictionary [TreeMap] to display the numbers in order; the method [forEach] receives each key/value pair;
  • line 35: the sum of the values, calculated by a stream;
  • line 38: the method ***[computeIfAbsent(clé, fonction)] returns the value associated with the key, after calculating it using the function and adding it if the key did not exist. As with [merge]*, the check and the addition form a single atomic operation: a [containsKey] check followed by a [put] would not be safe, since another thread could add the key in between.

docs.title: 8.9.2. Producer and consumers: BlockingQueue
docs.text:
The problem of readers and writers is a variation on the classic producer-consumer problem: some threads produce data that other threads consume. The [BlockingQueue<E>] interface solves this without any explicit synchronization tools:

  • [put(élément)] adds an element to the queue. If the queue has a limited capacity and is full, the producer is blocked until a spot becomes available;
  • [take()] removes the element at the head of the queue. If the queue is empty, the consumer is blocked until an element arrives;
  • [offer(élément, délai, unité)] and [poll(délai, unité)] do the same, with a maximum wait time; [offer(élément)] and [poll()], which have no timeout, never block: they return [false] or [null] in case of failure.

The queue is unaware that production has ended. A classic technique involves placing a special value—known in the English-speaking world as a “poison pill”—into the queue at the end of production: the consumer that retrieves it knows it must stop. Another technique is to interrupt the consumers, since [take] is interruptible. The program [Threads24.java] is as follows:

// producer/consumers with a blocking queue BlockingQueue

// the value that signals the end of production (“poison pill”)
static final int FIN = -1;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // a queue of at most 3 elements
    BlockingQueue<Integer> file = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(3);
    final int nbConsommateurs = 2;

     // the producer adds 8 numbers and then signals that they are finished
    var producteur = new Thread(() -> {
        try {
            for (int i = 1; i <= 8; i++) {
                 // blocks if the queue is full
                file.put(i);
                IO.println(heure() + " : P a déposé " + i
                        + " (éléments en attente : " + file.size() + ")");
                Thread.sleep(100);
            }
             // an end marker per consumer
            for (int i = 0; i < nbConsommateurs; i++) {
                file.put(FIN);
            }
            IO.println(heure() + " : P a terminé");
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }, "P");

     // Two consumers take the numbers up to the end marker
    var consommateurs = new Thread[nbConsommateurs];
    for (int i = 0; i < consommateurs.length; i++) {
        consommateurs[i] = new Thread(() -> {
            String nom = Thread.currentThread().getName();
            try {
                while (true) {
                     // blocks if the queue is empty
                    int nombre = file.take();
                    if (nombre == FIN) {
                        break;
                    }
                    IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " a pris " + nombre);
                     // processing the number
                    Thread.sleep(600);
                }
                IO.println(heure() + " : " + nom + " a terminé");
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }, "C" + (i + 1));
    }

     // launch and wait for all threads
    producteur.start();
    for (Thread consommateur : consommateurs) {
        consommateur.start();
    }
    producteur.join();
    for (Thread consommateur : consommateurs) {
        consommateur.join();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 4: the value that marks the end of production. It is a constant, declared outside any class: it is a static field of the implicit class;
  • line 8: a queue with at most 3 elements. [ArrayBlockingQueue] stores the elements in a fixed-size array; [LinkedBlockingQueue] has unlimited capacity by default;
  • lines 12–29: The producer places the numbers 1 through 8 into the queue, one every tenth of a second, followed by an end marker for each consumer (lines 22–24);
  • lines 34–51: Two consumers retrieve the numbers and spend 0.6 seconds processing each one. They consume them more slowly than the producer generates them;
  • line 39: blocking removal. Each number is removed by only one of the two consumers;
  • lines 40–42: a consumer that retrieves the end token exits its loop. Each consumer retrieves one, hence one token is deposited per consumer;
  • the producer and the consumers are lambdas that contain the instruction [try], because [put], [take], and [sleep] can invoke [InterruptedException].

> java Threads24.java

19:16:25.304 : C2 a pris 1
19:16:25.427 : P a déposé 2 (éléments en attente : 1)
19:16:25.428 : C1 a pris 2

19:16:25.927 : P a déposé 6 (éléments en attente : 3)

We see the producer quickly adding the first numbers, then, as soon as the queue contains 3 elements, only adding a number when a consumer removes one: it is blocked by [put] when the queue is full. The consumers share the numbers among themselves and stop when they remove the end marker. This rhythm is reproducible; the assignment of each number to C1 or C2 is not. The producer displays “P is finished” only after both of its end markers have been placed, that is, after C2 has removed the number 7 and freed up a slot.

We’ll revisit blocking queues in the next chapter, when discussing data transfer between asynchronous processes. With virtual threads, a consumer blocked on [take] does not occupy any system threads.

docs.title: 8.10.1. The Principle
docs.text:
Until now, to manage threads, we have created them and then launched them via [start()]. Creating a platform thread is a relatively costly operation: in particular, the system must allocate a stack to it, and each thread occupies memory as long as it exists. We’ll see in Chapter 10 that connection pools exist: open connections are kept in reserve and lent to threads that request them, since opening a connection is costly. A similar system exists for threads: the thread pool.

Java represents a thread pool using the [java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService] interface (an “executor”): threads are no longer created; instead, tasks are assigned to the executor, which has its threads execute them. A thread that has completed a task is not destroyed; it moves on to the next task. The [ThreadPoolExecutor] class, the most common implementation, works as follows:

  • it has a fixed number of threads (“core pool size”): as long as this number has not been reached, each new task triggers the creation of a new thread;
  • beyond that, tasks are placed in a queue (a [BlockingQueue]) from which the threads retrieve them;
  • if the queue is full, the pool creates additional threads, up to a maximum number (“maximum pool size”). These additional threads are destroyed if they remain inactive for longer than a certain amount of time;
  • if the maximum is reached and the queue is full, the task is rejected: by default, the method that submitted it throws the [RejectedExecutionException] exception.

The thread pool offers two advantages: it saves time spent creating threads (a few threads can handle hundreds of requests), and by limiting the number of threads, it prevents the application from becoming overwhelmed by too many requests.

An executor terminates via its [shutdown] method (it no longer accepts new tasks, and its threads stop once the tasks already submitted are completed), possibly followed by [awaitTermination] (which waits for the tasks to finish), or by [shutdownNow] (which interrupts the tasks in progress). Starting with Java 19, [ExecutorService] extends the [AutoCloseable] interface: its [close] method calls [shutdown] and then waits for all tasks to finish. You can therefore declare an executor in a [try] statement with a resource: upon exiting the block, all assigned tasks are completed. The program [Threads25.java] is as follows:

// a thread pool: ThreadPoolExecutor

void main() {
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");
     // 3 permanent threads, at most 5 threads, a queue of 2 jobs
    try (var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(3, 5, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2))) {
         // 8 jobs, each lasting 3 seconds, are assigned to the pool
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
            var data = new Donnees(i, LocalTime.now(), 3);
            try {
                pool.execute(() -> dormir(data, pool));
            } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
                IO.println(heure() + " : le travail n° " + i + " a été refusé par le pool");
            }
        }
        IO.println(heure() + " : le thread Main a confié les travaux au pool et attend leur fin");
         // The end of the try block closes the pool: close() waits for the assigned jobs to finish
    }
    IO.println(heure() + " : fin du thread Main");
}

// the job executed by a thread in the pool
static void dormir(Donnees data, ThreadPoolExecutor pool) {
     // Pool status
    IO.println("%s : le travail n° %d commence dans le thread %s (threads : %d, actifs : %d, en file : %d)"
            .formatted(heure(), data.numero(), Thread.currentThread().getName(),
                    pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size()));
     // idle for [duree] seconds
    try {
        Thread.sleep(data.duree() * 1000L);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
    double duree = Duration.between(data.debut(), LocalTime.now()).toMillis() / 1000.0;
    IO.println("%s : le travail n° %d se termine : programmé pour %d s, il a duré %.2f s depuis sa demande"
            .formatted(heure(), data.numero(), data.duree(), duree));
}

// information passed to each job
record Donnees(int numero, LocalTime debut, int duree) {
}

// current time, in hundredths of a second
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 6: the pool has 3 permanent threads, with a maximum of 5 threads; any additional thread that has been inactive for 60 seconds is destroyed; the task queue is a [ArrayBlockingQueue] with 2 slots. The pool is created in a [try] statement with a resource;
  • Lines 8–15: The pool is assigned 8 jobs, each lasting 3 seconds. The [execute(Runnable)] method assigns a task to the pool without waiting;
  • line 9: each job receives a [Donnees] object; this is a [record] (line 40), which is also defined outside of any class;
  • Lines 12–14: A job rejected by the pool triggers the [RejectedExecutionException] exception;
  • line 18: exiting the [try] block closes the pool and waits for the assigned jobs to finish;
  • lines 23–37: the job executed by a thread in the pool. The thread names ([pool-1-thread-1]…) are assigned by the pool;
  • line 27: the pool’s status: the number of its threads ([getPoolSize]), the number of threads currently executing a job ([getActiveCount]), and the number of jobs waiting in the queue ([getQueue().size()]);
  • line 45: times are displayed to the hundredth of a second ([SS]).

Results:

> java Threads25.java
19:16:31.71 : le travail n° 7 a été refusé par le pool
19:16:31.72 : le thread Main a confié les travaux au pool et attend leur fin
19:16:31.62 : le travail n° 1 commence dans le thread pool-1-thread-2 (threads : 2, actifs : 2, en file : 0)
19:16:31.72 : le travail n° 2 commence dans le thread pool-1-thread-3 (threads : 5, actifs : 5, en file : 2)
19:16:31.72 : le travail n° 6 commence dans le thread pool-1-thread-5 (threads : 5, actifs : 5, en file : 2)
19:16:31.71 : le travail n° 5 commence dans le thread pool-1-thread-4 (threads : 5, actifs : 5, en file : 2)
19:16:31.62 : le travail n° 0 commence dans le thread pool-1-thread-1 (threads : 2, actifs : 2, en file : 0)
19:16:34.81 : le travail n° 2 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 3,10 s depuis sa demande
19:16:34.81 : le travail n° 3 commence dans le thread pool-1-thread-3 (threads : 5, actifs : 5, en file : 1)
19:16:34.82 : le travail n° 5 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 3,10 s depuis sa demande
19:16:34.82 : le travail n° 4 commence dans le thread pool-1-thread-4 (threads : 5, actifs : 5, en file : 0)
19:16:34.82 : le travail n° 6 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 3,10 s depuis sa demande
19:16:34.82 : le travail n° 0 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 3,21 s depuis sa demande
19:16:34.82 : le travail n° 1 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 3,20 s depuis sa demande
19:16:37.82 : le travail n° 4 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 6,10 s depuis sa demande
19:16:37.81 : le travail n° 3 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 6,10 s depuis sa demande
19:16:37.82 : fin du thread Main
  • Jobs 0, 1, and 2 were assigned to the three permanent threads created for this purpose;
  • jobs 3 and 4 were placed in the queue, which was then full;
  • Jobs 5 and 6 triggered the creation of two additional threads ([pool-1-thread-4] and [pool-1-thread-5]): they started immediately, before jobs 3 and 4, which were waiting in the queue. This is the rule for [ThreadPoolExecutor]: the queue first, then the additional threads—which often comes as a surprise;
  • Job 7 was rejected: 5 threads busy, queue full;
  • Jobs 3 and 4 had to wait for a thread to become available after the first jobs finished: they reused threads 3 and 4. In total, they took a little over 6 seconds from the time of their request: 3 seconds of waiting and 3 seconds of processing;
  • The values displayed by each job when it starts (number of threads, queue) depend on the exact moment it obtained the processor: they vary from one execution to the next. However, the outcome of each job (immediate execution, waiting in the queue, or rejection) is reproducible.

You rarely build a *[ThreadPoolExecutor] yourself: the *[Executors] class provides methods for creating it in common scenarios:

MethodExecutor returned[newFixedThreadPool(n)]a pool of n permanent threads, with a queue of unlimited capacity[newCachedThreadPool()]a pool without permanent threads, which creates as many threads as necessary and destroys those that remain inactive for 60 seconds[newSingleThreadExecutor()]a single thread that executes tasks one after another, in the order they were submitted[newScheduledThreadPool(n)]A pool capable of executing tasks after a delay or periodically ([ScheduledExecutorService] interface)[newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()](Java 21) an executor without a pool, which creates a new virtual thread for each task

The last executor deserves a note: virtual threads are not placed in a pool. They are so inexpensive that a new one is created for each task; to limit resource usage, a semaphore is used, as in the program [Threads15.java].

docs.title: 8.10.2. Tasks with results: Callable and Future
docs.text:
The [execute] method passes a [Runnable] to the pool, which does not return a result. The [submit(tâche)] method also accepts a [Callable<V>], a functional interface whose [V call() throws Exception] method returns a result of type V and can throw controlled exceptions. It returns a [Future<V>] object that allows you to track the task:

Future<V> MethodRole[V get()], [V get(long délai, TimeUnit unité)]waits for the task to complete (at most for the duration of [délai]) and returns its result. If the task throws an exception, [get] throws a [ExecutionException] that wraps it (method [getCause])[boolean isDone()]indicates whether the task has completed (normally, due to an exception or cancellation)[Future.State state()](Java 19) the task’s status: [RUNNING], [SUCCESS], [FAILED], or [CANCELLED][V resultNow()], [Throwable exceptionNow()](Java 19) the result or exception of a task that has already completed, without waiting[boolean cancel(boolean interrompre)]cancels the task; if it has started and [interrompre] is equal to [true], the thread executing it is terminated

The executor’s [invokeAll(collection de Callable)] method submits all tasks in a collection, waits for them all to complete, and returns the list of their [Future] values, in the order of the collection. The [invokeAny] method returns the result of the first successfully completed task and cancels the others. The [Threads26.java] program is as follows:

// ExecutorService: Submit tasks and retrieve their results using Future

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    IO.println("Thread principal : " + Thread.currentThread());

     // 1 - a pool of 2 threads, automatically closed at the end of the try block
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
         // Three tasks, each returning a result of type Integer
        var futurs = new ArrayList<Future<Integer>>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            int numero = i;
            futurs.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                IO.println(heure() + " : la tâche " + numero + " s'exécute dans le thread "
                        + Thread.currentThread().getName());
                 // Task: A Callable can throw controlled exceptions
                Thread.sleep(500L * (numero + 1));
                 // the task’s result
                return numero * 10;
            }));
        }
         // the results: get() waits for the task to finish
        for (int i = 0; i < futurs.size(); i++) {
            Future<Integer> futur = futurs.get(i);
            try {
                IO.println("tâche " + i + " : résultat " + futur.get() + ", état " + futur.state());
            } catch (ExecutionException e) {
                IO.println("tâche " + i + " en erreur : " + e.getCause());
            }
        }

         // a task that throws an exception
        Future<Integer> enErreur = pool.submit(() -> echouer());
        try {
            enErreur.get();
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
             // the task's exception is wrapped in a ExecutionException
            IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " contenant " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()
                    + " : " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        }
        IO.println("tâche en erreur : état " + enErreur.state());
    }

     // 2 - one virtual thread per task; invokeAll submits a collection of tasks and waits for them to finish
    try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        List<Callable<String>> travaux = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            int numero = i;
            travaux.add(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(300);
                return "travail " + numero + " exécuté par " + Thread.currentThread();
            });
        }
        for (Future<String> futur : executeur.invokeAll(travaux)) {
             // the task is complete: resultNow() returns its result immediately
            IO.println(futur.resultNow());
        }
    }
}

// the work of the task that failed
static int echouer() {
    throw new IllegalStateException("test....");
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 7: a pool of 2 threads, created by [Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)] and closed at the end of the [try] block;
  • lines 12–19: Each task is a lambda that displays the thread executing it, sleeps for 0.5, 1, or 1.5 seconds, and then returns an integer result. Since the lambda returns a value, the compiler interprets it as a [Callable<Integer>], and [submit] yields a [Future<Integer>]. The [sleep] on line 16 does not need to be enclosed in a [try]: the [call] method of [Callable] declares [throws Exception];
  • line 25: [futur.get()] waits for the task to finish and returns its result; [futur.state()] returns its status;
  • line 32: a task that executes the [echouer] method (lines 61–63), which throws an exception;
  • lines 34–38: the exception thrown in the task is not lost: it is stored in the [Future] object, then rethrown in the thread requesting the result, wrapped in a [ExecutionException] whose [getCause] method throws the original exception;
  • lines 44–57: an executor that creates one virtual thread per task. The method [invokeAll] (line 53) assigns the three jobs from the list [travaux] to it and waits for them to finish. Once the tasks are complete, [resultNow] (line 55) returns their results immediately.

Results:

> java Threads26.java
Thread principal : Thread[#3,main,5,main]
19:16:39.815 : la tâche 0 s'exécute dans le thread pool-1-thread-1
19:16:39.816 : la tâche 1 s'exécute dans le thread pool-1-thread-2
19:16:40.333 : la tâche 2 s'exécute dans le thread pool-1-thread-1
tâche 0 : résultat 0, état SUCCESS
tâche 1 : résultat 10, état SUCCESS
tâche 2 : résultat 20, état SUCCESS
ExecutionException contenant IllegalStateException : test....
tâche en erreur : état FAILED
travail 0 exécuté par VirtualThread[#25]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1
travail 1 exécuté par VirtualThread[#27]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2
travail 2 exécuté par VirtualThread[#30]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1
  • the tasks run in the pool’s threads ([pool-1-thread-1] and [pool-1-thread-2]);
  • Task 2 did not start until Task 0 had finished, in the thread that Task 0 had freed up: the pool has only 2 threads, and Task 2 waited in the queue. This issue is reproducible;
  • the results are retrieved after the tasks have finished, and their status is [SUCCESS];
  • the exception from the task that failed was caught by the main thread, and the task’s status is [FAILED];
  • the three jobs in the second part were executed by three different virtual threads, mounted on the carrier threads [ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1] and [ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2].

Blocking a thread in [get] to wait for a result is simple, but you cannot chain processing operations to the completion of a task without waiting. The [CompletableFuture] class, presented in the next chapter, allows this. Finally, note that Java 25 offers, as a preview, structured concurrency ([StructuredTaskScope]), which treats a group of subtasks as a single unit of work (if one fails, the others are aborted); since it is not yet final, it is not used in this course.

docs.title: 8.11.1. Parallel streams
docs.text:
Let’s return to the first use of threads: utilizing all processors for a time-consuming computation. Streams from the API Stream (Chapter 5) can be executed in parallel: simply call [parallel()] on a stream, or [parallelStream()] instead of [stream()] on a collection. The stream then divides the data into chunks, has the chunks processed by multiple threads, and then combines the partial results. The threads used are those from the shared pool ([ForkJoinPool.commonPool()]), joined by the thread executing the flow. By default, the shared pool has as many threads as there are processors, minus one: the calling thread performs the count.

These flows are only suitable if the processing of each element is independent of the others: the processing order is undefined, and if the processing updates shared data, it must be protected. The program [Threads27.java] is as follows:

// parallel threads: parallelStream and IntStream.parallel

void main() {
     // 1 - count the prime numbers less than N
    final int N = 5_000_000;
     // Sequential version: a for loop
    long debut = System.nanoTime();
    int nbSequentiel = 0;
    for (int i = 2; i < N; i++) {
        if (estPremier(i)) {
            nbSequentiel++;
        }
    }
    IO.println("for séquentiel       : %,d nombres premiers en %d ms"
            .formatted(nbSequentiel, depuis(debut)));

     // Sequential version: a stream
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    long nbFlux = IntStream.range(2, N).filter(i -> estPremier(i)).count();
    IO.println("flux séquentiel      : %,d nombres premiers en %d ms".formatted(nbFlux, depuis(debut)));

     // parallel version: the same stream, made parallel
    debut = System.nanoTime();
    long nbParallele = IntStream.range(2, N).parallel().filter(i -> estPremier(i)).count();
    IO.println("flux parallèle       : %,d nombres premiers en %d ms".formatted(nbParallele, depuis(debut)));

     // the threads that ran and the number of prime numbers found by each
    var threads = new ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer>();
    IntStream.range(2, N).parallel()
            .filter(i -> estPremier(i))
            .forEach(i -> threads.merge(Thread.currentThread().getName(), 1, Integer::sum));
    new TreeMap<>(threads).forEach((nom, nb) ->
            IO.println("  thread %-30s : %,d nombres premiers trouvés".formatted(nom, nb)));

     // 2 - Processing a collection in parallel
    List<String> fichiers = List.of("a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt", "d.txt", "e.txt");
    fichiers.parallelStream().forEach(fichier -> {
        IO.println(heure() + " : traitement de " + fichier + " dans le thread "
                + Thread.currentThread().getName());
         // simulated processing
        dormir(500);
    });
    IO.println("forEach parallèle terminé");
    IO.println("Parallélisme du pool commun : " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism());
}

// prime test (intentionally simple)
static boolean estPremier(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

// the number of milliseconds elapsed since [debut] (in nanoseconds)
static long depuis(long debut) {
    return (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000;
}

// sleep duration of [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, accurate to the millisecond
static String heure() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • Lines 7–15: Prime numbers less than 5,000,000 are counted using a standard [for] loop. The function [estPremier] (lines 48–58) tests divisors up to the square root of the number: this is a time-consuming process, and the iterations are independent;
  • lines 18–20: the same calculation using a sequential workflow: [IntStream.range(2, N)] generates integers from 2 to N–1, [filter] keeps only the prime numbers, and [count] counts them;
  • lines 23–25: the same flow, made parallel by [parallel()]. Nothing else needs to be changed: each thread counts the prime numbers in its segments, and the flow adds up the partial counts. No data is shared between threads;
  • lines 28–33: To determine which threads have completed their work, the parallel stream counts, for each thread, the prime numbers it has found and stores them in a shared [ConcurrentHashMap]. This is shared data, updated by an atomic operation ([merge]);
  • lines 36–42: The method ***[parallelStream()], which takes a list of filenames, returns a parallel stream; *[forEach] processes each file (the processing is simulated by a half-second pause). With a parallel stream, [forEach] does not preserve the order of the list; [forEachOrdered] would preserve it, at the cost of some parallelism;
  • Line 44: the number of threads in the shared pool.

Results:

> java Threads27.java
for séquentiel       : 348 513 nombres premiers en 1419 ms
flux séquentiel      : 348 513 nombres premiers en 1253 ms
flux parallèle       : 348 513 nombres premiers en 780 ms
  thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 : 224 082 nombres premiers trouvés
  thread main                           : 124 431 nombres premiers trouvés
19:16:47.328 : traitement de b.txt dans le thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
19:16:47.328 : traitement de c.txt dans le thread main
19:16:47.838 : traitement de a.txt dans le thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
19:16:47.838 : traitement de e.txt dans le thread main
19:16:48.339 : traitement de d.txt dans le thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
forEach parallèle terminé
Parallélisme du pool commun : 1
  • All three versions find the same number of prime numbers;
  • two threads participated in the parallel processing: the thread [main] and the single thread from the shared pool ([ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1]): on this dual-processor machine, the shared pool has only one thread (line 13);
  • file processing occurs in pairs, half a second apart, and in an order that does not match the list;
  • the parallel flow was faster, but not twice as fast: the threads in our program were sharing the two processors with other very active programs at the time of the capture, and the measured times varied significantly from one run to the next. On a lightly loaded machine with n processors, a parallel flow like this one can be nearly n times faster than the sequential flow. Always measure before drawing conclusions: parallelization comes at a cost (work partitioning, synchronization, combining results) that is only worthwhile if processing each element requires a significant amount of computation.

docs.title: 8.11.2. Divide and conquer: ForkJoinPool and RecursiveTask
docs.text:
Parallel streams are based on the Fork/Join framework (Java 7), which can also be used directly. It is well-suited for “divide and conquer” algorithms: a task that is too large is broken down into subtasks, which are in turn broken down further, until the pieces are small enough to be processed directly; the results of the subtasks are then combined. A task is a class derived from [RecursiveTask<V>] (a task that returns a result of type V) or from [RecursiveAction] (no result), for which the method [compute] is overridden. In [compute], a subtask’s [fork()] method immediately submits it to the pool, and its [join()] method waits for its result.

The tasks are executed by a [ForkJoinPool], in which each thread has its own task queue. A thread that has nothing left to do “steals” tasks from another thread’s queue (“work stealing”): the load is thus distributed automatically. The threads carrying the virtual threads also form a [ForkJoinPool]: this is the one we saw in the textual representation of the virtual threads ([ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]). The program [Threads28.java] counts prime numbers using a recursive task:

// divide and conquer: ForkJoinPool and RecursiveTask

void main() {
    final int N = 5_000_000;
     // the shared pool, used by default by parallel streams
    long debut = System.nanoTime();
    int nb = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new CompterPremiers(2, N));
    IO.println("pool commun       : %,d nombres premiers en %d ms".formatted(nb, depuis(debut)));

     // a pool of 4 threads, closed at the end of the try block
    try (var pool = new ForkJoinPool(4)) {
        CompterPremiers.morceaux.clear();
        debut = System.nanoTime();
        nb = pool.invoke(new CompterPremiers(2, N));
        IO.println("pool de 4 threads : %,d nombres premiers en %d ms".formatted(nb, depuis(debut)));
        IO.println("tâches volées par un thread à un autre : " + pool.getStealCount());
    }
     // the distribution of segments among the threads of the last pool
    new TreeMap<>(CompterPremiers.morceaux).forEach((nom, nbMorceaux) ->
            IO.println("  %-25s : %d morceaux traités".formatted(nom, nbMorceaux)));
}

// a task that counts the prime numbers in the interval [start, end[
static class CompterPremiers extends RecursiveTask<Integer> {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
     // below this threshold, the segment is processed directly
    private static final int SEUIL = 100_000;
     // the number of chunks processed by each thread
    static final Map<String, Integer> morceaux = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    private final int debut;
    private final int fin;

    CompterPremiers(int debut, int fin) {
        this.debut = debut;
        this.fin = fin;
    }

    @Override
    protected Integer compute() {
         // If the segment is small enough, it is processed sequentially
        if (fin - debut <= SEUIL) {
            morceaux.merge(Thread.currentThread().getName(), 1, Integer::sum);
            int nb = 0;
            for (int i = debut; i < fin; i++) {
                if (estPremier(i)) {
                    nb++;
                }
            }
            return nb;
        }
         // otherwise, it is split in two
        int milieu = (debut + fin) >>> 1;
        var gauche = new CompterPremiers(debut, milieu);
        var droite = new CompterPremiers(milieu, fin);
         // the left half is assigned to the pool (another thread may “steal” it)
        gauche.fork();
         // the right half is processed by the current thread
        int nbDroite = droite.compute();
         // we wait for the result from the left half and combine the two results
        return gauche.join() + nbDroite;
    }
}

// prime test (intentionally simple)
static boolean estPremier(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

// the number of milliseconds elapsed since [debut] (in nanoseconds)
static long depuis(long debut) {
    return (System.nanoTime() - debut) / 1_000_000;
}

Comments:

  • lines 24–64: The task [CompterPremiers] counts prime numbers in the interval [start, end[. It is derived from [RecursiveTask<Integer>];
  • lines 25–26: Fork/Join tasks are serializable: the compiler’s [-Xlint:all] option therefore requires declaring the serialization version number [serialVersionUID], with the annotation [@Serial] (Java 14);
  • line 28: for fewer than 100,000 numbers, an interval is processed directly;
  • line 30: for each thread, the number of chunks it has processed;
  • lines 43–52: A sufficiently small chunk is processed sequentially;
  • lines 54–56: a chunk that is too large is split into two subtasks. The expression [(debut + fin) >>> 1] calculates the middle value using an unsigned right shift, which prevents an overflow if the sum exceeds the capacity of a [int];
  • line 58: the left half is assigned to the pool; another thread may “steal” it;
  • line 60: the right half is processed by the current thread via a direct call to [compute]. There is no need to assign both halves to the pool: the current thread would have nothing left to do but wait;
  • line 62: the thread waits for the result of the left half (which it will process itself if no one has “stolen” it) and combines the two results;
  • line 7: the task is first executed by the shared pool. The [invoke(tâche)] method submits the task and waits for its result;
  • lines 11–17: then by a pool of 4 threads, created in a [try] statement with a resource ([ForkJoinPool] is a [ExecutorService]). The [getStealCount] method returns the number of tasks stolen by one thread from another;
  • lines 19–20: the distribution of chunks among the threads in this pool.

Results:

> java Threads28.java
pool commun       : 348 513 nombres premiers en 1506 ms
pool de 4 threads : 348 513 nombres premiers en 648 ms
tâches volées par un thread à un autre : 6
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1   : 15 morceaux traités
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2   : 19 morceaux traités
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3   : 12 morceaux traités
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-4   : 18 morceaux traités
  • the shared pool was no faster than a sequential loop (compare with the previous program): on this machine, it has only one thread, and the main thread—which waits for the result in [invoke]—does not participate in the computation as it does in a parallel flow;
  • the 4-thread pool utilized both processors and was about twice as fast. Having more threads than processors offers no benefit for a pure computation, but doesn’t cost much here;
  • The 64 chunks (5,000,000 / 100,000, rounded up to the next power of 2 due to halving) were distributed roughly equally among the 4 threads, thanks to task stealing. This distribution varies from one run to the next.

Parallel streams are sufficient in most cases; a Fork/Join task is only written for a recursive algorithm that cannot be easily expressed as a stream (sorting, tree traversal, etc.).

docs.title: 8.12.1. The Principle
docs.text:
Consider a three-tier application:

Suppose the application is multi-user, such as a web application. Each user request is handled by a thread. The thread’s lifecycle is as follows:

  • the thread is created (virtual thread) or requested from a thread pool to fulfill a user’s request;
  • if this request requires data, the thread executes a method in the [ui] layer, which calls a method in the [metier] layer, which in turn calls a method in the [dao] layer;
  • the thread returns the response to the user. It then either terminates or is returned to the thread pool.

During the second step, it may be useful for the thread to have its own data—that is, data not shared with other threads. This data could, for example, belong to the specific user the thread is serving and be used across the various [ui, metier, dao] layers without being passed as a parameter to each method.

Java provides two tools for this purpose:

  • The [ThreadLocal<T>] class (Java 1.2): an object whose value—read by [get()] and written by [set(valeur)]—is different for each thread. The constructor [ThreadLocal.withInitial(fabrique)] provides the initial value for each thread; the method [remove()] clears the value of the current thread. The derived class [InheritableThreadLocal<T>] passes the value held by the creating thread to the newly created thread;
  • the class [ScopedValue<T>] (final in Java 25): a value bound, for a delimited scope of the code, to a thread, and which cannot be modified within that scope.

docs.title: 8.12.2. The ThreadLocal class
docs.text:
The program [Threads29.java] compares a regular static field, a [ThreadLocal], and a [InheritableThreadLocal]:

// Thread-specific data: ThreadLocal and InheritableThreadLocal

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");
     // the main thread writes its own values
    Contexte.partage = 100;
    Contexte.parThread.set(100);
    Contexte.utilisateur.set("admin");
    Contexte.langue.set("fr");

     // Three threads write and then read the data
    var threads = new Thread[3];
    for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) {
        int numero = i;
        threads[i] = new Thread(() -> {
             // write
            Contexte.partage = numero;
            Contexte.parThread.set(numero);
             // The thread T2 does not specify a user: it will have the initial value
            if (numero != 2) {
                Contexte.utilisateur.set("utilisateur" + numero);
            }
             // The thread T1 changes the language inherited from the main thread
            if (numero == 1) {
                Contexte.langue.set("en");
            }
             // the other threads are allowed to write in turn
            dormir(200);
             // re-read
            afficher();
        }, "T" + i);
        threads[i].start();
    }
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
     // re-read by the main thread
    afficher();
}

// displays the data seen by the current thread
static void afficher() {
    IO.println("%-4s : partage=%-3d parThread=%-3d utilisateur=%-20s langue=%s".formatted(
            Thread.currentThread().getName(), Contexte.partage, Contexte.parThread.get(),
            Contexte.utilisateur.get(), Contexte.langue.get()));
}

// the program's data
static class Contexte {
     // a static (volatile) field: a single instance, shared by all threads
    static volatile int partage;
     // one instance per thread; initial value is null
    static final ThreadLocal<Integer> parThread = new ThreadLocal<>();
     // one instance per thread, initialized for each thread by the provided factory
    static final ThreadLocal<String> utilisateur =
            ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> "anonyme (thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ")");
     // one instance per thread, whose initial value is inherited from the creating thread
    static final InheritableThreadLocal<String> langue = new InheritableThreadLocal<>();
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 51: a regular static field. There is only one instance of it, shared by all threads. It is [volatile], so that each thread sees the latest value written by the others;
  • line 53: a [ThreadLocal<Integer>] object. Each thread has its own value; as long as a thread hasn’t written to it, [get] returns [null];
  • lines 55–56: a [ThreadLocal<String>] object created by [ThreadLocal.withInitial(…)]. The lambda passed to this method is executed the first time a thread reads the value without having written it; it provides the initial value for that thread;
  • line 58: a [InheritableThreadLocal<String>] object: when a thread is created, its initial value is a copy of the value that the creating thread had at that time;
  • lines 6–9: the main thread writes its own values;
  • lines 17–26: Each thread writes its own values, except for thread T2, which does not set a user, and thread T1, which is the only one to change the language;
  • line 28: each thread waits for the others to write before reading the values again;
  • lines 42–46: the data viewed by the current thread is displayed.

Results:

> java Threads29.java
T1   : partage=2   parThread=1   utilisateur=utilisateur1         langue=en
T0   : partage=2   parThread=0   utilisateur=utilisateur0         langue=fr
T2   : partage=2   parThread=2   utilisateur=anonyme (thread T2)  langue=fr
Main : partage=2   parThread=100 utilisateur=admin                langue=fr
  • the ordinary field [partage] has the same value for all threads: the last value written (in this execution, that of thread T2; another execution may yield a different value);
  • [parThread] retained, in each thread, the value that thread had written to it;
  • [utilisateur] has the value written by each thread; the thread T2, which had not written to it, obtained the initial value provided by the lambda of [withInitial];
  • [langue] is equal to [fr] for threads T0 and T2, which inherited it from the main thread without ever writing to it. The thread T1 changed it to [en] only for itself: the main thread and the other threads do not see this change.

A [ThreadLocal] requires some precautions. A thread’s value exists only as long as the thread itself: with a thread pool, the thread that handles one request will then handle other requests, and [remove] must be called at the end of each request; otherwise, the next request would find the data from the previous one (and the memory would never be freed). With virtual threads, you can create millions of threads, each with its own copy of the data: [InheritableThreadLocal] then copies its values into each of them. Finally, a value that can be modified by any method of the thread makes the code difficult to follow. The [ScopedValue] class avoids these issues.

docs.title: 8.12.3. The ScopedValue class
docs.text:
A [ScopedValue<T>] value is bound to a value for the execution of a piece of code, called its scope:

  • [ScopedValue.newInstance()] creates a bindable value, typically stored in a [static final] field;
  • [ScopedValue.where(sv, valeur).run(action)] executes the action (a [Runnable]) by binding [sv] to [valeur]. During the execution of the action—and all the methods it calls—in the current thread, [sv.get()] creates [valeur]. When the action ends, the link disappears: there is nothing to clean up;
  • [ScopedValue.where(sv, valeur).call(op)] does the same with an operation that returns a result;
  • Within the scope, the value cannot be modified; it can only be bound to another value for a nested scope;
  • [isBound()] indicates whether the value is bound in the current thread; [orElse(autre)] binds the value, or, if that fails, [autre]. Outside any scope, [get()] throws the [NoSuchElementException] exception.

The program [Threads30.java] is as follows:

// values associated with a scope: ScopedValue (Java 25)

// the user on whose behalf the code is running
static final ScopedValue<String> UTILISATEUR = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    IO.println("Hors de toute portée, UTILISATEUR est-il lié ? " + UTILISATEUR.isBound());
    try {
        UTILISATEUR.get();
    } catch (NoSuchElementException e) {
        IO.println("get() hors portée : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }

     // 1 - two simultaneous processes, each for its own user
    Thread t1 = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> ScopedValue.where(UTILISATEUR, "alice").run(this::traiter));
    Thread t2 = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> ScopedValue.where(UTILISATEUR, "bob").run(this::traiter));
    t1.join();
    t2.join();

     // 2 - one scope can contain another, which temporarily binds a different value
    ScopedValue.where(UTILISATEUR, "admin").run(() -> {
        afficher("portée externe");
        ScopedValue.where(UTILISATEUR, "invité").run(() -> afficher("portée interne"));
        afficher("retour dans la portée externe");
         // A thread created within the scope does not inherit the binding
        Thread enfant = Thread.ofVirtual().start(
                () -> IO.println("thread enfant : lié ? " + UTILISATEUR.isBound()));
        try {
            enfant.join();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    });

     // 3 - call: a bound process that returns a result
    String message = ScopedValue.where(UTILISATEUR, "carole").call(() -> "bonjour " + UTILISATEUR.get());
    IO.println(message);
     // After the scope ends, the binding disappears
    IO.println("Après les portées : lié ? " + UTILISATEUR.isBound()
            + ", orElse : " + UTILISATEUR.orElse("personne"));
}

// The layer [metier] calls the layer [dao] without passing the user to it
void traiter() {
    afficher("couche [metier]");
    dao();
}

// The layer [dao] retrieves the user from the current scope
void dao() {
    afficher("couche [dao]");
}

// displays the associated user in the current scope
static void afficher(String endroit) {
    IO.println(endroit + " : UTILISATEUR = " + UTILISATEUR.get());
}

Comments:

  • line 4: the bound value [UTILISATEUR], a static field of the implicit class;
  • lines 7–12: outside any scope, the value is unbound, and [get] throws an exception;
  • lines 15–16: two virtual threads execute the method [traiter], each within a scope where [UTILISATEUR] is bound to a different user;
  • lines 44–52: the method [traiter] (the [metier] layer) calls the method [dao] (the [dao] layer) without passing the user to it: each retrieves it via [UTILISATEUR.get()] (line 56);
  • lines 21–33: a scope where [UTILISATEUR] is equal to [admin] contains a nested scope (line 23) where it is equal to [invité]. Upon exiting the nested scope, we find [admin];
  • lines 26–27: A thread created within the scope does not see the binding: unlike a *[InheritableThreadLocal]*, a *[ScopedValue] is not passed to threads created by *[Thread]. It is, however, passed to the sub-tasks of structured concurrency ([StructuredTaskScope], previewed in Java 25), which ensures that these sub-tasks complete before the scope ends;
  • line 36: [call] performs an operation within a scope and returns its result;
  • lines 39–40: after the scopes, the value is no longer bound.

Results:

> java Threads30.java
Hors de toute portée, UTILISATEUR est-il lié ? false
get() hors portée : NoSuchElementException
couche [metier] : UTILISATEUR = alice
couche [dao] : UTILISATEUR = alice
couche [metier] : UTILISATEUR = bob
couche [dao] : UTILISATEUR = bob
portée externe : UTILISATEUR = admin
portée interne : UTILISATEUR = invité
retour dans la portée externe : UTILISATEUR = admin
thread enfant : lié ? false
bonjour carole
Après les portées : lié ? false, orElse : personne

The messages from the virtual threads in lines 4–7 may appear in a different order (bob before alice); the rest is reproducible. A [ScopedValue] is suitable for context data passed “downward,” from the caller to the called methods: authenticated user, transaction, regional settings, etc. When a called method needs to modify the data for subsequent processing, a [ThreadLocal] is required.

docs.title: 8.12.4. Application: A Transaction Shared Across Layers
docs.text:
Consider the following three-tier application, in which the [dao] layer manages an item table:

Suppose that the interface of the [dao] layer is initially as follows:

interface IDao {
    int insertArticle(Article article);

    List<Article> getAllArticles();

    void deleteAllArticles();
}

Later, the need arises to insert a list of items within a transaction, because the system must operate on an all-or-nothing basis: either all items are inserted, or none are. A method named [insertArticles(List<Article> articles)] can be added to the interface. Then, for another application, the need arises to delete a list of items, again within a transaction… To meet different business requirements, the [dao] layer will grow. We can take a different approach:

  • include only the basic operations (insert, update, delete, read an item) in the [dao] layer;
  • move operations that simultaneously update multiple items to the [metier] layer. These operations use the basic operations from the [dao] layer.

The advantage of this solution is that the same [dao] layer can be used without modification with different [metier] layers. It introduces a challenge in managing the transaction that groups the updates to be performed atomically:

  • the transaction must be started by the [metier] layer before it calls the methods of the [dao] layer;
  • the methods in the [dao] layer must be aware of the transaction’s existence in order to participate in it;
  • The transaction must be completed (confirmed or canceled) by the [metier] layer.

To ensure that the methods of the [dao] layer are aware of any ongoing transaction, the transaction could be added as a parameter to each method of the [dao] layer. This parameter would then appear in the signature of the interface’s methods, thereby binding the interface to a specific data source. Thread-local data provides a more elegant solution: the [metier] layer places the transaction in the thread-local data, and that is where the [dao] layer retrieves it. The method signatures of the [dao] layer do not need to be changed. Multiple threads (multiple users) can work simultaneously: each has its own transaction.

Databases will be covered in Chapters 10 and 11. To keep the focus on threads, we are using an in-memory table and a simulated transaction here. The program [Threads31.java] combines all the layers into a single, compact source file. The entities are as follows:

// an article
record Article(int id, String nom, double prix, int stockActuel, int stockMinimum) {
}

// a simulated transaction: it notes how to roll back each update
static class Transaction {
    private static final AtomicInteger compteur = new AtomicInteger();
    private final Deque<Runnable> annulations = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int numero = compteur.incrementAndGet();

    int getNumero() {
        return numero;
    }

     // records the operation that reverses an update
    void journaliser(Runnable annulation) {
        annulations.push(annulation);
    }

     // commits the transaction: the updates are retained
    void commit() {
        annulations.clear();
    }

     // rolls back the transaction: updates are rolled back, from the last to the first
    void rollback() {
        Runnable annulation;
        while ((annulation = annulations.poll()) != null) {
            annulation.run();
        }
    }
}

// thread-local data shared by the layers
static class ContexteThread {
     // the thread’s current transaction (null if there is none)
    static final ThreadLocal<Transaction> transaction = new ThreadLocal<>();
}
  • line 68: an article is a [record] whose identifier [id] is set by the [dao] layer;
  • lines 72–98: a simulated transaction. Each update made within the transaction records the operation that allows it to be rolled back (method [journaliser]); [commit] commits the transaction while ignoring these operations; [rollback] rolls it back by executing the rollback operations, from the last to the first. The operations are stored in a stack: the method [push] of a [Deque] adds to the top, while the method [poll] removes from the top (and returns [null] if the stack is empty). A real database operates in a similar way, using a transaction log;
  • line 75: each transaction is assigned a unique number. Since transactions can be created by multiple threads simultaneously, the counter is a [AtomicInteger], incremented atomically;
  • lines 101–104: the thread-local data shared by the layers: the thread’s current transaction, or [null] if there is none.

The [dao] layer is as follows:

// the [dao] layer: an in-memory item table with a uniqueness constraint on the name
interface IDao {
    int insertArticle(Article article);

    List<Article> getAllArticles();

    void deleteAllArticles();
}

static class Dao implements IDao {
     // the table, shared by all threads, and its lock
    private final List<Article> table = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Object verrou = new Object();
    private int prochainId = 1;

    @Override
    public int insertArticle(Article article) {
         // Is there a transaction in progress in the current thread?
        Transaction transaction = ContexteThread.transaction.get();
        synchronized (verrou) {
            if (table.stream().anyMatch(a -> a.nom().equals(article.nom()))) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("un article nommé [" + article.nom() + "] existe déjà");
            }
            Article insere = new Article(prochainId++, article.nom(), article.prix(),
                    article.stockActuel(), article.stockMinimum());
            table.add(insere);
             // Within a transaction, we note how to roll back the insertion
            if (transaction != null) {
                transaction.journaliser(() -> {
                    synchronized (verrou) {
                        table.remove(insere);
                    }
                });
            }
