            String mode = transaction == null
                    ? "hors transaction"
                    : "dans la transaction " + transaction.getNumero();
            IO.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] [dao] insertion de " + insere.nom()
                    + " (id " + insere.id() + ") " + mode);
            return 1;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public List<Article> getAllArticles() {
        synchronized (verrou) {
            return List.copyOf(table);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void deleteAllArticles() {
        synchronized (verrou) {
            table.clear();
        }
    }
}
  • line 117: the item table, shared by all threads. Access to it is protected by the lock on line 118;
  • line 124: the method [insertArticle] retrieves any transaction that the [metier] layer has placed in the current thread’s local data;
  • lines 126–128: The table has a unique constraint on item names: inserting an item with a name that already exists throws an exception;
  • lines 129–131: The inserted item is a copy of the received item, with an identifier assigned by the [dao] layer. Since a [record] object is read-only, a new object is created;
  • lines 133–139: If there is a transaction, the [dao] layer participates by recording how to undo the insertion. The rollback lambda captures the variable [insere];
  • lines 140–144: a trace output shows the thread, the inserted item, and any transaction;
  • lines 150–154: The list of items returned is a read-only copy of the table ([List.copyOf]), so that the caller does not iterate through it while another thread is modifying it.

The [metier] layer is as follows:

// the [metier] layer
interface IMetier {
    void insertArticlesInTransaction(List<Article> articles);

    void insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(List<Article> articles);

    List<Article> getAllArticles();

    void deleteAllArticles();
}

static class Metier implements IMetier {
    private final IDao dao;

    Metier(IDao dao) {
        this.dao = dao;
    }

     // Inserting a list of items: all or nothing
    @Override
    public void insertArticlesInTransaction(List<Article> articles) {
         // Start of the transaction, recorded in the thread’s local data
        var transaction = new Transaction();
        ContexteThread.transaction.set(transaction);
        try {
            for (Article article : articles) {
                 // The [dao] layer will retrieve the transaction from the thread
                dao.insertArticle(article);
                 // simulated processing, which allows other threads time to intervene
                dormir(200);
            }
            transaction.commit();
            IO.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] [metier] transaction "
                    + transaction.getNumero() + " validée");
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            transaction.rollback();
            IO.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] [metier] transaction "
                    + transaction.getNumero() + " annulée");
             // The exception is rethrown to the caller
            throw e;
        } finally {
             // the thread no longer has an active transaction
            ContexteThread.transaction.remove();
        }
    }

     // insertion of a list of items without a transaction
    @Override
    public void insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(List<Article> articles) {
        for (Article article : articles) {
            dao.insertArticle(article);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public List<Article> getAllArticles() {
        return dao.getAllArticles();
    }

    @Override
    public void deleteAllArticles() {
        dao.deleteAllArticles();
    }
}
  • lines 176–180: The [dao] layer is injected by the constructor;
  • lines 186–187: the [insertArticlesInTransaction] method starts a transaction and saves it in the thread’s local data;
  • line 191: the insertion method of the [dao] layer is called for each item, without passing the transaction to it;
  • line 193: a pause simulates processing, in order to give another thread time to intervene during the transaction (third part of the test program);
  • line 195: if the program reaches this point, no exception has occurred: the transaction is committed;
  • Lines 198–203: If an exception occurs, the transaction is rolled back and the exception is rethrown to the caller;
  • line 206: in all cases, the thread no longer has an active transaction: [remove()] removes the transaction from the thread. This is essential if the thread is reused (a pooled thread);
  • Lines 212–216: The same insertion, without a transaction.

The test program is as follows:

// Thread-local data: the [metier] layer places the transaction there; the [dao] layer retrieves it from there

void main() throws InterruptedException {
     // the application layers
    IDao dao = new Dao();
    IMetier metier = new Metier(dao);
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");

     // Two items with the same name: the second violates the uniqueness constraint on the name
    List<Article> articles = List.of(new Article(0, "article", 100, 10, 1),
            new Article(0, "article", 100, 10, 1));

     // 1 - insertion outside a transaction
    IO.println("Insertion des articles hors transaction...");
    executer(() -> metier.insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articles));
    afficherArticles(metier);

     // 2 - insertion within a transaction
    metier.deleteAllArticles();
    IO.println("Insertion des articles dans une transaction...");
    executer(() -> metier.insertArticlesInTransaction(articles));
    afficherArticles(metier);

     // 3 - two concurrent threads: Thread A’s transaction is not visible to Thread B
    metier.deleteAllArticles();
    IO.println("Deux threads simultanés...");
    List<Article> articlesA = List.of(new Article(0, "clavier", 20, 5, 1), new Article(0, "souris", 10, 5, 1),
            new Article(0, "clavier", 20, 5, 1));
    List<Article> articlesB = List.of(new Article(0, "écran", 150, 2, 1));
    var threadA = new Thread(() -> executer(() -> metier.insertArticlesInTransaction(articlesA)), "A");
    var threadB = new Thread(() -> executer(() -> metier.insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articlesB)), "B");
    threadA.start();
    Thread.sleep(100);
    threadB.start();
    threadA.join();
    threadB.join();
    afficherArticles(metier);
}

// performs an action while displaying any exceptions
static void executer(Runnable action) {
    try {
        action.run();
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        IO.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void dormir(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// displays the list of items
static void afficherArticles(IMetier metier) {
    IO.println("Liste des articles :");
    for (Article article : metier.getAllArticles()) {
        IO.println("  " + article);
    }
}
  • Line 10: We create a list of two items with the same name. Attempting to insert the second item will be rejected. If the insertion is performed outside a transaction, the first item is inserted and remains in the list. If it is performed within a transaction, the first item is inserted and then removed when the transaction is rolled back;
  • Lines 13–16: Insert the list outside a transaction, then display the table;
  • Lines 18–22: Same procedure within a transaction;
  • lines 24–37: Two threads are working simultaneously. Thread A inserts three items within a transaction (the third violates the uniqueness constraint); meanwhile, Thread B inserts an item outside a transaction;
  • lines 41–48: the method [executer] executes an action and displays any exception, preceded by the thread name.

Results:

> java Threads31.java
Insertion des articles hors transaction...
[Main] [dao] insertion de article (id 1) hors transaction
[Main] IllegalStateException : un article nommé [article] existe déjà
Liste des articles :
  Article[id=1, nom=article, prix=100.0, stockActuel=10, stockMinimum=1]
Insertion des articles dans une transaction...
[Main] [dao] insertion de article (id 2) dans la transaction 1
[Main] [metier] transaction 1 annulée
[Main] IllegalStateException : un article nommé [article] existe déjà
Liste des articles :
Deux threads simultanés...
[A] [dao] insertion de clavier (id 3) dans la transaction 2
[B] [dao] insertion de écran (id 4) hors transaction
[A] [dao] insertion de souris (id 5) dans la transaction 2
[A] [metier] transaction 2 annulée
[A] IllegalStateException : un article nommé [clavier] existe déjà
Liste des articles :
  Article[id=4, nom=écran, prix=150.0, stockActuel=2, stockMinimum=1]
  • The insertion outside the transaction left the first record in the table (line 6). The method [toString] of a [record] displays the name and value of each of its components;
  • The insertion made within a transaction left no records in the table: the record with ID 2 was removed by the rollback;
  • In the third part, thread B inserted the monitor while transaction 2 of thread A was in progress: it did so outside the transaction, since the transaction is a local variable of thread A. The rollback of transaction 2 removed the keyboard and mouse inserted by A, but not the monitor inserted by B. This result is reproducible.

docs.title: 8.12.5. Conclusion
docs.text: The previous example demonstrated the value of thread-local data for transaction management. It should not be replicated exactly as shown, but it accurately describes how frameworks operate: Spring’s transaction management ([@Transactional] annotation) places the transaction and the database connection into [ThreadLocal], which the data access layers consult without their code having to manipulate the transaction; Hibernate can similarly associate the working session with the current thread. We’ll revisit these tools in Chapter 11. In new code, particularly when using virtual threads, a *[ScopedValue]* is the recommended way to pass this type of contextual information.

docs.title: 8.13. Further Reading
docs.text:
Thread synchronization is a challenging field. This chapter has introduced the main tools; to learn more:

  • the book by Brian Goetz et al., [Java Concurrency in Practice] (Addison-Wesley), which remains the definitive reference on the subject, even though it predates virtual threads;
  • the “Concurrency” section of Oracle’s Java tutorial: Lesson: Concurrency, which is outdated but still accurate for the basics;
  • the documentation for the [java.util.concurrent] package: Package java.util.concurrent, whose “Memory Consistency Properties” section summarizes the “earlier-than” relationships;
  • the Java enhancement proposals (JEP) that introduced virtual threads and scoped values: JEP 444: Virtual Threads and JEP 506: Scoped Values.

In modern code, [Thread] objects are rarely manipulated directly. Instead, executors ([ExecutorService]), parallel streams for computations, and virtual threads for waiting processes are preferred. The following chapter introduces asynchronous programming using the [CompletableFuture] class, which allows you to chain processes to run upon completion of a long-running operation (network access, database, file) without blocking a thread. Nevertheless, the concepts covered in this chapter remain essential: all these tasks run in threads, and the data they share must be protected using the same tools ([synchronized], locks, atomic classes, concurrent collections).

docs.title: 7. Functional Interfaces, Lambdas, and Events
docs.text:
In many programs, we need to pass not data but behavior to a method: the sorting criterion, the filtering condition, or the processing to be performed when something happens. Java addresses this need with a simple concept upon which this entire chapter is based: the functional interface—that is, an interface that declares only a single abstract method. An object that implements such an interface “carries” a function, which can be stored in a variable, passed as a parameter, returned as the result of a method, and executed at will.

Before Java 8 (2014), you had to write a class—often an anonymous class—for each behavior you wanted to express, which was verbose. Java 8 introduced lambda expressions and method references, which allow you to write this behavior in a single line. We’ve already used them without going into detail with the API Stream in Chapter 5: in [personnes.stream().filter(p -> p.age() >= 18)], we pass a lambda—that is, an instance of a functional interface—to the [filter] method. This chapter explains what lies behind this syntax. It concludes with events, which Java handles using “listeners”: objects—often lambdas—that register with an emitter to be notified of what is happening there. Java graphical user interfaces (Swing, JavaFX) and web frameworks alike rely on this mechanism: a button click or the arrival of a request (HTTP) are signaled to registered listeners. This course does not cover graphical user interfaces; all examples are console programs.

The programs in this chapter are compact source files located in the [07-lambdas] folder. They are run using [java LambdasNN.java]. Note that a compact source file automatically imports the entire [java.base] module: the interfaces from the [java.util.function], [java.util], or [java.util.concurrent] packages can be used there without any [import] statements.

docs.title: 7.1.1. The concept of a functional interface
docs.text:
A functional interface is an interface that has exactly one abstract method. It may also have as many [default] and [static] methods as desired (see Chapter 4): these do not count. This single abstract method describes a model (also called a signature or form) of a function: the types of its parameters and the type of its return value. A variable of the interface’s type can then refer to any object that provides a function of this form and execute it by calling the method.

The oldest example is the [java.lang.Runnable] interface, which has existed since Java 1.0 and represents a task to be executed (we’ll revisit it in connection with threads in Chapter 8). It boils down to a single method: [void run();]. It describes a function:

  • with no parameters;
  • returning no result ([void]).

There are three ways to create an object of type [Runnable]:

  • write a class that implements the interface, either named or anonymous. This was the only way to do it before Java 8;
  • write a lambda expression: [Runnable tache = () -> IO.println("tâche");];
  • write a method reference to an existing method that has the correct form: [Runnable tache = Fonctions::afficher;].

In the last two cases, the compiler creates the object that implements the interface itself: the lambda or the referenced method becomes the body of the method [run]. The function is then executed by calling the interface method: [tache.run()]. Unlike other languages, Java does not have a specific calling syntax: the interface method is always called by its name ([run], [apply], [test]…).

docs.title: 7.1.2. Interfaces in the java.util.function package
docs.text:
Before Java 8, each library defined its own single-method interfaces ([Runnable], [Comparator], [ActionListener]…). Java 8 introduced the [java.util.function] package, which provides 43 generic functional interfaces covering virtually all requirements. The main ones are as follows:

InterfaceAbstract MethodFunctions Represented[Runnable] ([java.lang])[void run()]No parameters, no results[Supplier<T>][T get()]No parameters, one result: a “supplier”[Consumer<T>][void accept(T t)]one parameter, no result: a “consumer”[BiConsumer<T, U>][void accept(T t, U u)]two parameters, no results[Function<T, R>][R apply(T t)]one parameter, one result of type [R] (always the last type)[BiFunction<T, U, R>][R apply(T t, U u)]two parameters, one result[UnaryOperator<T>][T apply(T t)]one [Function<T, T>]: parameter and result of the same type[BinaryOperator<T>][T apply(T t1, T t2)]a [BiFunction<T, T, T>][Predicate<T>][boolean test(T t)]one parameter, one Boolean result: a “predicate”[BiPredicate<T, U>][boolean test(T t, U u)]two parameters, a Boolean result[Comparator<T>] ([java.util])[int compare(T o1, T o2)]two parameters of the same type, an integer result[Callable<V>] ([java.util.concurrent])[V call() throws Exception]Same as [Supplier<V>], but may throw a controlled exception

Java generics apply only to object types: a [Function<Integer, Integer>] receives and returns [Integer], which requires automatic conversions (boxing and unboxing) between [int] and [Integer]. To avoid these, the package provides specialized versions for the primitive types [int], [long], and [double]: [IntBinaryOperator] ([int applyAsInt(int left, int right)]), [IntUnaryOperator], [IntPredicate], [IntSupplier], [IntConsumer], [IntFunction<R>] (with [int] as a parameter), [ToIntFunction<T>] (with [int] as the result), and their equivalents [Long…] and [Double…]. There is no predefined interface with three or more parameters; in that case, you must define your own (see the following paragraph).

The program [Lambdas01.java] uses these interfaces with method references:

// Java's predefined functional interfaces

void main() {
     // 1 - Runnable: no parameters, no return value: void run()
    Runnable tache = new Runnable() {
        @Override
        public void run() {
            Fonctions.afficher();
        }
    };
     // shorthand form: a method reference
    tache = Fonctions::afficher;
     // Execution: The interface’s single abstract method is called
    tache.run();

     // 2 - BiFunction<T, U, R>: two parameters, one return value
    BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> operation = Fonctions::ajouter;
    IO.println("operation.apply(2, 3)=" + operation.apply(2, 3));
     // Supplier<T>: no parameters, one result
    Supplier<String> saluer = Fonctions::saluer;
    IO.println("saluer.get()=" + saluer.get());
     // primitive version: IntBinaryOperator, int applyAsInt(int, int), without boxing
    IntBinaryOperator multiplier = Fonctions::multiplier;
    IO.println("multiplier.applyAsInt(2, 3)=" + multiplier.applyAsInt(2, 3));

     // 3 - Consumer<T>: one parameter, no return value
    Consumer<String> ecrire = IO::println;
    ecrire.accept("Consumer<String> a exécuté IO.println");

     // 4 - Predicate<T>: one parameter, one boolean result
    Predicate<Integer> estPair = Fonctions::estPair;
    IO.println("estPair.test(8)=" + estPair.test(8));
    List<Integer> nombres = new ArrayList<>(List.of(3, 8, 1, 6, 5, 4));
     // removeIf from Collection expects a Predicate
    boolean modifiee = nombres.removeIf(estPair);
    IO.println("nombres pairs retirés : " + modifiee + ", reste : " + nombres);

     // 5 - Comparator<T>: two T parameters, an int result
    List<String> noms = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Paul", "Mélanie", "Jo", "Sébastien"));
    noms.sort(Fonctions::comparerLongueurs);
    IO.println("triés par longueur : " + noms);

     // 6 - A lambda is an object: an instance of a generated class that implements the interface
    IO.println("classe : " + operation.getClass().getName());
    IO.println("interfaces : " + Arrays.toString(operation.getClass().getInterfaces()));
}

// the referenced methods, grouped into a class
// (the implicit class of a compact source file cannot be named)
class Fonctions {

    static void afficher() {
        IO.println("afficher() exécutée par Runnable.run()");
    }

    static int ajouter(int n1, int n2) {
        return n1 + n2;
    }

    static int multiplier(int n1, int n2) {
        return n1 * n2;
    }

    static String saluer() {
        return "Bonjour";
    }

    static boolean estPair(int n) {
        return n % 2 == 0;
    }

    static int comparerLongueurs(String s1, String s2) {
        return Integer.compare(s1.length(), s2.length());
    }
}

Results:

> java Lambdas01.java
afficher() exécutée par Runnable.run()
operation.apply(2, 3)=5
saluer.get()=Bonjour
multiplier.applyAsInt(2, 3)=6
Consumer<String> a exécuté IO.println
estPair.test(8)=true
nombres pairs retirés : true, reste : [3, 1, 5]
triés par longueur : [Jo, Paul, Mélanie, Sébastien]
classe : Lambdas01$$Lambda/0x0000000020165a28
interfaces : [interface java.util.function.BiFunction]

Comments:

  • Lines 5–10: Creation of a [Runnable] object using an anonymous class—that is, a class without a name—declared and instantiated right where it is needed. It implements the method [run], which calls the method [afficher] on line 52. This was the required syntax prior to Java 8;
  • line 12: the same thing using a method reference: [Fonctions::afficher] refers to the static method [afficher] of the class [Fonctions]. The compiler verifies that it has the same form as the method [run] (no parameters, no return value) and creates the object [Runnable] that calls it. This is the standard syntax today;
  • line 14: the function is executed by calling the method of the interface. The method [afficher] on line 52 is executed (line 2 of the results);
  • Lines 48–50: The referenced methods are grouped into a class named [Fonctions]. We would have liked to write them directly in the file, next to [main], and name them [Lambdas01::ajouter]. However, the implicit class that wraps a compact source file cannot be named in the code (the compiler returns [cannot find symbol]);
  • line 17: [BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer>] refers to a function with two parameters, [Integer], and returning a [Integer] (the last generic type). The method [ajouter] on line 56, which works with [int], is suitable: the compiler adds the conversions between [int] and [Integer]. The function is called via its method [apply] (line 18);
  • line 20: [Supplier<String>] refers to a parameterless function that returns a string. It is called via its method [get];
  • line 23: the primitive version [IntBinaryOperator] operates directly on [int] values, without conversion. Its method is called [applyAsInt]. This is the preferred type for computationally intensive tasks;
  • Line 27: [Consumer<String>] refers to a function that takes one parameter, [String], and returns nothing. The static method [IO.println(Object)] is appropriate: a [String] is a [Object]. It is executed via its method [accept];
  • line 31: a predicate is a function that returns a Boolean; it is executed via its method [test] (line 32). The method [removeIf] of the interface [Collection] (line 35) expects a parameter of type [Predicate]: it removes from the collection all elements for which the predicate returns [true], and returns [true] if it has removed at least one element;
  • line 40: the method [sort] of the interface [List] accepts a [Comparator] that compares two elements (result can be negative, zero, or positive, like [compareTo]). Here, the names are sorted in ascending order by length. The method [comparerLongueurs] (line 72) uses [Integer.compare], which compares two [int] objects without the risk of an overflow (which a simple subtraction does not guarantee);
  • Lines 44–45: A method reference, like a lambda, is an object. Its class, displayed on line 10 of the results, is a class generated at runtime by the virtual machine, whose name contains [$$Lambda] followed by an address that changes from one execution to the next. On line 11 of the results, we see that this class implements the [BiFunction] interface. A lambda is therefore not a new type of object: it is an instance of an ordinary class that implements a functional interface.

docs.title: 7.2. Defining Your Own Functional Interfaces
docs.text:
The predefined interfaces are often sufficient, but you can define your own. Simply write an interface with a single abstract method, for example:

  • [interface Operation { int calculer(int n1, int n2); }]

This interface represents a function that takes two integers and returns an integer. Compared to [IntBinaryOperator], the type [Operation] has a name that describes its purpose, its method has a descriptive name ([calculer] rather than [applyAsInt]), and its parameters have names ([n1], [n2]) that development tools display. It is preceded by the annotation [@FunctionalInterface]: this is not required, but it instructs the compiler to verify that the interface is functional, and it documents the developer’s intent.

A variable of type [Operation] named [op] references only one function at a time. Unlike other languages, which offer “multicast delegates,” Java does not provide a way to store multiple functions in a single variable and execute them all with a single call: when needed, functions are placed in a list and executed one by one. This is exactly what we will do with event listeners.

Consider the example [Lambdas02.java]:

// define your own functional interfaces

void main() {
     // a variable of type Operation receives the static method increase
    Operation op = Calculs::augmenter;
     // the operation is executed
    int n = op.calculer(4, 7);
    IO.println("n=" + n);

     // Create an object c1 of type Calculations
    var c1 = new Calculs();
     // The `add` method of the `c1` object is stored in `op`
    op = c1::ajouter;
    n = op.calculer(2, 3);
    IO.println("n=" + n);
     // then the `subtract` method of c1
    op = c1::soustraire;
    n = op.calculer(2, 3);
    IO.println("n=" + n);

     // A variable can only reference one function: to execute multiple functions, use a list
    List<Operation> operations = new ArrayList<>();
    operations.add(c1::ajouter);
    operations.add(c1::soustraire);
    operations.add((n1, n2) -> n1 * n2);
    for (Operation operation : operations) {
        IO.println("-> " + operation.calculer(10, 4));
    }

     // A default method of the interface creates a new operation
    Operation sommeAuCarre = ((Operation) c1::ajouter).puis(x -> x * x);
    IO.println("sommeAuCarre.calculer(1, 2)=" + sommeAuCarre.calculer(1, 2));

     // Operation and IntBinaryOperator have the same form but are two different types
    IntBinaryOperator autre = op::calculer;
    IO.println("autre.applyAsInt(5, 1)=" + autre.applyAsInt(5, 1));

     // A generic functional interface
    Transformation<String, Integer> longueur = String::length;
    Transformation<Integer, String> etoiles = "*"::repeat;
    IO.println("longueur(\"Bonjour\")=" + longueur.transformer("Bonjour"));
    IO.println("etoiles(5)=" + etoiles.transformer(5));
}

// Definition of a functional interface: a single abstract method
// that takes two integers as parameters and returns an integer
@FunctionalInterface
interface Operation {
    int calculer(int n1, int n2);

     // A default method does not count: the interface remains functional
    default Operation puis(IntUnaryOperator suite) {
        return (n1, n2) -> suite.applyAsInt(calculer(n1, n2));
    }
}

// A generic functional interface: T -> R
@FunctionalInterface
interface Transformation<T, R> {
    R transformer(T valeur);
}

// a class whose methods have the same form as the Operation interface
class Calculs {
     // two instance methods
    int ajouter(int n1, int n2) {
        IO.println("ajouter(" + n1 + "," + n2 + ")");
        return n1 + n2;
    }

    int soustraire(int n1, int n2) {
        IO.println("soustraire(" + n1 + "," + n2 + ")");
        return n1 - n2;
    }

     // a static method
    static int augmenter(int n1, int n2) {
        IO.println("augmenter(" + n1 + "," + n2 + ")");
        return n1 + 2 * n2;
    }
}

Results:

> java Lambdas02.java
augmenter(4,7)
n=18
ajouter(2,3)
n=5
soustraire(2,3)
n=-1
ajouter(10,4)
-> 14
soustraire(10,4)
-> 6
-> 40
ajouter(1,2)
sommeAuCarre.calculer(1, 2)=9
soustraire(5,1)
autre.applyAsInt(5, 1)=4
longueur("Bonjour")=7
etoiles(5)=*****

Comments:

  • lines 47–55: definition of the functional interface [Operation]. In a compact source file, type declarations (classes, interfaces, records, etc.) can be placed before or after the method [main]; we place them after it;
  • Lines 52–54: A functional interface can have methods [default]. The method [puis] constructs a new [Operation]: this method executes the current operation, then applies the function [suite] to its result. It returns a lambda, which we will examine in the next section. The composition methods for the predefined interfaces ([andThen], [compose]…, etc.) are written based on this model, which we will cover later;
  • Lines 64–81: The class [Calculs] has two instance methods, [ajouter] and [soustraire], and one static method, [augmenter], all three of which have the same form as the method [calculer];
  • line 5: the variable [op] is of type [Operation]. It is assigned a reference to the static method [Calculs.augmenter];
  • line 7: the operation is executed by the method [calculer]. The method [Calculs.augmenter] is executed, with the parameters passed to [calculer];
  • line 11: an instance [c1] of the class [Calculs] is created;
  • Line 13: The reference [c1::ajouter] refers to the method [ajouter] of the object [c1]. [augmenter] was a static method, while [ajouter] is an instance method: this makes no difference. In the second case, the object created by the compiler also stores the object [c1] on which the method will be called;
  • line 17: the same is done with the instance method [soustraire];
  • lines 22–28: To execute multiple operations, they are placed in a list [List<Operation>], which is then iterated over. Method references and lambdas can be mixed (line 25). Each result is retrieved (lines 8–12 of the results);
  • line 31: the method [default] [puis] is applied to the operation [c1::ajouter]. The [(Operation)] conversion is necessary: a method reference has no type of its own, and you cannot call a method on it until the compiler knows which interface it implements (we’ll come back to this). [sommeAuCarre.calculer(1, 2)] calculates (1+2)², which is 9 (lines 13–14 of the results);
  • line 35: [Operation] and [IntBinaryOperator] have exactly the same form, but they are two different types with no inheritance relationship. The assignment [IntBinaryOperator autre = op;] would be rejected ([incompatible types: Operation cannot be converted to IntBinaryOperator]). In contrast, the method reference [op::calculer] has the correct form: it creates a [IntBinaryOperator] that calls the method [calculer] of the object [op] ([c1::soustraire] at this stage of the program);
  • lines 57–61: a functional interface can be generic. [Transformation<T, R>] represents a function that takes a [T] and returns a [R]: this is equivalent to [Function<T, R>], with names chosen by us;
  • Line 39: [String::length] is suitable for a [Transformation<String, Integer>]: the method [length] will be called on the string passed as a parameter. Line 40: ["*"::repeat] refers to the method [repeat(int)] of the string object ["*"]; it takes an integer and returns a string. These are two different types of method references, which we will discuss in detail in the following section.

The annotation [@FunctionalInterface] comes into play if a second abstract method—for example, [int inverser(int n);]—is accidentally added to the interface [Operation]. The compiler then flags the annotation itself and each of the lambdas and method references that use the interface (abbreviated output):

> java Lambdas02.java
Lambdas02.java:5: error: incompatible types: Operation is not a functional interface
    Operation op = Calculs::augmenter;
                   ^
    multiple non-overriding abstract methods found in interface Operation
...
Lambdas02.java:47: error: Unexpected @FunctionalInterface annotation
@FunctionalInterface
^
  Operation is not a functional interface
    multiple non-overriding abstract methods found in interface Operation
9 errors
error: compilation failed

The messages from the [javac] compiler are in English: the JDK does not provide a French translation.

docs.title: 7.3. Anonymous classes, lambda expressions, and method references
7.3.1. From anonymous classes to lambdas
docs.text:
In the previous examples, each function is a named method written elsewhere in the program. For short functions used only once, this is cumbersome. Up until Java 7, the only alternative was the anonymous class: the class that implements the interface is written right where the object is created. Java 8 introduced a much more concise syntax—lambda expressions—which have virtually replaced anonymous classes for functional interfaces. The program [Lambdas03.java] demonstrates the different forms:

// anonymous classes with lambda expressions

void main() {
     // 1 - an anonymous class: the class that implements the interface is written in place
    IntBinaryOperator ajouter = new IntBinaryOperator() {
        @Override
        public int applyAsInt(int n1, int n2) {
            return n1 + n2;
        }
    };
    IO.println("classe anonyme : ajouter(2, 3)=" + ajouter.applyAsInt(2, 3));

     // 2 - the same thing with a lambda expression (Java 8): parameters -> body
    IntBinaryOperator soustraire = (int n1, int n2) -> {
        return n1 - n2;
    };
    IO.println("lambda à corps de bloc : soustraire(2, 3)=" + soustraire.applyAsInt(2, 3));

     // 3 - Parameter types are inferred from the target interface
    IntBinaryOperator multiplier = (n1, n2) -> n1 * n2;
    IO.println("lambda à corps d'expression : multiplier(2, 3)=" + multiplier.applyAsInt(2, 3));

     // 4 - a single parameter: parentheses are optional
    IntUnaryOperator carre = x -> x * x;
    Predicate<String> estVide = s -> s.isEmpty();
    IO.println("carre(7)=" + carre.applyAsInt(7) + ", estVide(\"\")=" + estVide.test(""));

     // 5 - no parameters: empty parentheses
    Supplier<String> saluer = () -> "Bonjour";
    Runnable bip = () -> IO.println("bip !");
    IO.println(saluer.get());
    bip.run();

     // 6 - a block body with multiple statements
    BiConsumer<String, Integer> repeter = (texte, fois) -> {
        for (int i = 0; i < fois; i++) {
            IO.print(texte);
        }
        IO.println();
    };
    repeter.accept("ab", 3);

     // 7 - anonymous parameters (Java 22): their values are not required
    BiConsumer<Object, String> ecouteur = (_, _) -> IO.println("événement reçu");
    ecouteur.accept(null, "clic");

     // 8 - a lambda passed directly as a method parameter
    List<Integer> nombres = new ArrayList<>(List.of(3, 8, 1, 6, 5, 4));
    List<Integer> pairs = new ArrayList<>(nombres);
    pairs.removeIf(n -> n % 2 != 0);
    IO.println("pairs : " + pairs);
    nombres.sort((n1, n2) -> Integer.compare(n2, n1));
    IO.println("ordre décroissant : " + nombres);
}

Results:

> java Lambdas03.java
classe anonyme : ajouter(2, 3)=5
lambda à corps de bloc : soustraire(2, 3)=-1
lambda à corps d'expression : multiplier(2, 3)=6
carre(7)=49, estVide("")=true
Bonjour
bip !
ababab
événement reçu
pairs : [8, 6, 4]
ordre décroissant : [8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 1]

Comments:

  • Lines 5–10: an anonymous class. The operator [new] is followed by the interface name, empty parentheses, and the body of a class that implements the interface. The compiler generates a class (with a name of its choosing, [Lambdas03$1]) and creates an instance of it. Six lines to express [n1 + n2];
  • lines 14–16: the same thing using a lambda expression. We write the list of parameters, the [->] operator (an arrow, which is read as “gives”), then the body. The interface name and method name have disappeared: the compiler knows them from the variable’s type, which is called the lambda’s target type. A lambda whose body is a block enclosed in curly braces is a block-bodied lambda;
  • line 20: the parameter types have disappeared. The compiler infers them from the target type [IntBinaryOperator]: [n1] and [n2] are of type [int]. The body is reduced to an expression, whose value is the result of the lambda: this is an expression-bodied lambda. This is the most common form;
  • line 24: with a single parameter whose type is not specified, parentheses are optional. [x -> x * x] reads “x gives x times x.” Line 25: a lambda with one parameter of type [String] returns a Boolean: it is a [Predicate<String>];
  • Lines 29–30: Without parameters, empty parentheses are used. A lambda whose body is a method call of type [void] is suitable for a [Runnable];
  • lines 35–40: A lambda with a block body can contain any statements: declarations, loops, tests, etc.;
  • line 44: The underscore character [_] denotes an anonymous parameter (Java 22). It is used when the interface’s signature requires parameters that the lambda does not need, which is common for event listeners. Multiple such parameters can be included in the same lambda;
  • lines 49–51: The most common use of lambdas is to pass them directly as parameters to a method that expects a functional interface. Compare with [Lambdas01.java]: it is no longer necessary to write a method [estPair]. Here, we’re working on a copy of the list, because [removeIf] modifies the list it operates on;
  • line 52: a lambda of type [Comparator<Integer>] that reverses the usual comparison: the list is sorted in descending order.

Let’s review the forms of a lambda expression:

FormExampletyped parameters, block body[(int a, int b) -> { return a + b; }]untyped parameters, expression body[(a, b) -> a + b]a single untyped parameter[x -> x * x]no parameters[() -> "Bonjour"]anonymous parameters[(_, _) -> IO.println("reçu")]Parameters declared with [var][(var a, var b) -> a + b]

Parameters are either all typed or all untyped: you cannot mix the two. Within a block body, a lambda that returns a result must have a [return] statement on every execution path, just like a method.

A lambda is not quite the same as a shorthand anonymous class. In an anonymous class, [this] refers to the instance of the anonymous class; in a lambda, [this] refers to the object of the method that encloses the lambda. Furthermore, an anonymous class creates a new scope: it can declare a variable with the same name as a variable in the method, which a lambda cannot do. Finally, an anonymous class can implement an interface with multiple methods or inherit from an abstract class, which is impossible with a lambda. In this course, we will use lambdas whenever possible.

docs.title: 7.3.2. Additional Information: Target Type and Method References
docs.text:
The [Lambdas04.java] program defines the concept of a target type and presents the four types of method references:

// Additional notes on lambdas and method references

void main() throws Exception {
     // 1 - A lambda does not have a type of its own: the context determines it
     // var double = x -> x *  2; // rejected: the lambda needs a target type
    var doubler = (IntUnaryOperator) x -> x * 2;
    IO.println("doubler(21)=" + doubler.applyAsInt(21));
     // The same lambda body can implement two different interfaces
    Supplier<String> fournisseur = () -> "Bonjour";
    Callable<String> appelable = () -> "Bonjour";
    IO.println(fournisseur.get() + " / " + appelable.call());

     // 2 - Parameters declared with `var` (Java 11): allows them to be annotated or marked as `final`
    BinaryOperator<String> concatener = (final var s1, final var s2) -> s1 + s2;
    IO.println(concatener.apply("lam", "bda"));

     // 3 - the four types of method references
     // a) static method: Class::methodeStatique
    Function<String, Integer> convertir = Integer::parseInt;
    IO.println("convertir(\"42\") + 1 = " + (convertir.apply("42") + 1));
     // b) Instance method of a given object: object::method
    String nom = "Pierre";
    Supplier<String> enMajuscules = nom::toUpperCase;
    IO.println("enMajuscules.get()=" + enMajuscules.get());
     // c) method of an instance of any object: Class::methodeInstance
         // the object on which the method is called becomes the first parameter
    UnaryOperator<String> majuscules = String::toUpperCase;
    Comparator<String> ignorerCasse = String::compareToIgnoreCase;
    IO.println("majuscules(\"paul\")=" + majuscules.apply("paul")
            + ", ignorerCasse(\"abc\", \"ABC\")=" + ignorerCasse.compare("abc", "ABC"));
     // d) constructor: Class::new
    Supplier<List<String>> creerListe = ArrayList::new;
    Function<String, StringBuilder> creerTampon = StringBuilder::new;
    IntFunction<int[]> creerTableau = int[]::new;
    List<String> liste = creerListe.get();
    liste.add("élément");
    IO.println(liste + " " + creerTampon.apply("abc").reverse() + " " + creerTableau.apply(3).length);

     // 4 - Controlled exceptions: Callable.call can throw them; Supplier.get cannot
    Callable<Integer> lire = () -> {
        throw new IOException("fichier absent");
    };
    try {
        lire.call();
    } catch (IOException ex) {
        IO.println("exception reçue : " + ex.getMessage());
    }

     // 5 - Each evaluation of a lambda or method reference may create a new object
    Supplier<String> r1 = nom::toUpperCase;
    Supplier<String> r2 = nom::toUpperCase;
    IO.println("r1 == r2 : " + (r1 == r2) + ", r1.equals(r2) : " + r1.equals(r2));
}

Results:

> java Lambdas04.java
doubler(21)=42
Bonjour / Bonjour
lambda
convertir("42") + 1 = 43
enMajuscules.get()=PIERRE
majuscules("paul")=PAUL, ignorerCasse("abc", "ABC")=0
[élément] cba 3
exception reçue : fichier absent
r1 == r2 : false, r1.equals(r2) : false

Comments:

  • line 5: A lambda does not have a type of its own. Its type is determined by the context: the type of the variable that receives it, the type of the parameter to which it is passed, or the type specified by a conversion. The declaration [var doubler = x -> x * 2;] is therefore rejected by the compiler: [cannot infer type for local variable doubler (lambda expression needs an explicit target-type)]. It would not know which interface to implement;
  • line 6: with a conversion to [IntUnaryOperator], the target type is known, and [var] becomes possible. In practice, we tend to write [IntUnaryOperator doubler = x -> x * 2;] instead;
  • Lines 9–10: The same lambda expression, [() -> "Bonjour"], implements a [Supplier<String>] here and a [Callable<String>] there. These are two objects of different classes, which share only the form of their method;
  • line 14: Since Java 11, lambda parameters can be declared using [var], which allows you to add a modifier ([final]) or an annotation to them—something that is not possible with an untyped parameter;
  • lines 17–37: the four types of method references:
    • line 19: a reference to a static method, [Classe::methode]. [Integer::parseInt] is equivalent to the lambda [s -> Integer.parseInt(s)];
    • line 23: the reference to an instance method of a given object, [objet::methode]. [nom::toUpperCase] is equivalent to [() -> nom.toUpperCase()]: the object [nom] is fixed once and for all;
    • Lines 27–28: a reference to an instance method of any object of a class, [Classe::methodeInstance]. The object on which the method will be called is not yet known: it becomes the first parameter of the function. [String::toUpperCase] is equivalent to [s -> s.toUpperCase()] (one parameter), and [String::compareToIgnoreCase] is equivalent to [(s1, s2) -> s1.compareToIgnoreCase(s2)] (two parameters), hence [Comparator<String>];
    • lines 32–34: the reference to a constructor, [Classe::new]. [ArrayList::new] is equivalent to [() -> new ArrayList<>()]; [StringBuilder::new], with a target type of [Function<String, StringBuilder>], selects the constructor that takes a string; [int[]::new] creates an array of the size passed as a parameter;
  • line 37: the three creation functions are used; [reverse] reverses the contents of [StringBuilder] (line 8 of the results);
  • Lines 40–47: A significant difference between [Callable] and [Supplier]. The method [call] is declared as [throws Exception]: a lambda of type [Callable] can therefore throw a controlled exception (see Chapter 3), in this case a [IOException]. The method [get] of [Supplier] does not declare any exceptions: the same lambda of type [Supplier<Integer>] would be rejected ([unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown]). No interface of type [java.util.function] allows controlled exceptions: a lambda that throws one must either catch it itself or use an interface whose method declares it. This is why [main] is declared as [throws Exception] (line 3): the calls to [appelable.call()] (line 11) and [lire.call()] (line 44) could theoretically invoke any [Exception], which the [catch] on line 45—limited to [IOException]—does not intercept;
  • lines 50–52: two evaluations of the same method reference [nom::toUpperCase] produce two different objects, which neither [==] nor [equals] consider to be equal (line 10 of the results). Keep this in mind: it will be important when unsubscribing from an event listener.

A method reference is simply a shorthand notation for a lambda that merely calls a method. We use it when it improves readability: [String::length] rather than [s -> s.length()].

docs.title: 7.3.3. Composing Functions
docs.text:
Predefined functional interfaces have methods [default] and [static] that create new functions from existing ones, such as the [puis] method in our [Operation] interface. The program [Lambdas05.java] lists the main ones:

// composing functions: andThen, compose, and, or, negate, comparing, thenComparing

void main() {
     // 1 - Function: andThen (first this, then the other) and compose (first the other)
    Function<Integer, Integer> plusUn = x -> x + 1;
    Function<Integer, Integer> foisDeux = x -> x * 2;
    IO.println("plusUn.andThen(foisDeux).apply(5)=" + plusUn.andThen(foisDeux).apply(5));
    IO.println("plusUn.compose(foisDeux).apply(5)=" + plusUn.compose(foisDeux).apply(5));
     // a processing chain built from a list of functions
    List<UnaryOperator<String>> etapes =
            List.of(String::strip, String::toLowerCase, s -> s.replace(' ', '-'));
    Function<String, String> normaliser = Function.identity();
    for (UnaryOperator<String> etape : etapes) {
        normaliser = normaliser.andThen(etape);
    }
    IO.println("normaliser(\"  Mon Beau Titre \")=" + normaliser.apply("  Mon Beau Titre "));

     // 2 - Predicate: and, or, negate, Predicate.not
    Predicate<String> court = s -> s.length() <= 4;
    Predicate<String> commenceParP = s -> s.startsWith("P");
    List<String> prenoms = List.of("Paul", "Mélanie", "Jo", "Sébastien", "Pierre");
    IO.println("court et P : " + filtrer(prenoms, court.and(commenceParP)));
    IO.println("court ou P : " + filtrer(prenoms, court.or(commenceParP)));
    IO.println("non court : " + filtrer(prenoms, court.negate()));
    IO.println("non vides : " + filtrer(List.of("a", "", "b"), Predicate.not(String::isEmpty)));

     // 3 - Consumer: andThen chains two processing steps on the same value
    List<String> journal = new ArrayList<>();
    Consumer<String> afficher = s -> IO.println("affichage : " + s);
    Consumer<String> memoriser = journal::add;
    Consumer<String> lesDeux = afficher.andThen(memoriser);
    lesDeux.accept("premier");
    lesDeux.accept("second");
    IO.println("journal : " + journal);

     // 4 - Comparator: comparing, thenComparing, reversed
    List<Personne> personnes = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Personne("Paul", 32),
            new Personne("Mélanie", 25), new Personne("Jo", 32), new Personne("Sébastien", 25)));
    personnes.sort(Comparator.comparing(Personne::age).thenComparing(Personne::nom));
    IO.println("par âge puis nom : " + personnes);
    personnes.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Personne::age).reversed()
            .thenComparing(Personne::nom, Comparator.reverseOrder()));
    IO.println("par âge décroissant puis nom décroissant : " + personnes);
     // BinaryOperator.minBy constructs a function from a comparator
    BinaryOperator<Personne> plusJeune = BinaryOperator.minBy(Comparator.comparingInt(Personne::age));
    IO.println("plusJeune(Paul, Mélanie)=" + plusJeune.apply(personnes.get(0), personnes.get(3)));
}

// keeps the elements that satisfy the predicate
static <T> List<T> filtrer(List<T> elements, Predicate<? super T> predicat) {
    List<T> resultat = new ArrayList<>();
    for (T element : elements) {
        if (predicat.test(element)) {
            resultat.add(element);
        }
    }
    return resultat;
}

record Personne(String nom, int age) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return nom + "(" + age + ")";
    }
}

Results:

> java Lambdas05.java
plusUn.andThen(foisDeux).apply(5)=12
plusUn.compose(foisDeux).apply(5)=11
normaliser("  Mon Beau Titre ")=mon-beau-titre
court et P : [Paul]
court ou P : [Paul, Jo, Pierre]
non court : [Mélanie, Sébastien, Pierre]
non vides : [a, b]
affichage : premier
affichage : second
journal : [premier, second]
par âge puis nom : [Mélanie(25), Sébastien(25), Jo(32), Paul(32)]
par âge décroissant puis nom décroissant : [Paul(32), Jo(32), Sébastien(25), Mélanie(25)]
plusJeune(Paul, Mélanie)=Mélanie(25)

Comments:

  • line 7: [f.andThen(g)] returns the result of applying [f] first, then [g]: (5 + 1) × 2 = 12;
  • line 8: [f.compose(g)] first applies [g], then [f]: 5 × 2 + 1 = 11;
  • lines 10–15: a dynamically constructed processing chain. We start with the identity function ([Function.identity()], which leaves its parameter unchanged) and add, via [andThen], each step in the list. The resulting function [normaliser] removes leading and trailing spaces, converts the text to lowercase, and replaces spaces with dashes. Each call to [andThen] creates a new function: existing functions are never modified. Similarly, the list of steps could be read from a configuration file;
  • lines 19–25: predicates are combined using [and] (and), [or] (or), and [negate] (not). The static method [Predicate.not] (Java 11) returns the negation of a predicate: it allows you to write [Predicate.not(String::isEmpty)], whereas [String::isEmpty.negate()] is rejected (a method reference has no type until it has a target type);
  • Lines 28–34: [c1.andThen(c2)] returns a [Consumer], which executes [c1] and then [c2] on the same value. This is the simplest way in Java to execute multiple operations with a single call. Line 30: [journal::add] is a reference to the [add] method of the [journal] object;
  • line 39: [Comparator.comparing(f)] constructs a comparator that compares the values of [f] (here, age); [thenComparing] specifies the tiebreaker to use in case of a tie (here, name). The record [Personne] (lines 60–65) provides the accessors [age()] and [nom()]; we have redefined its method [toString] to shorten the display output;
  • lines 41–42: [comparingInt] avoids converting the age to [Integer], [reversed] reverses the order obtained so far, and the second form of [thenComparing] takes, in addition to the criterion, the comparator to be used for that criterion: [Comparator.reverseOrder()], the reversed natural order;
  • lines 45–46: [BinaryOperator.minBy] converts a comparator into a function that returns the smaller of its two parameters;
  • lines 50–58: the method [filtrer] used for these tests. Its parameter is of type [Predicate<? super T>] rather than [Predicate<T>]: it therefore accepts, to filter a list of [String], a [Predicate<String>] as well as a [Predicate<Object>] or a [Predicate<CharSequence>]. This is the rule followed throughout the Java library: a functional parameter that consumes [T] is declared with [? super T], and a parameter that produces them is declared with [? extends T].

These methods allow you to write complex processes by combining simple functions, without writing a single class. We’ll revisit them with the API Stream.

docs.title: 7.3.4. Variable Capture and Closures
docs.text:
A lambda can use the local variables of the method in which it is defined. It is said to capture these variables. Java enforces an important rule in this regard, which distinguishes the language from many others (C#, JavaScript, Python): a captured local variable must be “effectively final,” meaning it is never modified after its initialization, neither in the method nor in the lambda. The program [Lambdas06.java] demonstrates what this rule allows and prohibits:

// variable capture and closures

// a field of the implicit class: lambdas can modify it
int nbAppels;

void main() {
     // 1 - a lambda can use the local variables surrounding it...
    int seuil = 5;
    Predicate<Integer> depasse = n -> n > seuil;
    IO.println("seuil=" + seuil + " : depasse(7)=" + depasse.test(7));
     // ... provided they are actually final: threshold = 10; would be rejected
    int autreSeuil = 10;
    Predicate<Integer> depasseAutre = n -> n > autreSeuil;
    IO.println("seuil=" + autreSeuil + " : depasse(7)=" + depasseAutre.test(7));

     // 2 - a lambda cannot modify a captured local variable...
     // int total = 0; IntConsumer accumulate = n -> total  += n; // rejected
     // ... but it can modify the object it references
    AtomicInteger total = new AtomicInteger();
    IntConsumer cumuler = n -> total.addAndGet(n);
    cumuler.accept(3);
    cumuler.accept(4);
    IO.println("total=" + total.get());
     // ... or a field of the current object (the lambda captures `this`)
    Runnable compter = () -> nbAppels++;
    compter.run();
    compter.run();
    IO.println("nbAppels=" + nbAppels);

     // 3 - a closure: the captured object survives the method that created it
    IntSupplier compteurA = creerCompteur();
    IntSupplier compteurB = creerCompteur();
    IO.println("A : " + compteurA.getAsInt() + " " + compteurA.getAsInt() + " " + compteurA.getAsInt());
    IO.println("B : " + compteurB.getAsInt() + " " + compteurB.getAsInt());

     // 4 - the for loop: the variable i changes; it cannot be captured
    List<Runnable> actions = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
         // actions.add(() -> IO.print(i +  " ")); // rejected: i is not actually final
        int copie = i;
        actions.add(() -> IO.print(copie + " "));
    }
    IO.print("for, capture d'une copie : ");
    actions.forEach(Runnable::run);
    IO.println();

     // The for-each loop declares a new variable on each iteration: it is effectively final
    actions.clear();
    for (int j : new int[] { 0, 1, 2 }) {
        actions.add(() -> IO.print(j + " "));
    }
    IO.print("for-each : ");
    actions.forEach(Runnable::run);
    IO.println();
}

// a method that returns a function
static IntSupplier creerCompteur() {
     // local object captured by the returned lambda
    AtomicInteger valeur = new AtomicInteger();
    return () -> valeur.incrementAndGet();
}

Results:

> java Lambdas06.java
seuil=5 : depasse(7)=true
seuil=10 : depasse(7)=false
total=7
nbAppels=2
A : 1 2 3
B : 1 2
for, capture d'une copie : 0 1 2 
for-each : 0 1 2

Comments:

  • Line 9: The lambda uses the local variable [seuil] declared on line 8. [seuil] is not a parameter of the lambda; it is a captured variable. The variable is never modified: it is effectively final, without the need to declare it as [final] (which was required up to Java 7 for anonymous classes);
  • Line 11: If we were to add [seuil = 10;] after the lambda is created, the compiler would reject the lambda on line 9: *[local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final]. To change the threshold, we create another variable and another lambda (lines 12–13). Conversely, the question “Does the lambda see the variable’s value at the time of its creation, or its value at the time of its execution?” does not arise in Java: the two are identical. Specifically, the lambda receives a copy* of the variable’s value when it is created;
  • line 17: for the same reason, a lambda cannot modify a captured local variable: [n -> total += n] is rejected, with the same message;
  • Lines 19–23: The captured variable [total] does not change; it still references the same object, [AtomicInteger]. However, nothing prevents the lambda from modifying the state of this object. The class [AtomicInteger] in the package [java.util.concurrent.atomic] encapsulates a mutable integer ([addAndGet], [incrementAndGet], [get]…), which can be safely used by multiple threads (Chapter 8). We also encounter the technique of a single-element array ([int[] total = {0};] followed by [total[0] += n]), which does not have this latter property;
  • lines 4 and 25–28: the rule applies only to local variables. A lambda can read and modify the fields of the current object: it then captures the reference [this], which itself does not change. The field [nbAppels] is a field of the implicit class of the compact source file; since the method [main] is an instance method, the lambda can increment it;
  • Lines 58–62: The method *[creerCompteur] returns a lambda that captures its local variable *[valeur]*. Normally, a local variable is destroyed when the method ends. Here, the returned lambda has retained a copy of the reference [valeur], and the referenced object [AtomicInteger] survives [creerCompteur]* as long as the lambda exists. The combination of the lambda and the values it captures is called a “closure.” To create it, the virtual machine stores the captured values in fields of the object it creates for the lambda;
  • lines 31–34: Each call to [creerCompteur] creates a new [AtomicInteger] object—and thus a new counter—that is independent of the others. The results (lines 6–7) confirm this;
  • lines 38–42: In a standard [for] loop, the variable [i] is modified on each iteration ([i++]): it is not effectively final, and the lambda on line 39 would be rejected. In other languages, this capture is allowed and leads to an unexpected result: the three lambdas share the same variable [i] and all print 3, its value, at the end of the loop. Java eliminates this pitfall at compile time. The solution is to declare a variable *[copie]* within the loop body—a new instance for each iteration that is never modified (line 40)—so that each lambda captures its own;
  • lines 49–51: with the “for each element” loop [for], the problem does not arise: the variable [j] is a new variable on each iteration, never modified, and therefore effectively final;
  • lines 44 and 53: the [forEach] method of the collections expects a [Consumer] and executes it on each element. Here, each element is itself a *[Runnable]*, and the reference *[Runnable::run]*** (any object of type *[Runnable]*, on which [run] is called) executes it.

The rule regarding effectively final variables may seem restrictive. However, it has a solid justification: a lambda may be executed later, or in another thread (Chapter 8). If it could modify the local variables of a method that may have already finished, or read them while another thread is modifying them, we would encounter behavior that is difficult to predict. By requiring that variables remain unchanged, Java prevents these situations; when a shared, mutable state is truly necessary, it is made explicit using an object ([AtomicInteger], collection…) whose behavior with respect to threads is specified.

docs.title: 7.4. Functional Interfaces or Interfaces?
docs.text:
In many languages, the concept of a “function passed as a parameter” (function pointer in C, delegate in C#) is distinct from the concept of an interface, and one might wonder which to choose. In Java, the question is framed differently, because the two concepts are one and the same: a lambda is an instance of an interface. Let’s take the example [Lambdas07.java], which is similar to [Lambdas02.java]:

// a parameter of type functional interface

void main() {
     // Execution of the add method
    IO.println(executer(Methodes::ajouter, 2, 3));
     // execution of the "subtract" method
    IO.println(executer(Methodes::soustraire, 2, 3));
     // Execution of a Java library method with the correct form
    IO.println(executer(Math::max, 2, 3));
     // execution of a lambda: no named method is required
    IO.println(executer((n1, n2) -> n1 * n2, 2, 3));
}

// Execution of an operation received as a parameter
static int executer(Operation op, int n1, int n2) {
    return op.calculer(n1, n2);
}

// Two methods with the form of the Operation interface
class Methodes {
    static int ajouter(int n1, int n2) {
        IO.println("ajouter(" + n1 + "," + n2 + ")");
        return n1 + n2;
    }

    static int soustraire(int n1, int n2) {
        IO.println("soustraire(" + n1 + "," + n2 + ")");
        return n1 - n2;
    }
}

// the functional interface
@FunctionalInterface
interface Operation {
    int calculer(int n1, int n2);
}

Results:

> java Lambdas07.java
ajouter(2,3)
5
soustraire(2,3)
-1
3
6

On line 15, the method *[executer] expects a parameter of the type defined by the functional interface *[Operation] on line 34. This allows us to pass different functions to it: static methods from our class [Methodes] (lines 5 and 7), a method from the Java library with the correct form (line 9: among the overloads of *[Math.max]*, the compiler chooses ***[int max(int a, int b)]*), and even a lambda (line 11): it was not necessary to write a multiplication method. This polymorphism is that of interfaces, covered in Chapter 4: the program [Lambdas08.java] demonstrates this by implementing the same interface with classes:

// Classes that implement the functional interface

void main() {
     // Execution of the Add operation
    IO.println(executer(new Ajouter(), 2, 3));
     // execution of the Subtract operation
    IO.println(executer(new Soustraire(), 2, 3));
     // The same `execute` method still accepts lambdas
    IO.println(executer((n1, n2) -> n1 * n2, 2, 3));
     // An interface with two abstract methods no longer accepts lambdas: a class is required
    OperationNommee division = new OperationNommee() {
        @Override
        public int calculer(int n1, int n2) {
            return n1 / n2;
        }

        @Override
        public String nom() {
            return "division entière";
        }
    };
    IO.println(division.nom() + " : " + division.calculer(7, 2));
}

// Execution of the single method of the Operation interface
static int executer(Operation op, int n1, int n2) {
    return op.calculer(n1, n2);
}

// Operation interface
interface Operation {
    int calculer(int n1, int n2);
}

// An interface that is not functional: two abstract methods
interface OperationNommee extends Operation {
    String nom();
}

// Add class
class Ajouter implements Operation {
    @Override
    public int calculer(int n1, int n2) {
        IO.println("Ajouter(" + n1 + "," + n2 + ")");
        return n1 + n2;
    }
}

// Subtract class
class Soustraire implements Operation {
    @Override
    public int calculer(int n1, int n2) {
        IO.println("Soustraire(" + n1 + "," + n2 + ")");
        return n1 - n2;
    }
}

Results:

> java Lambdas08.java
Ajouter(2,3)
5
Soustraire(2,3)
-1
6
division entière : 3

Comments:

  • Lines 31–33: The [Operation] interface defines a method [calculer]. It is not annotated [@FunctionalInterface]: The annotation is merely a check, and any interface with a single abstract method is functional;
  • lines 41–47 and 50–56: the classes [Ajouter] and [Soustraire] implement the interface [Operation];
  • lines 26–28: the method [executer], whose first parameter is of the type of the interface [Operation]. It receives, in succession, an instance of the [Ajouter] class, an instance of the [Soustraire] class (lines 5 and 7), and then a lambda (line 9). For [executer], these three objects are of the same type: objects that implement [Operation];
  • Lines 36–38: The [OperationNommee] interface inherits the [calculer] method and adds a [nom] method. With two abstract methods, it is no longer functional: it can no longer be implemented using a lambda; a class is required—in this case, an anonymous class (lines 11–21).

These two examples show that in Java, you don’t have to choose between two mechanisms: a method that expects an interface with a single method accepts objects from classes written for the occasion, method references, and lambdas alike. The real question, then, is: should the interface be functional, with a single method, or should it have multiple methods?

  • A single-method interface—whether predefined ([Function], [Predicate]…) or not—proves to be more flexible to use: any existing method with the correct form will do, and a lambda even allows you to write the function right at the point of the call. There is no class to write. This flexibility explains why modern libraries (the API Stream, the asynchronous programming in Chapter 9, Spring) make extensive use of functional interfaces;
  • an interface with multiple methods regains the advantage as soon as the behavior to be implemented involves several interrelated operations ([calculer] and [nom] above), or when it requires its own state and identity.

This is the case for the [IImpotDao] interface in the [dao] layer from Chapter 6: although it has only one method, [List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot()], its implementations have state (the chunks read, the file name), are created by the dependency injection container, and represent a clearly named role within the application. A [Supplier<List<TrancheImpot>>] would technically have sufficed, but it would have been much less descriptive. We therefore reserve functional interfaces for short, one-off behaviors (a criterion, a transformation, an action), and “business” interfaces for the application’s roles, regardless of the number of methods they contain.

docs.title: 7.5.1. The Listener Model
docs.text:
Functional interfaces are used to set up events. Java does not have a dedicated keyword for events: it uses a set of conventions, known as the “listener model,” established as early as Java 1.1 for graphical components and JavaBeans. A class [C1] that wants to signal an event [Xxx] proceeds as follows:

  • A [XxxEvent] class, derived from [java.util.EventObject], encapsulates the event information. [EventObject] stores the object that triggered the event—referred to as the source—which is obtained via [getSource()];
  • an interface [XxxListener], which extends the empty interface [java.util.EventListener] (a simple marker), defines the method(s) that will be called when the event occurs. With a single method, it is a functional interface: a listener can be a lambda;
  • The [C1] class manages a list of listeners and provides two public methods for subscribing to and unsubscribing from it: [addXxxListener(XxxListener l)] and [removeXxxListener(XxxListener l)];
  • When an instance of [c1] (derived from [C1]) wants to signal the event, it creates a [XxxEvent] object and calls the method of each registered listener, passing this object to it. By convention, this notification is handled by a protected method [fireXxx(XxxEvent e)] (“fire”), which a derived class can override to modify how the event is published;
  • if a [c2] object wants to be notified of the [Xxx] event from the [c1] object, it registers itself using [c1.addXxxListener(...)]. It can unsubscribe via [c1.removeXxxListener(...)] when it no longer wishes to be notified. Since [c1] manages a list, different objects can subscribe to be notified of the same event.

In this scenario, we have:

  • a class that signals (also called “publishes” or “emits”) an event;
  • objects that are notified of this event. They are said to subscribe to or register for the event: these are the listeners, or event handlers;
  • a listener interface that defines the signature of the methods that will be notified of the event.

This is the Observer design pattern: the emitter does not know its subscribers; it simply notifies them. This model offers the same protection as a dedicated keyword: the list of listeners is a private field of the emitter. From the outside, one can only subscribe or unsubscribe; one cannot clear the list, replace other listeners, or trigger the event in place of the emitter.

docs.title: 7.5.2. An example: excessively high temperature
docs.text:
Consider the following example:

  • A class named [Emetteur] encapsulates a temperature. When this temperature exceeds a certain threshold, an event must be triggered. We’ll call this event [TemperatureTropHaute]. Information about this event will be encapsulated in a [TemperatureTropHauteEvent] object, and the listeners will implement the [TemperatureTropHauteListener] interface;
  • a class named [Souscripteur] registers as a listener for the aforementioned event. When it is notified of the event, it displays a message on the console. A listener unsubscribes automatically after receiving a specified number of alerts;
  • A console program creates a publisher and two subscribers. It enters temperatures via the keyboard and stores them in the publisher. If any of them is too high, the publisher signals the [TemperatureTropHaute] event.

All these classes are grouped together in the compact source file [Lambdas09.java], which we present in three parts. First, here are the event class, the listener interface, and the class [Emetteur]:

// Information carried by the event
class TemperatureTropHauteEvent extends EventObject {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
     // Temperature at the time of the event
    private final double temperature;
     // time of the event
    private final LocalTime heure = LocalTime.now();

    TemperatureTropHauteEvent(Emetteur source, double temperature) {
        super(source);
        this.temperature = temperature;
    }

     // The source must be a Transmitter: we redefine getSource with a more specific type
    @Override
    public Emetteur getSource() {
        return (Emetteur) super.getSource();
    }

    double getTemperature() {
        return temperature;
    }

    LocalTime getHeure() {
        return heure;
    }
}

// the interface that event listeners must implement
@FunctionalInterface
interface TemperatureTropHauteListener extends EventListener {
    void temperatureTropHaute(TemperatureTropHauteEvent e);
}

// the class that signals the event
class Emetteur {
     // event trigger threshold
    static final double SEUIL = 19;
     // transmitter name
    private final String nom;
     // observed temperature
    private double temperature;
     // registered listeners
    private final List<TemperatureTropHauteListener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    Emetteur(String nom) {
        this.nom = nom;
    }

    String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    double getTemperature() {
        return temperature;
    }

    void setTemperature(double temperature) {
        this.temperature = temperature;
        if (temperature > SEUIL) {
             // The event is reported to the listeners
            fireTemperatureTropHaute(new TemperatureTropHauteEvent(this, temperature));
        }
    }

     // Listener registration
    void addTemperatureTropHauteListener(TemperatureTropHauteListener listener) {
        listeners.add(Objects.requireNonNull(listener));
    }

     // Unregistration of a listener
    void removeTemperatureTropHauteListener(TemperatureTropHauteListener listener) {
        listeners.remove(listener);
    }

     // Notification of the event to all registered listeners
    protected void fireTemperatureTropHaute(TemperatureTropHauteEvent e) {
        for (TemperatureTropHauteListener listener : listeners) {
            listener.temperatureTropHaute(e);
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 1–28: The class [TemperatureTropHauteEvent] derives from [EventObject], as per convention. Its constructor (lines 10–13) passes the event source to the constructor of [EventObject] ([super(source)]) and stores the temperature that triggered the event. We have added the event time, [heure] (line 8). The fields are [final], and the class has only read-only accessors: a listener must not be able to modify the event information for subsequent listeners;
  • lines 3–4: [EventObject] implements the [Serializable] interface (so that events can be logged or transmitted over a network). The compiler, when using the [-Xlint:all] option, then requires each derived class to declare a version number [serialVersionUID]. The [@Serial] annotation (Java 14) flags this specific field to the compiler;
  • lines 16–19: The [getSource] method of [EventObject] returns a [Object]. We redefine it with a more specific return type, [Emetteur], which Java allows (covariant return type): listeners will not have to cast the source. We cannot use a *[record]* here: a record cannot inherit from any class, and therefore cannot inherit from *[EventObject]*;
  • Lines 30–34: the listener interface. It extends [EventListener] and declares a single method, [temperatureTropHaute], which receives the event object: this is a functional interface;
  • line 39: the temperature threshold above which the [TemperatureTropHaute] event is triggered;
  • line 41: the emitter has a name for identification;
  • line 45: the list of registered listeners. This is a [CopyOnWriteArrayList] from the [java.util.concurrent] package, a list that, whenever it is modified, copies its contents into a new array. A current iteration therefore continues on the old array, even if the list is modified in the meantime. We’ll see later why this is essential here. This list is the standard type for listener lists: the list is traversed for each event, but it is rarely modified;
  • lines 59–65: the method [setTemperature] records the new temperature and signals the event if it exceeds the threshold;
  • line 63: Publishing is handled by the [fireTemperatureTropHaute] method, to which a [TemperatureTropHauteEvent] object is passed; this object originates from the transmitter itself ([this]) and contains the temperature that exceeded the threshold;
  • lines 68–70: Registering a listener adds it to the list. [Objects.requireNonNull] immediately rejects a listener [null], which would otherwise trigger a [NullPointerException] much later, during notification;
  • lines 73–75: Unregistration removes the listener from the list. The method [remove] searches for the object to be removed using [equals]; therefore, it must be passed the same object that was registered;
  • lines 78–82: The notification calls the [temperatureTropHaute] method for each registered listener, in the order in which they were registered. If there are no listeners, the loop does nothing: there are no special cases to handle.

Here is the [Souscripteur] class:

// A class that registers as a listener for the event
class Souscripteur {
     // subscriber name
    private final String nom;
     // maximum number of alerts accepted
    private final int nbAlertesMax;
     // number of alerts received
    private int nbAlertes;
     // the listener, created only once so it can be unsubscribed
    private final TemperatureTropHauteListener ecouteur = this::evtTemperatureTropHaute;

    Souscripteur(String nom, int nbAlertesMax) {
        this.nom = nom;
        this.nbAlertesMax = nbAlertesMax;
    }

     // registration with a sender
    void abonner(Emetteur emetteur) {
        emetteur.addTemperatureTropHauteListener(ecouteur);
    }

     // unsubscription
    void desabonner(Emetteur emetteur) {
        emetteur.removeTemperatureTropHauteListener(ecouteur);
    }

     // event manager TemperatureTropHaute
    private void evtTemperatureTropHaute(TemperatureTropHauteEvent e) {
        Emetteur emetteur = e.getSource();
        IO.println("Souscripteur [%s] : la source [%s] a signalé une température trop haute : [%.1f]"
                .formatted(nom, emetteur.getNom(), e.getTemperature()));
         // After receiving alerts from nbAlertesMax, the subscriber unsubscribes
        nbAlertes++;
        if (nbAlertes == nbAlertesMax) {
            desabonner(emetteur);
            IO.println("Souscripteur [%s] : désabonné après %d alerte(s)".formatted(nom, nbAlertes));
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 4–6: Each subscriber is identified by a name and is assigned the maximum number of alerts it accepts ([nbAlertesMax]);
  • line 10: the subscriber’s listener is a reference to its private method [evtTemperatureTropHaute]. We saw with [Lambdas04.java] that two evaluations of [this::evtTemperatureTropHaute] produce two different objects. If we were to write [emetteur.addTemperatureTropHauteListener(this::evtTemperatureTropHaute)] into [abonner] and then [emetteur.removeTemperatureTropHauteListener(this::evtTemperatureTropHaute)] into [desabonner], unsubscribing would not remove anything, and no error message would be displayed! So we create the listener once and store it in a field;
  • lines 18–20: subscription to a publisher. This is the subscriber’s responsibility; the subscriber knows which object to remove to unsubscribe;
  • lines 23–25: Unsubscribing removes the same object, [ecouteur]. Each subscriber has their own object, [ecouteur]: [remove] removes only the one belonging to the subscriber in question;
  • line 28: the event handler. It has the form specified by the [TemperatureTropHauteListener] interface. It is private: only the subscriber can register it with a publisher. Another very common approach is to have the [Souscripteur] class itself ([class Souscripteur implements TemperatureTropHauteListener]) implement the listener interface and register with [this]. The drawback of this approach is that it makes the [temperatureTropHaute] method public, which anyone could then call;
  • line 29: thanks to the redefinition of [getSource], the event source is directly of type [Emetteur];
  • lines 30–31: the handler displays the subscriber’s name, the name of the sender that reported the event, and the temperature that triggered it. The [%.1f] format displays the real number with one decimal place, in accordance with French conventions;
  • Lines 33–37: After the [nbAlertesMax] alerts, the subscriber unsubscribes from the publisher. The subscriber does this during the event notification, from its own handler—that is, while the [fireTemperatureTropHaute] method iterates through the list of listeners. This is safe thanks to [CopyOnWriteArrayList]: [remove] creates a new array, but the current iteration continues on the old one.

Here, finally, is the main program:

// Event management: a publisher and listeners

void main() {
     // creating an event publisher
    var e1 = new Emetteur("e");
     // Creating two subscribers that subscribe to e1
    List<Souscripteur> souscripteurs = List.of(new Souscripteur("s0", 3), new Souscripteur("s1", 1));
    for (Souscripteur souscripteur : souscripteurs) {
        souscripteur.abonner(e1);
    }
     // A third listener: a lambda
    e1.addTemperatureTropHauteListener(
            e -> IO.println("Journal : %.1f °C à %tT".formatted(e.getTemperature(), e.getHeure())));

     // Temperatures are read from the keyboard
    while (true) {
        String saisie = IO.readln("Température (rien pour arrêter) : ");
         // End of input? (readln returns null if standard input is closed)
        if (saisie == null || saisie.isBlank()) {
            break;
        }
        try {
             // Decimal point accepted
            double temperature = Double.parseDouble(saisie.strip().replace(',', '.'));
             // Temperature is correct—it is stored in the transmitter
            e1.setTemperature(temperature);
        } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
             // reporting the error
            IO.println("Température incorrecte");
        }
    }
}

Results:

> java Lambdas09.java
Température (rien pour arrêter) : 17
Température (rien pour arrêter) : 21
