Souscripteur [s0] : la source [e] a signalé une température trop haute : [21,0]
Souscripteur [s1] : la source [e] a signalé une température trop haute : [21,0]
Souscripteur [s1] : désabonné après 1 alerte(s)
Journal : 21,0 °C à 18:58:41
Température (rien pour arrêter) : abc
Température incorrecte
Température (rien pour arrêter) : 22,5
Souscripteur [s0] : la source [e] a signalé une température trop haute : [22,5]
Journal : 22,5 °C à 18:58:41
Température (rien pour arrêter) : 25
Souscripteur [s0] : la source [e] a signalé une température trop haute : [25,0]
Souscripteur [s0] : désabonné après 3 alerte(s)
Journal : 25,0 °C à 18:58:41
Température (rien pour arrêter) : 30
Journal : 30,0 °C à 18:58:41
Température (rien pour arrêter) :

Comments:

  • line 5: creation of the sender;
  • lines 7–10: creation of two subscribers, [s0] (up to 3 alerts) and [s1] (1 alert), which are registered with the sender;
  • lines 12–13: a third listener, a lambda, which acts as a log. The type of the parameter [e] is inferred from that of the parameter [addTemperatureTropHauteListener]. The format [%tT] displays a time in the form [HH:mm:ss]. This lambda cannot be unregistered: it would need to have been stored in a variable in order to pass it to [removeTemperatureTropHauteListener]. Therefore, lambdas written directly in the registration call are reserved for listeners that remain registered as long as the sender exists;
  • lines 16–31: loop for entering temperatures via the keyboard. [IO.readln(invite)] displays the prompt and reads a line; it returns [null] if standard input is closed, which is treated as an empty entry (line 19);
  • line 24: [Double.parseDouble] accepts only the decimal point. To allow a French user to type [22,5], the comma is replaced with a period. If the input is not a number, [parseDouble] triggers a [NumberFormatException], which is intercepted on line 27;
  • line 26: if the entered temperature is valid, it is transmitted to the [e1] transmitter, which signals the [TemperatureTropHaute] event if it is greater than 19 °C.

The results show (the standard input was fed by a file, which explains why all hours are identical):

  • line 2: 17 °C does not exceed the threshold: no event;
  • lines 3–7: 21 °C triggers the event. The three listeners are notified in the order in which they were registered. [s1], which accepts only one alert, unsubscribes immediately, but this does not prevent the log, registered after it, from being notified;
  • lines 10–12: [s1] is no longer notified;
  • lines 13–16: [s0] receives its third alert and unsubscribes in turn;
  • line 18: only the log remains.

What would happen if there were simply a [ArrayList] on line 45 of the first excerpt, in the [Emetteur] class? We tested this: when [s1] unsubscribes while the list is being processed, the subsequent elements are skipped and the processing stops immediately. The log is not notified of temperatures 21 and 25, with no error message. In other configurations, the iteration triggers a [ConcurrentModificationException]. A list of listeners must therefore always be able to handle changes while it is being iterated over: the [CopyOnWriteArrayList] is designed for this purpose, and it also supports subscriptions and unsubscriptions made by other threads (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.5.3. Property Change Events
docs.text:
The most common type of event occurs when an object’s property changes value: another object (a graphical user interface, a cache, a log) wants to be notified of this change. The Java library provides a ready-to-use class for this purpose, [java.beans.PropertyChangeSupport], which manages the list of listeners for us. Listeners implement the functional interface [PropertyChangeListener], whose method [void propertyChange(PropertyChangeEvent evt)] receives an event containing the source, the property name, and its old and new values. The program [Lambdas10.java] uses it:

// property change events: java.beans.PropertyChangeSupport

import java.beans.PropertyChangeListener;
import java.beans.PropertyChangeSupport;

void main() {
    var thermometre = new Thermometre("salon");
     // a listener for all properties
    PropertyChangeListener journal = e -> IO.println("Journal : %s.%s : %s -> %s".formatted(
            ((Thermometre) e.getSource()).getNom(), e.getPropertyName(), e.getOldValue(), e.getNewValue()));
    thermometre.addPropertyChangeListener(journal);
     // a listener for the temperature property only
    thermometre.addPropertyChangeListener("temperature", e -> {
        if ((double) e.getNewValue() > 19) {
            IO.println("Alerte : température trop haute");
        }
    });

    thermometre.setTemperature(18);
    thermometre.setTemperature(21.5);
     // same value: no events
    thermometre.setTemperature(21.5);
    thermometre.setNom("séjour");
     // unsubscription from the log
    thermometre.removePropertyChangeListener(journal);
    thermometre.setTemperature(22);
    IO.println("écouteurs restants : " + thermometre.getNbEcouteurs());
}

// a class whose properties signal changes
class Thermometre {
     // Listener management is delegated to an object PropertyChangeSupport
    private final PropertyChangeSupport changements = new PropertyChangeSupport(this);
    private String nom;
    private double temperature;

    Thermometre(String nom) {
        this.nom = nom;
    }

    String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    void setNom(String nom) {
        String ancien = this.nom;
        this.nom = nom;
        changements.firePropertyChange("nom", ancien, nom);
    }

    double getTemperature() {
        return temperature;
    }

    void setTemperature(double temperature) {
        double ancienne = this.temperature;
        this.temperature = temperature;
        changements.firePropertyChange("temperature", ancienne, temperature);
    }

     // registering and unregistering listeners
    void addPropertyChangeListener(PropertyChangeListener listener) {
        changements.addPropertyChangeListener(listener);
    }

    void addPropertyChangeListener(String propriete, PropertyChangeListener listener) {
        changements.addPropertyChangeListener(propriete, listener);
    }

    void removePropertyChangeListener(PropertyChangeListener listener) {
        changements.removePropertyChangeListener(listener);
    }

    int getNbEcouteurs() {
        return changements.getPropertyChangeListeners().length;
    }
}

Results:

> java Lambdas10.java
Journal : salon.temperature : 0.0 -> 18.0
Journal : salon.temperature : 18.0 -> 21.5
Alerte : température trop haute
Journal : séjour.nom : salon -> séjour
Alerte : température trop haute
écouteurs restants : 1

Comments:

  • lines 3–4: The package [java.beans] belongs to the module [java.desktop], not to the module [java.base]: it must be explicitly imported, even in a compact source file;
  • Line 33: The class [Thermometre] delegates the management of its listeners to an object [PropertyChangeSupport], which is constructed using the event source ([this]). The methods on lines 62–72 simply pass subscription and unsubscription events to it;
  • Lines 45–49 and 55–59: Each modifier stores the old value, records the new one, and calls [firePropertyChange] with the property name and both values. [firePropertyChange] notifies listeners only if the two values are different: line 22 produces no output;
  • lines 9–11: a first listener, a lambda stored in a variable so it can be unsubscribed (line 25). It is subscribed for all of the object’s properties. [e.getSource()] returns a [Object], which must be cast. The values are objects: the [double] objects have been converted to [Double], whose [toString] method uses the decimal point;
  • lines 13–17: a second sensor, registered solely for the [temperature] property. It triggers an alert when the temperature exceeds 19 °C;
  • lines 19–26: property changes. The name change (line 23) is reported only to the log. On line 5 of the results, the log displays the source’s new name, [séjour]: the event is reported after the change;
  • lines 26–27: After unsubscribing from the log, only the alert is displayed, and only one listener remains.

Without writing an event class or a listener interface, we thus obtain a complete mechanism. This is the one used by Swing GUI components and JavaBeans; JavaFX has its own, very similar mechanism based on observable properties.

docs.title: 7.6. Lambdas and the API Stream
docs.text:
In Chapter 5, we used the methods of the API Stream ([filter], [map], [sorted]…) by passing lambda expressions to them. We now know what these parameters are: the [filter] method is declared as follows in the [java.util.stream.Stream<T>] interface: [Stream<T> filter(Predicate<? super T> predicate)].

Its parameter is a [Predicate]: any method or lambda that takes one element and returns a boolean will work. Similarly, [map] expects a [Function<? super T, ? extends R>], [sorted] expects a [Comparator], [forEach] expects a [Consumer], [reduce] expects a [BinaryOperator]… To fully understand how API works, let’s write our own filtering and transformation operations. This is the [Lambdas11.java] program:

// Lambdas and the API Stream

void main() {
    List<Integer> nombres = List.of(3, 8, 1, 6, 5, 4, 9, 2);

     // 1 - `filter` and `map` expect a `Predicate<T>` and a `Function<T, R>`
    Predicate<Integer> estPair = n -> n % 2 == 0;
    Function<Integer, Integer> carre = n -> n * n;
    List<Integer> carresPairs = nombres.stream().filter(estPair).map(carre).toList();
    IO.println("Stream : " + carresPairs);

     // 2 - our own filtering method, called with a lambda followed by a method reference
    IO.println("filtrer(n > 4) : " + Outils.filtrer(nombres, n -> n > 4));
    IO.println("filtrer(estImpair) : " + Outils.filtrer(nombres, Outils::estImpair));

     // 3 - Execution is deferred: the predicate is only called by the terminal operation
    Stream<Integer> grands = nombres.stream().filter(n -> {
        IO.print("[test " + n + "] ");
        return n > 7;
    });
    IO.println("le flux est défini, rien n'a encore été exécuté");
    grands.forEach(n -> IO.print("-> " + n + " "));
    IO.println();

     // 4 - Our own intermediate operations with intermediate collectors (Gatherer, Java 24)
    List<String> villes = List.of("Angers", "Paris", "Lyon", "Nantes", "Aix");
    List<String> resultat = villes.stream()
            .gather(Outils.filtrer(v -> v.length() <= 5))
            .gather(Outils.transformer(String::toUpperCase))
            .toList();
    IO.println("gatherers : " + resultat);
}

class Outils {
     // filters a list using a predicate: the work performed by the `filter` method
    static <T> List<T> filtrer(List<T> source, Predicate<? super T> predicat) {
        List<T> resultat = new ArrayList<>();
        for (T element : source) {
            if (predicat.test(element)) {
                resultat.add(element);
            }
        }
        return resultat;
    }

    static boolean estImpair(int n) {
        return n % 2 != 0;
    }

     // an intermediate stream operation that only lets through elements that satisfy the predicate
    static <T> Gatherer<T, ?, T> filtrer(Predicate<? super T> predicat) {
        return Gatherer.of((_, element, aval) -> !predicat.test(element) || aval.push(element));
    }

     // an intermediate operation that transforms each element: the equivalent of `map`
    static <T, R> Gatherer<T, ?, R> transformer(Function<? super T, ? extends R> transformation) {
        return Gatherer.of((_, element, aval) -> aval.push(transformation.apply(element)));
    }
}

Results:

> java Lambdas11.java
Stream : [64, 36, 16, 4]
filtrer(n > 4) : [8, 6, 5, 9]
filtrer(estImpair) : [3, 1, 5, 9]
le flux est défini, rien n'a encore été exécuté
[test 3] [test 8] -> 8 [test 1] [test 6] [test 5] [test 4] [test 9] -> 9 [test 2] 
gatherers : [PARIS, LYON, AIX]

Comments:

  • Lines 7–9: The lambda from [filter] is first stored in a variable of type [Predicate<Integer>] to reveal its type. [map], in turn, receives a [Function<Integer, Integer>] that transforms each element: this yields the squares of the even numbers;
  • lines 36–44: our method [filtrer]. It is generic: it filters a list of elements of any type [T], using a predicate of type [Predicate<? super T>]. It iterates over the list, calls the predicate (line 39) on each element, and returns the list of selected elements;
  • Line 13: call to [filtrer] with a lambda. The type [T] is inferred from the list: [Integer]. Line 14: a method reference is passed to it: [estImpair] (line 46) receives a [int]; the compiler adds the conversion from [Integer];
  • Lines 17–20: a verbose predicate that displays each element it tests. The result (lines 5–6) shows that the flow definition does not execute anything: the message on line 21 is displayed before the first test. It is only when the terminal operation [forEach] (line 22) requests the elements that the predicate executes, and the tests alternate with the displays from [forEach]: each element passes through the entire flow before the next one enters it. This is deferred (or lazy) execution of the streams. Our method [filtrer], on the other hand, builds the entire result list before returning it;
  • lines 51–58: to write our own intermediate operations—lazy like those in API—we use the intermediate collectors ([Gatherer], Java 24), which are the counterparts for intermediate operations of the collectors ([Collector]) used by [collect]. [Gatherer.of] receives a lambda with three parameters, called for each element in the stream: a state (unnecessary here, hence the anonymous parameter [_]), the element, and the next stage in the flow ([aval]), to which an element is passed via [aval.push(...)]. The lambda returns [false] to stop the stream; our functions never decide this on their own: they return the result of [push], which is equal to [false] only if the downstream component no longer wants any elements (or [true] when the filter discards an element). The filter (line 52) transmits only the elements that satisfy the predicate; the transformation (line 57) transmits the result of the function applied to each element;
  • line 56: [transformer] is doubly generic: [T] is the type of the received elements, and [R] is the type of the produced elements. The parameter [Function<? super T, ? extends R>] follows the rule we’ve already encountered: the function consumes [T] and produces [R];
  • lines 27–30: The [gather] stream method inserts our operations into the string, which is written the same way as for the operations in API: we keep cities with 5 letters or fewer, then capitalize them.

The entire API stream is built on this model: operations that receive functional interfaces and produce new streams, whose elements are calculated only upon request by the terminal operation.

docs.title: 7.7. Expression Trees
docs.text:
Some languages, such as C#, allow a lambda to be converted not into executable code, but into a data structure that describes it (an “expression tree”): a program can then parse the lambda [t -> t.getLimite() > 20000] and translate it, for example, into a clause SQL [WHERE limite > 20000] executed by the database server.

Java has no equivalent. A Java lambda is always compiled into executable code: you can call it, but you cannot examine what it does. Database access libraries therefore use other means to express a query. Hibernate, which we will cover in Chapter 11, offers two solutions: a query language similar to SQL but expressed in terms of classes and properties, HQL (["from Tranche t where t.limite > 20000"]), and Jakarta Persistence’s API Criteria, which constructs the query through method calls ([cb.gt(t.get("limite"), 20000)]). In both cases, the query is data (a string or an object tree) that Hibernate translates into SQL, whereas a lambda passed to [filter] is executed within the Java program.

docs.title: 7.8. Conclusion
docs.text:
Key takeaways from this chapter:

  • A functional interface is an interface that has only one abstract method. The predefined interfaces in the [java.util.function] package ([Function], [Supplier], [Consumer], [Predicate], their two-parameter variants, and their primitive versions), along with [Runnable], [Callable], and [Comparator], usually eliminate the need to define your own; when one is defined, it is annotated as [@FunctionalInterface];
  • A functional interface can be implemented by a class (named or anonymous), by a lambda expression, or by a method reference ([Classe::statique], [objet::methode], [Classe::methode], [Classe::new]). A lambda has no type of its own: the target type determines it;
  • Lambdas capture the local variables surrounding them, provided that those variables are actually final; mutable state is handled through an object or a field;
  • The methods [andThen], [compose], [and], [negate], [comparing], [thenComparing]… build new functions from existing ones;
  • In Java, a lambda is an instance of an interface: a functional interface is chosen for short, one-time behavior, while an interface with multiple methods (or a “business” interface) is chosen for an application role;
  • an event is set up using the listener pattern: a class [XxxEvent] derived from [EventObject], an interface [XxxListener], methods [addXxxListener] / [removeXxxListener], and a list of listeners ([CopyOnWriteArrayList]) iterated over by a method [fireXxx]. To unsubscribe a listener, you must retain the subscribed object. [PropertyChangeSupport] provides this mechanism out of the box for property changes;
  • the API Stream is built on operations that accept functional interfaces; Java does not have expression trees, and Hibernate expresses its queries in HQL or using the API Criteria.

Lambdas will reappear in all subsequent chapters: a thread executes a [Runnable], and a [ExecutorService] executes a [Callable] (Chapter 8), a [CompletableFuture] chains functions (Chapter 9), and Spring Boot web services handle HTTP requests in methods that the framework calls as listeners (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 14. Further Reading
docs.text: This document introduced the Java language and the most commonly used libraries for writing layered applications, network clients and servers, and web services. Here are the main topics that build on this.

docs.title: 14.1. Processing XML documents
docs.text:
JSON has largely replaced XML for data exchange, but XML is still in use (configuration files such as Maven’s [pom.xml], document formats, and existing SOAP services). The JDK provides several API files within the [javax.xml] package:

  • DOM ([DocumentBuilder], [Document], [Element]): the document is loaded into memory as a tree, which is then traversed and modified;
  • StAX ([XMLStreamReader], [XMLStreamWriter]): the document is read or written on the fly, without being loaded entirely into memory;
  • XPath ([javax.xml.xpath]) to query a document, and XSLT ([javax.xml.transform]) to transform it.

Apart from JDK, the Jakarta XML Binding library (JAXB) maps Java classes to XML documents, just as Jackson does for JSON (Chapter 5); Jackson can also read and write XML using its [jackson-dataformat-xml] module.

docs.title: 14.2. Web Applications
docs.text:
Chapter 13 covers only web services (applications that generate data). For web applications that generate HTML pages, the Java ecosystem offers:

  • Spring MVC with a template engine such as Thymeleaf: server-side generated pages; the author wrote the course “Step-by-Step Introduction to the Spring Web Framework MVC” (September 2026);
  • Jakarta EE (formerly Java EE), the set of specifications that includes servlets, JPA (Jakarta Persistence, Chapter 11), CDI (dependency injection) and JAX-RS (services REST), implemented by application servers such as WildFly, Payara, or Open Liberty;
  • other lighter or more recent frameworks: Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon, Javalin;
  • interfaces written in JavaScript (Vue.js, Angular, React) that consume Java web services; the author wrote the course “Step-by-Step Introduction to the Vue.js Framework” (September 2026).

docs.title: 14.3. Desktop and Mobile Applications
docs.text: This document does not cover graphical user interfaces: today, management applications are most often built with web interfaces. JDK still provides the Swing library, and the JavaFX library (distributed separately since Java 11 by the OpenJFX project) enables the development of modern desktop interfaces. The concepts covered in Chapters 7 (event listeners) and 9 (asynchronous programming) apply directly here. On mobile devices, Android apps are written in Java or, increasingly, in Kotlin, a language that also generates bytecode for the Java Virtual Machine.

docs.title: 14.4. Tests
docs.text:
Chapter 6 introduces JUnit. It is often supplemented by:

  • the AssertJ library, which provides more readable assertions ([assertThat(liste).hasSize(7).contains(x)]);
  • the Mockito library, which creates “mocks” (simulated objects) of the layers on which the layer under test depends;
  • Testcontainers, which launches a real database (MySQL, PostgreSQL…) in a Docker container for the duration of integration tests;
  • Spring Boot testing tools ([@SpringBootTest], [MockMvc]) for testing a web service without deploying it.

docs.title: 14.5. Performance
docs.text:
The Java virtual machine compiles bytecode on the fly and optimizes it during execution, resulting in excellent performance for programs that run for extended periods. Among the tools that go a step further:

  • the JMH tool (“Java Microbenchmark Harness”) to precisely measure code performance, taking into account the virtual machine’s warm-up time;
  • JDK Flight Recorder and JDK Mission Control, which record and analyze a program’s behavior in production;
  • ahead-of-time compilation to native code with GraalVM Native Image: a standalone executable that starts up in a few milliseconds, at the cost of restrictions on reflection; Spring Boot and Quarkus can generate such executables;
  • the choice of garbage collector (G1 by default, ZGC for very short pauses on large memory heaps).

docs.title: 14.6. Deployment
docs.text: A Java program can be deployed in several ways: as a [.jar] archive executed by a JDK installed on the machine ([java -jar application.jar]; Spring Boot produces a standalone [.jar] that contains all its libraries), as a standalone application that embeds a virtual machine stripped down to only what it needs ([jlink] and [jpackage] tools from JDK), or in a Docker container (Spring Boot directly produces a container image via [mvn spring-boot:build-image]).

docs.title: 14.7. Resources
docs.text:
• the official Java developers’ website, with its tutorials: https://dev.java;
  • the Java 25 documentation: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/;
  • Java development proposals (JEP), to stay up to date on new features in upcoming versions: https://openjdk.org/jeps/0;
  • the source code for JDK, on GitHub: https://github.com/openjdk/jdk;
  • the books *Effective Java* by Joshua Bloch and *Java Concurrency in Practice* by Brian Goetz et al. (Addison-Wesley).

docs.title: 11. Hibernate
docs.text:
The previous chapter showed how a Java application communicates with a database through a driver JDBC: a connection is opened, commands SQL are written, the rows of the result are read column by column, and they are copied into objects. This process of copying—from rows to objects and from objects to the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands—is repetitive. It can be automated using a tool: an “Object-Relational Mapper” (ORM). This chapter introduces the most widely used ORM in the Java world, Hibernate, and the standard it implements, Jakarta Persistence.

The chapter revisits the sample database from the articles in Chapter 10 and concludes with version 7 of the tax calculation application, whose ORM layer uses Hibernate.

docs.title: 11.1.1. Objects and Tables
docs.text:
A Java application works with objects: an item has a name, a price, and a stock level; an order has a customer and a list of line items, each of which refers to an item. A relational database stores this same information in tables: one row in the [articles] table per item, one row in the [commandes] table per order, with the relationships between rows expressed by foreign keys. The two worlds do not quite align:

  • an object directly references other objects ([commande.getClient()]); a row contains the primary key value of another row ([client_id]);
  • an object can contain a collection ([commande.getLignes()]); a table contains only single values; the collection is represented by the rows of another table that point to the order;
  • Java types ([String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate], [boolean]) and the types SQL ([varchar(30)], [decimal(10,2)], [date], [bit]) are not the same;
  • objects are queried using Java (and the API stream), while tables are queried using SQL.

A ORM bridges the two worlds. We define the correspondence between classes and tables (the model, or “mapping”) once and for all; it then takes care of:

  • translating queries written in a language that refers to objects (HQL) or constructed by Java code (the API Criteria);
  • to create objects from the read lines (this is called materialization);
  • to store the read objects and detect those that have been modified, added, or deleted;
  • generate the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands that reflect these changes in the database;
  • and, if necessary, to create and update the database schema (tables, columns, indexes) based on the classes.

The architecture of an application that uses Hibernate with MySQL is as follows:

  • [1]: the application. Its [dao] layer no longer communicates directly with the JDBC driver but with Hibernate, through a [Session] object and HQL queries;
  • [2]: Hibernate, independent of SGBD: model, query translation, change tracking, schema generation;
  • [3]: the dialect specific to SGBD (here, [MySQLDialect]): it knows the SQL syntax of SGBD, its column types, and its functions. The dialects of the main SGBDs are part of Hibernate itself: nothing needs to be added to the project;
  • [4]: the JDBC driver for SGBD, the one from Chapter 10 (MySQL Connector/J): Hibernate does not replace JDBC; it uses it;
  • [5]: the SGBD.

docs.title: 11.1.2. Jakarta Persistence and Hibernate
docs.text:
Hibernate was created in 2001 by Gavin King in response to the cumbersomeness of the “entity beans” in the Java EE platform of the time. Its success was such that its concepts were incorporated into a standard, JPA (Java Persistence API), released in 2006 with Java EE 5. When Java EE was transferred to the Eclipse Foundation and renamed Jakarta EE, JPA became Jakarta Persistence, and its packages changed from [javax.persistence] to [jakarta.persistence] (version 3.0, 2020). The current version is Jakarta Persistence 3.2 (2024).

Jakarta Persistence is a specification: a set of interfaces ([EntityManagerFactory], [EntityManager]...), annotations ([@Entity], [@Id], [@Column]...), and a query language, JPQL. It is implemented by several products: Hibernate ORM (the most widely used, used by Spring Boot and Quarkus), EclipseLink (the reference implementation)... This course uses Hibernate ORM 7.4.5, which implements Jakarta Persistence 3.2.

Hibernate offers two ways to use it:

  • exclusively through the standard interfaces: in this case, the code depends only on [jakarta.persistence], and it would in principle be possible to switch implementations;
  • through its own, more feature-rich “native” API, whose interfaces extend those of the standard: a [SessionFactory] is a [EntityManagerFactory], and a [Session] is a [EntityManager].

We use Hibernate’s own API, as recommended in its documentation: It provides all the standard methods ([persist], [find], [merge], [remove]...) as well as Hibernate’s extensions. The annotations, on the other hand, are always those defined by the standard. The following table shows the correspondences:

Jakarta PersistenceHibernateRole[EntityManagerFactory][SessionFactory]Hibernate configuration for a database: a heavy object, created once, shared by the entire application[EntityManager][Session]A database session: a lightweight, short-lived object[EntityTransaction][Transaction]a transactionJPQLHQLthe query language; HQL is a superset of JPQL[CriteriaBuilder][HibernateCriteriaBuilder]Query construction using Java code

docs.title: 11.1.3. Libraries
docs.text:
The libraries used in this chapter are as follows (they are summarized in the appendix on Maven dependencies):

Maven DependencyRole[org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core] 7.4.5.FinalHibernate itself; it includes the API from Jakarta Persistence 3.2 ([jakarta.persistence-api]) and its own dependencies (Byte Buddy for class generation, ANTLR for query analysis, JBoss Logging for logging, etc.)[com.mysql:mysql-connector-j] 9.7.0the JDBC driver for MySQL, the one from Chapter 10[ch.qos.logback:logback-classic] 1.5.38Logback, which will receive the Hibernate log

Hibernate writes its log (executed SQL commands, warnings, etc.) through JBoss Logging, a small library that simply forwards messages to the logging system it finds in the classpath: Log4j 2, or Logback (via SLF4J), or, failing that, the one from JDK or [java.util.logging]. Without configuration, the latter displays each message on two lines, in red in most consoles, which makes the program output difficult to read. We therefore add Logback to our projects and configure it using a [logback.xml] file.

docs.title: 11.1.4. Code First or Database First
docs.text:
The model (the mapping between classes and tables) can be built in two ways:

  • "code first": we write the Java classes, and Hibernate derives the database schema from them, which it can create on its own. This is the approach taken in this chapter;
  • "Database First": The database already exists, and classes are generated from its schema using Hibernate’s reverse-engineering tools (Hibernate Tools) or those of the development environments (IntelliJ IDEA can generate entities from database tables). This is the approach for applications that need to work with an existing database. The generated code is similar to what we would write by hand.

docs.title: 11.2.1. The project
docs.text:
The examples in this chapter are modules of a multi-module Maven project (see Chapter 6), located in the [11-hibernate] folder:

11-hibernate/
  pom.xml                 le projet parent
  outils/                 bibliothèque : le journal SQL compact
  articles/               bibliothèque : l'entité Article et la base [hbarticles]
  premier/                un premier exemple
  modele/                 le modèle : annotations, fichier XML, script de création
  crud/                   persist, find, merge, remove
  hql/                    les requêtes HQL
  criteria/               les requêtes de l'API Criteria
  relations/              les relations entre entités
  clients/                l'évolution du schéma de la base
  asynchrone/             Hibernate et les threads virtuels
  transactions/           les transactions
  concurrence/            la concurrence optimiste
  sqlbrut/                le SQL natif
  majenmasse/             les mises à jour en masse
  injection/              Hibernate et Spring
  ImpotsV7/               l'application de calcul de l'impôt, version 7 (projet distinct)

The parent project sets the versions of the libraries and Maven extensions for all modules:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- the examples from Chapter 11: Hibernate; a Maven module, for example -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>exemples.hibernate</groupId>
    <artifactId>hibernate</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>

     <!-- modules, in the order of their dependencies -->
    <modules>
        <module>outils</module>
        <module>articles</module>
        <module>premier</module>
        <module>modele</module>
        <module>crud</module>
        <module>hql</module>
        <module>criteria</module>
        <module>relations</module>
        <module>clients</module>
        <module>asynchrone</module>
        <module>transactions</module>
        <module>concurrence</module>
        <module>sqlbrut</module>
        <module>majenmasse</module>
        <module>injection</module>
    </modules>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

     <!-- library versions, common to all modules -->
    <dependencyManagement>
        <dependencies>
             <!-- The two shared libraries from the chapter -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>exemples.hibernate</groupId>
                <artifactId>outils</artifactId>
                <version>1.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>exemples.hibernate</groupId>
                <artifactId>articles</artifactId>
                <version>1.0</version>
            </dependency>
             <!-- Hibernate ORM (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
                <artifactId>hibernate-core</artifactId>
                <version>7.4.5.Final</version>
            </dependency>
             <!-- the JDBC driver for MySQL -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
                <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
                <version>9.7.0</version>
            </dependency>
             <!-- Logging: Logback (via SLF4J) -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
                <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
                <version>1.5.38</version>
            </dependency>
             <!-- Spring Framework: dependency injection and transactions -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
                <version>7.0.9</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-orm</artifactId>
                <version>7.0.9</version>
            </dependency>
             <!-- connection pool HikariCP -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>com.zaxxer</groupId>

                <version>7.0.2</version>

        </dependencies>
    </dependencyManagement>

    <build>
        <pluginManagement>
            <plugins>
                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                    <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                    <version>3.15.0</version>
                    <configuration>
                        <parameters>true</parameters>

                    </configuration>
                </plugin>
                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>

  • lines 38–87: the [dependencyManagement] section specifies the version of each library. A module that requires it references it without a version;
  • lines 108–116: the [exec-maven-plugin] extension will execute the class specified by the [exec.mainClass] property, which each module defines.

The first example is the module [premier]. It is independent of the others:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>

        <exec.mainClass>premier.Main</exec.mainClass>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
         <!-- Hibernate and the driver JDBC from MySQL -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
            <artifactId>hibernate-core</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
            <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
        </dependency>
         <!-- Logback: it receives the Hibernate log -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
            <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
  • lines 8–12: the parent project;
  • line 18: the module’s main class;
  • lines 22–35: Hibernate, the JDBC driver for MySQL, and Logback, without a version number (it is provided by the parent project).

To run an example, build all the modules once and for all in the [11-hibernate] folder ([mvn install] installs the shared libraries in the local Maven repository), then navigate to the module’s folder:

> cd 11-hibernate
> mvn install
> cd premier
> mvn compile exec:java

The database used is the [hbpremier] database on the local MySQL server, which is the Laragon server (see appendices). It does not need to exist yet: MySQL will create it.

docs.title: 11.2.2. The entity [Article]
docs.text:
A class whose objects are stored in a table is called an entity. Our first entity is a store item, as in the table [articles] from Chapter 10:

package premier;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

// A store item: a regular Java class, plus a few annotations
@Entity
public class Article {

     // The primary key, generated by SGBD
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;
     // the other columns in the table
    private String nom;
    private BigDecimal prix;
    private int stockActuel;
    private int stockMinimum;

     // the parameterless constructor required by Hibernate
    protected Article() {
    }

     // the constructor used by the program
    public Article(String nom, BigDecimal prix, int stockActuel, int stockMinimum) {
        this.nom = nom;
        this.prix = prix;
        this.stockActuel = stockActuel;
        this.stockMinimum = stockMinimum;
    }

     // display
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[%d, %s, %.2f, %d, %d]".formatted(id, nom, prix, stockActuel, stockMinimum);
    }
}
  • Line 10: The annotation [@Entity] (package [jakarta.persistence]) makes the class an entity. It is almost a regular Java class, deriving from no Hibernate class: it is referred to as POJO (“Plain Old Java Object”);
  • lines 14–16: the primary key is designated by the [@Id] annotation. There is no naming convention: the annotation is required. [@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)] indicates that its values will be generated by SGBD (the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column of MySQL). Its type is [Integer], not [int]: the value [null] means “not yet recorded in the database”;
  • lines 18–21: Each field in the class becomes a column with the same name. Since the annotation [@Id] is applied to a field, Hibernate accesses the fields directly (it reads and writes them via reflection, even if they are private): the class does not need accessors;
  • lines 24–25: Jakarta Persistence requires a parameterless constructor, which Hibernate uses to create objects read from the database. It can be protected ([protected]): the application code will not use it;
  • lines 28–33: the constructor used by the program. No identifier is provided; it will be generated by SGBD;
  • lines 36–39: a convenient display of the item. The [%.2f] format displays the price with two decimal places, in accordance with local conventions (a comma in France).

An entity cannot be a record (Chapter 4): Hibernate must be able to create the empty object, fill in its fields, and modify those fields when the application changes them—something that the immutability of a record prevents. Records remain very useful with Hibernate for query results that are not entities (projections), as we will see.

docs.title: 11.2.3. [SessionFactory] and [Session]
docs.text:
The program uses three Hibernate objects:

  • [SessionFactory] represents Hibernate configured for a database: the list of entities, the database, and the options. Its creation is resource-intensive (Hibernate analyzes the entities, connects to the server to determine its version, and prepares the SQL for common operations): only one is created per database and per application, at startup. It is thread-safe: all threads in the application can use it;
  • The [Session] represents a work session with the database. It establishes a connection when needed, stores the records it has read or saved, and is able to update the database with any changes. It is a lightweight, short-lived object that is not thread-safe: one is opened for each unit of work and then closed;
  • [Transaction]: With Hibernate, all writes to the database occur within an explicit transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] (commit) or [rollback] (rollback).

[SessionFactory] and [Session] implement the [AutoCloseable] interface: they are created in a [try] statement with resources, which closes them at the end of the block.

docs.title: 11.2.4. The program
docs.text:
package premier;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // the SessionFactory: Hibernate configured for the [hbpremier] database
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("premier")
                 // the entities
                .managedClass(Article.class)
                 // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
                .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbpremier?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                 // display of SQL orders, formatted, without colors
                .showSql(true, true, false)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {

             // the tables are deleted and then recreated from the entities
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);

             // Adds three items in a single transaction
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                IO.println("--- persist");
                session.persist(new Article("vélo", BigDecimal.valueOf(500), 10, 5));
                session.persist(new Article("pompe", BigDecimal.valueOf(10), 10, 2));
                session.persist(new Article("arc", BigDecimal.valueOf(600), 4, 1));
                IO.println("--- commit");
                transaction.commit();
            }

             // Reading the table with a new session
            IO.println("--- lecture des articles");
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                List<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by nom", Article.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (Article article : articles) {
                    IO.println(article);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
  • lines 14–22: creation of [SessionFactory]. There are several ways to configure Hibernate (we’ll discuss them later); we use the [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration] class from Hibernate 7, an enhanced version of the [PersistenceConfiguration] class introduced with Jakarta Persistence 3.2, which allows everything to be configured via code. Its parameter is the name of the persistence unit—a freely chosen name that appears in Hibernate messages. Each method returns the configuration itself, allowing calls to be chained together;
  • line 16: the list of entities;
  • lines 18–19: the URL and JDBC from the [hbpremier] database, in the same format as in Chapter 10, and the user ([root], with no password in Laragon). The [createDatabaseIfNotExist=true] parameter of URL is an option of the MySQL driver: it creates the database if it does not exist;
  • Line 21: [showSql(true, true, false)] instructs Hibernate to print each SQL command it executes to the console, formatted across multiple lines (second parameter), without colors (third parameter). Looking at the SQL sent to the server is the best way to understand what Hibernate is doing: we’ll do this in all the examples;
  • line 22: [createEntityManagerFactory] constructs [SessionFactory] (the method name follows the standard; the returned type is Hibernate’s);
  • Lines 25–26: The [SchemaManager] object from [SessionFactory] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) manages the entity tables: [drop(false)] deletes them if they exist, [create(false)] creates them (the [false] parameter specifies that the database itself should not be deleted or created). This is convenient for examples and tests; a real-world application manages its database differently, as we will see;
  • line 29: [openSession()] opens a session;
  • line 30: the start of a transaction;
  • lines 32–34: [persist] adds three new items to the session: they will be saved to the database. No value is specified for the identifier; it will be generated by SGBD;
  • line 36: [commit] commits the transaction. Prior to this, the session sends the SQL commands to the server, which are still necessary to save the changes it has stored: this is referred to as “flushing” the session to the database;
  • lines 42–44: a query written in HQL, Hibernate’s query language: the items in alphabetical order by name. It refers to the entity [Article] and its field [nom], not to the table. The second parameter of [createSelectionQuery] is the result type: [getResultList] returns a [List<Article>].

The [src/main/resources/logback.xml] file in the module configures Logback. It displays Hibernate messages of level [INFO] or higher, one per line (level, log name, message):

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration: Hibernate informational messages, one per line -->
<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>
    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>

Comments:

  • Lines 2–17: Hibernate informational messages: the name of the persistence unit, the Hibernate version, and database characteristics (URL, driver, selected dialect, server version, transaction isolation level, connection pool size). Hibernate queried the server to select the [MySQLDialect] dialect appropriate for its version;
  • line 4: a warning. Hibernate manages its own small connection pool, which is not intended for a production application. We’ll see, with Spring, how to provide it with the HikariCP pool from Chapter 10; for our examples, the built-in pool is sufficient;
  • Lines 18–28: Deletion and subsequent creation of table [Article] based on the entity: the table name is the same as the entity name, the columns have the same names as the fields, and the column [id] is the primary key with a generated value ([auto_increment]). The columns for primitive-type fields ([int]) are [not null]: a [int] cannot equal [null]. Those for reference-type fields ([String], [BigDecimal]) accept the value [NULL];
  • note the default types: [varchar(255)] for a string, and [decimal(38,2)] for a [BigDecimal] (38 digits, including 2 decimal places). These are rarely the ones you want: the following paragraph shows how to specify them;
  • Lines 29–51: The three configured [INSERT] commands were executed as soon as [persist] was called, before [commit]. This is a consequence of the key being generated by SGBD ([IDENTITY]): the session must know an entity’s identifier as soon as it takes over that entity, and to obtain it, it must execute the insert operation (the JDBC driver returns the generated key; see Chapter 10). With other generation methods, the insert operations are deferred until the session is synchronized. The parameter values ([?]) are not displayed: we will see how to make them appear;
  • lines 53–63: the query HQL [from Article order by nom] was translated into a [SELECT ... ORDER BY] statement. Hibernate assigned the alias [a1_0] to the table and created a [Article] object for each row read (lines 64–66).

We did not write any SQL statements or any column-reading code: that is the whole point of a ORM. We can also see that this does not eliminate the need to understand SQL: to determine whether the generated SQL is correct and effective, you need to know how to read it.

docs.title: 11.3. The Model
docs.text:
Hibernate builds its model from entities in three steps:

  • First, it applies its default rules: anything that isn’t specified is assigned a reasonable value (this is known as “configuration by exception”);
  • it then supplements or corrects these values using the annotations placed on the entities;
  • finally, it applies the mapping files XML ([orm.xml]), which can fully describe a class without annotations or modify what its annotations specify.

docs.title: 11.3.1. Default Rules
docs.text:
We saw the basics of this in the first example:

  • an entity carries the annotation [@Entity] and has an identifier designated by [@Id]; both of these annotations are required;
  • the placement of the annotation [@Id] determines the access mode: when placed on a field, Hibernate reads and writes the fields directly; When placed on an accessor ([getId]), access occurs through the accessors ([getX]/[setX]). Access via fields is the most common: it allows the class to have whatever methods it wants;
  • any non-static field is stored in a column, unless it bears the annotation [@Transient] or the keyword [transient];
  • the table name is the entity name (the class’s simple name), and the column name is the field name. These names are then processed by a naming strategy: Hibernate’s strategy keeps the names as-is, while another strategy—which we’ll try below—converts them to “snake case” ([stockActuel] becomes [stock_actuel]). Spring Boot uses the latter by default;
  • A column of a primitive type ([int], [double], [boolean]) is [NOT NULL]; a column of a reference type ([Integer], [String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate]) accepts the value [NULL];
  • the types SQL are selected by the dialect. With MySQL: [integer] for [int], [bigint] for [long], [bit] for [boolean], [varchar(255)] for [String], [decimal(38,2)] for [BigDecimal], [date] for [LocalDate], [datetime(6)] (to the microsecond) for [LocalDateTime]. By default, an enumeration is recorded by its sequence number (see Chapter 3); the annotation [@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)] records it by its name, which is more reliable;
  • a field that refers to another entity, or to a collection of entities, defines a relationship (we’ll discuss this later).

docs.title: 11.3.2. The annotations and the mapping file XML
docs.text:
The module [modele] defines two entities configured in two different ways. The first is configured using annotations:

package modele;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import jakarta.persistence.Transient;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;

// an entity configured by annotations
@Entity
@Table(name = "produits")
public class Produit {

     // the primary key: @Id, regardless of its name
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer code;

     // required string of up to 50 characters
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    private String nom;

     // optional string (column NULL) of up to 200 characters
    @Column(length = 200)
    private String description;

     // Column name and type (SQL) are required
    @Column(name = "prix_ht", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal prixHT;

     // an optional date: an object may be null
    private LocalDate dateRetrait;

     // a field without a column
    @Transient
    private boolean selectionne;

    protected Produit() {
    }

     // A method is never registered: Hibernate accesses fields here, not methods
    public BigDecimal getPrixTTC() {
        return prixHT.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.2"));
    }

    public boolean isSelectionne() {
        return selectionne;
    }
}
  • lines 3–9: Jakarta Persistence annotations;
  • line 15: [@Table] specifies the table name;
  • lines 19–21: the primary key, designated by [@Id] regardless of its name;
  • lines 24–25: [@Column] specifies the column; [nullable = false] makes it required ([NOT NULL]), [length = 50] sets its length ([varchar(50)]);
  • lines 28–29: an optional description of up to 200 characters; the column will accept the value [NULL];
  • lines 32–33: [@Column] also specifies the column name ([prix_ht]) and, for a decimal number, its precision (the total number of digits) and its scale (the number of digits after the decimal point): [decimal(10,2)];
  • line 36: an optional date. The type [LocalDate] (Chapter 5) represents a date without a time: it is associated with the types SQL and [date];
  • lines 39–40: [@Transient] excludes a field from the model: in this case, information useful to the user interface that does not belong in the database;
  • lines 46–48: a method, even if named like a getter, is not registered, since Hibernate accesses the fields directly. If accessed via getters, the annotation [@Transient] would need to be added to it.

The second entity has no annotations:

package modele;

import java.time.LocalDateTime;

// a class with no annotations: its mapping is described by the file [fournisseur.orm.xml]
public class Fournisseur {

    private Integer numero;
    private String raisonSociale;
    private String telephone;
    private LocalDateTime dateCreation;

    protected Fournisseur() {
    }

    public Fournisseur(String raisonSociale, String telephone) {
        this.raisonSociale = raisonSociale;
        this.telephone = telephone;
    }
}

Its mapping to the table is described by a file named XML, located in the [src/main/resources/META-INF] folder of the module:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- the mapping of the class [Fournisseur] to its table, described in XML (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) -->
<entity-mappings xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm"
                 xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
                 xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm
                                     https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm/orm_3_2.xsd"
                 version="3.2">
    <entity class="modele.Fournisseur" access="FIELD">
        <table name="fournisseurs">
             <!-- a unique index: two suppliers cannot have the same company name -->
            <index name="ix_fournisseurs_raison_sociale" column-list="raisonSociale" unique="true"/>
        </table>
        <attributes>
            <id name="numero">
                <generated-value strategy="IDENTITY"/>
            </id>
            <basic name="raisonSociale">
                <column nullable="false" length="60"/>
            </basic>
            <basic name="telephone">
                <column name="tel" length="20"/>
            </basic>
             <!-- a default value calculated by SGBD: Hibernate never writes to this column -->
            <basic name="dateCreation">
                <column nullable="false" insertable="false" updatable="false"
                        column-definition="datetime(6) default current_timestamp(6)"/>
            </basic>
        </attributes>
    </entity>
</entity-mappings>
  • lines 3–7: the XML schema for Jakarta Persistence 3.2 mapping files;
  • line 8: the described class, with access via fields;
  • lines 9–12: the table, and a unique index on the company name: no two suppliers can have the same one. The equivalent annotation is [@Table(name = "fournisseurs", indexes = @Index(...))];
  • lines 14–16: the identifier, generated by SGBD;
  • lines 17–19: a required column of no more than 60 characters;
  • Lines 20–22: The field [telephone] is stored in the column [tel];
  • lines 24–27: The creation date has a default value, calculated by SGBD. The [column-definition] attribute returns the text SQL from the column definition, copied verbatim in the order [CREATE TABLE]; [insertable="false"] and [updatable="false"] indicate that Hibernate must never write to this column, which allows SGBD to use [current_timestamp(6)].

Everything that annotations do can be done in XML. Annotations have the advantage of placing the configuration next to the field, and this is the most common approach; the XML file, on the other hand, keeps the classes independent of Jakarta Persistence and consolidates the configuration in a single location. The two approaches can be combined: the XML file takes precedence in case of a conflict. Jakarta Persistence does not support configuring the model via Java code, as other frameworks (such as Entity Framework in C#) do.

The program displays the model built by Hibernate, followed by the SQL script that would create the tables:

package modele;

import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.Attribute;
import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.EntityType;
import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.SingularAttribute;
import java.io.StringWriter;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // The table creation script will be written to this object
        StringWriter script = new StringWriter();
         // a SessionFactory that never connects to the server
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("modele")
                 // An annotated entity and a mapping described in XML
                .managedClass(Produit.class)
                .mappingFile("META-INF/fournisseur.orm.xml")
                 // no database: SGBD and its version are provided for the SQL dialect
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_NAME, "MySQL")
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_MAJOR_VERSION, "8")
                .property(AvailableSettings.ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT, false)
                 // column names in "snake case": raisonSociale -> raison_sociale
                .property(AvailableSettings.PHYSICAL_NAMING_STRATEGY,
                        PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl.class.getName())
                 // the table creation script, without executing it
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, "create")
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
                .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {

             // the model built by Hibernate: entities and attributes (API Jakarta Persistence)
            for (EntityType<?> entite : sessionFactory.getMetamodel().getEntities()) {
                IO.println("entité %s (%s)".formatted(entite.getName(), entite.getJavaType().getName()));
                for (Attribute<?, ?> attribut : entite.getAttributes()) {
                    boolean id = attribut instanceof SingularAttribute<?, ?> s && s.isId();
                    IO.println("  %-14s %s%s".formatted(attribut.getName(),
                            attribut.getJavaType().getSimpleName(), id ? " (identifiant)" : ""));
                }
            }
        }
         // the table creation script, without removing 4 spaces from its lines
        IO.println("--- script de création");
        script.toString().strip().lines()
                .map(ligne -> ligne.startsWith("    ") ? ligne.substring(4) : ligne)
                .forEach(ligne -> IO.println(ligne.stripTrailing()));
    }
}
  • line 16: a [StringWriter] (package [java.io]), a write stream to a string in memory, will receive the SQL script;
  • lines 20–21: the annotated entity is declared by [managedClass], and the file XML by [mappingFile];
  • lines 23–25: The database [hbmodele] will never exist; this [SessionFactory] is used solely to examine the model. Therefore, there is no URL or JDBC. To select the SQL dialect without querying the server, Hibernate needs the name of the SGBD and its version; the property [ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT] ([hibernate.boot.allow_jdbc_metadata_access]) prevents it from connecting at startup. The names of the configuration properties are constants in the [AvailableSettings] interface;
  • lines 27–28: the “snake case” naming convention;
  • lines 30–33: Hibernate will write the table creation script (["create"]) to the [script] object without executing it; the commands are terminated by a semicolon and formatted across multiple lines;
  • line 37: the [getMetamodel] method (Jakarta Persistence) provides access to the model: its entities ([EntityType]) and, for each, its attributes ([Attribute]);
  • lines 38–43: for each entity, its name and class; for each attribute, its name, its Java type, and whether it is the identifier. The pattern filtering in line 40 ([instanceof SingularAttribute<?, ?> s && s.isId()], Chapter 4) checks the attribute’s type and, if appropriate, uses it immediately;
  • lines 48–50: the script output, without the four spaces that Hibernate adds to its lines.

Results:

> mvn compile exec:java

  dateRetrait    LocalDate

entité Fournisseur (modele.Fournisseur)

--- creation script
create table fournisseurs (
    numero integer not null auto_increment,
    date_creation datetime(6) default current_timestamp(6) not null,
    tel varchar(20),
    raison_sociale varchar(60) not null,
    primary key (numero)

create table produits (
