Comments:

  • Line 13: the Spring container, configured by the [Config] class. It is closed at the end of the [try] block, which closes the [SessionFactory] and the connection pool;
  • line 15: the [SessionFactory] constructed by Spring; it is used to recreate the product table;
  • line 21: a transaction (lines 3–4): within the same transaction, the current session remains the same (line 5);
  • lines 23–26: two calls, two transactions (lines 6–9), two different sessions; the first is closed, since its transaction is complete (line 10);
  • lines 28–32: outside a transaction, there is no current session: [getCurrentSession] launches a [HibernateException] (line 11). This is the classic error caused by a method that omitted the annotation [@Transactional];
  • line 36: a read-only transaction (lines 13–17);
  • Line 38: The sale of two bicycles. The transaction is confirmed, and the session synchronization sends the [UPDATE] (lines 20–33);
  • Lines 40–44: The sale of fifty pumps triggers an exception: Spring rolls back the transaction (line 40), and the [UPDATE] is never sent, since the session was not synchronized;
  • lines 46–47: database state: the bicycle inventory has changed to 8, while the pump inventory remains at 10 (lines 49 and 56).

In a Spring Boot application, all of this happens automatically: Spring Boot creates the connection pool, the factory (in its Jakarta Persistence form, a [EntityManagerFactory]), and the transaction manager from the [application.properties] file. Spring Data JPA is often used on top of Hibernate; it generates the [dao] layer from a simple interface: [interface ArticleRepository extends JpaRepository<Article, Integer>] provides [findAll], [findById], [save], [delete]..., and a declared method [List<Article> findByPrixLessThan(BigDecimal prix)] is automatically translated into a query.

docs.title: 11.15.1. The Architecture
docs.text:
Version 6 of the tax calculation application (Chapter 10) read the tax brackets from a MySQL database using JDBC. Version 7 does the same using Hibernate. As with version 6, only the [dao] layer changes: the [metier] and [ui] layers from version 5 (Chapter 6) are reused as-is via Maven dependencies.

The Maven project [ImpotsV7], located in the [11-hibernate] folder, consists of two modules:

ImpotsV7/
  pom.xml                           le projet parent
  impots-dao-hibernate/             bibliothèque : la couche [dao] Hibernate
    pom.xml
    src/main/java/impots/dao/
      Tranche.java                  l'entité
      HibernateImpot.java           l'implémentation de IImpotDao
      CreationBase.java             la création de la base [hbimpots]
    src/main/resources/
      logback.xml
  impots-ui-hibernate/              exécutable : intégration des couches
    pom.xml
    src/main/java/impots/ui/
      MainHibernate.java
    impots-hibernate.properties
    impots-hibernate-erreur.properties

The parent project ([exemples.impots:impots-v7:7.0]) is structured like the one in version 5: it declares the two modules and specifies the library versions, including those of the version 5 modules ([impots-dao], [impots-metier], [impots-ui], version 5.0), which are installed in the local Maven repository using the command [mvn install] entered in the [06-architectures/ImpotsV5] folder.

docs.title: 11.15.2. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [impots-dao-hibernate] module depends on the [dao] layer from version 5, which contains the application entities ([TrancheImpot], [ImpotException]) and the [IImpotDao] interface:

    <dependencies>
         <!-- the [dao] layer of version 5: entities, interface IImpotDao, HardwiredImpot -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-dao</artifactId>
        </dependency>
         <!-- Hibernate, the JDBC driver for MySQL, and Logback -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
            <artifactId>hibernate-core</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
            <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
            <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
             <!-- `mvn exec:java` creates the database [hbimpots] -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>impots.dao.CreationBase</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
  • lines 3–6: the [dao] layer of version 5;
  • lines 8–19: Hibernate, the JDBC driver for MySQL, and Logback;
  • lines 25–31: the class executed by [mvn exec:java] in the module’s directory: it creates the database, as we will see.

The [TrancheImpot] record in version 5 cannot be a Hibernate entity: it is a record, read-only, and has no identifier. It is not modified because it is part of the contract between the layers, shared by all versions. We create an entity specific to the [dao] layer, whose role is to represent a row in the table:

// A tax bracket as stored in the database: a Hibernate entity
@Entity
@Table(name = "tranches")
public class Tranche {

     // the primary key, which does not exist in the record TrancheImpot
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(name = "limite", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal limite;

    @Column(name = "coeffr", nullable = false, precision = 6, scale = 4)
    private BigDecimal coeffR;

    @Column(name = "coeffn", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal coeffN;

    protected Tranche() {
    }

    public Tranche(BigDecimal limite, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
        this.limite = limite;
        this.coeffR = coeffR;
        this.coeffN = coeffN;
    }
}
  • row 3: the table [tranches];
  • rows 7–9: the primary key, which is also used to sort the segments;
  • rows 11–18: the three columns, with appropriate [decimal] data types: the limit and the coefficient ([coeffN]) are amounts with two decimal places, and [coeffR] is a rate with four decimal places. Column names are in lowercase;
  • Lines 23–27: a constructor, which will be used to populate the table. The entity has no accessors: the rest of the application never sees it.

The class [HibernateImpot] implements the interface [IImpotDao]:

package impots.dao;

import impots.entites.ImpotException;
import impots.entites.TrancheImpot;
import jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

// a layer [dao] that reads tax brackets from a database using Hibernate
public class HibernateImpot implements IImpotDao {

     // error codes specific to this implementation
    public static final int ERREUR_ACCES = 1;
    public static final int TABLE_VIDE = 2;

     // tax brackets
    private final List<TrancheImpot> tranchesImpot;

     // constructor: the database is identified by its URL JDBC
    public HibernateImpot(String url, String utilisateur, String motDePasse) {
         // a short-lived SessionFactory, just long enough to read the table
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("impots")
                .managedClass(Tranche.class)
                .jdbcUrl(url)
                .jdbcCredentials(utilisateur, motDePasse)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
             // the table rows are projected onto the application record TrancheImpot
            String hql = "select limite, coeffR, coeffN from Tranche order by id";
            tranchesImpot = sessionFactory.fromSession(session -> session
                    .createSelectionQuery(hql, TrancheImpot.class)
                    .getResultList());
        } catch (PersistenceException e) {
             // Hibernate or SGBD error: it is encapsulated in a ImpotException
            throw new ImpotException("Erreur lors de la lecture des tranches d'impôt dans la base de données",
                    e, ERREUR_ACCES);
        }
         // The [metier] layer requires at least one slice
        if (tranchesImpot.isEmpty()) {
            throw new ImpotException("La table des tranches d'impôt est vide", TABLE_VIDE);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }
}
  • Lines 14–15: The error codes for this implementation, such as [FileImpot] and [JsonImpot];
  • line 21: the [dao] layer receives the URL from the database, along with the user and their password. It reads the segments once and for all in its constructor: it will be a singleton;
  • lines 23–27: a short-lived [SessionFactory], lasting only long enough to read the table, which is closed immediately. Since the layer accesses the database only once, there is no need to keep it; a [dao] layer that accessed the database on every call would instead receive a [SessionFactory] created once and for all, as in the previous example;
  • lines 29–32: reading the table in primary key order. The query is a projection onto the record [TrancheImpot]: Hibernate requests only the three relevant columns from SGBD and creates the application objects directly, without going through [Tranche] entities;
  • Lines 33–37: An error from Hibernate or SGBD (database inaccessible, table missing, etc.) manifests as a [PersistenceException] (the base class for Jakarta Persistence exceptions, from which Hibernate’s exceptions are derived). As in other implementations, it is encapsulated within a [ImpotException]. The exception can occur as early as the creation of the [SessionFactory] (line 27), which connects to the server: the [catch] clause of a [try] statement with resources also intercepts exceptions thrown during resource creation;
  • Lines 39–41: An empty table is also an error: the [metier] layer requires at least one segment.

docs.title: 11.15.3. The database
docs.text:
The database [hbimpots] is created by the class [CreationBase]. To avoid rewriting the scale segments, it reuses those from the class [HardwiredImpot] in version 5:

package impots.dao;

import impots.entites.TrancheImpot;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import org.hibernate.tool.schema.Action;

// creation of the database [hbimpots]: the table [tranches], populated with the slices from class HardwiredImpot
public class CreationBase {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("impots")
                .managedClass(Tranche.class)
                .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbimpots?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                 // Display of orders SQL, without formatting
                .showSql(true, false, false)
                 // the table is deleted and then recreated when SessionFactory is created
                .schemaToolingAction(Action.CREATE)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
             // the pay scale brackets from version 5, numbered starting at 1 by SGBD
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                for (TrancheImpot tranche : new HardwiredImpot().getTranchesImpot()) {
                    session.persist(new Tranche(tranche.limite(), tranche.coeffR(), tranche.coeffN()));
                }
            });
        }
    }
}
  • line 14: the database [hbimpots], created by MySQL if it does not exist;
  • line 17: displays the SQL orders, without formatting;
  • line 19: the table is deleted and then recreated when [SessionFactory] is created;
  • lines 22–26: one [Tranche] entity per batch of the [HardwiredImpot] class, persisted within a transaction.

The module also contains a file named [logback.xml], used by [CreationBase] and by the application, which only allows errors to pass through:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration: only Hibernate errors are displayed -->
<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger{0} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>
     <!-- Errors from SGBD are passed to the application as exceptions: they are not logged -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error" level="OFF"/>
    <root level="ERROR">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
  • line 10: Errors from SGBD, which Hibernate logs before throwing an exception, are not displayed: the application reports them itself;
  • Line 11: The other logs record only errors.

Execution:

> mvn compile exec:java
Hibernate: drop table if exists tranches

Hibernate: insert into tranches (coeffn,coeffr,limite) values (?,?,?)

We check the table contents:

> mysql -uroot -t hbimpots -e "SELECT id, limite, coeffr, coeffn FROM tranches"
+----+----------+--------+---------+
| id | limite   | coeffr | coeffn  |
+----+----------+--------+---------+
|  1 |  4962.00 | 0.0000 |    0.00 |
|  2 |  8382.00 | 0.0680 |  291.09 |
|  3 | 14753.00 | 0.1910 | 1322.92 |

We find the pay scale brackets, with the last one having a zero limit (it is not used by layer [metier], which takes the last bracket when no other applies).

To create the database on your own system:

  • start MySQL (in Laragon, see the appendix; user [root] with no password);
  • if you haven’t already, install the version 5 modules in the local Maven repository: [mvn install] in the [06-architectures/ImpotsV5] folder;
  • Build version 7: [mvn install] in the [11-hibernate/ImpotsV7] folder;
  • Navigate to the [11-hibernate/ImpotsV7/impots-dao-hibernate] folder and enter the command [mvn exec:java].

The database [hbimpots] is then created, with its table [tranches] populated. If the command fails, verify that MySQL is running and that the URL instance of the [CreationBase] class corresponds to your server (port 3306, username [root], empty password). Alternatively, if you prefer, you can create the table and its rows using a SQL script, as described in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 11.15.4. Layer Integration
docs.text:
The [impots-ui-hibernate] module combines the following layers:

    <dependencies>
         <!-- Layers [metier] and [ui] from version 5 remain unchanged -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-metier</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-ui</artifactId>
        </dependency>
         <!-- the new layer [dao] -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>exemples.impots</groupId>
            <artifactId>impots-dao-hibernate</artifactId>
        </dependency>
         <!-- the Spring dependency injection container -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
             <!-- `mvn exec:java` executes the main class -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>impots.ui.MainHibernate</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
  • lines 3–10: the [metier] and [ui] layers from version 5. The [impots-ui] module contains the main program for version 5; it is used here as a library, specifically for its [Dialogue] class;
  • lines 12–15: the new layer [dao], which provides Hibernate, the driver JDBC, and Logback;
  • lines 17–20: the Spring container;
  • line 30: the main class.

The configuration file [impots-hibernate.properties], located in the module folder, specifies the database:

# [Impots] application configuration, version 7: the tax bracket database
jdbc.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbimpots
jdbc.utilisateur=root
jdbc.motdepasse=

The file [impots-hibernate-erreur.properties] specifies a database named [hbimpotsabsente], which does not exist:

# a database that does not exist
jdbc.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbimpotsabsente
jdbc.utilisateur=root
jdbc.motdepasse=

The main program is the one from version 5, in which only the composition of the [dao] layer changes:

package impots.ui;

import impots.dao.HibernateImpot;
import impots.dao.IImpotDao;
import impots.entites.ImpotException;
import impots.metier.IImpotMetier;
import impots.metier.ImpotMetier;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.Reader;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Properties;
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext;

public class MainHibernate {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // the configuration file: impots-hibernate.properties by default, or the one passed as an argument
        String fichierConfig = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "impots-hibernate.properties";

         // layer integration
        IImpotMetier metier;
        try {
             // Reading the configuration from the current directory
            Properties config = new Properties();
            try (Reader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of(fichierConfig))) {
                config.load(reader);
            }
            String url = config.getProperty("jdbc.url");
            if (url == null) {
                throw new ImpotException("URL [jdbc.url] de la base absente du fichier " + fichierConfig);
            }
            String utilisateur = config.getProperty("jdbc.utilisateur", "root");
            String motDePasse = config.getProperty("jdbc.motdepasse", "");

             // the Spring container: layers are registered here
            GenericApplicationContext contexte = new GenericApplicationContext();
             // the layer [dao]: HibernateImpot, with the configuration base
            contexte.registerBean(IImpotDao.class, () -> new HibernateImpot(url, utilisateur, motDePasse));
             // the [metier] layer from version 5: the container will pass it the [dao] layer
            contexte.registerBean(ImpotMetier.class);

             // container startup: it creates the [dao] layer, then the [metier] layer
            contexte.refresh();
            metier = contexte.getBean(IImpotMetier.class);
        } catch (IOException | RuntimeException e) {
             // Displays the error and stops the program
            Dialogue.afficherErreur(e);
            System.exit(1);
            return;
        }

         // user dialog, the one from version 5
        Dialogue.run(metier);
    }
}
  • line 15: the class is not named [Main]: the [impots-ui] module from version 5, on which we depend, already contains a class named [impots.ui.Main];
  • Lines 29–34: the URL from the database, required, the username and password, read from the configuration;
  • line 39: the [dao] layer is a [HibernateImpot], created by a lambda that passes it the database parameters;
  • line 41: the [metier] layer in version 5: the container will pass the [dao] layer to its constructor;
  • line 54: the dialog for version 5.

With the configuration file [impots-hibernate-erreur.properties], which refers to a nonexistent database:

> mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.args="impots-hibernate-erreur.properties"
Chaîne des exceptions :
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'impots.dao.IImpotDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
----------------------------------------
impots.entites.ImpotException: Erreur lors de la lecture des tranches d'impôt dans la base de données
----------------------------------------
org.hibernate.service.spi.ServiceException: Unable to create requested service [org.hibernate.engine.jdbc.env.spi.JdbcEnvironment] due to: Error calling Driver.connect() [Unknown database 'hbimpotsabsente']
----------------------------------------
org.hibernate.exception.SQLGrammarException: Error calling Driver.connect() [Unknown database 'hbimpotsabsente']

  • line 12: the original exception, thrown by the JDBC driver;
  • lines 8 and 10: the Hibernate exceptions that encapsulate it: the error occurred during the creation of [SessionFactory], when Hibernate connected to the server to determine its version;
  • line 6: the [dao] layer wrapped the error in a [ImpotException];
  • Line 4: The Spring container, which was creating the [dao] layer, itself encapsulated the exception in a [BeanCreationException], which was displayed by the main program.

Changing SGBD is equivalent to changing the base URL and the dependency on the JDBC driver: Hibernate automatically selects the SQL dialect from the encountered SGBD, and the code for the [HibernateImpot] class, written in HQL, remains unchanged. Only the database creation—which depends on the column types—needs to be redone, which the [CreationBase] class does without any changes other than to its URL.

docs.title: 11.16. Conclusion: JDBC, JdbcClient, jOOQ, or Hibernate?
docs.text:
We now have two ways to access a database: JDBC (Chapter 10) and Hibernate (this chapter). There are other, intermediate approaches that are widely used:

  • JdbcClient, from the Spring Framework (library [spring-jdbc]), adds a lightweight API to JDBC, which executes a hand-written SQL query and automatically transforms the result rows into objects: [jdbcClient.sql("select * from articles where prix > :prix").param("prix", 200).query(Article.class).list()]. You write the SQL; Spring handles the parameters and copies the columns into the objects (including records). It is a “micro-ORM”;
  • jOOQ generates, based on the database schema, classes that allow you to write a SQL in Java that is verified by the compiler: [dsl.selectFrom(ARTICLES).where(ARTICLES.PRIX.gt(prix)).fetch()]. You retain full control over the SQL, with the safety of type checking.
StrengthsWeaknessesJDBCFull control over SQL; performance; no dependenciesa lot of repetitive code (parameters, reading columns); SQL in strings, not checked by the compilerJdbcClientSQL hand-written, without copy-and-paste code; performance similar to JDBCNo change tracking or generation of [INSERT]/[UPDATE]; SQL not verifiedjOOQSQL verified by the compiler; all features of SGBDCode generation with every schema change; no change tracking; paid license required for certain commercial SGBD versionsHibernateobject-oriented model; change tracking; relationships; HQL and API Criteria; Jakarta Persistence standard; independent of SGBDan additional layer to understand (sessions, states, lazy loading); generated SQL to monitor; less suitable for complex bulk processing

The following guidelines can be suggested:

  • Hibernate (often via Spring Data JPA) is suitable for most business applications: a model of interconnected entities, operations for reading and updating entities, and a schema that evolves with the application. It is the default choice for Spring Boot applications;
  • JDBC, JdbcClient or jOOQ are suitable when you want precise control over the SQL code being executed: complex statistical queries, stored procedures, processing very large volumes, or an existing database with a schema that is poorly suited to an object-oriented model;
  • These approaches can be combined: an application can use Hibernate for the most part and hand-written SQL, in native queries, with [JdbcClient] or with JDBC ([doWork]), for a few critical queries.

In any case, ORM does not eliminate the need to understand SQL and how SGBD works: the log of executed SQL commands, which we have displayed throughout this chapter, is the primary tool for verifying what Hibernate is actually doing.

To learn more, the Hibernate documentation is comprehensive, and its introductory guide is the best place to start: Hibernate ORM - documentation. The Jakarta Persistence specification is published by the Eclipse Foundation: Jakarta Persistence.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The PDF in the document is ICI.

The codes in this document are ICI.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It is the Java port of the course “Learning the C# Language 14 with .NET 10” (October 2026), which itself is a rewrite of the course “Learning the C# Language Version 3.0 with the .NET 3.5 written by Serge Tahé in May 2008. It retains the course outline, examples, and central theme, and rewrites them in modern Java:

  • the document uses Java 25 (September 2025), the latest long-term support version of Java (LTS), and presents the language’s new features throughout the chapters, ranging from Java 25’s compact source files to Java 21’s virtual threads, including records, sealed classes, and pattern matching;
  • where the two languages differ, the document does more than simply translate: C# properties, structures, operator overloading, and delegates do not exist in Java, which has its own solutions (getters, records, functional interfaces); conversely, Java has concepts unique to itself, such as controlled exceptions and virtual threads, and these are presented in detail;
  • Two chapters take on a different focus: asynchronous programming, which Java handles using the [CompletableFuture] classes and virtual threads rather than the [async] / [await] keywords, and the object-relational mapping, provided by Hibernate, the most widely used ORM in the Java world;
  • the libraries are those currently used in Java: [JUnit 6] for testing, [Spring Framework 7] for dependency injection, [Jackson 3] for JSON, the [MySQL Connector/J] driver for JDBC, [Hibernate 7], and [Spring Boot 4] for web services; the projects are built using [Maven].

This document is not a comprehensive course. Like the ones from which it is derived, it is intended for people who already know how to program and want to learn the basics of Java. It uses examples: more than two hundred programs (more than three hundred Java files), most of them short, with line-by-line comments.

docs.title: 1.1. Java from 1995 to 2026
docs.text:
Java was released by Sun Microsystems in May 1995. It is based on an idea that has been key to its success: the [javac] compiler does not produce machine code but rather an intermediate code—bytecode—stored in [.class] files, which the Java Virtual Machine (the JVM, “Java Virtual Machine”) executes by compiling it on the fly into machine code. A single compiled program can thus run on Windows, Linux, or macOS: “write once, run anywhere.” The Kotlin, Scala, and Groovy languages also produce bytecode and use the same libraries.

Key milestones:

  • 2006–2007: OpenJDK. Sun released the Java source code under an open-source license (JDK). All current Java distributions are built from OpenJDK;
  • 2010: Oracle acquires Sun and becomes the primary contributor to Java;
  • 2014: Java 8, a pivotal release: lambda expressions, API Stream, new date handling (API). Many programs in production are still written in this style;
  • Since 2017 (Java 9): A new version of Java is released every six months, in March and September. Some versions have long-term support (LTS, “Long-Term Support”): Java 11 (2018), 17 (2021), 21 (2023), and 25 (September 2025), which is used in this document; starting with Java 17, a new version is released every two years. The other versions are supported for only six months; new features often appear first as “previews” before being finalized in a subsequent version;
  • JDK is distributed by several vendors, all of which are based on OpenJDK and are equivalent for our purposes: Oracle, the Eclipse Foundation (Eclipse Temurin, Adoptium project), Microsoft, Amazon (Corretto), and Linux distributions.

The language has evolved significantly since Java 8. The following table summarizes the main new features presented in this document and indicates the chapter in which they appear:

VersionYearKey New FeaturesChapterJava 82014lambda expressions, method references, API Stream, interface methods, [default], [java.time], [CompletableFuture]5, 7, 9Java 92017modules (JPMS), [jshell], immutable collections [List.of], [Map.of]2, 4, 5Java 102018Type inference for local variables [var]3Java 112018client HTTP [java.net.http.HttpClient], direct execution of a source file [java Fichier.java], methods [strip], [repeat], [lines] strings2, 5, 12Java 142020expressions [switch] ([case ->], [yield]), detailed messages for [NullPointerException]3, 4Java 152020text blocks ["""]3Java 162021records, pattern filtering with [instanceof]4Java 172021Sealed classes and interfaces ([sealed], [permits])4Java 182022UTF-8 as the default encoding5Java 212023Virtual threads, sequenced collections, pattern filtering in [switch], record patterns3, 4, 5, 8, 9Java 222024Anonymous variables and parameters [_], launching programs from multiple source files3, 4, 7Java 242025Intermediate flow collectors ([Gatherers])5, 7Java 252025Compact source files and instance methods ([main]), class ([IO]), module imports, scoped values ([ScopedValue])2, 3, 8

In terms of libraries and tools, the new features presented include: the [Maven] build tool, modern collections, the API Stream, the API and [java.nio.file] file classes, the [java.util.concurrent] classes, the Java 11 client HTTP, and major frameworks in the ecosystem: JUnit, Spring, Jackson, Hibernate, and Spring Boot.

docs.title: 1.2. Document Contents
docs.text:
The document includes the following chapters:

  • Chapter 2: Setting up the development environment (JDK 25, IntelliJ, IDEA, or VS Code, Maven, the [java] and [javac] commands);
  • Chapter 3: Language Fundamentals (types, operators, control statements, checked and unchecked exceptions, enumerations, parameter passing);
  • Chapter 4: Classes, records, interfaces, inheritance, sealed classes, generics, packages, pattern matching;
  • Chapter 5: Commonly Used Java Classes: Strings, Arrays, Collections, API Streams, Text and Binary Files, JSON with Jackson, Regular Expressions;
  • Chapter 6: Layered architectures, unit testing with JUnit 6, and dependency injection with Spring;
  • Chapter 7: Functional interfaces, lambda expressions, and events;
  • Chapter 8: Execution threads, synchronization, and virtual threads;
  • Chapter 9: Asynchronous programming with [CompletableFuture] and virtual threads;
  • Chapter 10: Database access with JDBC;
  • Chapter 11: Hibernate;
  • Chapter 12: Web Programming (TCP/IP, TCP clients and servers, HTTP with [HttpClient]) ;
  • Chapter 13: Web Services with Spring Boot;
  • Chapter 14: Going Further;
  • Appendices: Installing Laragon and MySQL, the Maven dependencies used.

docs.title: 1.3. The Common Thread: Tax Calculation
docs.text:
The same problem is revisited throughout the document: calculating the income tax for a taxpayer who has only their salary to report. The tax bracket used is the original one (2003 income): it is no longer current, but it suffices for our purpose, which is to write the same application in several different ways. It is implemented in nine versions:

VersionChapterContent13A single program: validated input, calculation, display24Classes and interfaces: [TrancheImpot], [IImpot], [AbstractImpot], [HardwiredImpot]35calculation data read from a text file or a JSON file46A layered architecture ([dao], [metier], [ui]) within a single program56One Maven module per layer, unit tests, and integration of layers via dependency injection610a [dao] layer that reads data from a MySQL database using JDBC711a [dao] layer written with Hibernate812a TCP tax calculation server and its client913a REST web service for tax calculation, a console client, and a web client

Starting with version 5, subsequent versions reuse the layers from version 5 and replace only the layer that has changed: this is the whole point of the layered architecture presented in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 1.4. Examples
docs.text:
The code in this document is organized in a single folder named [java-oct-2026], with one subfolder per chapter:

java-oct-2026/
├── 02-installation/       premier programme, premiers projets Maven
├── 03-bases/              Bases01.java à Bases31.java, Impots1.java
├── 04-classes/            Classes01.java à Classes26.java, programmes de plusieurs fichiers, ImpotsV2
├── 05-classes-java/       chaînes, tableaux, collections, API Stream, fichiers, JSON, regex, ImpotsV3

├── 07-lambdas/            Lambdas01.java à Lambdas11.java

├── 09-async/              Async01.java à Async26.java

├── 12-internet/           Internet01.java à Internet19, ImpotsV8
└── 13-services-web/       services web Spring Boot et leurs clients (WsImpot, ClientWsImpot : version 9)

The small programs are compact source files: a single file named [.java], executed using the command [java Fichier.java] (Chapter 2). Multi-file programs that use only the libraries from JDK are launched in the same way. Programs that require an external library (Jackson, JUnit, Spring, the MySQL driver, Hibernate, Spring Boot) are Maven projects ([pom.xml]).

All programs in this document were compiled without errors or warnings by the [javac] compiler from JDK 25, using the [-Xlint:all] option that enables all warnings, and were run using the library versions listed in the appendix. The results reproduced in this document are those of these executions. They were obtained using the French language and country settings (fr-FR), as on a French Windows system: formatted floating-point numbers are displayed with a decimal point, and dates are in French. Two notes:

  • the error messages from JDK (exception messages, compiler messages) are in English: JDK does not provide a French translation for them;
  • the examples were run on Linux. For the most part, this makes no difference: Java is cross-platform. The few differences (file paths with / instead of \, terminal commands) are noted where they occur.

The results of multithreaded, asynchronous, or network programs, as well as the measured execution times, may vary from one run to another: the comments focus on what is reproducible.

docs.title: 1.5. Sources
docs.text:
The main sources for this document are:

  • the official Java documentation: the website https://dev.java (tutorials) and the documentation for the API Java SE 25: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/;
  • Java enhancement proposals (JEP, “JDK Enhancement Proposals”), which describe in detail each new feature of the language and platform: https://openjdk.org/jeps/0;

docs.title: 6.1. Introduction
docs.text:
Let’s revisit the latest version of the tax calculation application (version 3, Chapter 5). Stripped down to its essentials, its main program had the following structure (simplified diagram):

// creating a IImpot object from a text file or JSON
IImpot impot;
try {
    impot = nomFichier.toLowerCase().endsWith(".json") ? new JsonImpot(nomFichier) : new FileImpot(nomFichier);
} catch (ImpotException e) {
    IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : [Code=" + e.getCode() + ", Message=" + e.getMessage() + "]");
    return;
}
// input loop
while (true) {
    String parametres = IO.readln("Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : ...").strip();
    ...
     // The parameters are correct: the tax is calculated
    IO.println("Impôt=" + impot.calculer(marie.equals("o"), nbEnfants, salaire) + " euros");
}

This program combines three types of processing found in most applications:

  • retrieving data stored in files, databases, etc.: lines 1–8;
  • user interaction: lines 11–12 (input) and 14 (output);
  • the use of a business algorithm, the tax calculation: line 14. This calculation was previously performed by the abstract class [AbstractImpot], the parent class of [FileImpot] and [JsonImpot]: in version 3, data reading and calculation are still combined within a single object.

Practical experience has shown that isolating these different processes into separate classes improves application maintainability. The architecture of an application structured in this way is as follows:

This architecture is called “three-tier architecture.” The term “tier” normally refers to a part of the application that runs on a different machine. When the parts are on the same machine, the term “layered architecture” is used instead:

  • The [metier] layer contains the application’s business rules. For our application, these are the rules used to calculate a taxpayer’s tax. This layer requires data to function:
    • tax brackets, which change every year;
    • the number of children, the taxpayer’s marital status, and annual income;
  • the data access layer, or [dao] (DAO = Data Access Object), provides data already stored in files or databases. This includes the tax brackets, as in version 3 of the application;
  • the user interface layer, or [ui] (UI = User Interface), provides the data entered by the user and displays the results to the user. This applies here to the number of children, marital status, and the taxpayer’s annual income.

In general:

  • the [dao] layer handles access to persistent data (files, databases) or non-persistent data (network, sensors, etc.);
  • the [ui] layer handles interactions with the user, if there is one;
  • the three layers are made independent of one another through the use of interfaces.

We will revisit the [Impots] application, which we have already examined several times, to give it a layered architecture. First, we need to define the interfaces for the application’s various layers.

docs.title: 6.2. The interfaces of the [Impots] application
docs.text:
Remember that an interface defines a set of method signatures. Classes that implement the interface provide the implementation for these methods.

Let’s return to the layered architecture of our application:

In this type of architecture, it is often the user who takes the initiative. The user makes a request in [1] and receives a response in [8]. This is called the request-response cycle. Let’s take the example of calculating a taxpayer’s tax. This will require several steps:

  • The [ui] layer asks the user for their marital status, number of children, and annual salary. This is the [1] operation described above;
  • once this is done, layer [ui] asks layer [metier] to calculate the tax. To do this, it sends the data it received from the user to that layer. This is operation [2];
  • The [metier] layer needs certain information to complete its task: the tax brackets. It requests this information from layer [dao] via the path [3, 4, 5, 6]: [3] is the initial request, and [6] is the response to that request;
  • With all the data it needed, layer [metier] calculates the tax;
  • The [metier] layer can now respond to the request made by the [ui] layer in [2]. This is the path [7];
  • The [ui] layer formats this result and then presents it to the user. This is the path [8];
  • One could imagine that the user might run tax simulations and want to save them. They would use the same path, [1-8], to do so.

As seen in this description, a layer uses the resources of the layer to its right, never those of the layer to its left. Consider two adjacent layers:

The layer [A] makes requests to the layer [B]. In the simplest cases, a layer is implemented by a single class. But an application evolves over time, and the layer [B] may successively have different implementation classes: [B1], [B2], and so on. If the [B] layer is the [dao] layer, it may have an initial implementation, [B1], that retrieves data from a file. A few years later, you might want to store this data in a database: you would then create a second implementation class, [B2]. If, in the initial application, the [A] layer worked directly with the [B1] class, we would be forced to partially rewrite the code for the [A] layer. For example, suppose we wrote something like the following in the [A] layer:

B1 b1 = new B1(...);
...
b1.getData(...);
  • Line 1: An instance of the [B1] class is created;
  • line 3: data is requested from this instance.

If the new implementation class [B2] has methods with the same signature as the class [B1], you’ll need to change all instances of [B1] to [B2]. This is the best-case scenario, and it is quite unlikely if you have not paid attention to these signatures. In practice, it is common for the classes [B1] and [B2] to have different method signatures, meaning that a significant portion of the [A] layer must be rewritten.

We can improve this by placing an interface between the [A] and [B] layers. This freezes the method signatures that the [B] layer exposes to the [A] layer within an interface. The previous diagram becomes the following:

Layer [A] no longer communicates directly with layer [B] but instead with its interface [IB]. In the code for layer [A], the implementation class [Bi] of the [B] layer appears only once, when the object that implements the [IB] interface is created. After that, the [IB] interface—and not its implementation class—is used. The previous code becomes:

IB ib = new B1(...);
...
ib.getData(...);
  • Line 1: An instance of *[ib] that implements the *[IB] interface is created by instantiating the *[B1]* class;
  • Line 3: Data is requested from the [ib] instance.

Now, if we replace the [B1] implementation of the [B] layer with a [B2] implementation, and both of these implementations adhere to the same [IB] interface, only line 1 of the [A] layer needs to be modified. This is a major advantage that, on its own, justifies the systematic use of interfaces between two layers.

We can go even further and make the [A] layer completely independent of the [B] layer. In the code above, line 1 poses a problem because it hard-codes the class name [B1]. Ideally, the [A] layer should receive an implementation of the [IB] interface without having to specify a class name. This would be consistent with the diagram above: the [A] layer interfaces with the [IB] interface, and there is no reason why it would need to know the name of the class that implements that interface.

This is what dependency injection (DI) enables. The previous architecture evolves as follows:

A cross-cutting component—the dependency injection container—creates the objects that implement the layers and connects them to one another: it passes the [A] layer a reference to the object that implements the [B] layer. The code for the [A] layer then takes the following form:

// The layer [A] receives the layer [B] via its constructor
public class A {
    private final IB ib;

    public A(IB ib) {
        this.ib = ib;
    }

    public void travailler() {
        ...
        ib.getData(...);
    }
}
  • Lines 5–7: The [A] layer receives, via its constructor, a [ib] instance that implements the [IB] interface. It is not the [A] layer that creates it, but the container;
  • Line 11: Data is requested from the [ib] instance.

The implementation class [B1] no longer appears anywhere in the code of the [A] layer. When the implementation [B1] is replaced by a new implementation [B2], nothing will change in the code of the [A] layer: the only thing that will change is the single location in the application where the container is told which class implements [IB]. This location can even read the name of the implementation to use from a configuration file.

In the Java world, dependency injection was popularized in the early 2000s by the Spring framework, whose configuration was then written in XML files. The Spring Framework, now in version 7, remains the industry standard; it forms the basis of Spring Boot, which we will use in Chapter 13, “Web Services .” We’ll use its container in version 5 of the application (there are others, such as CDI, the Jakarta standard EE, or Google Guice). The combination of “Java interfaces + dependency injection” significantly improves application maintainability by making the layers independent of one another.

Let’s return to the layered architecture of our application. In simple cases, we can start with the [metier] layer to discover the application’s interfaces. To function, the application needs data:

  • already available in files, databases, or via the network. This data is provided by the [dao] layer;
  • not yet available. In that case, they are provided by the [ui] layer, which obtains them from the user.

What interface must the [dao] layer provide to the [metier] layer? The [dao] layer must provide the tax brackets to the [metier] layer. In our application, the [dao] layer uses existing data but does not create new data. Its interface can be as follows:

package dao;

import entites.TrancheImpot;
import java.util.List;

// the interface of layer [dao]
public interface IImpotDao {

     // the tax brackets
    List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot();
}
  • Line 1: The interface is located in the [dao] package. The file [IImpotDao.java] must therefore be located in a folder named [dao], as we will see;
  • Line 10: The [IImpotDao] interface defines the [getTranchesImpot] method, which provides the tax brackets to the [metier] layer. Java does not have properties: read-only data is exposed via a method named [getXxx], in accordance with the JavaBeans convention. The tax brackets are returned as a [List<TrancheImpot>] list rather than an array: we will see that the implementations return an immutable list, whereas the elements of an array can always be modified by the recipient;
  • line 3: imports the type [TrancheImpot], defined in the package [entites]:
package entites;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

// a tax bracket: a record, and therefore a non-modifiable class
public record TrancheImpot(BigDecimal limite, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
}

A tax bracket is represented by a record (Java 16): a non-modifiable class for which the compiler generates the constructor (based on the components declared in parentheses after the type name), the fields [private final], the accessors [limite()], [coeffR()] and [coeffN()], as well as the methods [equals], [hashCode], and [toString]. We write [new TrancheImpot(limite, coeffR, coeffN)] to create a slice. The three components are of type [BigDecimal], the Java class for exact decimal numbers: a [double] cannot exactly represent 0.068 or 291.09. Since a *[BigDecimal] is itself immutable, a slice cannot be modified once it has been created. A traditional JavaBean class, with [setXxx] methods, would have allowed this; we will see that this limitation eliminates a side effect of an older way of implementing the [metier]* layer.

What interface should the [metier] layer present to the [ui] layer? Let’s review the interactions between these two layers:

  • The [ui] layer asks the user for their marital status, number of children, and annual salary. This is operation [1] in the schema;
  • Once this is done, the [ui] layer asks the [metier] layer to calculate the tax. To do so, it sends the data it received from the user to the [metier] layer. This is operation [2].

The interface for layer [metier] might look like this:

package metier;

// the interface of the [metier] layer
public interface IImpotMetier {

    int calculerImpot(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire);
}
  • Line 1: Everything related to the [metier] layer is placed in the [metier] package;
  • line 6: the [IImpotMetier] interface defines only one method, which calculates a taxpayer’s tax based on their marital status, number of children, and annual salary. The methods of an interface are implicitly public and abstract: there is no need to write [public abstract].

We will now examine an initial implementation of this layered architecture.

docs.title: 6.3.1. The Project
docs.text:
Version 4 is a program consisting of several source files that does not use any external libraries. We will run it using the Java source code launcher, without creating a Maven project. Each layer occupies a separate folder:

ImpotsV4/
  Main.java                  intégration des couches
  DataImpot.txt              les tranches d'impôt
  DataImpotInvalide.txt      un fichier de tranches incorrect
  entites/
    TrancheImpot.java
    CodeErreur.java
    ImpotException.java
  dao/
    IImpotDao.java
    HardwiredImpot.java
    FileImpot.java
  metier/
    IImpotMetier.java
    ImpotMetier.java
  ui/
    Dialogue.java
  • The [entites] file contains the cross-layer types for the layers [ui], [metier], and [dao]: the record [TrancheImpot], the exception [ImpotException], and the enumeration [CodeErreur] of its error codes;
  • the [dao] file contains the interface and classes of the [dao] layer. We will use two implementations of the [IImpotDao] interface: the [HardwiredImpot] class, whose data is hard-coded (version 2), and the [FileImpot] class, which reads data from a text file (version 3). Reading a JSON file—the other option in version 3—will be covered in version 5;
  • the folder [metier] contains the interface and the class for the layer [metier];
  • the folder [ui] contains the class for the layer [ui];
  • The file [Main.java] creates the layers and links them together;
  • the file [DataImpot.txt] contains the tax brackets read by the [FileImpot] implementation of the [dao] layer.

Unlike in other languages, folder names matter here: in Java, a class from the [dao] package is located in a folder named [dao], a class in the [impots.dao] package is in a [impots/dao] folder, and these folders are relative to the source root. This is how the compiler and the virtual machine locate classes based on their fully qualified names.

The file [Main.java] is a compact source file: it has no package declaration and therefore belongs to the unnamed package at the source root. Starting with Java 22 (multi-file program launcher, JEP 458), the command [java Main.java], entered in the [ImpotsV4] folder, is sufficient to run the program: the source code launcher compiles [Main.java] in memory, and whenever it encounters a class from another file—for example, [dao.FileImpot]— it searches for the file [dao/FileImpot.java] starting from the directory of [Main.java] and compiles it in turn. No file named [.class] is written to disk. A class from the unnamed package can use classes from other packages, but the reverse is not possible: no class can import [Main]. This is why only the main program is placed there.

A IDE opens this folder as-is and runs [Main.java] without any special configuration. When the program requires external libraries (Jackson, Spring), in version 5, we will switch to a Maven project.

docs.title: 6.3.2. Application Components
docs.text:
We refer to types that span multiple layers as entities. These are generally the classes that encapsulate the data from the [dao] layer. These entities typically extend all the way up to the [ui] layer. The application entities are the [TrancheImpot] record, which has already been presented, and the [ImpotException] exception, along with its enumeration of error codes:

package entites;

import java.util.StringJoiner;

// error codes for the [dao] layer: each corresponds to a bit, so they can be combined
public enum CodeErreur {
    ACCES, LIGNE, CHAMP1, CHAMP2, CHAMP3;

     // the code bit: 1 for ACCES, 2 for LIGNE, 4 for CHAMP1, 8 for CHAMP2, 16 for CHAMP3
    public int bit() {
        return 1 << ordinal();
    }

     // the names of the codes present in a bit combination, for example, “CHAMP2, CHAMP3” for 24
    public static String noms(int code) {
        StringJoiner noms = new StringJoiner(", ");
        for (CodeErreur c : values()) {
            if ((code & c.bit()) != 0) {
                noms.add(c.name());
            }
        }
        return noms.toString();
    }
}
  • line 6: an enumeration ([enum]). In Java, the values of an enumeration are objects—unique instances of the [CodeErreur] class—and an enumeration can have methods;
  • line 7: the five error codes. The method [ordinal()], inherited from the class [Enum], returns the position of the value in the list: 0 for [ACCES], 4 for [CHAMP3];
  • Lines 10–12: Each code is associated with a bit, obtained by a left shift: [1 << ordinal()] equals 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. These powers of 2 can be combined using the operator [|]: the code [CHAMP2.bit() | CHAMP3.bit()] (8 + 16 = 24) means that fields 2 and 3 of a line are incorrect. Version 3 explicitly specified the value of each code ([ACCES(1)], [LIGNE(2)]…) and decoded a combination into a set [EnumSet]; calculating the bit based on the position eliminates the need for these values here. The exception’s error code remains a simple integer, which all implementations of the [dao] layer can use;
  • lines 15–23: The static method [noms] returns the names of the codes present in a bit combination: “CHAMP2, CHAMP3” for 24. The [values()] method, generated by the compiler, returns the array of enumeration values; [code & c.bit()] is not null if the bit corresponding to the code [c] is present in [code]; [name()] returns the name of the value. A [StringJoiner] (Java 8) concatenates strings, separating them with the separator provided to its constructor.
package entites;

import java.io.Serial;

// the exception thrown by the layer [dao]
// It derives from RuntimeException: it is an uncaught exception
public class ImpotException extends RuntimeException {

     // class version for serialization (an exception is serializable)
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

     // error code (a bit combination of CodeErreur)
    private final int code;

     // constructors
    public ImpotException(String message, int code) {
        this(message, null, code);
    }

    public ImpotException(String message, Throwable cause, int code) {
        super(message, cause);
        this.code = code;
    }

     // error code
    public int getCode() {
        return code;
    }
}
  • line 7: an application-specific exception is derived from the class [RuntimeException]: it is an unchecked exception. The methods that throw it do not need to declare it in a [throws] clause, and their callers are not required to catch it. This is the standard approach for errors that one layer reports to another layer;
  • lines 10–11: an exception is serializable (the class [Throwable] implements the interface [Serializable]). The [serialVersionUID] field specifies the class version for serialization; without it, the compiler, when using the [-Xlint:all] option, issues a warning. The [@Serial] annotation (Java 14) allows the compiler to verify the declaration of this field;
  • line 14: the error code, an integer that combines bits [CodeErreur]. The field is [final]: it is initialized in the constructor and cannot be changed afterward;
  • lines 17–24: two constructors, one with a message and a code, the other with the original exception (the cause) in addition, which will be accessible via the [getCause()] method. The first calls the second ([this(...)]), which calls the constructor of the parent class [RuntimeException] ([super(...)]);
  • lines 27–29: the error code accessor.

In this version, only the [FileImpot] class in the [dao] layer throws [ImpotException].

docs.title: 6.3.3. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
Let’s review the interface of the [dao] layer:

package dao;

import entites.TrancheImpot;
import java.util.List;

// [dao] layer interface
public interface IImpotDao {

     // tax brackets
    List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot();
}

We implement this interface in two different ways. First, with the [HardwiredImpot] class:

package dao;

import entites.TrancheImpot;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;

// a layer ([dao]) whose data is hard-coded in the program
public class HardwiredImpot implements IImpotDao {

     // tax brackets (2004 tax schedule for 2003 income): a non-editable list
    private final List<TrancheImpot> tranchesImpot = List.of(
            tranche("4962", "0", "0"),
            tranche("8382", "0.068", "291.09"),
            tranche("14753", "0.191", "1322.92"),
            tranche("23888", "0.283", "2668.39"),
            tranche("38868", "0.374", "4846.98"),
            tranche("47932", "0.426", "6883.66"),
            tranche("0", "0.481", "9505.54"));

    @Override
    public List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }

     // a bracket constructed from strings: the BigDecimal values are exact
    private static TrancheImpot tranche(String limite, String coeffR, String coeffN) {
        return new TrancheImpot(new BigDecimal(limite), new BigDecimal(coeffR), new BigDecimal(coeffN));
    }
}
  • Line 8: The class [HardwiredImpot] implements ([implements]) the interface [IImpotDao];
  • Lines 11–18: the tax brackets. [List.of] (Java 9) creates a read-only list: its methods [add], [set] or [remove] invoke a [UnsupportedOperationException]. The field is initialized in its declaration;
  • lines 20–23: the implementation of the interface method. The annotation [@Override] instructs the compiler to verify that the method correctly implements a method of the interface: a typo in its name would cause a compilation error;
  • Lines 26–28: A private method that creates a slice from three strings. A [BigDecimal] constructed from a string is exact: [new BigDecimal("0.068")] is exactly 0.068, whereas [new BigDecimal(0.068)] would be 0.0680000000000000049…, making [double] the closest to 0.068.

The [IImpotDao] interface is also implemented by the [FileImpot] class, which reads the tax brackets from a text file. The [DataImpot.txt] file is as follows:

4962:0:0
8382:0.068:291.09
14753:0.191:1322.92
23888:0.283:2668.39
38868:0.374:4846.98
47932:0.426:6883.66
0:0.481:9505.54

Each line describes a tax bracket in the format [limite:coeffR:coeffN]. Numbers are written with a decimal point, regardless of the system language; this ensures the file is readable on all machines. The values are those from the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, retained as-is: this is an exercise. The class [FileImpot] is as follows:

package dao;

import static entites.CodeErreur.ACCES;
import static entites.CodeErreur.CHAMP1;
import static entites.CodeErreur.CHAMP2;
import static entites.CodeErreur.CHAMP3;
import static entites.CodeErreur.LIGNE;

import entites.ImpotException;
import entites.TrancheImpot;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

// a layer [dao] that reads the tax brackets from a text file
// one line per tax bracket: limit:coeffR:coeffN (decimal point)
public class FileImpot implements IImpotDao {

     // data file related to the current folder
    private final String fileName;

     // tax brackets
    private final List<TrancheImpot> tranchesImpot;

     // builder
    public FileImpot(String fileName) {
         // the file name is stored
        this.fileName = fileName;
         // the tax brackets read
        List<TrancheImpot> tranches = new ArrayList<>();
         // read the file line by line
        int numLigne = 0;
        try {
            Path chemin = Path.of(fileName);
            if (!Files.exists(chemin)) {
                throw new NoSuchFileException(fileName, null, "Le fichier [" + fileName + "] n'existe pas");
            }
            for (String ligneLue : Files.readAllLines(chemin)) {
                numLigne++;
                 // empty lines are ignored
                String ligne = ligneLue.strip();
                if (ligne.isEmpty()) {
                    continue;
                }
                 // Line broken down into three fields separated by:
                String[] champs = ligne.split("\\s*:\\s*");
                int code = 0;
                BigDecimal limite = null, coeffR = null, coeffN = null;
                if (champs.length != 3) {
                    code = LIGNE.bit();
                } else {
                     // conversions of the 3 fields: each error adds a bit to the code
                    limite = parse(champs[0]);
                    coeffR = parse(champs[1]);
                    coeffN = parse(champs[2]);
                    if (limite == null) code |= CHAMP1.bit();
                    if (coeffR == null) code |= CHAMP2.bit();
                    if (coeffN == null) code |= CHAMP3.bit();
                }
                 // error?
                if (code != 0) {
                    throw new ImpotException("Ligne n° " + numLigne + " incorrecte : [" + ligne + "]", code);
                }
                 // the new tax bracket is stored
                tranches.add(new TrancheImpot(limite, coeffR, coeffN));
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
             // File access error: encapsulate it in a ImpotException
            throw new ImpotException("Erreur lors de la lecture du fichier " + fileName, e, ACCES.bit());
        }
         // returning a read-only copy of the list
        tranchesImpot = List.copyOf(tranches);
    }

    public String getFileName() {
        return fileName;
    }

    @Override
    public List<TrancheImpot> getTranchesImpot() {
        return tranchesImpot;
    }

     // A positive or zero number written with digits and a decimal point; null if incorrect
    private static BigDecimal parse(String champ) {
        return champ.matches("\\d+(\\.\\d+)?") ? new BigDecimal(champ) : null;
    }
}
  • Lines 3–7: Static import ([import static], Java 5) allows you to use the static members of a class without prefixing them with the class name. The values of an enum are static members: we write [CHAMP1] instead of [CodeErreur.CHAMP1];
  • line 21: the class [FileImpot] implements the interface [IImpotDao];
  • Lines 24, 27: the file name and the read segments. These [final] fields are initialized only once, in the constructor (lines 32 and 76). They are returned by the methods on lines 79–86; [getTranchesImpot] is the interface method;
  • line 30: the constructor receives the name of the tax bracket file;
  • line 34: the read tax brackets are accumulated in a list named [ArrayList];
  • line 38: [Path.of] (Java 11) creates the file path. A relative path is relative to the current directory, the one in which the [java] command was entered;
  • Lines 39–41: If the file does not exist, a [NoSuchFileException] ([java.nio.file] package) is launched with a message in French. Its three-parameter constructor takes the file name, the name of a possible second file (here, [null]), and the reason for the error. The exception messages for JDK are in English: without this test, [Files.readAllLines] would itself launch a [NoSuchFileException] whose message would consist solely of the file name;
  • Line 42: [Files.readAllLines] reads the entire file using UTF-8 and returns a list of its lines. The method opens and closes the file itself. For a large file, it would be preferable to read it in real time using [Files.lines] or [BufferedReader];
  • line 45: [strip()] (Java 11) removes leading and trailing spaces;
  • line 50: the line is split by [split], whose parameter is a regular expression: the separator is a colon, possibly surrounded by spaces ([\s*] matches zero or more spaces). In a Java string, the backslash is doubled;
  • Lines 53–54: A line that does not have three fields is invalid;
  • lines 57–62: conversion of the three fields. Each incorrect field adds a bit to the error code using the operator [|=];
  • lines 65–67: an invalid line triggers a [ImpotException], whose message provides the line number and content. This exception is not a [IOException]: it is not caught on line 71 and is propagated as-is to the caller;
  • line 69: the read block is added to the list;
  • Lines 71–74: All I/O errors stem from [IOException]: file not found ([NoSuchFileException]), insufficient permissions ([AccessDeniedException]), file not in UTF-8 ([MalformedInputException]), etc. The error is wrapped in a [ImpotException] with code [ACCES]; the original exception is retained as the cause;
  • line 76: [List.copyOf] (Java 10) returns a read-only copy of the list;
  • Lines 89–91: Conversion of a field to [BigDecimal]. The [matches] method verifies that the entire string matches the regular expression [\d+(\.\d+)?]: one or more digits, optionally followed by a period and more digits. Thus, “0.191” is rejected, as is any negative number. The constructor [BigDecimal(String)] is not dependent on the user’s language: it always expects a decimal point. In case of an error, the method returns [null].

docs.title: 6.3.4. The [metier] layer
docs.text:
Let’s review the interface for this layer:

package metier;

// the interface of the [metier] layer
public interface IImpotMetier {

    int calculerImpot(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire);
}

Its implementation, [ImpotMetier], is as follows:

package metier;

import dao.IImpotDao;
import entites.TrancheImpot;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.MathContext;
import java.util.List;

// the [metier] layer receives the [dao] layer via its constructor
public class ImpotMetier implements IImpotMetier {

     // the tax brackets, requested once and for all from the [dao] layer
    private final List<TrancheImpot> tranches;

     // creator
    public ImpotMetier(IImpotDao dao) {
        tranches = dao.getTranchesImpot();
    }

     // tax calculation
    @Override
    public int calculerImpot(boolean marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire) {
         // parameter verification
        if (nbEnfants < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("nbEnfants (" + nbEnfants + ") doit être positif ou nul");
        }
        if (salaire < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("salaire (" + salaire + ") doit être positif ou nul");
        }
         // number of shares
        BigDecimal nbParts = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbEnfants).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
                .add(BigDecimal.valueOf(marie ? 2 : 1));
        if (nbEnfants >= 3) {
            nbParts = nbParts.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
        }
         // taxable income and family quotient
        BigDecimal revenu = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salaire));
        BigDecimal qf = revenu.divide(nbParts, MathContext.DECIMAL128);
         // the tax bracket: the first one with a threshold greater than or equal to QF,
         // the last bracket if none of the others apply (its threshold is not used)
        TrancheImpot tranche = tranches.getLast();
        for (int i = 0; i < tranches.size() - 1; i++) {
            if (qf.compareTo(tranches.get(i).limite()) <= 0) {
                tranche = tranches.get(i);
                break;
            }
        }
         // tax (whole part)
        return revenu.multiply(tranche.coeffR()).subtract(nbParts.multiply(tranche.coeffN())).intValue();
    }
}
  • Line 10: The class [ImpotMetier] implements the interface [IImpotMetier]. The [metier] layer must collaborate with the [dao] layer: it therefore receives, via its constructor (line 16), a reference to the object that implements the [IImpotDao] interface;
  • Lines 13, 16–18: When the object is constructed, the [metier] layer requests the tax brackets from the [dao] layer once and for all and stores them in a [final] field. Note that the [metier] layer knows the [dao] layer only through its [IImpotDao] interface: it does not know whether the tax brackets come from the code, a file, or, later, a database;
  • lines 24–29: The [metier] layer does not trust its callers. An incorrect parameter triggers a [IllegalArgumentException], the uncaught exception that Java provides for this case, with a message that identifies the parameter;
  • lines 31–35: the number of shares. A [BigDecimal] has no arithmetic operators: instead, its methods [add], [subtract], [multiply], and [divide] are used. Since it is immutable, each operation returns a new object, hence the notation [nbParts = nbParts.add(...)]. Division by [BigDecimal.TWO] (a constant added in Java 19) is exact: 3 children result in 1.5 shares;
  • lines 37–38: taxable income and the family quotient. Division by the number of shares can result in an infinite number of decimal places (division by 3, for example): without specified precision, [divide] would then launch a [ArithmeticException]. [MathContext.DECIMAL128] limits the result to 34 significant digits;
  • lines 41–47: We search for the first bracket whose threshold is greater than or equal to the family quotient. The [BigDecimal] values are compared with [compareTo], which returns a negative, zero, or positive number: [qf.compareTo(limite) <= 0] means [qf <= limite]. The last bracket, [tranches.getLast()] (Java 21), is used if none of the others apply: its threshold (0) is not used;
  • line 49: the tax. [intValue()] returns the integer part of the result.

A method that was once common involved modifying the limit of the last bracket (something like [tranches[tranches.length - 1].setLimite(qf + 1)]) before the search so that the search loop would always stop. This instruction modified the array provided by the [dao] layer: a side effect on data shared by all layers. We could no longer write it here, since a [TrancheImpot] is unmodifiable, as is the list that contains them. Modern code simply takes the last segment when no boundary is suitable, without modifying the data it receives.

docs.title: 6.3.5. The [ui] layer
docs.text:
In versions 2 and 3, the user interface was written in the main program, following the creation of the calculation object. The only difference was in how this object was created. We now isolate this interaction in a class within the [ui] layer, which knows the [metier] layer only through its interface:

package ui;

import metier.IImpotMetier;

// the console dialog with the user: it only recognizes the interface of the [metier] layer
public final class Dialogue {

     // help displayed in case of incorrect input
    private static final String SYNTAXE = """
            syntaxe : Marié NbEnfants Salaire
            Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié
            NbEnfants : nombre d'enfants
            Salaire : salaire annuel en euros""";

     // Utility class: no instance
    private Dialogue() {
    }

     // dialog loop: parameter entry, calculation, display
    public static void run(IImpotMetier metier) {
        while (true) {
             // prompt for tax calculation parameters
            String saisie = IO.readln("Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : "
                    + "Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : ");
            String parametres = saisie == null ? "" : saisie.strip();
             // Is there anything to do?
            if (parametres.isEmpty()) {
                break;
            }
             // Checking the number of parameters
            String[] champs = parametres.split("\\s+");
            if (champs.length != 3) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE);
                continue;
            }
             // married
            String marie = champs[0].toLowerCase();
            if (!marie.equals("o") && !marie.equals("n")) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument Marié incorrect : tapez o ou n");
                continue;
            }
             // Number of children
            int nbEnfants = entier(champs[1]);
            if (nbEnfants < 0) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument NbEnfants incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
                continue;
            }
             // Salary
            int salaire = entier(champs[2]);
            if (salaire < 0) {
                IO.println(SYNTAXE + "\nArgument Salaire incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
                continue;
            }
             // The parameters are correct: the calculation is requested from the [metier] layer
            IO.println("Impôt=" + metier.calculerImpot(marie.equals("o"), nbEnfants, salaire) + " euros");
        }
    }

     // a positive integer or zero; -1 if the string is not an integer
    private static int entier(String champ) {
        try {
            return Integer.parseInt(champ);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return -1;
        }
    }
}
  • Line 6: The class [Dialogue] has no state of its own and contains only static members. Java does not have top-level static classes: we declare the class [final] (which cannot be subclassed) and give it a private constructor (lines 16–17), which prevents instances from being created;
  • lines 9–13: the help message is a text block (Java 15), delimited by three quotation marks. It can span multiple lines; the standard indentation of the lines is removed. Since the closing quotation marks are placed at the end of the last line, the text does not end with a line break;
  • line 20: the method [run] receives the layer [metier] in the form of its interface [IImpotMetier]*. It knows nothing about the class that implements it or the layer [dao]*;
  • Lines 23–25: [IO.readln] (Java 25) prints its parameter and then reads a line from the keyboard. It returns [null] at the end of the input stream; line 25 then replaces [null] with the empty string: an end-of-stream signal terminates the dialog just like an empty line;
  • line 31: the entered line is split by spaces; the regular expression [\s+] (one or more spaces) ignores multiple spaces;
  • lines 37–38: the strings are compared with [equals], never with [==], which compares references;
  • lines 43–53: the number of children and the salary must be positive integers or zero. The [entier] method (lines 60–66) returns -1 if the field is not an integer: [Integer.parseInt] then calls [NumberFormatException], which is intercepted. A negative number and an incorrect entry are thus rejected by the same check;
  • line 55: the parameters are correct: the calculation is requested from the [metier] layer.

docs.title: 6.3.6. Integrating the layers
docs.text:
All that remains is to create the layers and link them together. This is the role of the main program [Main.java]:

import dao.FileImpot;
import dao.HardwiredImpot;
import dao.IImpotDao;
import entites.CodeErreur;
import entites.ImpotException;
import metier.IImpotMetier;
import metier.ImpotMetier;
import ui.Dialogue;

// layer integration: this is the only place where the implementation classes are named
// argument: “hardwired” for HardwiredImpot,
// otherwise, the name of the file read by FileImpot (DataImpot.txt by default)
void main(String[] args) {
    String source = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "DataImpot.txt";
    IImpotMetier metier;
    try {
         // creation of the layer [dao]
        IImpotDao dao = source.equals("hardwired") ? new HardwiredImpot() : new FileImpot(source);
         // creation of the layer [metier], which receives the layer [dao]
        metier = new ImpotMetier(dao);
    } catch (ImpotException e) {
         // Display the error and terminate the program with exit code 1
        String origine = e.getCause() == null ? "" : ", exception d'origine : " + e.getCause().getMessage();
        IO.println("L'erreur suivante s'est produite : [Code=" + CodeErreur.noms(e.getCode())
                + ", Message=" + e.getMessage() + origine + "]");
        System.exit(1);
        return;
    }

     // The [ui] layer: user interaction
    Dialogue.run(metier);
}
  • Lines 1–8: A compact source file (Java 25) does not have a class declaration, but it may contain imports. The compiler places its contents in an implicit class;
  • line 13: the [main] method receives command-line arguments in the [args] array. The argument selects the implementation of the [dao] layer: [hardwired] for the [HardwiredImpot] class; otherwise, the name of the file read by the [FileImpot] class—[DataImpot.txt] by default;
  • line 18: creation of layer [dao]. This is the only place in the program where the classes [HardwiredImpot] and [FileImpot] are named;
  • line 20: creation of layer [metier], which receives layer [dao];
  • Lines 21–28: The creation of layer [dao] may trigger a [ImpotException]. The error is then displayed, along with the message from the original exception (if any), and the program terminates with exit code 1 ([System.exit(1)]). The error code is displayed in plain text using the [CodeErreur.noms] method. The [return] statement on line 27 is never executed, but the compiler is unaware that [System.exit] does not yield control: without it, the compiler would report that the variable [metier] may not be initialized on line 31;
  • Line 31: The layers are ready: the [ui] layer interacts with the user.
